Reads the LDAP server's cn=Monitor backend for connections, operation counters, waiters and thread state; supports OpenLDAP and 389 Directory Server.
CPU, memory, disk, network, processes and kernel parameters out of the box; templates cover Categraf, node_exporter and Telegraf metric names.
Collects pipeline event in/out and filter time, queue state and JVM health from Logstash's node API; rules watch event backlog and JVM pressure.
MinIO ships a Prometheus endpoint; scrape the cluster, bucket and node paths together or the object, bucket, process and disk panels stay empty.
Embeds the mongodb_exporter collector for connections, op counters, replica set and sharding state; the dashboards need the compatible metric names turned on.
Categraf embeds mtail: extract counters, gauges and histograms from log files with regular expressions and expressions, without shipping the logs to a log system first.

documents.t: Connects to the instance and runs SHOW STATUS, SHOW VARIABLES and replica status; slow-query pileups, connection exhaustion and broken or lagging replication come with rules and runbooks.
Checks whether a local or remote port accepts connections and responds as expected; result codes 0 to 4 mean success, timeout, connection failure, read failure and content mismatch.
stub_status covers connections and request totals, the VTS module adds per-server and per-upstream status codes and latency; an upstream_check input reads health-check results.
Reads nsqd's /stats endpoint for per-topic and per-channel depth, in-flight, timeouts and client counts; rules watch growing backlog and lost consumers.
Two ways to collect NVIDIA GPUs: nvidia-smi is light and usually enough, DCGM gives more; dashboards cover a fleet overview, single cards and training jobs.
Collects resources and quotas from Nova, Neutron, Cinder, Glance, Keystone and Heat through the OpenStack API, plus the state of every instance.
Runs a customizable set of SQL queries with a read-only account to collect sessions, tablespaces, wait events and cache hit ratios; a Linux Categraf can monitor Oracle on Windows remotely.
With pm.status_path enabled, the input reads the PHP-FPM pool status over HTTP or a Unix socket: active and idle processes, request queue, slow requests and max-children hits.
Ping a list of targets from wherever Categraf runs and get packet loss, round-trip latency and jitter; the simplest liveness check there is.
Collects connections, transactions, cache hit ratio, locks and replication state with a read-only pg_monitor account; custom queries against business tables are supported.
On 3.8+ scrape the built-in Prometheus plugin on port 15692; older versions go through the management API. Templates are split by version; rules watch queue backlog, unacked messages and node state.
Runs INFO against Redis to collect memory, hit ratio, connections, slowlog and replication state; includes a Sentinel input and templates for redis_exporter.
Runs smartctl to read S.M.A.R.T. health attributes from HDDs, SSDs and NVMe drives, so you see reallocated sectors, temperature and wear before a disk actually dies.
Collect any network device by listing OIDs, with OID values usable as labels; the template ships Cisco, Juniper and generic switch dashboards and dozens of rules.

documents.t: Collects connections, waits, buffer pool, log usage and database state from DMVs and performance counters; VIEW SERVER STATE is all the permission it needs.
Give it a list of IPs and it detects the device model and collects CPU, memory and per-port traffic, errors and state; SNMP v2c only.

Scrape Cloud Monitor metrics converted to Prometheus format by the tencentcloud-exporter; templates cover CVM, CKafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, TDSQL-C and load balancers.
TiDB, PD and TiKV all expose Prometheus metrics on /metrics; the templates cover SQL latency, Region scheduling, storage and node health.
Reads the /manager/status/all endpoint of the Manager app for JVM memory, per-connector threads and requests, traffic and errors; needs the manager-gui role.
Both the single-node and cluster editions expose /metrics; templates cover vmsingle as well as the vmstorage, vmselect and vminsert cluster components.
Pulls CPU, memory, disk and network performance counters for ESXi hosts, virtual machines, datastores and clusters through the vCenter API.
Categraf reports the same metric names on Windows as on Linux, so host dashboards and rules carry over; extra dashboards cover AD, DNS and ADFS via windows_exporter.

documents.t: An alert rule is only half the job: when it fires at 3 a.m., someone needs to know what to check first. This library collects 238 PromQL alert rules from Nightingale's integration templates, and every one of them comes with runbook steps written for the person on call. The rules use standard exporter metric names (node_exporter, kube-state-metrics, mysqld_exporter and so on), so they work with plain Prometheus as well as with Nightingale. Service Rules Metrics from Download Kubernetes 77 kube-state-metrics, cAdvisor (kubelet), apiserver kubernetes.yml Prometheus 30 Prometheus's own /metrics, Prometheus Operator prometheus.yml Linux 76 node_exporter, Categraf, Telegraf linux.yml MySQL 11 mysqld_exporter, Categraf mysql.yml Redis 12 redis_exporter, Categraf redis.yml Elasticsearch 11 elasticsearch_exporter, Categraf elasticsearch.yml MongoDB 8 mongodb_exporter mongodb.yml Windows 13 windows_exporter, Categraf windows.yml

These standard alert names, used by kubernetes-mixin and kube-prometheus, each have their own page with the meaning, common causes, the rule and the runbook. Kubernetes: KubeClientCertificateExpiration, KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn, KubeAggregatedAPIDown, KubeContainerWaiting, KubeCPUOvercommit, KubeDaemonSetMisScheduled, KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch, KubeDeploymentRolloutStuck, KubeHpaMaxedOut, KubeJobFailed, KubeletDown, KubeletTooManyPods, KubeMemoryOvercommit, KubeNodeNotReady, KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp, KubePodCrashLooping, KubePodNotReady, KubeQuotaAlmostFull, KubeStatefulSetReplicasMismatch Prometheus: PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources, PrometheusBadConfig, PrometheusNotConnectedToAlertmanagers, PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind, PrometheusRemoteWriteDesiredShards, PrometheusRuleFailures, PrometheusTargetLimitHit

Each service page lists every rule with its PromQL condition, severity, for duration and runbook steps, grouped by the collector that produces the metrics. Standard alert names with their own page appear there as a short entry with a link. Each .yml file is a standard Prometheus rules file and passes promtool check rules. Severity is a severity label (critical / warning / info), the summary is in annotations.summary, and annotations.runbook_url links to the rule page. Thresholds are starting points, not recommendations for every environment. Review them before you enable a rule.

A rule without a runbook moves the investigation to whoever is on call. The steps here say what to look at first (the log before the last restart, the exit code, the slow query list, the replication thread state) and what usually fixes it, so the alert carries its own first response.

Rule expressions are partly adapted from community collections: kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0), kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0), awesome-prometheus-alerts (CC BY 4.0). Runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0).
Integrations: collector config and dashboards for each service Alert rules in Nightingale Rule design practices

Elasticsearch alert rules for cluster health turning yellow or red, JVM heap usage climbing, disk space running low or out, unassigned, initializing and relocating shards, pending cluster tasks, and an index that has stopped receiving new documents. The exporter group uses prometheus-community/elasticsearch_exporter metric names; the Categraf group runs the same checks on Categraf-collected metrics.
documents.s: Elasticsearch alert rules for Prometheus: 11 rules with runbooks

documents.t: 11 rules, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a for duration and runbook steps Metrics from: elasticsearch_exporter, Categraf Download: elasticsearch.yml, a standard Prometheus rules file (groups: format), checked with promtool check rules Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

Rule Severity For Elastic Cluster Red status Critical — Elastic Cluster Yellow status Warning 10m Elasticsearch disk out of space of the instance Critical 2m Elasticsearch disk space low of the instance Warning 2m Elasticsearch Heap Usage Too High of the instance Critical 2m Elasticsearch Heap Usage warning of the instance Warning 2m Elasticsearch initializing shards of the instance Warning 15m Elasticsearch no new documents of the instance Warning 5m Elasticsearch pending tasks of the instance Warning 15m Elasticsearch relocation shards of the instance Warning 15m Elasticsearch unassigned shards of the instance Critical —
All rules in this group also apply unchanged to instances collected by Categraf, which produces the same metric names.

Critical · — · Trigger: elasticsearch_cluster_health_status{color="red"} == 1 Runbook: Run GET _cluster/health?level=indices to find the indices that are red; Run GET _cluster/allocation/explain to see exactly why the primary shard cannot be allocated; The usual cause is a node dropping out — bring the node back so shards recover automatically; If the node's data is genuinely corrupted, restore the index from a snapshot with POST _snapshot/<repo>/<snap>/_restore.

Warning · 10m · Trigger: elasticsearch_cluster_health_status{color="yellow"} == 1 Runbook: Run GET _cluster/allocation/explain to find why the replica shards cannot be allocated; On a single-node cluster, set the index replica count to 0: PUT <index>/_settings {"index.number_of_replicas":0}; On a multi-node cluster, check whether a node dropped out or a disk watermark is blocking allocation; Once handled, confirm the health goes back to green.

Critical · 2m · Trigger: elasticsearch_filesystem_data_available_bytes / elasticsearch_filesystem_data_size_bytes * 100 < 10 Runbook: Run GET _cat/allocation?v to find the nodes that are short on disk; Delete or archive expired indices (DELETE <index>), or use ILM to move cold data to cold nodes; After freeing disk, lift the read-only block by hand: PUT _all/_settings {"index.blocks.read_only_allow_delete":null}; Longer term, expand the disk or add data nodes.
documents.s: Elasticsearch disk out of space of the instance

documents.t: Warning · 2m · Trigger: elasticsearch_filesystem_data_available_bytes / elasticsearch_filesystem_data_size_bytes * 100 < 20 Runbook: Run GET _cat/allocation?v to check the disk watermark on each node; Clean up expired indices or adjust the ILM policy to roll data to cold nodes earlier; Review whether the cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.* thresholds match your actual capacity; Schedule expansion early so it never drops to flood stage and turns indices read-only.
documents.s: Elasticsearch disk space low of the instance

documents.t: Critical · 2m · Trigger: (elasticsearch_jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} / elasticsearch_jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"}) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Run GET _nodes/stats/jvm to identify which node is under heap pressure; Run GET _cat/indices?v&s=store.size:desc to find the largest indices and close or archive the unused ones; Run GET _tasks?actions=search&detailed to find large aggregations or deep pagination queries and cancel them; Longer term, set the heap to half of physical memory (never above 31G), or add nodes to spread the load.
documents.s: Elasticsearch Heap Usage Too High of the instance

documents.t: Warning · 2m · Trigger: (elasticsearch_jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} / elasticsearch_jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"}) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Compare against elasticsearch_jvm_gc_collection_seconds_count to see whether old GC is becoming more frequent; Run GET _cat/indices?v&s=store.size:desc to check whether any index has grown sharply recently; Run GET _nodes/stats/indices/fielddata to inspect fielddata and query cache usage; Plan capacity or cleanup ahead of time so it does not climb to 90% and trigger full GC.
documents.s: Elasticsearch Heap Usage warning of the instance

documents.t: Warning · 15m · Trigger: elasticsearch_cluster_health_initializing_shards > 0 Runbook: Run GET _cat/recovery?v&active_only=true to see whether recovery is still making progress; If it is stuck, run GET _cluster/allocation/explain to find the reason (insufficient disk, saturated node bandwidth); Temporarily raise indices.recovery.max_bytes_per_sec if the recovery throttle is the bottleneck; Confirm no node is repeatedly dropping out and causing shards to be rebuilt over and over.
documents.s: Elasticsearch initializing shards of the instance

documents.t: Warning · 5m · Trigger: rate(elasticsearch_indices_docs{es_data_node="true"}[5m]) == 0 Runbook: First confirm this cluster is genuinely expected to receive continuous writes, otherwise disable this rule; Check that the upstream writers (Filebeat/Logstash/application bulk clients) are alive and whether their logs show rejected bulk requests; Run GET _cat/thread_pool/write?v to see whether the write thread pool's rejected counter is growing; Confirm the indices have not been made read-only (a disk watermark triggers read_only_allow_delete).
documents.s: Elasticsearch no new documents of the instance

documents.t: Warning · 15m · Trigger: elasticsearch_cluster_health_number_of_pending_tasks > 10 Runbook: Run GET _cluster/pending_tasks to see the queued tasks and their priorities; Run GET _cat/master?v to confirm the master is not flapping; Run GET _cat/shards to count total shards and check whether a large number of tiny indices is bloating the cluster state; Reduce the shard count (merge small indices, tune ILM) and, if needed, scale the master nodes separately.
documents.s: Elasticsearch pending tasks of the instance

documents.t: Warning · 15m · Trigger: elasticsearch_cluster_health_relocating_shards > 0 Runbook: Run GET _cat/recovery?v&active_only=true to see whether the relocation is still progressing; If it has stalled, run GET _cluster/allocation/explain to check whether a disk watermark or an allocation filter is blocking it; Confirm whether someone triggered a large reroute by hand, or whether nodes are joining and leaving; If needed, temporarily raise cluster.routing.allocation.node_concurrent_recoveries and the recovery throttle.
documents.s: Elasticsearch relocation shards of the instance

documents.t: Critical · — · Trigger: elasticsearch_cluster_health_unassigned_shards > 0 Runbook: Run GET _cluster/allocation/explain to get the exact reason the shards are unassigned; If a node dropped out, bring it back into the cluster first; If the replica count exceeds the number of available nodes, lower index.number_of_replicas; If a disk watermark was hit, free disk space first and then run POST _cluster/reroute?retry_failed=true.
documents.s: Elasticsearch unassigned shards of the instance

documents.t: With Prometheus or vmalert: download elasticsearch.yml, add it to rule_files (or -rule for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a severity label (critical / warning / info), and runbook_url points back to this page, or to the rule's own page where it has one. With Nightingale: the same rules ship in the Elasticsearch integration template. Open the integration center, import the rules into a business group, and enable them one by one. Nightingale keeps the runbook with each alert and can evaluate the rules against Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and other data sources.
The runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates (Elasticsearch, Apache-2.0). Corrections are welcome as pull requests there.
Monitor Elasticsearch with Nightingale: collector config, dashboards and metric reference Write a metric rule in Nightingale All alert rules

Alert rules for Kubernetes clusters built on the metrics every cluster already exposes: kube-state-metrics for object state, cAdvisor through the kubelet for container resources, and the apiserver, kubelet, scheduler and controller-manager endpoints for the control plane. They cover crash-looping and unready pods, stuck rollouts, replica mismatches, failed jobs, resource overcommit, quota pressure, certificate expiry and control-plane outages. Most rules keep the alert names used by kubernetes-mixin and kube-prometheus (KubePodCrashLooping, KubeNodeNotReady, KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn…), so they match the names you already see in Alertmanager.
documents.s: Kubernetes alert rules for Prometheus: 77 rules with runbooks

Critical · 1m · Trigger: kube_deployment_status_replicas_unavailable and kube_deployment_status_replicas_available{} / kube_deployment_status_replicas{} * 100 < 70 and kube_deployment_status_replicas{} > 9 Runbook: Run kubectl describe deploy <name> -n <ns> for Conditions and Events; Run kubectl get pod -n <ns> -l <selector> to see the state and reason of the unready Pods; Common causes are insufficient resources for scheduling, image pull failures, and failing readiness probes; Follow the Pod's specific state; for resource shortage, add nodes or lower requests.
documents.s: Deployment Pod availability below 70% (replicas above 9 pods)

documents.t: Info · 1m · Trigger: kube_job_status_failed{} > 0 Runbook: Run kubectl get job <job> -n <ns> for the failure count, then kubectl logs job/<job> for the reason; Run kubectl describe job for Events and whether it gave up after exhausting backoffLimit; After fixing the root cause, kubectl delete job and resubmit, or let the CronJob run again on schedule; Confirm whether the failure has downstream impact (missing output, skipped cleanup) and redo it manually if needed.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{} == 1 Runbook: Run kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> and use the Event timestamps to see whether it is stuck pulling the image, mounting a volume, or in an init container; For slow pulls, check image size and registry bandwidth, and consider pre-warming images or a local registry; For slow mounts, check the PV/CSI driver state; If the application itself starts slowly, optimise startup and set a sensible readiness probe initialDelaySeconds.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: kube_pod_status_phase{phase=~"Pending|Unknown|Failed"} > 0 Runbook: Run kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o wide for STATUS and READY, then kubectl describe pod for Events; Pending usually means insufficient resources or scheduling constraints (affinity, taints, unbound PVC); for ImagePullBackOff check the image address and pull credentials; Running but not Ready — check the readiness probe and kubectl logs <pod> for startup errors; Confirm whether the replica count is now too low to carry traffic, and scale healthy replicas first if so.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{}[5m]) > 3 Runbook: Run kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --previous to see the log before the last exit — this is the key step; Run kubectl describe pod for the exit code and Events: 137 usually means OOM or killed, 1/2 usually means the application failed to start; For config or dependency problems (unreachable database, missing ConfigMap/Secret), fix the dependency first; For OOM, compare resources.limits.memory against actual usage, or fix the application's memory leak.

Info · 1m · Trigger: 100 * sum by (namespace, pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!="", container!="POD"}[2m])) / sum by (namespace, pod, container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="cpu"}) > 80 Runbook: Run kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> --containers to compare actual usage against the limit; Check the CPUThrottlingHigh metric to confirm whether it is already being throttled; For genuine growth, raise resources.limits.cpu or scale out with an HPA; For abnormal usage, capture a CPU profile in the application rather than papering over it with more quota.

Info · 1m · Trigger: 100 * sum by (namespace, pod, container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!="", container!="POD"}) / sum by (namespace, pod, container) (container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{container!="", container!="POD"} > 0) > 80 Runbook: Run kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> --containers to compare usage against the limit; Check the history curve to tell a steady climb (likely a leak) from a normal traffic peak; For normal peaks, raise resources.limits.memory with headroom; For a steady climb, capture a heap profile in the application — raising the quota only postpones it.

Info · 1m · Trigger: 100-cpu_usage_idle{cpu="cpu-total"} > 90 Runbook: Run kubectl top node for the overall picture and kubectl top pod -A --sort-by=cpu for the biggest consumers; Check whether too many high-load Pods landed on this node and drain some if needed; Check whether Pod requests are set too low, causing overcommit; If the cluster is running hot overall, add nodes.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: mem_used_percent > 90 Runbook: Run kubectl top node and kubectl top pod -A --sort-by=memory to find the biggest consumers; Check for Pods without a memory limit growing without bound; Use kubectl drain to move some Pods off, confirming the target nodes have headroom; Review the kubelet eviction thresholds, and add nodes if the cluster is tight overall.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready",status="true"} == 0 Runbook: Run kubectl describe node <node> for Conditions and Events to tell MemoryPressure, DiskPressure and a lost kubelet apart; Log in to the node and check kubelet and the container runtime (systemctl status kubelet containerd); Use journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 to locate the problem; If the node cannot recover soon, run kubectl drain so the Pods move promptly instead of waiting for the eviction timeout.

Info · 1m · Trigger: disk_used_percent > 90 Runbook: On the node run df -h to find the mount point, usually /var/lib/docker or /var/lib/containerd; Run crictl rmi --prune or docker system prune to clean unused image layers — the fastest win; Check whether a Pod is writing large amounts of data to an emptyDir or hostPath; After cleaning, confirm the kubelet DiskPressure taint was removed automatically.
A client certificate used to authenticate to the apiserver is expiring in less than 7.0 days. Warning · — · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeClientCertificateExpiration
A client certificate used to authenticate to the apiserver is expiring in less than 24.0 hours. Critical · — · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeClientCertificateExpiration

An aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has reported errors. The number of errors have increased for it in the past five minutes. High values indicate that the availability of the service changes too often. Warning · — · Trigger: sum by(name, namespace)(increase(aggregator_unavailable_apiservice_count[5m])) > 2 Runbook: Run kubectl get apiservice to see which APIService is False; Run kubectl describe apiservice <name> for the specific error; If the backing service is down, check its Deployment/Service health (commonly metrics-server); For certificate problems, verify the CA bundle configuration.

An aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has been only {{ $value | humanize }}% available over the last 10m. Warning · 5m · Trigger: (1 - max by(name, namespace)(avg_over_time(aggregator_unavailable_apiservice[10m]))) * 100 < 85 Runbook: Run kubectl get apiservice to identify the APIService; Run kubectl -n <ns> get pod to check its backing Pods; Read that Pod's logs for startup or runtime errors; After recovery, verify with something like kubectl top node that the functionality is back.

KubeAPI has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery. Critical · 15m · Trigger: absent(up{job="apiserver"} == 1) Runbook: On the control plane node, check the kube-apiserver process/static Pod state and logs; For multi-replica deployments, confirm whether only some instances are down and whether the load balancer removed the faulty ones; Common root causes are unavailable etcd, expired certificates and resource exhaustion; Restore etcd and certificates first — apiserver usually recovers on its own.
The API server is burning too much error budget. Critical · 2m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn
The API server is burning too much error budget. Critical · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn
The API server is burning too much error budget. Warning · 60m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn
The API server is burning too much error budget. Warning · 180m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn

Deployment {{ $labels.deployment }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has mismatched replicas. Warning · 10m · Trigger: kube_deployment_spec_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_deployment_status_replicas_available{job="kube-state-metrics"} Runbook: Run kubectl describe deploy <name> -n <ns> for Conditions and Events; Run kubectl get pod -n <ns> -l <selector> to see the state and reason of the unready Pods; Common causes are insufficient resources for scheduling, image pull failures, and failing readiness probes; Follow the Pod's specific state; for resource shortage, add nodes or lower requests.

StatefulSet {{ $labels.statefulset }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has mismatched replicas. Warning · 10m · Trigger: kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_statefulset_spec_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} Runbook: Run kubectl get pod -n <ns> -l <selector> and check by ordinal which replica is stuck; Run kubectl describe pod to check whether its PVC bound successfully — this is the most common sticking point for stateful services; For storage problems, check the PV/StorageClass and the CSI driver; For application problems check kubectl logs; once fixed, the StatefulSet continues automatically.

DaemonSet {{ $labels.daemonset }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has unready pods. Warning · 10m · Trigger: kube_daemonset_status_number_ready{job="kube-state-metrics"} < kube_daemonset_status_desired_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} Runbook: Run kubectl describe ds <name> -n <ns> for Events and desired/current counts; Compare node taints against the DaemonSet's tolerations — a taint mismatch is the most common cause; Check whether nodeSelector/affinity excludes those nodes; For resource shortage, lower the DaemonSet's requests or free node resources.

HPA {{ $labels.hpa }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has scale up failures. Warning · 5m · Trigger: kube_hpa_status_failed_scale_up_total{job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0 Runbook: Run kubectl describe hpa <name> -n <ns> and read the reason in Conditions; ScalingLimited means it hit the min/max boundary; FailedGetScale means the target workload has a problem; For metric failures, check whether metrics-server or the custom metrics adapter is healthy; If new replicas stay Pending for lack of resources, add nodes.

Pod {{ $labels.pod }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has failed. Warning · 5m · Trigger: kube_pod_status_phase{job="kube-state-metrics",phase="Failed"} == 1 Runbook: Run kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o wide for STATUS and READY, then kubectl describe pod for Events; Pending usually means insufficient resources or scheduling constraints (affinity, taints, unbound PVC); for ImagePullBackOff check the image address and pull credentials; Running but not Ready — check the readiness probe and kubectl logs <pod> for startup errors; Confirm whether the replica count is now too low to carry traffic, and scale healthy replicas first if so.

Job {{ $labels.job_name }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} has failed. Warning · 5m · Trigger: kube_job_status_failed{job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0 Runbook: Run kubectl get job <job> -n <ns> for the failure count, then kubectl logs job/<job> for the reason; Run kubectl describe job for Events and whether it gave up after exhausting backoffLimit; After fixing the root cause, kubectl delete job and resubmit, or let the CronJob run again on schedule; Confirm whether the failure has downstream impact (missing output, skipped cleanup) and redo it manually if needed.

{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} throttling of CPU in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} for container {{ $labels.container }} in pod {{ $labels.pod }}. Info · 15m · Trigger: sum(increase(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{container!="", }[5m])) by (container, pod, namespace) / sum(increase(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{}[5m])) by (container, pod, namespace) > ( 25 / 100 ) Runbook: Run kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> --containers and compare against resources.limits.cpu; Note that runtimes like Java that do not detect the cgroup limit may spawn too many threads and worsen throttling — check the JVM version and flags; Raise limits.cpu, or scale out horizontally with an HPA; A limit far above the request is easily squeezed by overcommit — consider bringing them closer together.

Kubernetes aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has been only {{ $value | humanize }}% available over the last 10m. Warning · 5m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeAggregatedAPIDown

Kubernetes aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has reported errors. It has appeared unavailable {{ $value | humanize }} times averaged over the past 10m. Warning · — · Trigger: sum by(name, namespace, cluster)(increase(aggregator_unavailable_apiservice_total{job="apiserver"}[10m])) > 4 Runbook: Run kubectl get apiservice to see which one is False; Run kubectl describe apiservice <name> for the specific error; If the backing service is down, check its Deployment/Service; For certificate problems, verify the CA bundle configuration.

The kubernetes apiserver has terminated {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its incoming requests. Warning · 5m · Trigger: sum(rate(apiserver_request_terminations_total{job="apiserver"}[10m])) / ( sum(rate(apiserver_request_total{job="apiserver"}[10m])) + sum(rate(apiserver_request_terminations_total{job="apiserver"}[10m])) ) > 0.20 Runbook: Check the apiserver_flowcontrol metrics to see which flow schema is being throttled; Identify the client making the flood of requests (usually an Operator or script doing full LIST calls); Rate limit that client or fix its request pattern; If more capacity is genuinely needed, tune the FlowSchema and PriorityLevelConfiguration.

Kubernetes API server client '{{ $labels.job }}/{{ $labels.instance }}' is experiencing {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} errors.' Warning · 15m · Trigger: (sum(rate(rest_client_requests_total{job="apiserver",code=~"5.."}[5m])) by (cluster, instance, job, namespace) / sum(rate(rest_client_requests_total{job="apiserver"}[5m])) by (cluster, instance, job, namespace)) > 0.01 Runbook: Use the alert labels to identify the component/instance that is erroring; Read the specific error code in that component's log: 401/403 is an RBAC problem, 429 is throttling, 5xx is an apiserver-side problem; For permissions, verify the ServiceAccount's Role/ClusterRoleBinding; For throttling, check whether the component is doing high-frequency LIST calls and switch to Watch or add a resourceVersion.

pod/{{ $labels.pod }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} on container {{ $labels.container}} has been in waiting state for longer than 1 hour. Warning · 60m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeContainerWaiting

KubeControllerManager has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery. Critical · 15m · Trigger: absent(up{job="kube-controller-manager"} == 1) Runbook: On the control plane node, check the kube-controller-manager static Pod or process state and logs; For multi-replica deployments, confirm leader election is failing over correctly; Common root causes are an unavailable apiserver or expired certificates; After recovery, confirm workloads with wrong replica counts start self-healing.

Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Pods by {{ $value }} CPU shares and cannot tolerate node failure. Warning · 10m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeCPUOvercommit

Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Namespaces. Warning · 5m · Trigger: sum(min without(resource) (kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="hard", resource=~"(cpu|requests.cpu)"})) by (cluster) / sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="cpu", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster) > 1.5 Runbook: Run kubectl describe node | grep -A5 'Allocated resources' to sum up allocation per node; This is a capacity planning signal rather than an immediate outage — assess whether there is still headroom to absorb a node failure; Check for Pods with requests set far above actual usage; lowering them frees a lot of schedulable capacity; If headroom is genuinely insufficient, add nodes.

{{ $value }} Pods of DaemonSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.daemonset }} are running where they are not supposed to run. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeDaemonSetMisScheduled

{{ $value }} Pods of DaemonSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.daemonset }} are not scheduled. Warning · 10m · Trigger: kube_daemonset_status_desired_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} - kube_daemonset_status_current_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0 Runbook: Run kubectl describe ds <name> -n <ns> for Events and desired/current counts; Compare node taints against the DaemonSet's tolerations — a taint mismatch is the most common cause; Check whether nodeSelector/affinity excludes those nodes; For resource shortage, lower the DaemonSet's requests or free node resources.

DaemonSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.daemonset }} has not finished or progressed for at least 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · Trigger: ( ( kube_daemonset_status_current_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_daemonset_status_desired_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) or ( kube_daemonset_status_number_misscheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} != 0 ) or ( kube_daemonset_status_updated_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_daemonset_status_desired_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) or ( kube_daemonset_status_number_available{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_daemonset_status_desired_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) ) and ( changes(kube_daemonset_status_updated_number_scheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"}[5m]) == 0 ) Runbook: Run kubectl rollout status ds/<name> -n <ns> to see which nodes are stuck; Run kubectl describe pod to see why the new Pod is not ready; If it cannot be fixed quickly, kubectl rollout undo ds/<name>; Check whether the updateStrategy maxUnavailable is too conservative.

Deployment generation for {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} does not match, this indicates that the Deployment has failed but has not been rolled back. Warning · 15m · Trigger: kube_deployment_status_observed_generation{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_deployment_metadata_generation{job="kube-state-metrics"} Runbook: Run kubectl describe <kind> <name> -n <ns> and compare generation with observedGeneration; Check whether kube-controller-manager is healthy — a stalled controller is the most common cause; Look for errors about this object in the controller-manager log; Confirm apiserver and etcd are healthy; once the controller recovers, generation catches up automatically.

Deployment {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch
Rollout of deployment {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} is not progressing for longer than 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeDeploymentRolloutStuck
HPA {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.horizontalpodautoscaler }} has been running at max replicas for longer than 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeHpaMaxedOut

HPA {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.horizontalpodautoscaler }} has not matched the desired number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · Trigger: (kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_desired_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"}) and (kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} > kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_spec_min_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"}) and (kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} < kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_spec_max_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"}) and changes(kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"}[15m]) == 0 Runbook: Run kubectl describe hpa <name> -n <ns> and read the reason in Conditions; ScalingLimited means it hit the min/max boundary; FailedGetScale means the target workload has a problem; For metric failures, check whether metrics-server or the custom metrics adapter is healthy; If new replicas stay Pending for lack of resources, add nodes.

Job {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.job_name }} failed to complete. Removing failed job after investigation should clear this alert. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeJobFailed

Job {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.job_name }} is taking more than {{ "43200" | humanizeDuration }} to complete. Warning · — · Trigger: time() - max by(namespace, job_name, cluster) (kube_job_status_start_time{job="kube-state-metrics"} and kube_job_status_active{job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0) > 43200 Runbook: Run kubectl get job <job> -n <ns> for elapsed time and completions; Run kubectl logs job/<job> to see where it is stuck; Determine whether the task is genuinely long-running or hung — for a hang, kubectl delete job, fix it and rerun; Set a sensible activeDeadlineSeconds so Jobs cannot hang indefinitely.

Client certificate for Kubelet on node {{ $labels.node }} expires in {{ $value | humanizeDuration }}. Kubelet on node {{ $labels.node }} has failed to renew its client certificate ({{ $value | humanize }} errors in the last 5 minutes). Warning · 15m · Trigger: increase(kubelet_certificate_manager_client_expiration_renew_errors[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Check the kubelet log for certificate rotation errors; Check whether CSRs are stuck Pending: kubectl get csr, and approve manually with kubectl certificate approve if needed; Confirm the cluster has a CSR auto-approval controller (kube-controller-manager's --cluster-signing-cert-file setting); After fixing, confirm new CSRs are auto-approved and signed.
Kubelet has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery. Critical · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeletDown

The Kubelet Pod Lifecycle Event Generator has a 99th percentile duration of {{ $value }} seconds on node {{ $labels.node }}. Warning · 5m · Trigger: node_quantile:kubelet_pleg_relist_duration_seconds:histogram_quantile{quantile="0.99"} >= 10 Runbook: On the node run crictl ps and crictl info to gauge container runtime responsiveness; Check whether the node has too many containers and whether disk IO is saturated — these are the main causes of slow PLEG; For a stalled runtime, consider restarting containerd (briefly affects that node); If it persists, reduce the Pod density on that node.

Kubelet Pod startup 99th percentile latency is {{ $value }} seconds on node {{ $labels.node }}. Warning · 15m · Trigger: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kubelet_pod_worker_duration_seconds_bucket{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"}[5m])) by (cluster, instance, le)) * on(cluster, instance) group_left(node) kubelet_node_name{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} > 60 Runbook: Run kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> and use the Event timestamps to see whether it is stuck pulling the image, mounting a volume, or in an init container; For slow pulls, check image size and registry bandwidth, and consider pre-warming images or a local registry; For slow mounts, check the PV/CSI driver state; If the application itself starts slowly, optimise startup and set a sensible readiness probe initialDelaySeconds.

Server certificate for Kubelet on node {{ $labels.node }} expires in {{ $value | humanizeDuration }}. Warning · — · Trigger: kubelet_certificate_manager_server_ttl_seconds < 604800 Runbook: Run kubeadm certs check-expiration (kubeadm clusters) or openssl x509 -noout -dates to confirm the expiry; On kubeadm clusters run kubeadm certs renew all and restart the control plane components; kubelet client certificates usually rotate automatically — if not, check the rotateCertificates setting and CSR approval; After renewal, verify the components loaded the new certificate (restart them) and re-check every node.

Kubelet on node {{ $labels.node }} has failed to renew its server certificate ({{ $value | humanize }} errors in the last 5 minutes). Warning · 15m · Trigger: increase(kubelet_server_expiration_renew_errors[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Check the kubelet log for certificate rotation errors; Check whether CSRs are stuck Pending: kubectl get csr, and approve manually with kubectl certificate approve if needed; Confirm the cluster has a CSR auto-approval controller (kube-controller-manager's --cluster-signing-cert-file setting); After fixing, confirm new CSRs are auto-approved and signed.
Kubelet '{{ $labels.node }}' is running at {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its Pod capacity. Info · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeletTooManyPods

Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted memory resource requests for Pods by {{ $value | humanize }} bytes and cannot tolerate node failure. Warning · 10m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeMemoryOvercommit

Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted memory resource requests for Namespaces. Warning · 5m · Trigger: sum(min without(resource) (kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="hard", resource=~"(memory|requests.memory)"})) by (cluster) / sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster) > 1.5 Runbook: Run kubectl describe node | grep -A5 'Allocated resources' to sum up allocation per node; This is a capacity planning signal rather than an immediate outage — assess whether there is still headroom to absorb a node failure; Check for Pods with requests set far above actual usage; lowering them frees a lot of schedulable capacity; If headroom is genuinely insufficient, add nodes.
{{ $labels.node }} has been unready for more than 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeNodeNotReady

The readiness status of node {{ $labels.node }} has changed {{ $value }} times in the last 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · Trigger: sum(changes(kube_node_status_condition{job="kube-state-metrics",status="true",condition="Ready"}[15m])) by (cluster, node) > 2 Runbook: Run kubectl describe node <node> and read the timeline of Condition changes; On the node, check the kubelet log — common root causes are resource pressure, a stalled container runtime, or an unstable network to apiserver; While it flaps, kubectl cordon the node so no new Pods land on it; Uncordon only after the root cause is fixed — do not repeatedly restart kubelet during the flapping.

{{ $labels.node }} is unreachable and some workloads may be rescheduled. Warning · 15m · Trigger: (kube_node_spec_taint{job="kube-state-metrics",key="node.kubernetes.io/unreachable",effect="NoSchedule"} unless ignoring(key,value) kube_node_spec_taint{job="kube-state-metrics",key=~"ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoscaler|cloud.google.com/impending-node-termination|aws-node-termination-handler/spot-itn"}) == 1 Runbook: First confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh — if it is down, handle it as a host outage; If it is alive, investigate the node's network and certificates to apiserver (the kubelet log states the error clearly); Check whether any single-replica critical service runs on that node and start it elsewhere first; After recovery, confirm the node is Ready again and Pod states are normal.

The persistent volume {{ $labels.persistentvolume }} has status {{ $labels.phase }}. Critical · 5m · Trigger: kube_persistentvolume_status_phase{phase=~"Failed|Pending",job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0 Runbook: Run kubectl describe pv <pv> and kubectl describe pvc <pvc> -n <ns> and read the errors in Events; Common causes are an unavailable storage backend, insufficient capacity, or wrong StorageClass parameters; Check whether the CSI driver Pods are healthy (usually in kube-system); For a storage backend failure, follow that system's own procedure — Pods stay Pending meanwhile.

The PersistentVolume claimed by {{ $labels.persistentvolumeclaim }} in Namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} is only {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} free. Critical · 1m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp

The PersistentVolume claimed by {{ $labels.persistentvolumeclaim }} in Namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} only has {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} free inodes. Critical · 1m · Trigger: ( kubelet_volume_stats_inodes_free{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} / kubelet_volume_stats_inodes{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} ) < 0.03 and kubelet_volume_stats_inodes_used{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} > 0 unless on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_access_mode{ access_mode="ReadOnlyMany"} == 1 unless on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_labels{label_excluded_from_alerts="true"} == 1 Runbook: kubectl exec into a Pod using the volume and run df -i; Count files level by level to find the directories with the most small files; Clean up useless small files (cache fragments, temporary files); If it cannot be reduced, expand the volume or change storage type.
Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} ({{ $labels.container }}) is in waiting state (reason: "CrashLoopBackOff"). Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubePodCrashLooping

Warning · 15m · Trigger: kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="used"} / ignoring(instance, job, type) (kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="hard"} > 0) > 1 Runbook: Run kubectl describe quota -n <ns> to see which item (cpu/memory/pods/storage) topped out; Use kubectl get pod -n <ns> -o custom-columns to sum requests per workload and find the biggest consumers; Check for stopped-but-uncleaned resources still holding quota; If more quota is genuinely needed, ask the cluster admin to adjust the ResourceQuota.

Namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} is using {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its {{ $labels.resource }} quota. KubeScheduler has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery. StatefulSet generation for {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.statefulset }} does not match, this indicates that the StatefulSet has failed but has not been rolled back. StatefulSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.statefulset }} has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: KubeStatefulSetReplicasMismatch

StatefulSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.statefulset }} update has not been rolled out. Warning · 15m · Trigger: ( max without (revision) ( kube_statefulset_status_current_revision{job="kube-state-metrics"} unless kube_statefulset_status_update_revision{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) * ( kube_statefulset_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_statefulset_status_replicas_updated{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) ) and ( changes(kube_statefulset_status_replicas_updated{job="kube-state-metrics"}[5m]) == 0 ) Runbook: Run kubectl rollout status sts/<name> -n <ns> to see which replica it is stuck on; StatefulSets update in order, so one stuck replica blocks all the rest — focus on the one currently updating; Run kubectl describe pod to find why it is not ready (PVC, probe, image); If it cannot be fixed quickly, kubectl rollout undo.

With Prometheus or vmalert: download kubernetes.yml, add it to rule_files (or -rule for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a severity label (critical / warning / info), and runbook_url points back to this page, or to the rule's own page where it has one. With Nightingale: the same rules ship in the Kubernetes integration template. Open the integration center, import the rules into a business group, and enable them one by one. Nightingale keeps the runbook with each alert and can evaluate the rules against Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and other data sources.

Many rule expressions are adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates (Kubernetes, Apache-2.0). Corrections are welcome as pull requests there.
