An aggregated API, an APIService that the Kubernetes API server proxies to another service, has been available less than 85% of the time over the last 10 minutes. The most common one is v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io from metrics-server; others come from prometheus-adapter, custom metrics adapters and various operators. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 5m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeAggregatedAPIDown alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: (1 - max by(name, namespace, cluster)(avg_over_time(aggregator_unavailable_apiservice{job="apiserver"}[10m]))) * 100 < 85 Alert message: Kubernetes aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has been only {{ $value | humanize }}% available over the last 10m.

The backing Pods (metrics-server, prometheus-adapter) are crashing, not ready, or scaled to zero. The API server cannot reach the backing service: a network policy, a firewall, or a broken Service or endpoints. TLS problems between the API server and the backend, such as an expired serving certificate or a wrong caBundle on the APIService. The APIService still exists but points to a service that was uninstalled.

Run kubectl get apiservice to identify the APIService; Run kubectl -n <ns> get pod to check its backing Pods; Read that Pod's logs for startup or runtime errors; After recovery, verify with something like kubectl top node that the functionality is back.

Effects depend on the API. When the metrics API is down, kubectl top fails and HPAs that scale on CPU or memory stop scaling. A broken APIService can also stall namespace deletion, because the namespace controller cannot list resources from that group. The expression selects job="apiserver". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
aggregator_unavailable_apiservice (kube-apiserver)

KubeAggregatedAPIErrors: Kubernetes aggregated API …/… has reported errors. It has appeared unavailable … times averaged over the past 10m. KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn: The API server is burning too much error budget. KubeHpaReplicasMismatch: HPA …/… has not matched the desired number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeAggregatedAPIDown expr: |- (1 - max by(name, namespace, cluster)(avg_over_time(aggregator_unavailable_apiservice{job="apiserver"}[10m]))) * 100 < 85 for: 5m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Kubernetes aggregated API {{ $labels.name }}/{{ $labels.namespace }} has been only {{ $value | humanize }}% available over the last 10m." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeaggregatedapidown" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

The Kubernetes API server is failing or slowing down requests fast enough to use up its error budget early. The rules use the multi-window burn-rate method from the Google SRE workbook against a 99% availability target. Each pairs a long and a short window, and both must exceed the threshold: 14.4 over 1h and 5m, and 6 over 6h and 30m, are critical; 3 over 1d and 2h, and 1 over 3d and 6h, are warnings. At a burn rate of 14.4 a 30-day error budget is gone in about two days. Controllers, kubectl and CI pipelines all go through the API server, so its errors spread everywhere. Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: The template splits this alert into 4 rules with different thresholds, windows and severities. Load all of them together.
Critical (critical) · Fires after: 2m sum(apiserver_request:burnrate1h) > (14.40 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate5m) > (14.40 * 0.01000)
Critical (critical) · Fires after: 15m sum(apiserver_request:burnrate6h) > (6.00 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate30m) > (6.00 * 0.01000)
Warning (warning) · Fires after: 60m sum(apiserver_request:burnrate1d) > (3.00 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate2h) > (3.00 * 0.01000)

Warning (warning) · Fires after: 180m sum(apiserver_request:burnrate3d) > (1.00 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate6h) > (1.00 * 0.01000) Alert message: The API server is burning too much error budget.

etcd is slow, most often because of disk latency, which drags down writes in particular. Clients issue expensive requests, such as LIST calls across all namespaces without a resourceVersion, which push latency past the SLO. An aggregated API (metrics-server, an admission webhook backend) is failing, and requests that depend on it fail with it. An admission webhook is slow or down, and every write it intercepts waits for it. The API server is short of CPU or memory, or one replica of several is unhealthy.

Look at the apiserver error code and latency distribution to tell read from write degradation; For write degradation, check etcd disk latency first — that is the most common root cause; For read degradation, look for clients doing wide LIST calls (full enumeration without a resourceVersion); Rate limit the offending client and consider enabling APF (API Priority and Fairness).
The expressions read the apiserver_request:burnrate* recording rules from kubernetes-mixin. Load those recording rules too, or the rules never fire.

apiserver_request:burnrate1h (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) apiserver_request:burnrate5m (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) apiserver_request:burnrate6h (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) apiserver_request:burnrate30m (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) apiserver_request:burnrate1d (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) apiserver_request:burnrate2h (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) apiserver_request:burnrate3d (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin)

KubeAPIDown: KubeAPI has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery. KubeClientErrors: Kubernetes API server client '…/…' is experiencing … errors.' KubeAggregatedAPIDown: Kubernetes aggregated API …/… has been only …% available over the last 10m.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn-S1-120s expr: |- sum(apiserver_request:burnrate1h) > (14.40 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate5m) > (14.40 * 0.01000) for: 2m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "The API server is burning too much error budget." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeapierrorbudgetburn" - alert: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn-S1-900s expr: |- sum(apiserver_request:burnrate6h) > (6.00 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate30m) > (6.00 * 0.01000) for: 15m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "The API server is burning too much error budget." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeapierrorbudgetburn" - alert: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn-S2-3600s expr: |- sum(apiserver_request:burnrate1d) > (3.00 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate2h) > (3.00 * 0.01000) for: 60m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "The API server is burning too much error budget." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeapierrorbudgetburn" - alert: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn-S2-10800s expr: |- sum(apiserver_request:burnrate3d) > (1.00 * 0.01000) and sum(apiserver_request:burnrate6h) > (1.00 * 0.01000) for: 180m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "The API server is burning too much error budget." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeapierrorbudgetburn" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Of the client certificates presented to the API server over the last 5 minutes, at least 1% expire within 7 days (warning) or within 24 hours (critical). The rules take the 1st percentile of their remaining lifetime. When they expire, those clients get 401 Unauthorized. If they belong to a kubelet, a controller or the scheduler, nodes go NotReady or the control plane stops reconciling. Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeClientCertificateExpiration alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: The template splits this alert into 2 rules with different thresholds, windows and severities. Load all of them together.

Warning (warning) · Fires after: — apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_count{job="apiserver"} > 0 and on(job) histogram_quantile(0.01, sum by (job, le) (rate(apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_bucket{job="apiserver"}[5m]))) < 604800

Critical (critical) · Fires after: — apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_count{job="apiserver"} > 0 and on(job) histogram_quantile(0.01, sum by (job, le) (rate(apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_bucket{job="apiserver"}[5m]))) < 86400 Alert message: A client certificate used to authenticate to the apiserver is expiring in less than 7.0 days.

kubeadm issues control-plane certificates for one year and renews them during kubeadm upgrade. A cluster that has not been upgraded for a year runs into this. Kubelet client certificate rotation is off, or the CSRs it creates are not being approved. Long-lived kubeconfig files issued to people or CI systems with client certificates. Certificates generated by hand or by an external tool that has no renewal job.

Run kubeadm certs check-expiration (kubeadm clusters) or openssl x509 -noout -dates to confirm the expiry; On kubeadm clusters run kubeadm certs renew all and restart the control plane components; kubelet client certificates usually rotate automatically — if not, check the rotateCertificates setting and CSR approval; After renewal, verify the components loaded the new certificate (restart them) and re-check every node.

The metric is built from the certificates clients actually present, so it only reflects clients that have connected recently. It does not tell you which client is affected. On kubeadm clusters kubeadm certs check-expiration lists the control plane's own certificates. The expression selects job="apiserver". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_count (kube-apiserver) apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_bucket (kube-apiserver)

KubeletClientCertificateExpiration: Client certificate for Kubelet on node … expires in …. KubeletServerCertificateExpiration: Server certificate for Kubelet on node … expires in …. KubeNodeNotReady: … has been unready for more than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeClientCertificateExpiration-S2 expr: |- apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_count{job="apiserver"} > 0 and on(job) histogram_quantile(0.01, sum by (job, le) (rate(apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_bucket{job="apiserver"}[5m]))) < 604800 labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "A client certificate used to authenticate to the apiserver is expiring in less than 7.0 days." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeclientcertificateexpiration" - alert: KubeClientCertificateExpiration-S1 expr: |- apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_count{job="apiserver"} > 0 and on(job) histogram_quantile(0.01, sum by (job, le) (rate(apiserver_client_certificate_expiration_seconds_bucket{job="apiserver"}[5m]))) < 86400 labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "A client certificate used to authenticate to the apiserver is expiring in less than 24.0 hours." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeclientcertificateexpiration" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A container has been in the Waiting state for more than an hour: it is neither running nor terminated. The waiting reason tells you which step it is stuck on, from pulling the image to mounting volumes to the back-off between crash restarts. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 60m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeContainerWaiting alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: sum by (namespace, pod, container, cluster) (kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{job="kube-state-metrics"}) > 0 Alert message: pod/{{ $labels.pod }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} on container {{ $labels.container}} has been in waiting state for longer than 1 hour.

ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull: wrong image name or tag, missing pull credentials, or the registry is unreachable or rate limiting. CreateContainerConfigError: a ConfigMap, Secret or key that the container references does not exist. ContainerCreating for a long time: a volume cannot be attached or mounted, or the network plugin cannot set up the Pod network. CrashLoopBackOff: the container keeps crashing; KubePodCrashLooping fires as well. PodInitializing: an init container has not finished.

Run kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> and read the Waiting Reason; For ImagePullBackOff, check the image name, tag and pull credentials (imagePullSecrets); For CreateContainerConfigError, check the referenced ConfigMap/Secret exists; For CrashLoopBackOff, follow the crash loop path and read the --previous logs.

The rule sums kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason without filtering on the reason, so every waiting reason counts. Group the alert by the reason label, or check it with kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].state.waiting}'. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason (kube-state-metrics)
KubePodCrashLooping: Pod …/… (…) is in waiting state (reason: "CrashLoopBackOff"). KubePodNotReady: Pod …/… has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeContainerWaiting expr: |- sum by (namespace, pod, container, cluster) (kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{job="kube-state-metrics"}) > 0 for: 60m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "pod/{{ $labels.pod }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} on container {{ $labels.container}} has been in waiting state for longer than 1 hour." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubecontainerwaiting" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

The CPU requested by all Pods in the cluster is more than the cluster could provide if its largest node went away. In other words, the cluster cannot survive losing one node: the Pods from that node would have nowhere to be rescheduled. It is a capacity warning, not an outage, and it is about requests, not actual CPU usage. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 10m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeCPUOvercommit alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: sum(namespace_cpu:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum{job="kube-state-metrics",}) by (cluster) - (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster)) > 0 and (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster)) > 0 Alert message: Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Pods by {{ $value }} CPU shares and cannot tolerate node failure.

Workloads grew (more replicas, HPAs scaling out) without the node pool growing. Nodes were removed or scaled down, by hand or by an autoscaler. Requests are set far above what containers actually use, so the cluster looks fuller than it is. One node is much larger than the others, so the "lose the largest node" reserve is big.

Run kubectl describe node | grep -A5 'Allocated resources' to sum up allocation per node; This is a capacity planning signal rather than an immediate outage — assess whether there is still headroom to absorb a node failure; Check for Pods with requests set far above actual usage; lowering them frees a lot of schedulable capacity; If headroom is genuinely insufficient, add nodes.

The expression uses the namespace_cpu:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum recording rule from kubernetes-mixin. Without that recording rule loaded, the rule never fires. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
namespace_cpu:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) kube_node_status_allocatable (kube-state-metrics)

KubeMemoryOvercommit: Cluster … has overcommitted memory resource requests for Pods by … bytes and cannot tolerate node failure. KubeCPUQuotaOvercommit: Cluster … has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Namespaces. KubeHpaMaxedOut: HPA …/… has been running at max replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeCPUOvercommit expr: |- sum(namespace_cpu:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum{job="kube-state-metrics",}) by (cluster) - (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster)) > 0 and (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="cpu"}) by (cluster)) > 0 for: 10m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Pods by {{ $value }} CPU shares and cannot tolerate node failure." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubecpuovercommit" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Some of a DaemonSet's Pods are running on nodes where, according to the DaemonSet's current node selector, affinity and the node's taints, they should not run. It rarely breaks anything by itself, but it means the DaemonSet's placement and the cluster's node layout disagree. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeDaemonSetMisScheduled alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: kube_daemonset_status_number_misscheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0 Alert message: {{ $value }} Pods of DaemonSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.daemonset }} are running where they are not supposed to run.

Node labels changed and no longer match the DaemonSet node selector or affinity. A NoSchedule taint was added to nodes. Pods already there keep running, but they no longer count as correctly placed. The DaemonSet spec was updated to target fewer nodes.

Run kubectl get pod -n <ns> -l <selector> -o wide to see which nodes they landed on; Check whether the DaemonSet's nodeSelector/affinity matches the node labels; This usually follows a node label change or a DaemonSet update — after correcting it the extra Pods are cleaned up automatically; Delete any leftovers manually.

Decide which side is right. If the DaemonSet should still run there, fix its selector or add a toleration. If it should not, remove the leftover Pods. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_daemonset_status_number_misscheduled (kube-state-metrics)
KubeDaemonSetNotScheduled: … Pods of DaemonSet …/… are not scheduled. KubeDaemonSetRolloutStuck: DaemonSet …/… has not finished or progressed for at least 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeDaemonSetMisScheduled expr: |- kube_daemonset_status_number_misscheduled{job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0 for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "{{ $value }} Pods of DaemonSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.daemonset }} are running where they are not supposed to run." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubedaemonsetmisscheduled" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A Deployment has had fewer available replicas than it asks for, for 15 minutes, while no rollout is in progress: the number of updated replicas has not changed in the last 10 minutes. Some replicas are missing or unready, so the service runs below its planned capacity. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: ( kube_deployment_spec_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} > kube_deployment_status_replicas_available{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) and ( changes(kube_deployment_status_replicas_updated{job="kube-state-metrics"}[10m]) == 0 ) Alert message: Deployment {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

New Pods cannot be scheduled: not enough CPU or memory, or affinity rules and taints leave no eligible node. Pods are crash looping or failing their readiness probe, so they never count as available. Images cannot be pulled on some nodes. The namespace quota is exhausted, so the ReplicaSet cannot create the missing Pods (look for exceeded quota events on the ReplicaSet). A node failure removed replicas and the replacements are stuck for one of the reasons above.

Run kubectl describe deploy <name> -n <ns> for Conditions and Events; Run kubectl get pod -n <ns> -l <selector> to see the state and reason of the unready Pods; Common causes are insufficient resources for scheduling, image pull failures, and failing readiness probes; Follow the Pod's specific state; for resource shortage, add nodes or lower requests.

The changes(...[10m]) == 0 clause keeps the rule quiet during a normal rolling update. A rollout that stops making progress is reported by KubeDeploymentRolloutStuck instead. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_deployment_spec_replicas (kube-state-metrics) kube_deployment_status_replicas_available (kube-state-metrics) kube_deployment_status_replicas_updated (kube-state-metrics)

KubeDeploymentRolloutStuck: Rollout of deployment …/… is not progressing for longer than 15 minutes. KubePodNotReady: Pod …/… has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes. KubePodCrashLooping: Pod …/… (…) is in waiting state (reason: "CrashLoopBackOff"). KubeHpaMaxedOut: HPA …/… has been running at max replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch expr: |- ( kube_deployment_spec_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} > kube_deployment_status_replicas_available{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) and ( changes(kube_deployment_status_replicas_updated{job="kube-state-metrics"}[10m]) == 0 ) for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Deployment {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubedeploymentreplicasmismatch" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A Deployment's Progressing condition is False. Kubernetes sets this, with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded, when a rollout has not made progress within progressDeadlineSeconds (600 seconds by default). Kubernetes does not roll back on its own: old and new ReplicaSets stay as they are, so you may be running a mix of versions until someone acts. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeDeploymentRolloutStuck alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: kube_deployment_status_condition{condition="Progressing", status="false",job="kube-state-metrics"} != 0 Alert message: Rollout of deployment {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} is not progressing for longer than 15 minutes.

The new version crashes or fails its readiness probe, so new Pods never become available. The new Pods cannot be scheduled, or their image cannot be pulled. The new version needs more CPU or memory than the namespace quota or the nodes have left. maxUnavailable is 0 and the cluster has no room for the extra surge Pod.

Run kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> -n <ns> to see which replica it is stuck on; Run kubectl describe pod to see why the new Pod is not ready (image, probe, resources); If it cannot be fixed quickly, kubectl rollout undo deploy/<name> to roll back; After fixing, redeploy and review whether maxSurge/maxUnavailable are sensible.

kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> -n <ns> exits with an error once the deadline is exceeded, so the same signal can fail a CI/CD pipeline before this alert fires. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_deployment_status_condition (kube-state-metrics)

KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch: Deployment …/… has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes. KubePodCrashLooping: Pod …/… (…) is in waiting state (reason: "CrashLoopBackOff"). KubeContainerWaiting: pod/… in namespace … on container … has been in waiting state for longer than 1 hour.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeDeploymentRolloutStuck expr: |- kube_deployment_status_condition{condition="Progressing", status="false",job="kube-state-metrics"} != 0 for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Rollout of deployment {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.deployment }} is not progressing for longer than 15 minutes." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubedeploymentrolloutstuck" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A HorizontalPodAutoscaler has been running at maxReplicas for 15 minutes. It cannot add more replicas, so if load keeps rising, each replica takes more of it and latency or error rates follow. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeHpaMaxedOut alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} == kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_spec_max_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} Alert message: HPA {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.horizontalpodautoscaler }} has been running at max replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Real growth in traffic or work that has outgrown the configured maximum. maxReplicas was set low on purpose (for cost or a downstream limit) and is now the bottleneck. The target is too low for the metric. For CPU, utilization is measured against requests, so a container with small requests looks busy all the time. The application slowed down (a slow dependency, a regression), so each replica handles less and the HPA keeps scaling out.

Run kubectl describe hpa <name> -n <ns> to see the gap between the current and target metric; Confirm the cluster still has resources for more replicas (node headroom); With headroom, raise maxReplicas; without it, add nodes first; Also assess whether per-replica capacity is too low — optimising the application beats scaling replicas indefinitely.

Raising maxReplicas only helps if the cluster has room for the extra Pods. Check KubeCPUOvercommit and KubeMemoryOvercommit, or the cluster autoscaler, before you raise it. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas (kube-state-metrics) kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_spec_max_replicas (kube-state-metrics)

KubeHpaReplicasMismatch: HPA …/… has not matched the desired number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes. KubeCPUOvercommit: Cluster … has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Pods by … CPU shares and cannot tolerate node failure. KubeMemoryOvercommit: Cluster … has overcommitted memory resource requests for Pods by … bytes and cannot tolerate node failure. KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch: Deployment …/… has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeHpaMaxedOut expr: |- kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} == kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_spec_max_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "HPA {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.horizontalpodautoscaler }} has been running at max replicas for longer than 15 minutes." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubehpamaxedout" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.

A Job has been marked Failed (kube_job_failed > 0): it used up its backoffLimit (6 retries by default) or ran past activeDeadlineSeconds, and the batch work it was meant to do (a backup, a report, a data sync) did not happen. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeJobFailed alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: kube_job_failed{job="kube-state-metrics"} > 0 Alert message: Job {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.job_name }} failed to complete. Removing failed job after investigation should clear this alert.

The task itself errors out: bad input data, a failed query, a dependency that is down. Pods are killed for exceeding their memory limit, or evicted from a node under pressure. The Job ran longer than activeDeadlineSeconds. The container image or command changed and no longer works with the Job arguments.

Run kubectl get job <job> -n <ns> for the failure count, then kubectl logs job/<job> for the reason; Run kubectl describe job for Events and whether it gave up after exhausting backoffLimit; After fixing the root cause, kubectl delete job and resubmit, or let the CronJob run again on schedule; Confirm whether the failure has downstream impact (missing output, skipped cleanup) and redo it manually if needed.

The alert keeps firing for as long as the failed Job object exists, even after a later run succeeds. Delete the Job once you have looked at it. For CronJobs, failedJobsHistoryLimit (1 by default) controls how many failed Jobs are kept. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_job_failed (kube-state-metrics)
KubeJobNotCompleted: Job …/… is taking more than … to complete. KubePodCrashLooping: Pod …/… (…) is in waiting state (reason: "CrashLoopBackOff").

Prometheus has no kubelet target reporting up == 1. Because the rule wraps the whole selector in absent(), it only fires when every kubelet is missing or failing to scrape. One broken node does not trigger it. When it fires you lose kubelet and cAdvisor metrics (container CPU and memory, volume usage) for the whole cluster, and any rule built on them goes quiet. Severity: Critical (critical) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeletDown alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: absent(up{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} == 1) Alert message: Kubelet has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery.

The scrape configuration changed: the ServiceMonitor for the kubelet was deleted, or its selector, port name or path no longer matches. Prometheus cannot authenticate to the kubelet on port 10250: an expired or missing bearer token, a TLS verification error, or RBAC that no longer grants nodes/metrics. A network policy or firewall now blocks Prometheus from reaching the nodes. Less often, the kubelets really are down across the cluster, for example after a bad configuration rollout.

On the node run systemctl status kubelet to check the process; Use journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager to find the exit or error reason; Common causes are expired certificates, config errors and an unavailable container runtime; After recovery, confirm the node is Ready again and check whether Pods were wrongly evicted meanwhile.

A single dead kubelet shows up as KubeNodeNotReady, not as this alert. Treat KubeletDown first as a monitoring problem: open the Prometheus /targets page and read the scrape error for the kubelet job. The expression selects job="kubelet". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
up (Prometheus's own metrics)
KubeNodeNotReady: … has been unready for more than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeletDown expr: |- absent(up{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} == 1) for: 15m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "Kubelet has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubeletdown" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A node is running more than 95% of the Pods it can hold, as set by the kubelet's maxPods (110 by default). When it reaches the limit, new Pods that would land there stay Pending, and a crowded node is more likely to show kubelet slowness. Severity: Info (info) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeletTooManyPods alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: count by(cluster, node) ( (kube_pod_status_phase{job="kube-state-metrics",phase="Running"} == 1) * on(instance,pod,namespace,cluster) group_left(node) topk by(instance,pod,namespace,cluster) (1, kube_pod_info{job="kube-state-metrics"}) ) / max by(cluster, node) ( kube_node_status_capacity{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="pods"} != 1 ) > 0.95 Alert message: Kubelet '{{ $labels.node }}' is running at {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its Pod capacity.

Many small Pods packed onto large nodes, which hit the Pod limit before CPU or memory run out. DaemonSets and sidecar-heavy workloads using up slots on every node. Completed or failed Pods that have not been garbage-collected yet. On some managed clusters the Pod limit is tied to the number of IP addresses a node can get, so it is lower than 110. On Amazon EKS with the VPC CNI, for example, it depends on the instance type.

Run kubectl get pod -A -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> | wc -l for the actual count; Compare against the kubelet maxPods setting (110 by default); Use kubectl drain or scheduling policy to move some Pods to other nodes; If you genuinely need higher density, raise maxPods but reassess node CPU/memory/PLEG pressure at the same time.

The ratio counts Pods in the Running phase against the node capacity reported by kube-state-metrics. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_pod_status_phase (kube-state-metrics) kube_pod_info (kube-state-metrics) kube_node_status_capacity (kube-state-metrics)
KubeNodeNotReady: … has been unready for more than 15 minutes. KubePodNotReady: Pod …/… has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeletTooManyPods expr: |- count by(cluster, node) ( (kube_pod_status_phase{job="kube-state-metrics",phase="Running"} == 1) * on(instance,pod,namespace,cluster) group_left(node) topk by(instance,pod,namespace,cluster) (1, kube_pod_info{job="kube-state-metrics"}) ) / max by(cluster, node) ( kube_node_status_capacity{job="kube-state-metrics",resource="pods"} != 1 ) > 0.95 for: 15m labels: severity: info annotations: summary: "Kubelet '{{ $labels.node }}' is running at {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its Pod capacity." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubelettoomanypods" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

The memory requested by all Pods in the cluster is more than the cluster could provide if its largest node went away, so a single node failure would leave Pods unschedulable. Like its CPU twin it is about requests, not usage, but memory is less forgiving: Pods that do not fit stay Pending instead of running slower. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 10m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeMemoryOvercommit alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: sum(namespace_memory:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum{}) by (cluster) - (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster)) > 0 and (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster)) > 0 Alert message: Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted memory resource requests for Pods by {{ $value | humanize }} bytes and cannot tolerate node failure.

Workloads grew without the node pool growing. Nodes were removed or scaled down. Memory requests are set well above actual usage. One node is much larger than the rest, so the reserve for losing it is large.

Run kubectl describe node | grep -A5 'Allocated resources' to sum up allocation per node; This is a capacity planning signal rather than an immediate outage — assess whether there is still headroom to absorb a node failure; Check for Pods with requests set far above actual usage; lowering them frees a lot of schedulable capacity; If headroom is genuinely insufficient, add nodes.

The expression uses the namespace_memory:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum recording rule from kubernetes-mixin. Without it, the rule never fires. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
namespace_memory:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum (recording rule from kubernetes-mixin) kube_node_status_allocatable (kube-state-metrics)

KubeCPUOvercommit: Cluster … has overcommitted CPU resource requests for Pods by … CPU shares and cannot tolerate node failure. KubeMemoryQuotaOvercommit: Cluster … has overcommitted memory resource requests for Namespaces. KubeHpaMaxedOut: HPA …/… has been running at max replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeMemoryOvercommit expr: |- sum(namespace_memory:kube_pod_container_resource_requests:sum{}) by (cluster) - (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster)) > 0 and (sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster) - max(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="memory", job="kube-state-metrics"}) by (cluster)) > 0 for: 10m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has overcommitted memory resource requests for Pods by {{ $value | humanize }} bytes and cannot tolerate node failure." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubememoryovercommit" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A node's Ready condition has not been True for 15 minutes; it is either False (the kubelet reports a problem) or Unknown (the kubelet has stopped reporting). New Pods are not scheduled there, and Pods already on it are evicted once the not-ready or unreachable taint outlasts their toleration, which is 300 seconds by default. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeNodeNotReady alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: kube_node_status_condition{job="kube-state-metrics",condition="Ready",status="true"} == 0 Alert message: {{ $labels.node }} has been unready for more than 15 minutes.

The kubelet or the container runtime (containerd, CRI-O) has stopped or keeps restarting. The node cannot reach the API server: network partition, firewall change, or a broken route. The node is out of resources: memory, disk, or process IDs, so the kubelet itself cannot work. The kubelet client certificate expired and the node can no longer authenticate. The machine was shut down, rebooted or reclaimed (for example a spot instance) without being drained.

Run kubectl describe node <node> for Conditions and Events to tell MemoryPressure, DiskPressure and a lost kubelet apart; Log in to the node and check kubelet and the container runtime (systemctl status kubelet containerd); Use journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 to locate the problem; If the node cannot recover soon, run kubectl drain so the Pods move promptly instead of waiting for the eviction timeout.

The expression status="true" == 0 covers both False and Unknown. kubectl describe node <node> shows which one and the last heartbeat time, which separates "the kubelet says something is wrong" from "the kubelet is gone". The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_node_status_condition (kube-state-metrics)

KubeletDown: Kubelet has disappeared from Prometheus target discovery. KubePodNotReady: Pod …/… has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes. KubeletTooManyPods: Kubelet '…' is running at … of its Pod capacity.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeNodeNotReady expr: |- kube_node_status_condition{job="kube-state-metrics",condition="Ready",status="true"} == 0 for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "{{ $labels.node }} has been unready for more than 15 minutes." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubenodenotready" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A PersistentVolume has less than 3% of its space left, as reported by the kubelet on the node that mounts it. Databases, queues and other stateful services usually stop accepting writes or crash once the volume is full, so this one is critical. Severity: Critical (critical) Fires after: 1m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: ( kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} / kubelet_volume_stats_capacity_bytes{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} ) < 0.03 and kubelet_volume_stats_used_bytes{job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"} > 0 unless on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_access_mode{ access_mode="ReadOnlyMany"} == 1 unless on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_labels{label_excluded_from_alerts="true"} == 1 Alert message: The PersistentVolume claimed by {{ $labels.persistentvolumeclaim }} in Namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} is only {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} free.

Data has simply grown: tables, indexes, topic logs or object counts outpaced the size chosen at creation. Retention or cleanup stopped working: log rotation, compaction, TTL jobs or backups that delete old copies. Temporary files, dumps or core files written to the data volume and never removed. The volume was sized for a test environment and reused in production.

Run kubectl get pvc -n <ns> to find the PVC and PV; kubectl exec into a Pod using the volume and use du to find the largest directories; Clean up logs and temporary data; If the StorageClass supports online expansion, kubectl edit pvc and raise spec.resources.requests.storage; otherwise migrate the data.

Volumes mounted read-only by many Pods (ReadOnlyMany) are skipped. You can also silence one PVC by labelling it excluded_from_alerts=true, but kube-state-metrics only exports PVC labels that are listed in its --metric-labels-allowlist flag, so add that label there first. The metrics come from the kubelet (kubelet_volume_stats_*). Volumes whose driver does not report usage statistics never produce them, so the rule stays silent for those volumes. The expression selects job="kubelet". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.

kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes (kubelet) kubelet_volume_stats_capacity_bytes (kubelet) kubelet_volume_stats_used_bytes (kubelet) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_access_mode (kube-state-metrics) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_labels (kube-state-metrics)

KubePersistentVolumeInodesFillingUp: The PersistentVolume claimed by … in Namespace … only has … free inodes. KubePersistentVolumeErrors: The persistent volume … has status …. KubeStatefulSetReplicasMismatch: StatefulSet …/… has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A container keeps exiting and the kubelet is restarting it with a growing back-off delay (from 10 seconds up to 5 minutes), so its waiting reason reads CrashLoopBackOff. The rule fires when kube-state-metrics has reported that reason at any point in the last 5 minutes, for 15 minutes in a row. While the loop lasts the container serves nothing; if every replica is looping, the workload is down. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubePodCrashLooping alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: max_over_time(kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{reason="CrashLoopBackOff", job="kube-state-metrics"}[5m]) >= 1 Alert message: Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} ({{ $labels.container }}) is in waiting state (reason: "CrashLoopBackOff").

The application exits on startup: a bad configuration value, a missing environment variable, or a failed migration. A dependency is unreachable (database, message queue, another service) and the process exits instead of retrying. The container is killed for exceeding its memory limit. lastState.terminated.reason shows OOMKilled and the exit code is 137. A liveness probe that is too strict, or that starts before the application is ready, keeps killing a healthy container. The image runs the wrong command or entrypoint, or is built for a different CPU architecture.

Run kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --previous to see the log before the last exit — this is the key step; Run kubectl describe pod for the exit code and Events: 137 usually means OOM or killed, 1/2 usually means the application failed to start; For config or dependency problems (unreachable database, missing ConfigMap/Secret), fix the dependency first; For OOM, compare resources.limits.memory against actual usage, or fix the application's memory leak.

The quickest way to see why the last run ended is kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].lastState.terminated}', which prints the reason, exit code and timestamps. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason (kube-state-metrics)

KubeContainerWaiting: pod/… in namespace … on container … has been in waiting state for longer than 1 hour. KubePodNotReady: Pod …/… has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes. KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch: Deployment …/… has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubePodCrashLooping expr: |- max_over_time(kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{reason="CrashLoopBackOff", job="kube-state-metrics"}[5m]) >= 1 for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} ({{ $labels.container }}) is in waiting state (reason: \"CrashLoopBackOff\")." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubepodcrashlooping" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A Pod that is not owned by a Job has been in the Pending, Unknown or Failed phase for 15 minutes. A Pending Pod has not started all its containers (often it has not even been scheduled), an Unknown Pod usually sits on a node that has stopped reporting, and a Failed Pod has terminated for good. Either way the Pod is not serving, and the workload is running with fewer replicas than it asked for. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubePodNotReady alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: sum by (namespace, pod, cluster) ( max by(namespace, pod, cluster) ( kube_pod_status_phase{job="kube-state-metrics", phase=~"Pending|Unknown|Failed"} ) * on(namespace, pod, cluster) group_left(owner_kind) topk by(namespace, pod, cluster) ( 1, max by(namespace, pod, owner_kind, cluster) (kube_pod_owner{owner_kind!="Job"}) ) ) > 0 Alert message: Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes.

No node can take the Pod: not enough CPU or memory to satisfy its requests, or node selectors, affinity rules and taints rule out every node. A PersistentVolumeClaim it mounts is not bound, or the volume is in a different zone from every eligible node. The image cannot be pulled (wrong name or tag, missing imagePullSecrets, registry rate limits). The node it runs on lost contact with the control plane, which puts the Pod into Unknown. The namespace hit its ResourceQuota, so the Pod could not be admitted.

Run kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o wide for STATUS and READY, then kubectl describe pod for Events; Pending usually means insufficient resources or scheduling constraints (affinity, taints, unbound PVC); for ImagePullBackOff check the image address and pull credentials; Running but not Ready — check the readiness probe and kubectl logs <pod> for startup errors; Confirm whether the replica count is now too low to carry traffic, and scale healthy replicas first if so.

Despite its name, the rule looks at the Pod phase, not the Ready condition. A Pod that is Running but failing its readiness probe does not trigger it; KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch or KubeStatefulSetReplicasMismatch usually catch that case. Pods owned by Jobs are excluded, so finished or failed batch work does not page anyone through this rule. Use KubeJobFailed for those. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_pod_status_phase (kube-state-metrics) kube_pod_owner (kube-state-metrics)

KubeContainerWaiting: pod/… in namespace … on container … has been in waiting state for longer than 1 hour. KubePodCrashLooping: Pod …/… (…) is in waiting state (reason: "CrashLoopBackOff"). KubeNodeNotReady: … has been unready for more than 15 minutes. KubeQuotaAlmostFull: Namespace … is using … of its … quota.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubePodNotReady expr: |- sum by (namespace, pod, cluster) ( max by(namespace, pod, cluster) ( kube_pod_status_phase{job="kube-state-metrics", phase=~"Pending|Unknown|Failed"} ) * on(namespace, pod, cluster) group_left(owner_kind) topk by(namespace, pod, cluster) ( 1, max by(namespace, pod, owner_kind, cluster) (kube_pod_owner{owner_kind!="Job"}) ) ) > 0 for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubepodnotready" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A namespace is using between 90% and 100% of one of its ResourceQuota limits (CPU, memory, Pod count, storage and so on). Nothing is broken yet. Once the quota is full, the API server rejects new Pods and objects in that namespace, which typically shows up as a failed rollout or a scale-out that never happens. Severity: Info (info) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeQuotaAlmostFull alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="used"} / ignoring(instance, job, type) (kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="hard"} > 0) > 0.9 < 1 Alert message: Namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} is using {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its {{ $labels.resource }} quota.

The team has grown its workloads and the quota was never revisited. An HPA scaled out and is now near the ceiling the quota allows. Finished Pods, old ReplicaSets or unused PVCs still count against the quota. A rollout needs room for surge Pods on top of the current replicas.

Run kubectl describe quota -n <ns> to see which item (cpu/memory/pods/storage) topped out; Use kubectl get pod -n <ns> -o custom-columns to sum requests per workload and find the biggest consumers; Check for stopped-but-uncleaned resources still holding quota; If more quota is genuinely needed, ask the cluster admin to adjust the ResourceQuota.

This is an info-level rule meant for the namespace owner. KubeQuotaFullyUsed and KubeQuotaExceeded are the louder follow-ups. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_resourcequota (kube-state-metrics)
KubeQuotaFullyUsed: Namespace … is using … of its … quota. KubeQuotaExceeded: Namespace … is using … of its … quota. KubePodNotReady: Pod …/… has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeQuotaAlmostFull expr: |- kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="used"} / ignoring(instance, job, type) (kube_resourcequota{job="kube-state-metrics", type="hard"} > 0) > 0.9 < 1 for: 15m labels: severity: info annotations: summary: "Namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} is using {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of its {{ $labels.resource }} quota." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubequotaalmostfull" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A StatefulSet has had a different number of ready replicas than it runs, for 15 minutes, with no update in progress. Stateful services are often quorum-based (etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka, databases), so one missing replica can mean reduced redundancy, and two can mean an outage. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Kubernetes alert rules (kubernetes.yml)
documents.s: KubeStatefulSetReplicasMismatch alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: ( kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_statefulset_status_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) and ( changes(kube_statefulset_status_replicas_updated{job="kube-state-metrics"}[10m]) == 0 ) Alert message: StatefulSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.statefulset }} has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

A Pod's PersistentVolumeClaim cannot bind or attach, for example because the volume is in a different zone from the node (volume node affinity conflict). A replica is crash looping or failing its readiness probe, often because its data on disk is corrupted or its peers won't let it rejoin. The Pod cannot be scheduled: no node fits its requests, anti-affinity rules, or zone constraints. With the default OrderedReady pod management policy, one stuck Pod blocks every Pod with a higher ordinal from being created.

Run kubectl get pod -n <ns> -l <selector> and check by ordinal which replica is stuck; Run kubectl describe pod to check whether its PVC bound successfully — this is the most common sticking point for stateful services; For storage problems, check the PV/StorageClass and the CSI driver; For application problems check kubectl logs; once fixed, the StatefulSet continues automatically.

Check Pods by ordinal (<name>-0, <name>-1, …). The lowest ordinal that is not ready is usually the one to fix; the rest are waiting behind it. The expression selects job="kube-state-metrics". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready (kube-state-metrics) kube_statefulset_status_replicas (kube-state-metrics) kube_statefulset_status_replicas_updated (kube-state-metrics)

KubePodNotReady: Pod …/… has been in a non-ready state for longer than 15 minutes. KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp: The PersistentVolume claimed by … in Namespace … is only … free. KubePersistentVolumeErrors: The persistent volume … has status …. KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch: Deployment …/… has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Kubernetes rule at once as kubernetes.yml. - alert: KubeStatefulSetReplicasMismatch expr: |- ( kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready{job="kube-state-metrics"} != kube_statefulset_status_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"} ) and ( changes(kube_statefulset_status_replicas_updated{job="kube-state-metrics"}[10m]) == 0 ) for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "StatefulSet {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.statefulset }} has not matched the expected number of replicas for longer than 15 minutes." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/kubernetes/kubestatefulsetreplicasmismatch" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kubernetes-mixin (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Host-level alert rules for Linux servers and Kubernetes nodes: memory exhaustion and pressure, disks and inodes running out (including "will fill up within 24 hours" predictions), disk latency, network errors, packet loss and saturation, CPU load and steal, OOM kills, conntrack and file-handle exhaustion, clock skew, crashed system services, missing processes, and failed PING, port and HTTP probes. The node_exporter group uses standard node_* metric names; the Categraf and Telegraf groups cover the same ground for hosts collected by those agents.
documents.s: Linux alert rules for Prometheus: 76 rules with runbooks

documents.t: 76 rules, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a for duration and runbook steps Metrics from: node_exporter, Categraf, Telegraf Download: linux.yml, a standard Prometheus rules file (groups: format), checked with promtool check rules Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

Node out of memory (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100 < 10 Runbook: On the node run free -h to check available memory and swap; Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head for the biggest consumers; On Kubernetes nodes, prefer kubectl top pod -A --sort-by=memory to find the Pod; For a leak, fix it in the application; for capacity, move Pods off or add nodes.

Node under memory pressure (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: rate(node_vmstat_pgmajfault[1m]) > 1000 Runbook: Run vmstat 1 and check the si/so columns for swapping; Use sar -B or /proc/vmstat to watch pgmajfault growth; Find the heaviest process or Pod and assess whether it can be moved; Review the swap setting — Kubernetes nodes normally have swap disabled, since enabling it masks memory problems.

Host unusual network throughput in (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 5m · Trigger: sum by (instance) (rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total[2m])) / 1024 / 1024 > 100 Runbook: Use iftop or nethogs to find the processes/connections consuming the most bandwidth; On Kubernetes nodes, check whether a Pod is doing bulk data transfer (backup, data sync, image pull); Confirm whether the NIC is saturated and throttle or reschedule if so; For abnormal traffic, check for a misconfiguration causing a traffic loop.

Host unusual network throughput out (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 5m · Trigger: sum by (instance) (rate(node_network_transmit_bytes_total[2m])) / 1024 / 1024 > 100 Runbook: Use iftop or nethogs to find the processes/connections consuming the most bandwidth; On Kubernetes nodes, check whether a Pod is doing bulk data transfer (backup, data sync, image pull); Confirm whether the NIC is saturated and throttle or reschedule if so; For abnormal traffic, check for a misconfiguration causing a traffic loop.

Host unusual disk read rate (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 5m · Trigger: sum by (instance) (rate(node_disk_read_bytes_total[2m])) / 1024 / 1024 > 50 Runbook: Run iostat -x 1 to see which disk it is and the actual await and %util; Run iotop -oP to find the process doing the most IO; On Kubernetes nodes it is usually container log writes, image pull/unpack, or one Pod's data writes; Move deferrable work off peak; for sustained load, consider SSDs or spreading the data.

Host unusual disk write rate (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: sum by (instance) (rate(node_disk_written_bytes_total[2m])) / 1024 / 1024 > 50 Runbook: Run iostat -x 1 to see which disk it is and the actual await and %util; Run iotop -oP to find the process doing the most IO; On Kubernetes nodes it is usually container log writes, image pull/unpack, or one Pod's data writes; Move deferrable work off peak; for sustained load, consider SSDs or spreading the data.

Host out of disk space (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: (node_filesystem_avail_bytes * 100) / node_filesystem_size_bytes < 10 and ON (instance, device, mountpoint) node_filesystem_readonly == 0 Runbook: Run df -h to find the mount point and du -x --max-depth=1 to drill into the largest directories; For the container runtime directory (/var/lib/containerd or /var/lib/docker) run crictl rmi --prune to clean unused images; Clean container logs (/var/log/pods) and confirm log rotation is working; Use lsof +L1 for deleted files whose handles are still open.

Host disk will fill up within 24 hours (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: (node_filesystem_avail_bytes * 100) / node_filesystem_size_bytes < 10 and ON (instance, device, mountpoint) predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes{fstype!~"tmpfs"}[1h], 24 * 3600) < 0 and ON (instance, device, mountpoint) node_filesystem_readonly == 0 Runbook: Run du -x --max-depth=1 to find the fastest-growing directory; Determine whether the growth is normal business or abnormal (an application looping on logs, backups piling up); Prune unused images and container logs; If the growth is genuine, plan disk expansion or data migration — do not wait until it is full.

documents.t: Host out of inodes (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: node_filesystem_files_free{mountpoint ="/rootfs"} / node_filesystem_files{mountpoint="/rootfs"} * 100 < 10 and ON (instance, device, mountpoint) node_filesystem_readonly{mountpoint="/rootfs"} == 0 Runbook: Run df -i to find the mount point; Count files level by level to find the directories with the most small files; On Kubernetes nodes it is usually container layers and log fragments — pruning unused images typically frees a lot of inodes; Longer term, raise inode density or isolate small-file workloads to a dedicated partition.

documents.t: Host unusual disk read latency (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: rate(node_disk_read_time_seconds_total[1m]) / rate(node_disk_reads_completed_total[1m]) > 0.1 and rate(node_disk_reads_completed_total[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run iostat -x 1 and look at r_await/w_await and queue depth; High latency with low IOPS suggests a disk hardware problem — check with smartctl -a; If IOPS is also high, treat it as disk saturation and find the heavy IO process; For cloud disks, check whether the specification's IOPS/throughput ceiling triggered throttling.

Host unusual disk write latency (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: rate(node_disk_write_time_seconds_total[1m]) / rate(node_disk_writes_completed_total[1m]) > 0.1 and rate(node_disk_writes_completed_total[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run iostat -x 1 and look at r_await/w_await and queue depth; High latency with low IOPS suggests a disk hardware problem — check with smartctl -a; If IOPS is also high, treat it as disk saturation and find the heavy IO process; For cloud disks, check whether the specification's IOPS/throughput ceiling triggered throttling.

Host high CPU load (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · — · Trigger: 100 - (avg by(instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[2m])) * 100) > 80 Runbook: Run uptime to see the 1/5/15 minute trend and judge spike versus sustained; Check %wa in top — high means the bottleneck is disk rather than CPU; Use the r/b columns in vmstat 1 to separate CPU-bound from IO-blocked; On Kubernetes nodes use kubectl top pod to find the heavy Pods and consider moving them.

Host CPU steal noisy neighbor (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · — · Trigger: avg by(instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="steal"}[5m])) * 100 > 10 Runbook: Use top or vmstat to confirm the sustained level of the st column; This is contention at the hypervisor level and cannot be fixed from inside the VM; In the cloud, contact the provider or move to a dedicated instance type (no steal); On self-hosted virtualization, check the host's overcommit ratio and migrate VMs.
documents.s: CPU stolen by other cloud guests

documents.t: Host context switching (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · — · Trigger: (rate(node_context_switches_total[5m])) / (count without(cpu, mode) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"})) > 1000 Runbook: Run vmstat 1 and check the cs column; Run pidstat -w 1 to find the processes switching most; Common root causes are too many threads, heavy lock contention, or many short-lived processes; Reducing thread pool sizes and lock granularity in the application is the real fix.

Host swap is full (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: (1 - (node_memory_SwapFree_bytes / node_memory_SwapTotal_bytes)) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run free -h and swapon -s to check swap usage; Use smem or VmSwap in /proc/<pid>/status to find the processes swapped out most; Kubernetes nodes should generally have swap disabled — leaving it on masks real memory pressure and breaks QoS; The root cause is insufficient memory, so follow the memory alert path.

Host systemd service crashed (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · — · Trigger: node_systemd_unit_state{state="failed"} == 1 Runbook: Run systemctl --failed to list the failed units; Use journalctl -u <unit> -n 100 --no-pager to find the cause; On Kubernetes nodes pay special attention to kubelet, containerd and kube-proxy; After fixing, run systemctl reset-failed and confirm recovery.

Host kernel version deviation (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 360m · Trigger: count(sum(label_replace(node_uname_info, "kernel", "$1", "release", "([0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+).*")) by (kernel)) > 1 Runbook: Run kubectl get node -o wide to compare kernel versions; Determine whether the difference is temporary (mid-upgrade) or long standing; Bring the lagging nodes' kernels in line step by step; Before upgrading, confirm the container runtime and CNI plugin support the target kernel.

Host OOM kill detected (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · — · Trigger: increase(node_vmstat_oom_kill[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to see which process was killed and how much memory it held; Match it against kubectl get pod -A to find the Pod and whether its limit is set too low; If the node is tight overall, move Pods off or add capacity; Repeated kills require finding the application memory leak — raising the limit alone will just recur.

Host network receive errors (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: rate(node_network_receive_errs_total[2m]) / rate(node_network_receive_packets_total[2m]) > 0.01 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> and ethtool -S <nic> for the error counters and types; Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match the peer; Check the cable/optical module, or open a cloud provider ticket; If redundancy exists, move traffic away first.

Host network transmit errors (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: rate(node_network_transmit_errs_total[2m]) / rate(node_network_transmit_packets_total[2m]) > 0.01 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> and ethtool -S <nic> for the error counters and types; Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match the peer; Check the cable/optical module, or open a cloud provider ticket; If redundancy exists, move traffic away first.

Host network interface saturated (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 1m · Trigger: (rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total{device!~"^tap.*"}[1m]) + rate(node_network_transmit_bytes_total{device!~"^tap.*"}[1m])) / node_network_speed_bytes{device!~"^tap.*"} > 0.8 < 10000 Runbook: Use iftop/nethogs to find the connections consuming the most bandwidth; On Kubernetes nodes, check for high-traffic Pods or large image pulls; Move deferrable jobs off peak; If more bandwidth is genuinely needed, upgrade the NIC or move some workloads.

Host conntrack limit (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 5m · Trigger: node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit > 0.8 Runbook: Run sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count and nf_conntrack_max to check the level; On Kubernetes nodes, kube-proxy in iptables mode creates many conntrack entries, especially at high Pod density; Raise nf_conntrack_max and the bucket count together; Longer term, consider switching to IPVS mode to reduce conntrack pressure.

Host clock skew (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: (node_timex_offset_seconds > 0.05 and deriv(node_timex_offset_seconds[5m]) >= 0) or (node_timex_offset_seconds < -0.05 and deriv(node_timex_offset_seconds[5m]) <= 0) Runbook: Run chronyc tracking to check the offset and upstream source state; Confirm chronyd/ntpd is running and enabled at boot; Check that 123/UDP to the NTP server is allowed; For a large offset use chronyc makestep, then confirm all nodes agree on the time.

Host clock not synchronising (instance {{ $labels.instance }}) Warning · 2m · Trigger: min_over_time(node_timex_sync_status[1m]) == 0 and node_timex_maxerror_seconds >= 16 Runbook: Run chronyc tracking to check the offset and upstream source state; Confirm chronyd/ntpd is running and enabled at boot; Check that 123/UDP to the NTP server is allowed; For a large offset use chronyc makestep, then confirm all nodes agree on the time.
