documents.t: {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of conntrack entries are used. Warning · 5m · Trigger: (node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit) > 0.75 Runbook: Run sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count and nf_conntrack_max to check the level; On Kubernetes nodes, kube-proxy in iptables mode creates many conntrack entries, especially at high Pod density; Raise nf_conntrack_max and the bucket count together; Longer term, consider switching to IPVS mode to reduce conntrack pressure.

Node Exporter text file collector failed to scrape. Warning · — · Trigger: node_textfile_scrape_error{job="node-exporter"} == 1 Runbook: Check the permissions and format of the .prom files in the textfile directory; The writer is usually a cron script — confirm it succeeds and writes atomically (write .tmp then mv); Validate format errors with promtool check metrics; Clean up leftover temporary files, which break parsing.

Network interface "{{ $labels.device }}" changing it's up status often on node-exporter {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }}" Warning · 2m · Trigger: changes(node_network_up{job="node-exporter",device!~"veth.+"}[2m]) > 2 Runbook: Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'link is' for the flap timeline; Check the cable and optical module — flapping usually means a bad physical connection; Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match the peer; Ask the network team about the switch port state, or open a ticket in the cloud.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: (node_filesystem_device_error{mountpoint!~"/var/lib/.*",mountpoint!~"/run.*"}) > 0 Runbook: Run dmesg -T | grep -iE 'i/o error|ata|scsi' to see the exact kernel error and device name; Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and focus on Reallocated_Sector_Ct and Current_Pending_Sector; Confirm the data on that disk has a replica or backup — data safety comes before hardware work; Once confirmed a hardware fault, schedule downtime to swap the disk; in a RAID array, check the degraded state first.
documents.s: A certain disk is unable to read/write normally

documents.t: Critical · 1m · Trigger: (100 - ((node_filesystem_avail_bytes * 100) / node_filesystem_size_bytes) ) > 92 Runbook: Run df -h to find the mount point, then du -x --max-depth=1 <mount> | sort -h to find the largest directories; On a system disk the usual suspects are /var/log and container image layers (docker system df to inspect, docker system prune to clean); Use lsof +L1 to check for deleted-but-unreleased file handles; Longer term, expand the disk or move large data directories to a dedicated disk.
documents.s: Disk needs to be cleaned - utilization has reached 92% - node exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: avg (node_load1) by (instance)/count(count(node_cpu_seconds_total) by (cpu,instance)) by (instance) >10 Runbook: Run uptime to see the 1/5/15 minute load trend and judge spike versus sustained; Run top and look at %wa (IO wait) — high means the bottleneck is disk rather than CPU, so follow the disk IO path; Run vmstat 1 and use the r (run queue) and b (blocked) columns to separate CPU-bound from IO-blocked; Once you have the specific process, continue down the CPU or IO path and scale out if needed.
documents.s: Insufficient computational resources - average load per core of the machine is greater than 10 - node exporter

documents.t: You can increase the file handle limit or expand the capacity Warning · 1m · Trigger: (node_filefd_allocated/node_filefd_maximum*100) > 90 Runbook: Run cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr to see allocated versus the limit; Run lsof | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head to find the processes holding the most handles; As an emergency measure raise it with sysctl -w fs.file-max=<larger value>, and check the process's ulimit -n and systemd LimitNOFILE; The root cause is usually connections or files never closed — fix the leak in the application.
documents.s: Insufficient file handles - usage exceeds 90% - node exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: (100 - ((node_filesystem_files_free * 100) / node_filesystem_files))>90 Runbook: Run df -i to see which mount point is short on inodes; Drill down with for d in /path/*; do echo "$(find $d | wc -l) $d"; done | sort -rn | head to find the directories with the most small files; Common sources are session files, mail queues, cache fragments and uncleaned container layers — confirm with the owner and bulk delete; Longer term, raise inode density at format time or move small-file workloads to a dedicated partition.
documents.s: Insufficient inode resources - usage exceeds 90% - node exporter

documents.t: Expansion or upgrading of configuration is required Warning · 1m · Trigger: (node_memory_MemTotal_bytes - node_memory_MemFree_bytes - (node_memory_Cached_bytes + node_memory_Buffers_bytes))/node_memory_MemTotal_bytes*100 > 75 Runbook: Run free -h to check available memory and swap usage; Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head to find the largest consumers and compare against their memory history to judge whether it is a leak; If the kernel is slow to reclaim, sync; echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches frees page cache (use with care in production); Determine whether it is growth or a process leak — a leak must be located with a heap profile, not just a restart.
documents.s: Insufficient memory resources - utilization is greater than 75% - node exporter

documents.t: Critical · 1m · Trigger: (node_memory_MemTotal_bytes - node_memory_MemFree_bytes - (node_memory_Cached_bytes + node_memory_Buffers_bytes))/node_memory_MemTotal_bytes*100 > 95 Runbook: Run free -h to check available memory and swap usage; Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head to find the largest consumers and compare against their memory history to judge whether it is a leak; If the kernel is slow to reclaim, sync; echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches frees page cache (use with care in production); Determine whether it is growth or a process leak — a leak must be located with a heap profile, not just a restart.
documents.s: Insufficient memory resources - utilization is greater than 95% - node exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: rate(node_network_receive_drop_total{device=~"e.*"}[1m]) > 3 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> to confirm RX dropped/errors are growing; Run ethtool -S <nic> to see the specific drop reason (rx_no_buffer, rx_missed_errors, etc.); If ring buffers are too small, raise them with ethtool -G <nic> rx <larger value> and check net.core.netdev_max_backlog; If softirq CPU is also high (%si in top), enable RPS/RSS to spread interrupts across cores.
documents.s: Packet loss in the inbound direction of the network card - node exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: rate(node_network_transmit_drop_total{device=~"e.*"}[1m]) > 3 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> to confirm TX dropped/errors are growing; Run ethtool -S <nic> for the specific counters and tc -s qdisc show dev <nic> to see whether the queue is overflowing; If the transmit queue is too small, raise txqueuelen and ethtool -G <nic> tx; Check whether the link is saturated — if so throttle or add bandwidth, otherwise investigate the NIC driver and peer device.
documents.s: Packet loss in the outbound direction of the network card - node exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit*100 > 80 Runbook: Run sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count and nf_conntrack_max to see the current level; Run conntrack -L | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to see which protocol or source the entries concentrate on; As an emergency measure raise it: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=<larger value>, raising nf_conntrack_buckets to match; Also shorten timeouts such as nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait, or mark traffic that needs no tracking NOTRACK in the iptables raw table.
documents.s: System conntrack needs to be adjusted - usage exceeds 80% - node exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: increase(node_vmstat_oom_kill[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to see which process was killed and how much memory it held; Use free -h and that process's memory history to tell a leak apart from a limit set too high; Lower oom_score_adj for critical processes and set cgroup memory limits on secondary ones; If it is a leak, capture a heap profile in the application — adding memory alone will just postpone the recurrence.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: node_procs_running > 3000 Runbook: Run ps -eo ppid | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head to find the parent forking the most children; Determine whether this is a normal multi-process model (php-fpm, nginx workers) or a runaway fork; For a runaway, stop that parent to stop the bleeding, then fix the fork logic in the code; For genuine growth, tune the worker count and evaluate whether to scale out.
documents.s: Too many running processes - exceeding 3000 - node exporter

documents.t: For hosts and instances collected by Categraf; metric names follow Categraf plugins. 8 of the 24 rules in this group also apply unchanged to instances collected by Telegraf, which produces the same metric names.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: conntrack_ip_conntrack_count / conntrack_ip_conntrack_max > 0.8 Runbook: Run sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count and nf_conntrack_max to see the current level; Run conntrack -L | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to see which protocol or source the entries concentrate on; As an emergency measure raise it: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=<larger value>, raising nf_conntrack_buckets to match; Also shorten timeouts such as nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait, or mark traffic that needs no tracking NOTRACK in the iptables raw table.

Info · 1m · Trigger: cpu_usage_active>75 cpu_usage_active>85 cpu_usage_active>95 Runbook: Run top -H or pidstat 1 to find the busiest processes and threads; Use perf top or a language profiler (arthas/async-profiler for Java, pprof for Go) to locate the hot functions; Tell natural traffic growth apart from a code problem (infinite loop, regex backtracking, frequent GC); For growth, scale out or rate limit; for a code problem, fix and release.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: http_response_result_code != 0 Runbook: Reproduce it by hand on the collector host with curl -sv <target URL> and see whether it is a connection failure, a timeout or an unexpected status code; For a connection failure, first confirm the target port is reachable and the process is alive; For an unexpected status code, check the target service logs; Confirm the probe's timeout, expected status code and certificate verification settings match reality, so the config itself is not causing the alert.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: rate(diskio_io_time[1m])/10 > 99 Runbook: Run iostat -x 1 to see which disk it is and the actual await and %util values; Run iotop -oP or pidstat -d 1 to find the process doing the most IO; The usual culprits are large database queries, backup jobs and log flushing — move deferrable work off peak; If it is sustained rather than a spike, consider SSDs or spreading hot data across disks.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: ntp_offset_ms > 1000 or ntp_offset_ms < -1000 Runbook: Run chronyc tracking (or ntpq -p) to see the current offset and upstream source state; If upstream is unreachable, check the network and whether the firewall allows 123/UDP; Run chronyc sources -v to see whether every source is marked unusable, and switch NTP servers if needed; When the offset is large chrony refuses to slew, so use chronyc makestep to step the clock (prepare time-sensitive workloads first).

Warning · 1m · Trigger: ping_result_code != 0 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with ping -c 5 <target>, then use mtr -n <target> to find which hop is dropping packets; If the target host is alive, check whether it blocks ICMP (many security policies do) — if so this probe does not apply and you should switch to a port probe; For loss at an intermediate hop, involve the network team; Confirm the target host itself is not down or suffering a NIC failure.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: netstat_tcp_time_wait > 20000 Runbook: Run ss -s to see the connection state distribution; Run ss -tan state time-wait | awk '{print $4}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to see which peer they concentrate on; The root cause is usually too many short-lived connections — switching the application to long-lived connections or a pool is by far the most effective fix; As an emergency measure enable net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 and widen net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range (do not enable tcp_tw_recycle — it drops packets behind NAT).

Info · 1m · Trigger: mem_available_percent < 25 mem_available_percent < 15 mem_available_percent < 5 Runbook: Run free -h to check available memory and swap usage; Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head to find the largest consumers and compare against their memory history to judge whether it is a leak; If the kernel is slow to reclaim, sync; echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches frees page cache (use with care in production); Determine whether it is growth or a process leak — a leak must be located with a heap profile, not just a restart.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: linux_sysctl_fs_file_nr/linux_sysctl_fs_file_max>0.9 Runbook: Run cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr to see allocated versus the limit; Run lsof | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head to find the processes holding the most handles; As an emergency measure raise it with sysctl -w fs.file-max=<larger value>, and check the process's ulimit -n and systemd LimitNOFILE; The root cause is usually connections or files never closed — fix the leak in the application.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: system_load_norm_1>3 Runbook: Run uptime to see the 1/5/15 minute load trend and judge spike versus sustained; Run top and look at %wa (IO wait) — high means the bottleneck is disk rather than CPU, so follow the disk IO path; Run vmstat 1 and use the r (run queue) and b (blocked) columns to separate CPU-bound from IO-blocked; Once you have the specific process, continue down the CPU or IO path and scale out if needed.
documents.s: Average load per CPU core exceeds 3

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: disk_inodes_used/disk_inodes_total >0.9 Runbook: Run df -i to see which mount point is short on inodes; Drill down with for d in /path/*; do echo "$(find $d | wc -l) $d"; done | sort -rn | head to find the directories with the most small files; Common sources are session files, mail queues, cache fragments and uncleaned container layers — confirm with the owner and bulk delete; Longer term, raise inode density at format time or move small-file workloads to a dedicated partition.

Info · 1m · Trigger: disk_free/1024/1024/1024 < 20 and disk_total/1024/1024/1024 >= 200 disk_free/1024/1024/1024 < 10 and disk_total/1024/1024/1024 >= 200 disk_free/1024/1024/1024 < 2 and disk_total/1024/1024/1024 >= 200 Runbook: Run df -h to find the mount point, then du -x --max-depth=1 <mount> | sort -h to find the largest directories; Clean up logs and expired data, and use lsof +L1 to check for deleted-but-unreleased files; Evaluate whether the data directory should move to its own disk or the disk should be expanded; For a database or object-store data disk, tier cold data off according to the business archiving policy.
documents.s: Disk monitoring - disk larger than 200G is running out of space

documents.t: Info · 1m · Trigger: disk_used_percent > 90 and disk_total/1024/1024/1024 < 200 disk_used_percent > 95 and disk_total/1024/1024/1024 < 200 disk_used_percent > 99 and disk_total/1024/1024/1024 < 200 Runbook: Run df -h to find the mount point, then du -x --max-depth=1 <mount> | sort -h to find the largest directories; On a system disk the usual suspects are /var/log and container image layers (docker system df to inspect, docker system prune to clean); Use lsof +L1 to check for deleted-but-unreleased file handles; Longer term, expand the disk or move large data directories to a dedicated disk.
documents.s: Disk monitoring - disk smaller than 200G is running out of space

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: disk_device_error>0 Runbook: Run dmesg -T | grep -iE 'i/o error|ata|scsi' to see the exact kernel error and device name; Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and focus on Reallocated_Sector_Ct and Current_Pending_Sector; Confirm the data on that disk has a replica or backup — data safety comes before hardware work; Once confirmed a hardware fault, schedule downtime to swap the disk; in a RAID array, check the degraded state first.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: predict_linear(disk_free[1h], 4*3600) < 0 Runbook: Run df -h to identify the mount point, then drill down with du -x --max-depth=1 <mount> | sort -h to find the fastest-growing directory; Start with logs (journalctl --vacuum-size=500M, rotate out *.log.N) and temporary files — that is the quickest win; Use lsof +L1 to find deleted files whose handles are still open; the owning process must be restarted to actually free the space; Confirm whether something abnormal is writing (an application looping on logs, backups piling up) — without fixing the root cause, cleanup only buys time.
documents.s: Disk monitoring - disk predicted to be full within 4 hours

documents.t: Warning · — · Trigger: increase(kernel_vmstat_oom_kill[2m]) > 0 Runbook: Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to see which process was killed and how much memory it held; Use free -h and that process's memory history to tell a leak apart from a limit set too high; Lower oom_score_adj for critical processes and set cgroup memory limits on secondary ones; If it is a leak, capture a heap profile in the application — adding memory alone will just postpone the recurrence.

Info · 1m · Trigger: increase(net_drop_in[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> to confirm RX dropped/errors are growing; Run ethtool -S <nic> to see the specific drop reason (rx_no_buffer, rx_missed_errors, etc.); If ring buffers are too small, raise them with ethtool -G <nic> rx <larger value> and check net.core.netdev_max_backlog; If softirq CPU is also high (%si in top), enable RPS/RSS to spread interrupts across cores.

Info · 1m · Trigger: increase(net_err_in[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run ethtool -S <nic> and look at rx_crc_errors, rx_frame_errors and similar counters; Run ethtool <nic> to confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match the peer (half duplex is the classic source of errors); Check the cable/optical module, swapping the cable or port to cross-check; Ask the network team for the error counters on the corresponding switch port.

Info · 1m · Trigger: increase(net_drop_out[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> to confirm TX dropped/errors are growing; Run ethtool -S <nic> for the specific counters and tc -s qdisc show dev <nic> to see whether the queue is overflowing; If the transmit queue is too small, raise txqueuelen and ethtool -G <nic> tx; Check whether the link is saturated — if so throttle or add bandwidth, otherwise investigate the NIC driver and peer device.

Info · 1m · Trigger: increase(net_err_out[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run ethtool -S <nic> and look at tx_errors, tx_carrier_errors and similar counters; Run ethtool <nic> to confirm speed and duplex match the peer; Check the cable/optical module and cross-check by swapping; Verify the NIC driver and firmware versions and upgrade if needed.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: net_response_result_code != 0 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with telnet <target> <port> or nc -vz <target> <port>; On the target host, run ss -lntp | grep <port> to confirm a process is listening; If it is listening, check the firewall, security groups, and whether it is bound only to 127.0.0.1; If nothing is listening, start the service through its own recovery procedure.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: procstat_lookup_count == 0 Runbook: Run ps -ef | grep <process keyword> to confirm it is really gone and rule out a wrong match rule on the collector side; Check that process's log and dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to tell a crash, an OOM kill and a manual stop apart; Start it through the service's own procedure and confirm the systemd Restart policy is effective; If it keeps exiting, find the root cause before starting it again to avoid a restart loop.
documents.s: Process monitoring - a process count is 0, the process may be down

documents.t: Info · 1m · Trigger: procstat_rlimit_num_fds_soft < 2048 Runbook: Run cat /proc/<pid>/limits to see the soft and hard Max open files; For systemd services, add LimitNOFILE=65535 to the unit file, then systemctl daemon-reload and restart; For non-systemd, add ulimit -n 65535 to the startup script or edit /etc/security/limits.conf; Note the process must be restarted for a changed soft limit to take effect.
documents.s: Process monitoring - process file handle limit too small

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: processes_total > 600 Runbook: Run ps -eo ppid | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head to find the parent forking the most children; Determine whether this is a normal multi-process model (php-fpm, nginx workers) or a runaway fork; For a runaway, stop that parent to stop the bleeding, then fix the fork logic in the code; For genuine growth, tune the worker count and evaluate whether to scale out.
For hosts collected by Telegraf with Prometheus-style output.

Info · 1m · Trigger: cpu_usage_idle{cpu="cpu-total"} < 25 Runbook: Run top -H or pidstat 1 to find the busiest processes and threads; Use perf top or a language profiler (arthas/async-profiler for Java, pprof for Go) to locate the hot functions; Tell natural traffic growth apart from a code problem (infinite loop, regex backtracking, frequent GC); For growth, scale out or rate limit; for a code problem, fix and release.
documents.s: Machine load - high CPU, please pay attention - telegraf

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: mem_available_percent < 25 Runbook: Run free -h to check available memory and swap usage; Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head to find the largest consumers and compare against their memory history to judge whether it is a leak; If the kernel is slow to reclaim, sync; echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches frees page cache (use with care in production); Determine whether it is growth or a process leak — a leak must be located with a heap profile, not just a restart.
documents.s: Machine load - high memory, please pay attention - telegraf

documents.t: Critical · 1m · Trigger: procstat_lookup_result_code != 0 Runbook: Reproduce the configured match by hand on the collector host with ps/pgrep; If the process is genuinely gone, follow the service's recovery procedure; If the process exists but the probe fails, check the procstat pid_file / exe / pattern settings and whether the collector account can read /proc; In containers, confirm categraf mounts the host's /proc.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: procstat_lookup_running == 0 Runbook: Run ps -ef | grep <process keyword> to confirm it is really gone and rule out a wrong match rule on the collector side; Check that process's log and dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to tell a crash, an OOM kill and a manual stop apart; Start it through the service's own procedure and confirm the systemd Restart policy is effective; If it keeps exiting, find the root cause before starting it again to avoid a restart loop.
documents.s: there are processes with 0 count, a certain process may have crashed - telegraf

documents.t: With Prometheus or vmalert: download linux.yml, add it to rule_files (or -rule for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a severity label (critical / warning / info), and runbook_url points back to this page, or to the rule's own page where it has one. With Nightingale: the same rules ship in the Kubernetes and Linux integration template. Open the integration center, import the rules into a business group, and enable them one by one. Nightingale keeps the runbook with each alert and can evaluate the rules against Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and other data sources.

Many rule expressions are adapted from awesome-prometheus-alerts (CC BY 4.0). The runbook steps and the remaining rules come from Nightingale's integration templates (Kubernetes, Linux, Apache-2.0). Corrections are welcome as pull requests there.

Monitor Kubernetes with Nightingale: collector config, dashboards and metric reference Monitor Linux with Nightingale: collector config, dashboards and metric reference Write a metric rule in Nightingale All alert rules

MongoDB alert rules for an instance that has crashed or just restarted, connections approaching the limit, high average operation latency, assertion errors, cursor timeouts, page faults and replica-set lag. They use mongodb_exporter metric names.
documents.s: MongoDB alert rules for Prometheus: 8 rules with runbooks

documents.t: 8 rules, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a for duration and runbook steps Metrics from: mongodb_exporter Download: mongodb.yml, a standard Prometheus rules file (groups: format), checked with promtool check rules Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

Rule Severity For MongoDB average operation latency exceeds 250ms - exporter Warning 10m Mongo connection number has exceeded 80% - exporter Warning 2m Mongo has encountered an Assert error - exporter Info 30m Mongo has encountered cursor timeout - exporter Warning 30m Mongo has encountered page fault interrupt - exporter Warning 30m Mongo has just restarted, please pay attention - exporter Info — Mongo instance has crashed - exporter Critical — Mongo replica set master-slave delay exceeds 30 seconds - exporter Critical 1m

Warning · 10m · Trigger: rate(mongodb_mongod_op_latencies_latency_total[5m]) / rate(mongodb_mongod_op_latencies_ops_total[5m]) > 250000 Runbook: Run db.currentOp({"secs_running":{$gt:5}}) to find long-running operations and db.killOp(opid) to stop the bleeding if needed; Enable the profiler to find slow queries: db.setProfilingLevel(1,100), then db.system.profile.find().sort({millis:-1}).limit(10); Run explain("executionStats") on the slow queries to see whether they do a COLLSCAN and add indexes; Check whether a bulk write or an index rebuild is saturating disk IO.
documents.s: MongoDB average operation latency exceeds 250ms - exporter

documents.t: Warning · 2m · Trigger: avg by (instance) (mongodb_connections{state="current"}) / (avg by (instance) (mongodb_connections{state="current"}) + avg by (instance) (mongodb_connections{state="available"})) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run db.serverStatus().connections to see the real current and available levels; Run db.currentOp(true) and group by client to find the application with an abnormal connection count; Tell business growth apart from a driver connection pool leak (maxPoolSize set too high, or the MongoClient is not reused); As an emergency measure raise net.maxIncomingConnections on mongod, and confirm the system ulimit -n is high enough.
documents.s: Mongo connection number has exceeded 80% - exporter

documents.t: Info · 30m · Trigger: rate(mongodb_asserts_total{type=~"regular|message"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run db.adminCommand({getLog:"global"}) to see the context of the asserts in the log; Run db.serverStatus().asserts to see whether the regular or message counter is growing; Regular asserts usually point to the storage layer — check disk health and data file integrity; message asserts usually mean a protocol or driver mismatch, so verify the driver version; Check whether it lines up with a recent upgrade or schema change.
documents.s: Mongo has encountered an Assert error - exporter

documents.t: Warning · 30m · Trigger: rate(mongodb_mongod_metrics_cursor_timed_out_total[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run db.serverStatus().metrics.cursor and watch timedOut against open.total; On the application side, confirm cursors are close()d after use and that a single batch does not take too long; For long traversals use noCursorTimeout and manage the lifecycle yourself, or lower batchSize to consume faster; Check whether a slow query is holding a cursor past cursorTimeoutMillis (10 minutes by default).
documents.s: Mongo has encountered cursor timeout - exporter

documents.t: Warning · 30m · Trigger: rate(mongodb_extra_info_page_faults_total[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache and compare "bytes currently in the cache" against the configured limit; Compare db.stats() and index sizes against physical memory to judge whether the working set exceeds RAM; Start by dropping unused indexes and archiving cold data to shrink the working set; Confirm the host is not swapping, and add memory or shard if necessary.
documents.s: Mongo has encountered page fault interrupt - exporter

documents.t: Info · — · Trigger: mongodb_instance_uptime_seconds < 60 Runbook: Read the tail of the mongod log to tell a crash, an OOM kill and a manual restart apart; If it was an OOM, compare wiredTigerCacheSizeGB against host memory and lower it; For a replica set, run rs.status() to confirm a new primary was elected automatically and applications reconnected; For an unplanned restart, check whether systemd or the container orchestrator is repeatedly restarting it.
documents.s: Mongo has just restarted, please pay attention - exporter

documents.t: Critical · — · Trigger: mongodb_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status mongod or docker ps to confirm the process is alive; If it is alive, connect by hand with mongosh to tell a hung instance apart from a network or authentication problem; If it is not running, read the tail of the log to identify the cause (OOM, full disk, corrupted data files) before starting it — do not blindly restart; For a replica set, run rs.status() immediately to confirm failover completed and that the application has taken this node out of rotation.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: (max by (rs_nm) (mongodb_rs_members_optimeDate) - min by (rs_nm) (mongodb_rs_members_optimeDate)) / 1000 > 30 Runbook: Run rs.status() on the primary and compare optimeDate and lastHeartbeat across members to find the lagging one; On the lagging node, check the mongod log for oplog fetch errors or disk IO bottlenecks; On the primary, run db.currentOp() to check whether a bulk write is flooding the oplog faster than the secondary can apply; If it falls behind the oplog window the secondary needs a fresh initial sync — move read traffic away first.
documents.s: Mongo replica set master-slave delay exceeds 30 seconds - exporter

documents.t: With Prometheus or vmalert: download mongodb.yml, add it to rule_files (or -rule for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a severity label (critical / warning / info), and runbook_url points back to this page, or to the rule's own page where it has one. MySQL alert rules for the failures that page people in practice: an instance that is down or has just restarted, slow queries piling up, connections approaching max_connections, too many running threads, InnoDB log waits, open files nearing the limit, and replication problems (IO or SQL thread stopped, replica lag). The exporter group uses mysqld_exporter metric names (mysql_global_status_*, mysql_slave_status_*); each rule comes with the first commands to run, such as SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST and pt-query-digest, when it fires.
documents.s: MySQL alert rules for Prometheus: 11 rules with runbooks

documents.t: 11 rules, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a for duration and runbook steps Metrics from: mysqld_exporter, Categraf Download: mysql.yml, a standard Prometheus rules file (groups: format), checked with promtool check rules Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

Rule Severity For More than 60% of the connections in MySQL are in a running state Warning 2m More than 80% of MySQL files open Warning 2m MySQL connection count has exceeded 80% Warning 2m Mysql has just restarted. Please be advised - exporter Info — MySQL slow queries are piling up Warning 2m MysqlInnodbLogWaits - exporter Warning — MysqlSlaveIoThreadNotRunning - exporter Critical — MysqlSlaveReplicationLag - exporter Critical 1m MysqlSlaveSqlThreadNotRunning - exporter Critical — The MySQL instance is down Critical — Mysql has opened a large number of file handles. Please be aware - categraf Warning 2m
9 of the 10 rules in this group also apply unchanged to instances collected by Categraf, which produces the same metric names.

Warning · 2m · Trigger: avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_threads_running) / avg by (instance) (mysql_global_variables_max_connections) * 100 > 60 Runbook: Run SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST to see which SQL statement and which table the piled-up threads are concentrated on; Run SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS to check for lock waits or deadlocks; KILL the offending SQL to stop the bleeding, then add indexes or apply rate limiting; Check whether an upstream traffic spike or a slow dependency is keeping connections from being released.
documents.s: More than 60% of the connections in MySQL are in a running state

documents.t: More than 80% of MySQL files open Warning · 2m · Trigger: avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_innodb_num_open_files) / avg by (instance)(mysql_global_variables_open_files_limit) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Open_files' and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'open_files_limit' to confirm the current level; Raise open_files_limit in my.cnf and raise the system ulimit -n and the systemd LimitNOFILE to match; Check whether table_open_cache is set too large and inflating the handle count; Check whether a large number of partitioned or small tables are being accessed at once.
documents.s: More than 80% of MySQL files open

documents.t: More than 80% of MySQL connections are in use Warning · 2m · Trigger: avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_threads_connected) / avg by (instance) (mysql_global_variables_max_connections) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST and group connections by source host to find the application with an abnormal connection count; Tell a traffic spike apart from an application connection pool leak (many long-lived Sleep connections piling up); As an emergency measure raise max_connections, checking free memory at the same time to avoid an OOM; For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and shorten wait_timeout.

MySQL has just been restarted, less than one minute ago Info · — · Trigger: mysql_global_status_uptime < 60 Runbook: Check the error log (the file pointed to by SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_error') to tell a crash, an OOM kill and a manual restart apart; If it was an OOM, compare innodb_buffer_pool_size against the machine's physical memory and lower it; If the restart was unplanned, check whether systemd or the container orchestrator is repeatedly restarting it; After the restart, confirm replication resumed automatically and application connection pools reconnected.
documents.s: Mysql has just restarted. Please be advised - exporter

documents.t: MySQL slow queries are piling up over the last 5 minutes Warning · 2m · Trigger: increase(mysql_global_status_slow_queries[5m]) > 10 Runbook: Run SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST to find long-running SQL and KILL <id> to stop the bleeding if needed; Use mysqldumpslow -s t -t 10 <slow_log> or pt-query-digest to find the top slow queries; Run EXPLAIN on the queries you found to inspect the plan, then add indexes or rewrite them; If the noise comes from long_query_time being set too low, tune that parameter instead of ignoring the alert.
documents.s: MySQL slow queries are piling up

documents.t: MySQL innodb log writes stalling Warning · — · Trigger: rate(mysql_global_status_innodb_log_waits[15m]) > 10 Runbook: Raise innodb_log_buffer_size (typically doubling the 16M default up to 64M~256M); Check whether innodb_log_file_size is too small and causing frequent checkpoints; Run iostat -x 1 to see whether the disk holding the redo log is already at full utilization; Check for large transactions writing too much data at once and split them into smaller batches.

MySQL Slave IO thread not running Critical · — · Trigger: mysql_slave_status_master_server_id > 0 and ON (instance) mysql_slave_status_slave_io_running == 0 Runbook: Run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G on the replica and read Last_IO_Error; The usual causes are the primary being unreachable, an invalid replication account, or the required binlog having been purged — fix the network, reset the account with CHANGE MASTER TO, or rebuild the replica from a backup respectively; Then run START SLAVE IO_THREAD and confirm Slave_IO_Running=Yes; Take read traffic off this replica before you start.

Critical · 1m · Trigger: mysql_slave_status_master_server_id > 0 and ON (instance) (mysql_slave_status_seconds_behind_master - mysql_slave_status_sql_delay) > 30 Runbook: Run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and read Seconds_Behind_Master together with the event the SQL thread is currently applying; On the primary, run SHOW PROCESSLIST to check for a large transaction or a bulk DML loading data; If the replica applies single-threaded, enable parallel replication (slave_parallel_workers / slave_parallel_type=LOGICAL_CLOCK); If the lag keeps growing, move read traffic back to the primary or to another replica.

MySQL Slave SQL thread not running Critical · — · Trigger: mysql_slave_status_master_server_id > 0 and ON (instance) mysql_slave_status_slave_sql_running == 0 Runbook: Run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G on the replica and read Last_SQL_Error to identify the event it is stuck on; If it is a conflict that can be safely skipped (such as a duplicate primary key), verify the data is consistent, then run SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter=1 followed by START SLAVE SQL_THREAD; If the primary and replica data have already diverged, rebuild the replica from a backup instead of blindly skipping; Take read traffic off this replica before you start.

Critical · — · Trigger: mysql_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status mysqld or docker ps to confirm the process is alive; If it is alive, connect by hand with mysql -h<host> -P<port> -u<user> -p to tell a hung instance apart from a network or account problem; If it is not running, read the tail of the error log to identify the cause (OOM, full disk, corrupted data files) before starting it — do not blindly restart; If replication is in use, immediately assess whether to fail over, and confirm the application has taken this node out of rotation.
For hosts and instances collected by Categraf; metric names follow Categraf plugins.

More than 80% of MySQL files open Warning · 2m · Trigger: avg by (instance) (mysql_global_status_open_files) / avg by (instance)(mysql_global_variables_open_files_limit) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Open_files' and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'open_files_limit' to confirm the current level; Raise open_files_limit in my.cnf and raise the system ulimit -n and the systemd LimitNOFILE to match; Check whether table_open_cache is set too large and inflating the handle count; Check whether a large number of partitioned or small tables are being accessed at once.

Rules that watch Prometheus itself: a bad configuration reload, failing or missed rule evaluations, a notification queue backing up, no connection to Alertmanager, remote write falling behind, TSDB compactions or reloads failing, scrape and label limits being hit, and the Prometheus Operator failing to reconcile. When these fire, every other alert you rely on may be silently missing, so they are worth routing to the people who own the monitoring stack rather than to application teams.
documents.s: Prometheus alert rules for Prometheus: 30 rules with runbooks

documents.t: 30 rules, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a for duration and runbook steps Metrics from: Prometheus's own /metrics, Prometheus Operator Download: prometheus.yml, a standard Prometheus rules file (groups: format), checked with promtool check rules Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

Rule Severity For ConfigReloaderSidecarErrors Warning 10m PrometheusOperatorListErrors Warning 15m PrometheusOperatorNodeLookupErrors Warning 10m PrometheusOperatorNotReady Warning 5m PrometheusOperatorReconcileErrors Warning 10m PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources Warning 5m PrometheusOperatorSyncFailed Warning 10m PrometheusOperatorWatchErrors Warning 15m PrometheusBadConfig Critical 10m PrometheusDuplicateTimestamps Warning 10m PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToAnyAlertmanager Critical 15m PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToSomeAlertmanagers Warning 15m PrometheusHighQueryLoad Warning 15m PrometheusLabelLimitHit Warning 15m PrometheusMissingRuleEvaluations Warning 15m PrometheusNotConnectedToAlertmanagers Warning 10m PrometheusNotificationQueueRunningFull Warning 15m PrometheusNotIngestingSamples Warning 10m PrometheusOutOfOrderTimestamps Warning 10m PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures Critical 15m PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind Critical 15m PrometheusRemoteWriteDesiredShards Warning 15m PrometheusRuleFailures Critical 15m PrometheusScrapeBodySizeLimitHit Warning 15m PrometheusScrapeSampleLimitHit Warning 15m PrometheusSDRefreshFailure Warning 20m PrometheusTargetLimitHit Warning 15m PrometheusTargetSyncFailure Critical 5m PrometheusTSDBCompactionsFailing Warning 240m PrometheusTSDBReloadsFailing Warning 240m

Errors encountered while the {{$labels.pod}} config-reloader sidecar attempts to sync config in {{$labels.namespace}} namespace. As a result, configuration for service running in {{$labels.pod}} may be stale and cannot be updated anymore. Warning · 10m · Trigger: max_over_time(reloader_last_reload_successful{namespace=~".+"}[5m]) == 0 Runbook: Run kubectl logs <pod> -c config-reloader -n <ns> for the specific error; It is usually a config syntax error causing the reload to be rejected; Validate with promtool check config / amtool check-config; After fixing, confirm the reload succeeded and verify the new config on Prometheus's /config page.

Errors while performing List operations in controller {{$labels.controller}} in {{$labels.namespace}} namespace. Warning · 15m · Trigger: (sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_list_operations_failed_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[10m])) / sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_list_operations_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[10m]))) > 0.4 Runbook: Run kubectl logs -n <ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error; For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources; For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule); For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

Errors while reconciling Prometheus in {{ $labels.namespace }} Namespace. Warning · 10m · Trigger: rate(prometheus_operator_node_address_lookup_errors_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0.1 Runbook: Run kubectl logs -n <ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error; For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources; For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule); For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

Prometheus operator in {{ $labels.namespace }} namespace isn't ready to reconcile {{ $labels.controller }} resources. Warning · 5m · Trigger: min by (cluster,controller,namespace) (max_over_time(prometheus_operator_ready{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) == 0) Runbook: Run kubectl logs -n <ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error; For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources; For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule); For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of reconciling operations failed for {{ $labels.controller }} controller in {{ $labels.namespace }} namespace. Warning · 10m · Trigger: (sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_reconcile_errors_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))) / (sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_reconcile_operations_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))) > 0.1 Runbook: Run kubectl logs -n <ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error; For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources; For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule); For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

Prometheus operator in {{ $labels.namespace }} namespace rejected {{ printf "%0.0f" $value }} {{ $labels.controller }}/{{ $labels.resource }} resources. Warning · 5m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources

Controller {{ $labels.controller }} in {{ $labels.namespace }} namespace fails to reconcile {{ $value }} objects. Warning · 10m · Trigger: min_over_time(prometheus_operator_syncs{status="failed",job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run kubectl logs -n <ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error; For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources; For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule); For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

Errors while performing watch operations in controller {{$labels.controller}} in {{$labels.namespace}} namespace. Warning · 15m · Trigger: (sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_watch_operations_failed_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])) / sum by (cluster,controller,namespace) (rate(prometheus_operator_watch_operations_total{job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]))) > 0.4 Runbook: Run kubectl logs -n <ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error; For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources; For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule); For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.
Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to reload its configuration. Critical · 10m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: PrometheusBadConfig

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is dropping {{ printf "%.4g" $value }} samples/s with different values but duplicated timestamp. Warning · 10m · Trigger: rate(prometheus_target_scrapes_sample_duplicate_timestamp_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Find the duplicated targets on the /targets page (the same instance appearing under several jobs); Check whether ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor selectors are too broad and overlapping; Tighten the selectors so each target is scraped by exactly one job; After fixing, confirm the discard counter stops growing.

{{ printf "%.1f" $value }}% minimum errors while sending alerts from Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} to any Alertmanager. Critical · 15m · Trigger: min without (alertmanager) ( rate(prometheus_notifications_errors_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring",alertmanager!~``}[5m]) / rate(prometheus_notifications_sent_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring",alertmanager!~``}[5m]) ) * 100 > 3 Runbook: Check whether the Alertmanager instances are healthy and reachable; Confirm Alertmanager discovery on the Prometheus /status page; If the queue is full, check whether Alertmanager processing is stuck or the alert volume spiked abnormally; After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

{{ printf "%.1f" $value }}% errors while sending alerts from Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} to Alertmanager {{$labels.alertmanager}}. Warning · 15m · Trigger: ( rate(prometheus_notifications_errors_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) / rate(prometheus_notifications_sent_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) ) * 100 > 1 Runbook: Check whether the Alertmanager instances are healthy and reachable; Confirm Alertmanager discovery on the Prometheus /status page; If the queue is full, check whether Alertmanager processing is stuck or the alert volume spiked abnormally; After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} query API has less than 20% available capacity in its query engine for the last 15 minutes. Warning · 15m · Trigger: avg_over_time(prometheus_engine_queries{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) / max_over_time(prometheus_engine_queries_concurrent_max{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0.8 Runbook: Check the query engine concurrency and queue metrics on the /status page; Use topk-style queries or the query log to find the heaviest queries; The usual root causes are high-cardinality labels and over-wide time ranges — narrow the range and reduce group by dimensions; If it stays high after tuning, scale Prometheus or use federation/sharding.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has dropped {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} targets because some samples exceeded the configured label_limit, label_name_length_limit or label_value_length_limit. Warning · 15m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_target_scrape_pool_exceeded_label_limits_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Find the rejected targets and the specific reason on the /targets page; On the target side, work out why the label count is so high — usually high-cardinality data (user ID, request ID) was made into labels; Fix the metric design at the source, or drop the excess labels with metric_relabel_configs; If more labels are genuinely needed, raise label_limit after assessing the cardinality impact.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has missed {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} rule group evaluations in the last 5m. Warning · 15m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_rule_group_iterations_missed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Check the log for rule evaluation timeout errors; Find the rule group with the longest evaluation time, usually recording rules with heavy queries; Split the rule group, lengthen evaluation_interval, or optimise the queries in the rules; If resources are short, scale Prometheus.
Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is not connected to any Alertmanagers. Warning · 10m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: PrometheusNotConnectedToAlertmanagers

Alert notification queue of Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is running full. Warning · 15m · Trigger: # Without min_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. ( predict_linear(prometheus_notifications_queue_length{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m], 60 * 30) > min_over_time(prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) ) Runbook: Check whether the Alertmanager instances are healthy and reachable; Confirm Alertmanager discovery on the Prometheus /status page; If the queue is full, check whether Alertmanager processing is stuck or the alert volume spiked abnormally; After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is not ingesting samples. Warning · 10m · Trigger: ( rate(prometheus_tsdb_head_samples_appended_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) <= 0 and ( sum without(scrape_job) (prometheus_target_metadata_cache_entries{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}) > 0 or sum without(rule_group) (prometheus_rule_group_rules{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}) > 0 ) ) Runbook: Check on the /targets page whether every target is down; Check that service discovery is working (the /service-discovery page); If a config error left the target list empty, treat it as a configuration problem; This is total monitoring blindness and should be the highest priority.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is dropping {{ printf "%.4g" $value }} samples/s with timestamps arriving out of order. Warning · 10m · Trigger: rate(prometheus_target_scrapes_sample_out_of_order_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Identify which target is reporting out-of-order data; The usual root causes are an unsynchronised clock on the target, or metrics aggregated from multiple sources with mixed timestamps; Correct the target machine's clock first (chronyc); For Pushgateway-style setups, review how the pusher handles timestamps.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} failed to send {{ printf "%.1f" $value }}% of the samples to {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }} Critical · 15m · Trigger: ( (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])) / ( (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])) + (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_succeeded_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m])) ) ) * 100 > 1 Runbook: Check the Prometheus log for remote_write or tsdb errors; For remote write failures, confirm remote storage availability and credentials, and check for throttling; For local storage failures, check disk space and permissions — a corrupted TSDB may require clearing the WAL; Confirm the queue backlog is draining; if not, raise queue_config or reduce the write volume.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} remote write is {{ printf "%.1f" $value }}s behind for {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}. Critical · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} remote write desired shards calculation wants to run {{ $value }} shards for queue {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}, which is more than the max of {{ printf prometheus_remote_storage_shards_max\{instance="%s",job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"\} $labels.instance | query | first | value }}. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: PrometheusRemoteWriteDesiredShards
Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to evaluate {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} rules in the last 5m. Critical · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: PrometheusRuleFailures

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} scrapes in the last 5m because some targets exceeded the configured body_size_limit. Warning · 15m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_target_scrapes_exceeded_body_size_limit_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Find the rejected targets on the /targets page; curl that target's /metrics by hand to see the actual size and whether the metric count has ballooned; High-cardinality metrics are the usual cause — fix at the source or drop with metric_relabel_configs; If a higher limit is genuinely needed, raise body_size_limit.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} scrapes in the last 5m because some targets exceeded the configured sample_limit. Warning · 15m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_target_scrapes_exceeded_sample_limit_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Find the rejected targets and their sample counts on the /targets page; Run curl /metrics | wc -l by hand to confirm the actual scale; High-cardinality metrics are the main cause — reduce label dimensions at the source or drop unneeded metrics with metric_relabel_configs; If a higher limit is genuinely needed, raise sample_limit after assessing storage and query impact.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to refresh SD with mechanism {{$labels.mechanism}}. Warning · 20m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_sd_refresh_failures_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[10m]) > 0 Runbook: Check the log for service discovery errors; For Kubernetes SD, check that Prometheus's RBAC covers the required resources; For other SD types (Consul, file, …), check backend reachability and credentials; After fixing, confirm the target list is updated on the /service-discovery page.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has dropped {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} targets because the number of targets exceeded the configured target_limit. Warning · 15m · PromQL, common causes and runbook: PrometheusTargetLimitHit

{{ printf "%.0f" $value }} targets in Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} have failed to sync because invalid configuration was supplied. Critical · 5m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_target_sync_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[30m]) > 0 Runbook: Check the log for the specific target sync error; It is usually a relabel misconfiguration producing an invalid target address; Review recently changed ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor configurations; After fixing, confirm the targets are healthy again on the /targets page.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has detected {{$value | humanize}} compaction failures over the last 3h. Warning · 240m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_tsdb_compactions_failed_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[3h]) > 0 Runbook: Check the log for compaction errors; The most common cause is insufficient disk space — confirm the free space first; A corrupted block may need its directory deleted (losing that time range); After fixing, confirm subsequent compactions complete successfully.

Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has detected {{$value | humanize}} reload failures over the last 3h. Warning · 240m · Trigger: increase(prometheus_tsdb_reloads_failures_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[3h]) > 0 Runbook: Check the log for reload errors and which block is involved; It is usually a corrupted block or a permissions problem; For permissions, fix the data directory owner; a corrupted block can only be deleted (losing that time range); After fixing, restart Prometheus and confirm the data is queryable.

The last attempt to reload the Prometheus configuration failed. Prometheus keeps running with the previous configuration, so nothing breaks at once. But every change made since then (new scrape targets, new rule files, new Alertmanager settings) is not in effect, and the next restart may not come back up if the file stays broken. Severity: Critical (critical) Fires after: 10m Part of the Prometheus alert rules (prometheus.yml)
