documents.t: # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. max_over_time(prometheus_config_last_reload_successful{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) == 0 Alert message: Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to reload its configuration.

A YAML syntax error or an unknown field in prometheus.yml. A rule file listed in rule_files that fails to parse. A referenced file (TLS certificate, password file, file_sd target list) that is missing or unreadable. On Kubernetes, a ServiceMonitor, PodMonitor or PrometheusRule that the Operator turned into an invalid configuration.

Find the config parse error line in kubectl logs or the instance log; Validate locally with promtool check config prometheus.yml; On Kubernetes the config is usually generated by the Operator — check ServiceMonitor/PrometheusRule for invalid fields; After fixing, confirm /-/reload succeeded and the /config page shows the new configuration.

Run promtool check config prometheus.yml before each reload. With the Operator the generated configuration lives in a Secret; the config-reloader sidecar logs show the reload error. The expression selects job="prometheus-k8s", namespace="monitoring". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
prometheus_config_last_reload_successful (Prometheus's own metrics)

PrometheusRuleFailures: Prometheus …/… has failed to evaluate … rules in the last 5m. PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources: Prometheus operator in … namespace rejected … …/… resources. PrometheusOperatorReconcileErrors: … of reconciling operations failed for … controller in … namespace.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Prometheus rule at once as prometheus.yml. - alert: PrometheusBadConfig expr: |- # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. max_over_time(prometheus_config_last_reload_successful{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) == 0 for: 10m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to reload its configuration." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus/prometheusbadconfig" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Prometheus has discovered no Alertmanager to send alerts to. Rules are still evaluated and alerts still show as firing on the Prometheus /alerts page, but no notifications go out. Everything is silent and nothing looks wrong, which is why this alert should be routed through a channel that does not depend on the same Alertmanager. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 10m Part of the Prometheus alert rules (prometheus.yml)
documents.s: PrometheusNotConnectedToAlertmanagers alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. max_over_time(prometheus_notifications_alertmanagers_discovered{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) < 1 Alert message: Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is not connected to any Alertmanagers.

The alerting section of the configuration is missing or was removed. Alertmanager discovery returns nothing: wrong service name, namespace or port name. With the Operator, check spec.alerting.alertmanagers in the Prometheus resource. Prometheus lacks RBAC permissions to list the endpoints of the Alertmanager service. All Alertmanager Pods are down, so the service has no endpoints.

Check whether the Alertmanager instances are healthy and reachable; Confirm Alertmanager discovery on the Prometheus /status page; If the queue is full, check whether Alertmanager processing is stuck or the alert volume spiked abnormally; After recovery, confirm Alertmanager actually received the alerts so nothing fails silently.

The Prometheus /status page (Runtime & Build Information) lists the Alertmanagers it has discovered. The expression selects job="prometheus-k8s", namespace="monitoring". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
prometheus_notifications_alertmanagers_discovered (Prometheus's own metrics)

PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToAnyAlertmanager: …% minimum errors while sending alerts from Prometheus …/… to any Alertmanager. PrometheusErrorSendingAlertsToSomeAlertmanagers: …% errors while sending alerts from Prometheus …/… to Alertmanager …. PrometheusNotificationQueueRunningFull: Alert notification queue of Prometheus …/… is running full.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Prometheus rule at once as prometheus.yml. - alert: PrometheusNotConnectedToAlertmanagers expr: |- # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. max_over_time(prometheus_notifications_alertmanagers_discovered{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) < 1 for: 10m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} is not connected to any Alertmanagers." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus/prometheusnotconnectedtoalertmanagers" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

The Prometheus Operator rejected one or more monitoring resources (ServiceMonitor, PodMonitor, Probe, PrometheusRule, AlertmanagerConfig) and left them out of the generated configuration. The resources still exist in the cluster and kubectl apply succeeded, but the targets they describe are not scraped and the rules they contain are not loaded. Nothing else tells you this has happened. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 5m Part of the Prometheus alert rules (prometheus.yml)
documents.s: PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: min_over_time(prometheus_operator_managed_resources{state="rejected",job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Alert message: Prometheus operator in {{ $labels.namespace }} namespace rejected {{ printf "%0.0f" $value }} {{ $labels.controller }}/{{ $labels.resource }} resources.

A PrometheusRule contains a rule that does not parse, such as invalid PromQL or a bad duration. A ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor reads a file from the Prometheus filesystem (bearerTokenFile, TLS file paths) while the Operator is configured to forbid it. A resource references a Secret or ConfigMap that does not exist or is in a namespace the Operator cannot read. An AlertmanagerConfig uses a receiver or field that does not pass the Operator's validation.

Run kubectl logs -n <ns> deploy/prometheus-operator for the specific error; For permission errors, verify the Operator's ClusterRole covers the required resources; For Reconcile/Sync failures, check the corresponding CRD objects (kubectl describe servicemonitor/prometheusrule); For rejected resources, kubectl describe shows the rejection reason, usually failed field validation.

The controller and resource labels on the alert tell you which kind of object was rejected. The Operator logs name the object and the reason. The expression selects job="prometheus-operator", namespace="monitoring". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
prometheus_operator_managed_resources (Prometheus Operator)

PrometheusOperatorReconcileErrors: … of reconciling operations failed for … controller in … namespace. PrometheusOperatorSyncFailed: Controller … in … namespace fails to reconcile … objects. PrometheusBadConfig: Prometheus …/… has failed to reload its configuration.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Prometheus rule at once as prometheus.yml. - alert: PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources expr: |- min_over_time(prometheus_operator_managed_resources{state="rejected",job="prometheus-operator",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 for: 5m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Prometheus operator in {{ $labels.namespace }} namespace rejected {{ printf \"%0.0f\" $value }} {{ $labels.controller }}/{{ $labels.resource }} resources." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus/prometheusoperatorrejectedresources" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Remote write is more than 2 minutes behind: the newest sample Prometheus has ingested is more than 120 seconds newer than the newest sample it has sent to a remote endpoint. Dashboards and alerts that read from the remote store (VictoriaMetrics, Thanos Receive, Mimir, a managed service) see stale data. If the lag keeps growing, samples can be dropped before they are sent. Severity: Critical (critical) Fires after: 15m Part of the Prometheus alert rules (prometheus.yml)
documents.s: PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. ( max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) - ignoring(remote_name, url) group_right max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) ) > 120 Alert message: Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} remote write is {{ printf "%.1f" $value }}s behind for {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}.

The remote endpoint is slow or rejecting writes: overloaded, rate limiting with HTTP 429, or returning errors. Network latency or bandwidth between Prometheus and the endpoint is not enough for the write volume. Remote write is capped at too few shards for the series count (see PrometheusRemoteWriteDesiredShards). A spike in series count, for example from a new high-cardinality label, multiplied the write volume. After a restart, Prometheus is replaying a large WAL and catching up.

Check the Prometheus log for remote_write or tsdb errors; For remote write failures, confirm remote storage availability and credentials, and check for throttling; For local storage failures, check disk space and permissions — a corrupted TSDB may require clearing the WAL; Confirm the queue backlog is draining; if not, raise queue_config or reduce the write volume.
The expression selects job="prometheus-k8s", namespace="monitoring". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds (Prometheus's own metrics) prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds (Prometheus's own metrics)

PrometheusRemoteWriteDesiredShards: Prometheus …/… remote write desired shards calculation wants to run … shards for queue …:…, which is more than the max of {{ printf prometheus_remote_storage_shards_max\{instance="%s",job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"\} $labels.instance | query | first | value }}. PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures: Prometheus …/… failed to send …% of the samples to …:…

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Prometheus rule at once as prometheus.yml. - alert: PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind expr: |- # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. ( max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) - ignoring(remote_name, url) group_right max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) ) > 120 for: 15m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} remote write is {{ printf \"%.1f\" $value }}s behind for {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus/prometheusremotewritebehind" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Remote write calculates how many parallel shards it needs to keep up with the incoming samples. This alert fires when that number has been above the configured max_shards for 15 minutes. Remote write cannot add the shards it needs, so it will fall behind (PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind) unless something changes. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Prometheus alert rules (prometheus.yml)
documents.s: PrometheusRemoteWriteDesiredShards alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. ( max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_shards_desired{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_shards_max{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) ) Alert message: Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} remote write desired shards calculation wants to run {{ $value }} shards for queue {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}, which is more than the max of {{ printf prometheus_remote_storage_shards_max\{instance="%s",job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"\} $labels.instance | query | first | value }}.

The number of series or the scrape frequency grew, so there are more samples per second to send. Each send became slower because the remote endpoint or the network is slower, so more shards are needed for the same throughput. max_shards in queue_config is set lower than the workload needs.

Check the Prometheus log for remote_write or tsdb errors; For remote write failures, confirm remote storage availability and credentials, and check for throttling; For local storage failures, check disk space and permissions — a corrupted TSDB may require clearing the WAL; Confirm the queue backlog is draining; if not, raise queue_config or reduce the write volume.

Fix the cause before raising the limit. If the endpoint is slow, more shards only add pressure on it. If the volume really grew, raise max_shards, or max_samples_per_send to send larger batches, and make sure Prometheus has the memory for the larger queues. The expression selects job="prometheus-k8s", namespace="monitoring". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
prometheus_remote_storage_shards_desired (Prometheus's own metrics) prometheus_remote_storage_shards_max (Prometheus's own metrics)
PrometheusRemoteWriteBehind: Prometheus …/… remote write is …s behind for …:…. PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures: Prometheus …/… failed to send …% of the samples to …:…

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Prometheus rule at once as prometheus.yml. - alert: PrometheusRemoteWriteDesiredShards expr: |- # Without max_over_time, failed scrapes could create false negatives, see # https://www.robustperception.io/alerting-on-gauges-in-prometheus-2-0 for details. ( max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_shards_desired{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > max_over_time(prometheus_remote_storage_shards_max{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) ) for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} remote write desired shards calculation wants to run {{ $value }} shards for queue {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}, which is more than the max of {{ printf `prometheus_remote_storage_shards_max{instance=\"%s\",job=\"prometheus-k8s\",namespace=\"monitoring\"}` $labels.instance | query | first | value }}." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus/prometheusremotewritedesiredshards" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Prometheus failed to evaluate one or more alerting or recording rules in the last 5 minutes. A rule that fails to evaluate produces no result, so an alert that should be firing stays silent, and recording rules leave gaps that other rules and dashboards then read. Severity: Critical (critical) Fires after: 15m Part of the Prometheus alert rules (prometheus.yml)
documents.s: PrometheusRuleFailures alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: increase(prometheus_rule_evaluation_failures_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Alert message: Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to evaluate {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} rules in the last 5m.

Vector matching errors that appear only with certain data: many-to-many matching not allowed or found duplicate series for the match group after a new label or a duplicate target shows up. A query that exceeds the query timeout or the maximum number of samples it may load. A rule that reads a recording rule or metric that has been renamed, so it now returns errors in a combined expression. Remote read or storage errors while the rule is being evaluated.

Check the log for the failing rule name and error; Common causes are a query syntax error in the rule, a reference to a non-existent metric, or an oversized result; Validate the rule files with promtool check rules; After fixing, confirm the rule shows ok on the /rules page.

The /rules page in the Prometheus UI shows the last error for each rule; this is quicker than searching the logs. Some of these errors depend on the data, so promtool check rules can pass while evaluation still fails. The expression selects job="prometheus-k8s", namespace="monitoring". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
prometheus_rule_evaluation_failures_total (Prometheus's own metrics)

PrometheusMissingRuleEvaluations: Prometheus …/… has missed … rule group evaluations in the last 5m. PrometheusBadConfig: Prometheus …/… has failed to reload its configuration. PrometheusOperatorRejectedResources: Prometheus operator in … namespace rejected … …/… resources.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Prometheus rule at once as prometheus.yml. - alert: PrometheusRuleFailures expr: |- increase(prometheus_rule_evaluation_failures_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 for: 15m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has failed to evaluate {{ printf \"%.0f\" $value }} rules in the last 5m." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus/prometheusrulefailures" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

A scrape job discovered more targets than its target_limit allows. Prometheus does not scrape just the first N in that case: it marks every target of that scrape pool as failed and scrapes none of them. A whole job goes dark at once, and its up series turn to 0. Severity: Warning (warning) Fires after: 15m Part of the Prometheus alert rules (prometheus.yml)
documents.s: PrometheusTargetLimitHit alert: what it means and how to fix it

documents.t: increase(prometheus_target_scrape_pool_exceeded_target_limit_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 Alert message: Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has dropped {{ printf "%.0f" $value }} targets because the number of targets exceeded the configured target_limit.

A ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor selector is too broad and now matches Services or Pods it was not meant to. The monitored workload scaled out past the limit, for example a large DaemonSet or an HPA scaling out. Relabeling that used to drop unwanted targets was changed or removed. The limit was set for a smaller cluster and never revisited.

Confirm the current target count against the limit on the /targets page; Check whether the ServiceMonitor selector is too broad and picking up unwanted targets; Tighten the selector or split across multiple Prometheus instances by business domain; If more targets are genuinely needed, raise target_limit and size the resources accordingly.

The /targets page shows the affected job with an error that mentions the target limit. With the Operator, the limit can come from targetLimit on a ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor, or enforcedTargetLimit on the Prometheus resource. The expression selects job="prometheus-k8s", namespace="monitoring". If your scrape job or namespace is named differently, change these matchers or the rule never matches.
prometheus_target_scrape_pool_exceeded_target_limit_total (Prometheus's own metrics)

PrometheusScrapeSampleLimitHit: Prometheus …/… has failed … scrapes in the last 5m because some targets exceeded the configured sample_limit. PrometheusLabelLimitHit: Prometheus …/… has dropped … targets because some samples exceeded the configured label_limit, label_name_length_limit or label_value_length_limit. PrometheusTargetSyncFailure: … targets in Prometheus …/… have failed to sync because invalid configuration was supplied.

Add this to a rules file loaded through rule_files, or download every Prometheus rule at once as prometheus.yml. - alert: PrometheusTargetLimitHit expr: |- increase(prometheus_target_scrape_pool_exceeded_target_limit_total{job="prometheus-k8s",namespace="monitoring"}[5m]) > 0 for: 15m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Prometheus {{$labels.namespace}}/{{$labels.pod}} has dropped {{ printf \"%.0f\" $value }} targets because the number of targets exceeded the configured target_limit." runbook_url: "https://n9e.github.io/alert-rules/prometheus/prometheustargetlimithit" With Nightingale: this rule ships in the Kubernetes integration template; import it into a business group and Nightingale attaches the runbook to every alert it sends.
The rule expression is adapted from kube-prometheus (Apache-2.0). The runbook steps come from Nightingale's integration templates (Apache-2.0); the explanation and causes are written for this page.

Redis alert rules for high memory usage, a rising eviction rate, rejected connections, too many client connections, a falling cache hit ratio, high command or ping latency, and an instance that has just restarted. The exporter group uses oliver006/redis_exporter metric names; the Categraf group covers the same checks for instances collected by Categraf.
documents.s: Redis alert rules for Prometheus: 12 rules with runbooks

documents.t: 12 rules, each with a PromQL condition, a severity, a for duration and runbook steps Metrics from: redis_exporter, Categraf Download: redis.yml, a standard Prometheus rules file (groups: format), checked with promtool check rules Thresholds are starting points. Adjust them to your environment before enabling the rules.

Rule Severity For High Redis client connection count - exporter Warning 1m High Redis eviction rate - exporter Warning 1m High Redis latency - exporter Warning 1m High Redis memory usage rate - exporter Warning 1m Low Redis hit rate - exporter Warning 1m Redis connection refused - exporter Warning — Redis has just been restarted, please be aware - exporter Info — High Redis eviction rate Warning 1m High Redis memory usage rate Warning 1m High Redis Ping latency (above 100 milliseconds) Warning 1m Low Redis hit rate Warning 1m Redis connection refused Warning —
1 of the 7 rules in this group also apply unchanged to instances collected by Categraf, which produces the same metric names.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: (redis_connected_clients / redis_config_maxclients) > 0.85 Runbook: Use CLIENT LIST grouped by source address to find the application holding the most connections; Tell a scale-out apart from a connection pool leak (many idle connections never released); As an emergency measure run CONFIG SET maxclients <larger value> and check the system ulimit -n to match; For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and enable connection reuse.
documents.s: High Redis client connection count - exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: rate(redis_evicted_keys_total[5m]) / sum without (db) (redis_db_keys) > 0.1 Runbook: Use INFO memory to compare used_memory against maxmemory and confirm whether it has topped out; Use redis-cli --bigkeys to find abnormally large keys and clean up or split them; Confirm maxmemory-policy matches expectations (allkeys-lru for a pure cache; data you cannot afford to lose must not be left evictable); If capacity is genuinely insufficient, scale up memory or shard.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: sum without (cmd) (rate(redis_commands_duration_seconds_total[5m])) / rate(redis_commands_processed_total[5m]) > 0.25 Runbook: Run SLOWLOG GET 10 to find the slowest commands; Focus on O(N) commands such as KEYS, HGETALL and SMEMBERS and on big-key operations, switching to SCAN or batched processing; Check INFO persistence to see whether an RDB/AOF rewrite fork is causing the stall; Check whether the host CPU is saturated or the machine is swapping.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: redis_memory_max_bytes > 0 and (redis_memory_used_bytes / redis_memory_max_bytes) > 0.85 Runbook: Check used_memory_rss and the fragmentation ratio mem_fragmentation_ratio in INFO memory — enable activedefrag if fragmentation is high; Use redis-cli --bigkeys / --memkeys to find big keys and split them or add TTLs; Check whether keys without an expiry are piling up; Confirm maxmemory-policy, then scale up memory or shard as needed.
documents.s: High Redis memory usage rate - exporter

documents.t: Warning · 1m · Trigger: rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[5m]) / (rate(redis_keyspace_misses_total[5m]) + rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[5m])) < 0.9 Runbook: First rule out a cold start after a restart or scale-out (check redis_uptime_in_seconds); Compare the growth of keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses in INFO stats to tell unwarmed new keys apart from heavy eviction; If an eviction alert fired at the same time, treat it as insufficient memory (scale up or clean up big keys); Review the cache key design and whether the TTL is too short on the application side.

Warning · — · Trigger: (rate(redis_rejected_connections_total[5m])) > 0 Runbook: Compare connected_clients from INFO clients against CONFIG GET maxclients; Use CLIENT LIST grouped by source address to find the application leaking connections; As an emergency measure run CONFIG SET maxclients <larger value>, confirming the system ulimit -n is high enough; For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and enable connection reuse.

Info · — · Trigger: redis_uptime_in_seconds < 600 Runbook: Check the Redis log to tell an OOM kill, a crash and a manual restart apart; If the system OOM killer was involved, compare maxmemory against free host memory and lower maxmemory; Confirm the RDB/AOF loaded correctly and the data is complete (check rdb_last_load_keys_loaded in INFO persistence); After the restart, watch the hit rate and the backend database load, and warm the cache if needed.
documents.s: Redis has just been restarted, please be aware - exporter

documents.t: For hosts and instances collected by Categraf; metric names follow Categraf plugins.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: rate(redis_evicted_keys[5m]) / sum without (db) (redis_keyspace_keys) > 0.1 Runbook: Use INFO memory to compare used_memory against maxmemory and confirm whether it has topped out; Use redis-cli --bigkeys to find abnormally large keys and clean up or split them; Confirm maxmemory-policy matches expectations (allkeys-lru for a pure cache; data you cannot afford to lose must not be left evictable); If capacity is genuinely insufficient, scale up memory or shard.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: redis_maxmemory > 0 and (redis_used_memory / redis_maxmemory) > 0.85 Runbook: Check used_memory_rss and the fragmentation ratio mem_fragmentation_ratio in INFO memory — enable activedefrag if fragmentation is high; Use redis-cli --bigkeys / --memkeys to find big keys and split them or add TTLs; Check whether keys without an expiry are piling up; Confirm maxmemory-policy, then scale up memory or shard as needed.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: redis_ping_use_seconds > 0.1 Runbook: Use redis-cli --latency and SLOWLOG GET 10 to check whether slow commands (KEYS, HGETALL, big-key operations) are blocking the main thread; Check INFO persistence to see whether an RDB/AOF rewrite fork is causing the stall; Check whether the host CPU is saturated or the machine is swapping; Once you find the slow command, replace it with SCAN or batched operations.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: rate(redis_keyspace_hits[5m]) / (rate(redis_keyspace_misses[5m]) + rate(redis_keyspace_hits[5m])) < 0.9 Runbook: First rule out a cold start after a restart or scale-out (check redis_uptime_in_seconds); Compare the growth of keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses in INFO stats to tell unwarmed new keys apart from heavy eviction; If an eviction alert fired at the same time, treat it as insufficient memory (scale up or clean up big keys); Review the cache key design and whether the TTL is too short on the application side.

Warning · — · Trigger: (rate(redis_rejected_connections[5m])) > 0 Runbook: Compare connected_clients from INFO clients against CONFIG GET maxclients; Use CLIENT LIST grouped by source address to find the application leaking connections; As an emergency measure run CONFIG SET maxclients <larger value>, confirming the system ulimit -n is high enough; For the root cause, cap the application connection pool and enable connection reuse.

With Prometheus or vmalert: download redis.yml, add it to rule_files (or -rule for vmalert), check the metric names against your exporter version, and tune thresholds. Severity is set as a severity label (critical / warning / info), and runbook_url points back to this page, or to the rule's own page where it has one. Warning · 1m · Trigger: 100 * sum by (instance) (rate(windows_cpu_time_total{mode != 'idle'}[5m])) / count by (instance) (windows_cpu_core_frequency_mhz) > 80 Runbook: Open Task Manager, or run Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 to find the busiest processes; Use Resource Monitor (resmon) to see whether user or kernel time dominates — high kernel time points at drivers or antivirus; Tell traffic growth apart from a program fault (infinite loop, frequent GC); For growth, scale out or rate limit; for a fault, restart the service and fix it.

Warning · 1m · Trigger: 100 * (windows_cs_physical_memory_bytes - windows_os_physical_memory_free_bytes) / windows_cs_physical_memory_bytes > 80 Runbook: Run Get-Process | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 to find the largest consumers; Use perfmon to watch Available MBytes and Pages/sec — a sustained high Pages/sec means it is already paging heavily; Determine whether it is growth or a process leak — a leak must be located in the application, a restart only helps temporarily; Confirm the page file is sized sensibly and add memory if needed.

kube-state-metrics vs metrics-server vs cAdvisor vs node_exporter November 1, 2026 · 7 min read Eric Qin Kubernetes metrics come from four places, and their names look alike. kube_pod_container_resource_limits, container_memory_working_set_bytes, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes and the numbers in kubectl top all sound like they describe the same thing. They are made by different components and they answer different questions. Only three of the four are meant for monitoring. This post explains what each component measures and how to tell which one a metric came from. It also covers the renames that make a query copied from a 2019 blog post return nothing. The short answer​ Component Measures Where it gets the data Metric prefix Use it for kube-state-metrics The state of Kubernetes objects: desired vs actual replicas, pod phase, container restarts, resource requests and limits Watches the API server kube_ Alerting and dashboards cAdvisor What each container actually uses: CPU, memory, throttling, filesystem, network Built into the kubelet, served at /metrics/cadvisor container_ Alerting and dashboards node_exporter The machine underneath: CPU modes, memory, disks, filesystems, network interfaces A DaemonSet reading /proc and /sys on each node node_ Alerting and dashboards metrics-server A CPU and memory snapshot for each pod and node Scrapes the kubelet's /metrics/resource none; it serves the Metrics API (metrics.k8s.io) kubectl top, the Horizontal and Vertical Pod Autoscalers You will also meet two more sources. The kubelet's own /metrics endpoint provides things like kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes, which tells you how full a PersistentVolume is. The API server exposes apiserver_* metrics about itself. Neither belongs to the four above, and alert rules use both. kube-state-metrics: what the API server believes​ kube-state-metrics listens to the API server and turns objects into metrics. Its README calls this "the health of the various objects inside" the cluster, as opposed to the health of the cluster components themselves. It exposes the values as the API returns them. It does not apply the heuristics kubectl uses, which is why its numbers sometimes differ from what kubectl get prints. That makes it the right source for questions about intent: Does the Deployment have the replicas it asked for? kube_deployment_spec_replicas vs kube_deployment_status_replicas_available. Is a container stuck in CrashLoopBackOff? kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason. Why did the last run end? kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason, where reason="OOMKilled" is the one you usually want. Is a node NotReady? kube_node_status_condition. It tells you nothing about usage. A pod at 100% of its CPU limit and an idle pod look the same to kube-state-metrics. For usage you need cAdvisor. The rename that breaks old queries. kube-state-metrics 2.0 removed the per-resource metrics such as kube_pod_container_resource_limits_cpu_cores and kube_pod_container_resource_requests_memory_bytes. Their replacements are kube_pod_container_resource_limits and kube_pod_container_resource_requests, with resource and unit labels: # kube-state-metrics 1.x (removed in 2.0) kube_pod_container_resource_limits_cpu_cores # kube-state-metrics 2.x kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="cpu", unit="core"} A query that uses the old name does not fail. It returns an empty result, and an alert rule built on it never fires. We found exactly this in our own Kubernetes template while writing this post: the container CPU rule still used the 1.x metric name and the old pod_name label. It now uses the current names. cAdvisor: what containers actually use​ cAdvisor is compiled into the kubelet, so there is nothing extra to deploy. Prometheus scrapes it from each node at /metrics/cadvisor. These are the metrics you reach for when a pod is slow or keeps getting killed: container_cpu_usage_seconds_total: CPU time consumed. Take a rate() to get cores in use. container_memory_working_set_bytes: memory the kernel cannot easily reclaim. The kubelet uses the working set for eviction decisions, and kubectl top shows the same number. container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total and container_cpu_cfs_periods_total: how often the container hit its CPU limit and was paused. The CPUThrottlingHigh rule is the ratio of the two. Two things trip people up: Extra series. cAdvisor also reports cgroups that are not your application container: a pod-level series with container="" and, on older Docker-based nodes, the pause container as container="POD". Summing without a filter counts the same memory twice. Add container!="" (and container!="POD" on old nodes) when you aggregate. Label names changed. Before Kubernetes 1.16, cAdvisor labelled series pod_name and container_name. They are now pod and container. A rule that groups by (pod_name) returns nothing on a current cluster. Usage becomes useful when you compare it with a limit, and the limit lives in kube-state-metrics. Both sides share the namespace, pod and container labels, so the join is direct: sum by (namespace, pod, container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""}) / sum by (namespace, pod, container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"}) > 0.9 node_exporter: the machine underneath​ node_exporter runs as a DaemonSet with access to the host's /proc and /sys. It knows nothing about pods. It reports the operating system: node_cpu_seconds_total by mode, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes, node_filesystem_avail_bytes, disk I/O and network errors. Use it for the questions Kubernetes does not answer. Is the node's root filesystem filling up? Is the clock drifting? Is a NIC dropping packets? Is the kernel OOM killer firing (node_vmstat_oom_kill)? Node-level memory includes page cache and every process on the host, so it will not add up to the sum of your containers. That is expected. The Linux rule set covers the common host checks, including disk-fill prediction with predict_linear. metrics-server: for autoscaling, not alerting​ metrics-server collects CPU and memory every 15 seconds from each kubelet's /metrics/resource endpoint and serves them through the Metrics API. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reads it, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler reads it, and kubectl top reads it. It keeps only the latest value, in memory. There is no history to query and no Prometheus endpoint to scrape. The project's README says it plainly: metrics-server is meant for autoscaling, and you should not use it to forward metrics to monitoring solutions. If you want those numbers in your monitoring system, scrape the kubelet's /metrics/resource endpoint directly. So when kubectl top and your dashboard disagree by a few percent, neither is wrong. They read different endpoints at different moments. Which component answers your question​ Question Metric Source Is the pod restarting? kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total kube-state-metrics Was it OOM-killed? kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"} kube-state-metrics Is a container close to its memory limit? container_memory_working_set_bytes ÷ kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"} cAdvisor + kube-state-metrics Is it being CPU-throttled? container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total ÷ container_cpu_cfs_periods_total cAdvisor Does the Deployment have the replicas it wants? kube_deployment_status_replicas_available vs kube_deployment_spec_replicas kube-state-metrics Is a node NotReady? kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready"} kube-state-metrics Is a node's disk filling up? node_filesystem_avail_bytes node_exporter Is a PersistentVolume filling up? kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes kubelet How much CPU is the pod using right now? kubectl top pod metrics-server Ready-made rules, sorted by source​ Most of the standard Kubernetes alerts read kube-state-metrics. Each of these pages explains what the alert means, its common causes and the steps to fix it, and lists the metrics it uses: kube-state-metrics: KubePodCrashLooping, KubePodNotReady, KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch, KubeNodeNotReady, KubeJobFailed, KubeHpaMaxedOut kubelet: KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp cAdvisor: CPUThrottlingHigh API server: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn, KubeClientCertificateExpiration The full Kubernetes rule set is available as a Prometheus rules file you can download and load with rule_files. With Nightingale​ Nightingale does not replace any of these four components. It queries the store where their metrics already land, such as Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics, and runs alert rules against it. The Kubernetes integration ships the rules above, each with its runbook attached, and you can import them into a business group in one step. documents.t: MCP server for alerting: six design decisions November 1, 2026 · 7 min read Eric Qin Since v9, the Nightingale process is also an MCP server. Claude Code, Cursor or any other MCP client can connect to /mcp and ask which alerts are firing, which rules are noisiest, or what a metric did over the last hour. The tool list was the easy part. The hard questions were about trust. Whose permissions does the AI client have? What can it change? How do you find out afterwards what it did? This post walks through the six decisions we made, and one caveat we haven't solved. What this is not: an autonomous agent that resolves incidents on its own. It is a way for a model to read, and with explicit opt-in to change, an alerting system with the same permissions as the person who connected it. 1. No separate server: the endpoint lives in the process​ There is nothing extra to deploy. POST /mcp is served by the same n9e process that serves the UI and the API, and it is on by default. It uses MCP's Streamable HTTP transport in stateless mode. Every POST is self-contained. The server returns an Mcp-Session-Id on initialize but never validates it, and GET /mcp returns 405 because there is no standalone event stream. The practical benefit: several Nightingale instances behind a load balancer need no sticky sessions. Any instance can answer any request. 2. A tool call is an internal API call​ When a client calls list_alert_rules, the MCP server does not read the database. It dispatches the call, in-process, onto Nightingale's own HTTP route (/api/n9e/busi-group/{gid}/alert-rules), carrying the caller's token through the full middleware chain: authenticate, resolve the user, check the permission point, check the business group. So the answer to "can the AI get around RBAC?" is structural: no. It walks the same path as a click in the UI. There is no separate permission model for AI to configure, audit and keep in sync. The consequence is that a client has exactly the permissions of its token's owner. To limit what the AI can see, you give it a limited account: a dedicated user with the Guest or Standard role, in a team that can read only the business groups you choose. list_busi_groups returns only groups that user can reach, so the model can only ever pick from that set. Do not give the AI account the Admin role. Admin bypasses the business-group layer. OAuth tokens get one more restriction. A token issued through OAuth works on /mcp and /a2a only; the rest of the API rejects it. 3. Write tools are not registered, not just refused​ There are 74 tools. 42 read and 32 write. By default only the 42 read tools exist. The write tools sit in a separate registration list that is skipped unless you set: [HTTP.A2A] MCPEnableWriteTools = true We chose "not registered" over "registered and refused" on purpose. A model plans with the tools it can see. If write tools appear in tools/list and fail at call time, the model keeps trying them, or tries to work around the error. If they are absent, the model never considers them. This gate sits outside RBAC. Even if a client is handed root's token by mistake, under the default config it cannot change anything. Every tool also carries MCP's readOnlyHint annotation for clients that use it, and it always agrees with the registration list. 4. No delete tools at all​ None of the 74 tools deletes anything. "Write" means create and update. Deleting a rule, a user or a business group is not reachable through MCP. This changes the worst case from "gone" to "changed wrongly", which is easier to notice and to fix. It does not make write tools harmless. Some of them are among the most powerful operations in the product: Tool Why it is dangerous reset_user_password Resets any user's password create_user, update_user_profile Assign roles as a side effect, which is privilege escalation bind_role_operations Replaces a role's whole permission set; a short payload silently removes permissions create_notify_channel, update_notify_channel A webhook channel sends alert content to any address it is given upsert_datasource Stores data source credentials and probes the address it is given set_dashboard_public Makes a dashboard readable without login toggle_alert_rules, set_datasource_status, create_mute Create blind spots: rules disabled, a data source off, alerts silenced 5. Toolsets are an allowlist, and typos don't fall back​ The 74 tools are grouped into 13 toolsets: alerts, targets, datasource, mutes, busi_groups, notify_rules, alert_subscribes, event_pipelines, users, metrics, logs, dashboards and roles. An empty list exposes all of them; a list exposes only those named: [HTTP.A2A] MCPToolsets = ["alerts", "busi_groups", "targets", "metrics"] A misspelled name is dropped with a warning in the log. It does not fall back to "everything". A list made entirely of typos exposes zero tools, not 74. Failing closed is less convenient and much safer. Work backwards from what you want the AI to do: Use Toolsets On-call triage: what is firing, which rule, who owns it alerts, busi_groups, targets Plus "explain this spike" add metrics Noise review: noisiest rules, mutes, subscriptions add mutes, alert_subscribes Letting the AI change configuration turn on writes, and remove users and roles first 6. Every call is attributable​ Two trails answer "who changed this, and was it the AI?": The object itself. A rule, mute or dashboard changed over MCP records the token owner's username in update_by, exactly as if they had edited it in the UI. The request log. Every /mcp request writes a start line with the full request body (tool name and arguments) and a done line with the user and status code, joined by a trace_id: grep '"method":"tools/call"' n9e.log | grep -oE '"name":"[a-z_]+"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn Oversized bodies are truncated, and the log line says so. A dedicated account per client makes both trails useful. If every client shares one token, update_by tells you nothing. The caveat: query_logs and SQL data sources​ One read-only tool deserves care. query_logs in the logs toolset passes the query body to Nightingale's log query endpoint, which dispatches on the data source type. If you have SQL data sources registered (MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Doris or TDengine), the SQL runs as written. There is a read-only check on that path. It is a keyword blocklist that rejects statements containing INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, ALTER, CREATE, TRUNCATE, REPLACE, GRANT or REVOKE. That stops the obvious cases. It is not a SQL parser, so treat it as a second line of defence rather than a guarantee. If you have SQL data sources, leave logs out of MCPToolsets, or give the AI account a role that cannot reach those data sources. Registering them with read-only database credentials is a sensible extra layer. MCP or the built-in assistant?​ Nightingale also has a built-in assistant in the UI. For configuration changes it is the safer of the two: its update operations are two-phase. The first call computes the change and shows a confirmation card, and nothing is written until a person confirms. MCP has no such step. A write tool writes on its first call. So a reasonable split is: use an MCP client for reading and triage, where its own model and tools shine, and use the built-in assistant when something needs to change. Try it​ Create a token for a dedicated, least-privileged user under Profile → Token management, then add Nightingale to your MCP client: ~/.claude.json { "mcpServers": { "nightingale": { "type": "http", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:17000/mcp", "headers": { "X-User-Token": "<token of the AI account>" } } } } Then ask something you can check: "Which alerts are firing right now? Group them by severity." or "List every business group I can see." The second one is also a quick test that the account is scoped the way you intended. More detail is in the docs: Enable the MCP endpoint, Permission inheritance and RBAC, Read and write toolsets and Enable write tools safely. documents.t: Migrating from Zabbix to Prometheus November 1, 2026 · 7 min read Eric Qin Moving from Zabbix to Prometheus is not a data migration. There is no export file that turns into rule files, and no tool that converts triggers into PromQL. The two systems model monitoring differently. Most of the work is translating concepts, then rebuilding a smaller set of rules on top of them. This post maps each Zabbix concept to its Prometheus counterpart, lists the parts that have no equivalent, and suggests an order of work that keeps Zabbix running until the end. The difference that explains everything else​ Zabbix is host-centric. You create a host, attach templates, and the templates define items (what to collect) and triggers (when to alert) for that host. 40 database servers with one template give you 40 copies of each trigger. Prometheus is query-centric. Exporters expose metrics, Prometheus scrapes them, and an alert rule is a query. A rule matches every series the query returns. One rule covers all 40 servers, and the 41st server is covered as soon as it is scraped. Most of the translation follows from this. You rarely port triggers one by one; you merge them. Concept map​ Collection and storage​ Zabbix Prometheus Notes Zabbix server and database Prometheus server and its local TSDB Local retention is short by default (15 days). Long-term storage is a separate component Zabbix agent Exporters: node_exporter for hosts, mysqld_exporter for MySQL and so on Prometheus pulls over HTTP; the agent's active checks push. Targets must be reachable from Prometheus Zabbix proxy A Prometheus server per site, or Prometheus in agent mode with remote_write Agent mode scrapes and forwards without evaluating rules locally Item A metric name plus labels Which metrics exist is decided by the exporter, not by the monitoring server Item key vfs.fs.size[/,pfree] node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} ÷ node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"} Percentages are usually computed in the query Calculated item Recording rule History and trends Raw samples; downsampling only in long-term stores such as Thanos There is no built-in hourly min/avg/max like Zabbix trends Text and log items None Prometheus stores numbers only. Logs go to Loki, Elasticsearch or similar Hosts, templates and discovery​ Zabbix Prometheus Notes Host A scrape target, identified by the instance label Host group Labels such as team or env, added through relabeling Groups become labels you can filter on Template An exporter, a rule file and a dashboard The community equivalent of a template collection is a monitoring mixin Low-level discovery (LLD) Service discovery for targets; labels for things on a target New filesystems or interfaces appear as new series automatically. No discovery rule needed User macros {$THRESHOLD} Hard-coded thresholds, or a threshold metric joined in the query Per-host overrides need a pattern, see below Triggers and alerting​ Zabbix Prometheus Notes Trigger Alerting rule: a PromQL expr plus for One rule, many series Trigger severity (six levels) A severity label A convention, not a built-in. Most teams use three: critical, warning, info Recovery expression, hysteresis No direct equivalent keep_firing_for delays recovery; true hysteresis needs a query trick nodata() absent(), absent_over_time(), or up == 0 absent() only works for series you name explicitly Trigger dependencies Alertmanager inhibit_rules Inhibition mutes target alerts while a source alert fires, matched on labels Event correlation None in Prometheus or Alertmanager Notification​ Zabbix Prometheus Notes Action and operations Alertmanager routes and receivers Routing matches on labels Media type Receiver integration: email, Slack, webhook and others Escalation steps Not built in Alertmanager repeats notifications (repeat_interval) but has no escalation chain. That is an on-call tool's job Maintenance period Silences, plus mute_time_intervals for recurring windows Silences are ad hoc; time intervals cover the weekly window Acknowledgement None in Alertmanager Usually handled in the on-call or chat tool The parts with no equivalent​ Plan for these before you start. They are where migrations stall. Escalations. Zabbix can notify the on-call engineer, then the team lead after 30 minutes, then the manager. Alertmanager cannot. If you rely on escalation, you need an on-call tool behind Alertmanager. Per-host thresholds. In Zabbix you override {$DISK_PFREE_MIN} on one host. In Prometheus a threshold is part of the query. The common workaround is a small metric that carries thresholds, joined in the rule: (node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes) * 100 < on(instance) group_left() disk_free_threshold_percent Or keep a default rule and split the exceptions out by label: disk_profile="large" gets its own rule. SNMP traps. The SNMP exporter polls; it does not receive traps. Traps need a separate receiver that turns them into metrics or logs. Text and log items. If Zabbix watches log files or string values, those move to a log system, not Prometheus. Trigger dependencies, partly. inhibit_rules cover the common case of "switch down mutes everything behind it". They need a label that links the two alerts, such as a shared site or rack. Zabbix's dependency tree has no labels to rely on, so you add them first. An order that keeps Zabbix running​ Zabbix stays up and keeps paging people until the very last step. Each step can be checked on its own. Deploy exporters next to the Zabbix agents. Start with one group of hosts. Leave the agents installed. Check: the targets are up in Prometheus. Pick the storage you will keep. A single Prometheus for a start; a pair and a long-term store if you need HA or longer retention. Decide now, because changing stores later is a project of its own. Import existing rule sets instead of porting templates. The community rules for node_exporter, MySQL, Redis, Kubernetes and others cover most of what stock Zabbix templates do. Our alert rule library has them as downloadable rule files, each with a runbook. Port the custom triggers, merged. List your custom triggers, group them by item and threshold, and write one rule per group. Use labels for the exceptions. Send Prometheus alerts somewhere nobody is paged. A dedicated channel or mailbox. Compare it with Zabbix every day: fired only in Zabbix (missed rule or metric), fired only in Prometheus (threshold typo, or a Zabbix dependency or maintenance window you forgot), fired in both at different severity. Move notification one channel at a time. Chat first, then email, then phone. Disable the matching Zabbix action as each channel moves, but keep Zabbix evaluating so the daily comparison continues. Stop Zabbix last. After a week with no differences, stop the agents. Keep the database read-only for as long as you need the history. History does not migrate. Zabbix or Prometheus at all?​ Not every Zabbix setup should move. Zabbix suits fleets of long-lived hosts and network devices, teams that want everything configured in one UI, and environments that need agents to push through firewalls. Prometheus suits environments where targets come and go (containers, autoscaling), where configuration lives in Git, and where software already exposes /metrics. Many organisations run both for years: Zabbix for network gear and legacy hosts, Prometheus for Kubernetes and new services. With Nightingale​ Nightingale sits on top of Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics as the alerting layer. It manages rules in a UI with business groups and permissions, and handles notification, muting and subscriptions, so step 6 does not require learning Alertmanager's routing tree. It does not import Zabbix templates or triggers; the rebuild described above still applies. Two Nightingale pages go deeper: From Zabbix: every Zabbix object mapped to a Nightingale one, including the ones with no equivalent. Coexistence and rollback plan: the daily comparison and channel-by-channel cutover in detail, with a rollback for each stage. If you are still choosing, see Nightingale vs Zabbix. How long should a Prometheus alert wait? Data from 692 rules November 1, 2026 · 9 min read Eric Qin Every alert rule answers two questions: what counts as bad, and how long it has to stay bad. Most review effort goes into the first one, the expression and the threshold. The second is the for duration, and it often gets whatever value the tool filled in. We wanted to know how often that happens, so we counted. Nightingale ships alert rule templates for 49 integrations. 692 rules, and 304 of them (44%) have a for duration of exactly 60 seconds, which is the default in Nightingale's rule editor. This post walks through what the numbers show and what for value suits which kind of alert. What for does​ An alert rule is evaluated on a schedule. When the expression first returns a series, the alert is pending. It becomes firing only once the same series has kept matching on every evaluation for at least the for duration. If the series disappears for even one evaluation, the clock starts over. Three consequences follow: Detection time is about for plus one evaluation interval. A rule with for: 5m evaluated every minute fires five to six minutes after the problem starts. A series that flaps never fires. If the condition comes and goes faster than for, no alert is created, and no recovery either. That is the point of for, and also a risk. The defaults differ by tool. In Prometheus, leaving out for means 0, so the alert fires on the first evaluation that matches. In Nightingale's rule editor, a new rule starts at a 60-second for and a 60-second evaluation interval. The bundled templates set their own interval, almost always 15 or 30 seconds. How we counted​ The data is the alert rule templates bundled with Nightingale's integrations: Kubernetes, Linux, MySQL, Redis, Elasticsearch and 44 more. They are published in the alert rule library and on each integration page. 705 rules in total, 692 after removing exact duplicates (same integration, same name, same expression). Some checks exist twice on purpose, once for Categraf metrics and once for a Prometheus exporter, because the metric names differ. We count those separately. These are templates, not production configs. They show what template authors chose. They say nothing about what users changed after importing them. Counted on 2026-11-01, after the two changes described in Finding 4. The distribution​ for Rules Share 0 51 7.4% 60s 304 43.9% 2m 59 8.5% 3m 67 9.7% 5m 86 12.4% 10m 38 5.5% 15m 58 8.4% Over 15m 26 3.8% Three rules use 15s or 90s and are left out of the table. Finding 1: the default wins, unless someone chose deliberately​ The 60-second spike is the obvious feature. We can't tell from the data whether 304 authors thought about it and picked 60s, or simply kept what the form offered. What we can see is a clear difference between where the rules came from: 86 rules in the Kubernetes template keep the standard alert names from kubernetes-mixin and the Prometheus monitoring mixins, the community rule sets behind most Kubernetes monitoring stacks. 46 of them use 15 minutes, and only 2 use 60 seconds. The mixin authors set for alert by alert. Rules written for Categraf and for Prometheus exporters have a median of 60 seconds. Only 4 of the 352 use 15 minutes. Neither is wrong as a whole. The point is that a default is a choice someone else made for you, before they knew what the rule would watch. With the templates' 15- or 30-second evaluation intervals, a 60-second for means "matched on two to four evaluations in a row". That is reasonable for CPU, memory and latency. It is too short for things that recover on their own, and too long for events that are over in seconds. Finding 2: for: 0 is right for events, if the window is wide enough​ 51 rules fire on the first match (four of them are host heartbeat checks with no PromQL). Most of the rest watch something that has already happened, so waiting adds nothing: A counter went up: increase(node_vmstat_oom_kill[1m]) > 0. The OOM kill happened; it will not un-happen in five minutes. A deadline is close: kubelet_certificate_manager_client_ttl_seconds < 604800. Under seven days is under seven days. A process restarted: mysql_global_status_uptime < 60. The restart check hides a trap. uptime < 60 is only true for the first 60 seconds after a restart. Any for of 60 seconds or more means the alert can never fire, because uptime passes 60 before the duration is met. And the window has to fit several evaluations: copy uptime < 60 into a rule evaluated every 60 seconds, and it gets one chance per restart, which scrape delay can easily push out of the window. The templates get this right in different ways. The MySQL and MongoDB rules use uptime < 60 with for: 0, and they evaluate every 15 seconds, so each restart gets about four chances. The Redis rules widen the window to uptime_in_seconds < 600. The Apache, EMQX and OpenLDAP rules use uptime < 300 with for: 60s. Make the window several evaluation intervals wide, keep for well under it, and keep both in mind if you change the evaluation interval. Finding 3: some rules move the waiting into the expression​ Of the 47 for: 0 rules that have a PromQL expression, 22 wrap their metric in a range function, so the persistence check happens inside PromQL: # GitLab's ServiceDown template, for: 0 avg_over_time(up[5m]) * 100 < 50 This is not the same as up == 0 with for: 5m: up == 0 with for: 5m avg_over_time(up[5m]) < 0.5 with for: 0 Fires when Every evaluation in the last 5 minutes saw the target down The target was down for more than half of the last 5 minutes One good scrape in the middle Resets the clock Barely moves the average Good for "Continuously broken" "Mostly broken", for flapping targets Pick the one that matches what you mean. A target that answers one scrape in four is broken, and only the second form will say so. Finding 4: a few instant checks deserved a longer wait​ Counting also turned up for: 0 rules that compare a sampled value against a threshold with no window at all. Two of them we changed while writing this post: elasticsearch_cluster_health_status{color="yellow"} == 1. A cluster goes yellow on every rolling restart while replicas are reallocated. It now waits 10 minutes. (node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit) > 0.75. A single busy scrape was enough to trigger it. It now waits 5 minutes, the same as the sibling rule at 80%. The tables in this post already include both changes. The general rule: give sampled gauges a few evaluation intervals, or a range function as in Finding 3. Keep for: 0 for the checks that really are binary: mysql_up == 0, a failed systemd unit, a replication thread that stopped. Finding 5: long waits are for slow problems​ 26 rules wait longer than 15 minutes. Most of them watch something that develops slowly: The node filesystem predictions from kubernetes-mixin use one hour. A predict_linear forecast swings a lot on short windows; an hour of consistent prediction means the trend is real. Prometheus TSDB compaction failures wait four hours. One failed compaction is noise; a run of them is a problem. A kernel version mismatch across nodes waits six hours. It is a hygiene check, not an incident. The slow windows of the Kubernetes API error budget burn alerts wait one and three hours. They are designed to catch slow, steady burns. Long for values pair naturally with a lower severity. Nobody should be paged at 3 a.m. for something that took six hours to become true. The severity side​ The same templates carry a severity. Nightingale has three levels: S1 (critical), S2 (warning) and S3 (info). Severity Rules Share S2 / warning 490 71% S1 / critical 137 20% S3 / info 60 9% Five rules have no rule-level severity. When seven rules in ten share a level, the level stops helping anyone route or prioritize. A workable split: S1: someone must act now. Users are affected or data is about to be lost. S2: someone should look today. Capacity trends, single replicas down with redundancy left. S3: record it, don't notify. Useful context during an incident. 24 templates put several severities on one rule. The Linux CPU rule, for example, uses cpu_usage_active > 75 as S3, > 85 as S2 and > 95 as S1. One rule with three tiers keeps the thresholds side by side, which is easier to review than three separate rules that drift apart. Rules of thumb​ What the rule watches for Example Something that already happened 0 OOM kill counter increased, certificate under 7 days A binary up/down state 0 to 1 evaluation interval mysql_up == 0 A sampled gauge: CPU, memory, latency, error rate 2–3 evaluation intervals CPU over 90% Something that often recovers by itself Longer than its normal recovery time A queue that usually drains in 5 minutes: 10m A slow trend 30m to several hours, lower severity Disk full within 24 hours for only controls when an alert starts. If an alert fires and recovers over and over, for is not the fix. Use a recovery delay instead: keep_firing_for in Prometheus, or the recover duration in Nightingale. See Evaluation interval and recovery. Where to look next​ Every rule in the alert rule library shows its severity and its for value ("Fires after"), and links to a runbook. You can download a whole rule set as a Prometheus rules file, or import it into Nightingale from the matching integration. documents.t: Prometheus high availability: storage vs alerting November 1, 2026 · 7 min read Eric Qin Ask how to make Prometheus highly available and the usual answer is "run two of them". That is correct, and it is only half the job. Two replicas give you two copies of every alert and two slightly different copies of every time series. Each needs its own fix, and the fixes don't share a configuration. This post separates the two problems: keeping alerts flowing exactly once, and keeping the data queryable without gaps. It ends with a checklist. How Prometheus does HA​ Prometheus has no clustering. High availability means running two (or more) identical servers. Each one scrapes the same targets, evaluates the same rules and keeps its own local copy of the data. They don't talk to each other. The copies are never identical. Each replica scrapes at its own moment, so the timestamps differ. When one replica restarts, it has a gap that the other doesn't. That is fine for alerting, and a problem for dashboards. The usual convention is to give each replica an external label that says which one it is: # prometheus-a.yml (prometheus-b.yml says replica: b) global: external_labels: cluster: prod-eu replica: a Problem 1: alerts should arrive once, even when a replica dies​ Both replicas evaluate every rule, so both send every alert. Deduplication happens in Alertmanager. Cluster the Alertmanagers. Alertmanager instances gossip with each other. You start each one with --cluster.peer pointing at the others, and they share notification state and silences. When two replicas send the same alert, the cluster sends one notification. Point every Prometheus at every Alertmanager. The Alertmanager README is explicit: do not load-balance traffic between Prometheus and its Alertmanagers. Give each Prometheus the full list, because every alert has to reach every instance: alerting: alertmanagers: - static_configs: - targets: ['am-0:9093', 'am-1:9093', 'am-2:9093'] Drop the replica label from alerts. Alerts carry the external labels. If replica A sends {alertname="X", replica="a"} and replica B sends {alertname="X", replica="b"}, Alertmanager sees two different alerts and notifies twice. Strip the label on the way out: alerting: alert_relabel_configs: - action: labeldrop regex: replica The Prometheus Operator does this for you with its own replica label. Hand-built setups often miss it, and the symptom is that every page arrives twice. With these three in place, alerting HA works well. If replica A dies, replica B was evaluating the same rules all along, so there is no gap in detection. If an Alertmanager dies, Prometheus is still sending to the others. Problem 2: dashboards and queries should not show gaps​ This is the half that "run two" does not solve. Point Grafana at replica A, and you see replica A's gaps. Put a load balancer in front of both, and consecutive refreshes can hit different replicas and draw slightly different lines. The fix is a layer that knows the two replicas hold the same data and merges them. The three common options handle the replica label in different ways, and that difference matters: Store How it deduplicates What the replicas' labels must look like Thanos Thanos Querier merges series that differ only in the label named by --query.replica-label Different: each replica has its own replica value Grafana Mimir The HA tracker elects a leader replica per cluster, keeps its samples and drops the rest. It switches leader if the current one sends nothing for 30 seconds by default Different: cluster plus a __replica__ label by default VictoriaMetrics -dedup.minScrapeInterval keeps one sample per series per interval. Set it equal to your scrape_interval Identical: the docs require the HA pair to write the same series, so no per-replica label So a setup moved from Thanos to VictoriaMetrics needs its replica label removed, and a setup moved the other way needs one added. Mixing the conventions gives you either doubled series or a store that silently keeps one replica. Long-term retention is a separate decision from HA. Thanos, Mimir and VictoriaMetrics also keep data longer than a local Prometheus. But you can have deduplicated HA with short retention, or long retention with a single replica. Decide each one on its own. Scaling is not HA​ Federation, functional sharding (one Prometheus per team or per cluster) and hashmod sharding spread load. They don't add redundancy: each shard is still a single point of failure until you run it as a pair. If you shard, every shard needs the replica treatment above. Where a separate alerting engine changes the picture​ Everything above assumes Prometheus evaluates the rules. Some setups move evaluation out of Prometheus: Grafana Alerting, vmalert, Thanos Ruler, or Nightingale. Then storage HA and alerting HA become two different systems. Nightingale takes a different approach from a Prometheus pair, with a different trade-off: It queries one deduplicated data source. Prometheus behind Thanos Querier, VictoriaMetrics or Mimir. The storage-side HA from Problem 2 is still needed, and Nightingale doesn't replace it. Rules are shared out, not duplicated. Several n9e instances share one MySQL and one Redis. Each live instance sends a heartbeat every second. The live instances form a consistent hash ring per data source, and each rule runs on exactly one instance. One evaluation means one event, so no Alertmanager-style deduplication is needed. The trade-off is a failover gap. An instance counts as dead after 30 seconds without a heartbeat, and only then does its share of rules move to another instance. A freshly started instance also waits 30 seconds before evaluating. A Prometheus pair has no such gap, because the other replica was evaluating all along. Shared dependencies need their own HA. If MySQL is down, everything is down. If Redis is unreachable at startup, the process exits. Running several n9e instances protects against losing an n9e process, and nothing else. Neither design is better in general. Duplicate evaluation with downstream deduplication gives zero-gap failover and costs you a deduplication layer that must be configured exactly right. Single evaluation with a hash ring avoids duplicates by construction and costs you up to 30 seconds of blindness for the rules on a failed instance. The details are in High availability and failure domains. Checklist​ Alerting Two or more Prometheus replicas with identical rule files. Alertmanager clustered with --cluster.peer; the cluster port reachable between instances. Every Prometheus lists every Alertmanager. No load balancer in between. The replica label dropped in alert_relabel_configs. Tested: stop one replica and one Alertmanager, fire a test alert, and get exactly one notification. Storage and queries A deduplicating layer: Thanos Querier, Mimir's HA tracker or VictoriaMetrics deduplication. Replica labels set the way that layer expects. Thanos and Mimir need them to differ; VictoriaMetrics needs them identical. Dashboards and alert rules query the deduplicated endpoint, not a single replica. Tested: restart one replica and check that a dashboard over that window shows no gap. Everything The monitoring system is monitored from outside itself. A dead-man's-switch alert that always fires, and pages when it stops arriving, catches the case where the whole alerting path is down. The last item is the one most often skipped. Every check above runs inside the system it is checking.
