documents.t: Symptom-based alerting with Prometheus November 1, 2026 · 7 min read Eric Qin At 3 a.m. an alert says CPU is at 92% on db-3. The on-call engineer opens the dashboards. Checkout is fast, errors are flat, and nobody is affected. The alert was true and useless. A week later, checkout fails for 20 minutes because a dependency returns errors. CPU is fine, memory is fine, every host looks healthy. No alert fires. Both failures have the same root cause: the rules watch causes, not symptoms. This post explains the difference, shows what symptom rules look like in PromQL, and explains where cause alerts still earn their place. Symptoms and causes​ A symptom is what users experience: requests failing, pages loading slowly, a service unreachable, data arriving late. A cause is why: a saturated CPU, a full disk, a crashed pod, a slow query. The idea comes from Google's SRE book. Chapter 6, "Monitoring Distributed Systems", argues that paging should be driven by symptoms, and proposes four golden signals to watch on every user-facing system: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Rob Ewaschuk's essay "My Philosophy on Alerting", written while he was an SRE at Google, makes the same case in more detail. Cause-based paging fails in two directions: Causes without symptoms create noise. High CPU, a pod restart, one replica out of three down. Systems absorb these all the time. Each page that turns out to be harmless teaches people to ignore the next one. Symptoms without a known cause create silence. You can only write cause rules for failures you have imagined. A new failure mode, a dependency outage or a bad deploy that leaves every resource metric normal goes unnoticed. A symptom rule catches both the failures you predicted and the ones you didn't, because it watches the outcome instead of the mechanism. What symptom rules look like​ The metric names below follow common conventions. Yours will depend on your instrumentation library, ingress controller or service mesh. Errors: the share of requests that fail. sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout", code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m])) > 0.02 Use a ratio, not a count. 50 errors a minute is a disaster at 100 requests and noise at 100,000. Latency: how slow the slow requests are. histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout"}[5m])) ) > 1 Alert on a high percentile, not the average. An average of 200 ms can hide one request in fifty taking ten seconds. Availability from outside. A probe that calls the service the way a user would catches DNS, TLS, load balancer and network failures that internal metrics never see. With the Prometheus blackbox exporter that is probe_success == 0. Our Linux rule set includes an "HTTP probe failed" rule for Categraf's HTTP checks. Freshness and throughput for things that are not request-driven. Did the nightly job run? Is the queue draining? time() - batch_job_last_success_timestamp_seconds{job="nightly-export"} > 26 * 3600 Three details that make symptom rules work​ Measure where users are. The ingress or load balancer sees every request, including the ones that never reached a healthy pod. Per-pod error rates miss requests that were dropped before reaching any pod. Aggregate across instances. sum(...) over the whole service, not one alert per pod. Users don't care which replica failed them. Guard against low traffic. At three requests a minute, one failure is a 33% error ratio. Add a minimum volume: ( sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout", code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m])) ) > 0.02 and sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m])) > 1 Where cause alerts still belong​ "Alert on symptoms" doesn't mean "delete every cause alert". Some causes deserve a notification. They just shouldn't wake anyone up. Deadlines. A disk that will be full in 24 hours, or a certificate that expires in 7 days, is a symptom waiting to happen, with a known date. Alert on these during working hours, at warning severity. The Linux library has a predict_linear rule for disks; the Kubernetes library has certificate expiry rules. Lost redundancy. One replica of three is down. Users are fine, but the next failure will hurt them. That is worth a ticket today, not a page tonight. The monitoring itself. If a scrape target or collector stops reporting, every rule that depends on it looks healthy. up == 0, or a dead-man's-switch alert that always fires, is a cause alert you need from day one. Explanation. Everything else, such as CPU, memory, GC pauses and connection counts, belongs on a dashboard or as a low-severity alert that someone looks at while investigating a symptom. The Kubernetes rules in our library follow this: "Node CPU usage exceeds 90%" ships at info severity, while the symptom-shaped rules such as KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn go up to critical. Connecting symptoms to causes​ A symptom alert tells you that something is wrong. The responder then needs to know where to look. Two ways to close that gap: Put the causes in the runbook. Every symptom alert should link to a list of likely causes and the commands that confirm each one. Each page in our alert rule library follows that shape: what the alert means, common causes, then the steps to fix it. KubePodCrashLooping is a typical example. Mute symptoms while a known cause is active. If a whole site loses its uplink, every service there reports errors. Alertmanager's inhibit_rules, or an equivalent, can mute the dependent alerts while the upstream alert is firing. That needs a shared label such as site on both. A worked example​ Here is a rule set for a checkout service built on these ideas: Rule Kind Severity Who hears about it Error ratio above 2% for 5 minutes Symptom Critical Page p99 latency above 1 s for 10 minutes Symptom Critical Page External probe failing from 2 or more locations Symptom Critical Page Error ratio above 0.5% for 30 minutes Symptom, slow burn Warning Team channel Disk full within 24 hours Cause with a deadline Warning Team channel One of three replicas down for 15 minutes Lost redundancy Warning Team channel Scrape target down Monitoring Warning Team channel CPU, memory, GC, DB connections Cause Info or dashboard Nobody, until someone investigates Three rules can page, and all three describe something a customer would notice. Auditing a rule set you already have​ For each rule that can page, ask: if this fires and users are fine, would anyone do anything? If the answer is no, lower its severity or move it to a dashboard. Then look at the data. List the rules that fired most often in the last month and how many of those firings led to an action. Also list the rules that never fired in a year. They are usually broken rather than lucky: a renamed metric, a label that changed, a threshold that cannot be reached. Nightingale's built-in assistant can answer both questions directly ("which rules fired most often in the last 7 days, and which have never fired?"); see Common investigation workflows. For the rules that stay, the rule design best practices page covers naming, labels and how much one rule should cover. View all tags kube-state-metrics vs metrics-server vs cAdvisor vs node_exporter November 1, 2026 · 7 min read Eric Qin Kubernetes metrics come from four places, and their names look alike. kube_pod_container_resource_limits, container_memory_working_set_bytes, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes and the numbers in kubectl top all sound like they describe the same thing. They are made by different components and they answer different questions. Only three of the four are meant for monitoring. This post explains what each component measures and how to tell which one a metric came from. It also covers the renames that make a query copied from a 2019 blog post return nothing. Tags: Kubernetes Prometheus Alerting Read more How long should a Prometheus alert wait? Data from 692 rules November 1, 2026 · 9 min read Eric Qin Every alert rule answers two questions: what counts as bad, and how long it has to stay bad. Most review effort goes into the first one, the expression and the threshold. The second is the for duration, and it often gets whatever value the tool filled in. COLLECTOR Categraf Nightingale evaluates alerts on data you already have. Categraf is one way to put it there: a single agent covering operating systems, middleware, databases, network gear and Kubernetes, writing over Prometheus Remote Write. MIT licensed, built by the team behind Nightingale. 100+Collection plugins MITLicensed 1Agent per host Install and run Download a release build Archives are per platform and already contain the conf directory, so the agent runs straight out of the tarball. Linux ships for amd64 and arm64, Windows as a zip. Two variants sit beside the default build: -with-cgo-plugin adds the NVIDIA DCGM collector, and categraf-slim drops everything but metrics collection. tar xzf categraf-v<version>-linux-amd64.tar.gzcd categraf-v<version>-linux-amd64 The version is part of the filename, so there is no fixed “latest” URL — pick the build from the releases page. Releases on GitHub → Docker The image carries the binary at /usr/bin/categraf and the sample config at /etc/categraf/conf. Set N9E_HOST and the entrypoint rewrites the server address inside config.toml for you; mount your own conf directory when you need more than that. docker pull flashcatcloud/categraf:latestdocker run -d --name categraf -e N9E_HOST=192.168.1.10:17000 flashcatcloud/categraf:latest Build from source Go 1.25 or newer. Package the binary together with conf so the agent keeps its sample configuration alongside it. go buildtar zcvf categraf.tar.gz categraf conf On macOS use gnu-tar (gtar) — the bundled bsdtar produces an archive Categraf refuses to load. See what it collects before writing anywhere Test mode prints metrics straight to stdout, so you can confirm a plugin works before pointing the agent at a server. ./categraf --test./categraf --test --inputs system:mem Run it Configuration lives in the conf directory — config.toml for the agent itself, one input.<plugin> directory per collector. Restrict the run to specific plugins with --inputs. ./categraf./categraf --configs /path/to/conf-directory./categraf --inputs system:mem Connecting it to Nightingale, tagging hosts, and what to check when no data arrives are covered step by step in the docs. Categraf docs → Kubernetes A DaemonSet collects node and cAdvisor metrics, a Deployment covers cluster-level targets such as apiserver and CoreDNS, and a sidecar covers one service. The manifests ship in the repository. kubectl apply -n monitoring -f k8s/daemonset.yamlkubectl apply -n monitoring -f k8s/deployment.yamlkubectl apply -n monitoring -f k8s/sidecar.yaml What it collects Every plugin is a directory under inputs/ with its own sample config. A selection of what ships today: Operating system cpu mem disk diskio net netstat processes procstat system kernel systemd ntp Databases mysql postgresql oracle sqlserver mongodb redis clickhouse elasticsearch greenplum cassandra Middleware kafka rabbitmq nats nsq activemq zookeeper consul ldap Web and app servers nginx apache tomcat jboss weblogic phpfpm haproxy tengine jenkins logstash Containers and Kubernetes docker cadvisor kubernetes kubelet kube_state_metrics kube_proxy Network gear and hardware snmp snmp_trap switch_legacy ipmi redfish smart modbus gnmi vsphere GPU nvidia_smi dcgm amd_rocm_smi hy_smi Cloud aliyun cloudwatch googlecloud appdynamics Probes ping http_response net_response dns_query x509_cert whois Generic exec prometheus node_exporter mtail tpl Where the data goes Categraf pushes over the Prometheus Remote Write protocol, so it writes into Nightingale, Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or anything else that speaks it. Push means the agent opens the connection — which matters when network policy will not let a central server reach into every subnet. Register it as a data source → Not the only option Nightingale does not require Categraf. Telegraf, the Datadog Agent and standard Prometheus exporters write in the same way, and a Prometheus that already scrapes your targets can stay exactly as it is. Categraf source and releases →

Nothing in the collection path changes. 2 Move the rules across The migration guides map every entry of an alertmanager.yml or a Grafana alert rule onto a Nightingale object, and say plainly which ones have no equivalent. 3 Run both, cut over by channel Compare what fires each day, switch one notification channel at a time, and back out of any stage in about a minute. Coexistence and rollback plan → Questions people ask before switching Can I keep Grafana? Yes, and it is the most common setup: chart in Grafana, alert in Nightingale. A Nightingale dashboard can also embed a Grafana dashboard by URL. Do I have to replace Prometheus? No. Prometheus keeps scraping and storing; Nightingale takes over rules, noise reduction and routing on top of it, so nothing has to move. Can Alertmanager rules be migrated? Rules, routes, silences and receivers each map onto a Nightingale object. The migration guide takes an alertmanager.yml apart entry by entry and lists the few that have no equivalent. Can Nightingale read Zabbix data? No. Moving from Zabbix is a rebuild: hosts become targets, templates become integrations, triggers become rules, and Categraf takes over collection. Zabbix never has to stop while you do it. When should I not switch? At moderate scale, with a GitOps-comfortable team and a rule count you can hold in your head, Prometheus + Alertmanager is enough. For network gear and SNMP-first estates, Zabbix is still home ground. Not sure? Run both. Nightingale reads the storage you already have. documents.t: Comparisons Grafana Alerting Nightingale vs Grafana Alerting The short answer: Grafana is a visualization platform that ships alerting as one module; Nightingale (n9e) is an open-source alerting engine that makes alerting the whole product. Nightingale does not try to replace Grafana dashboards, so the comparison is about the alerting layer, and for many teams the answer is both: chart in Grafana, alert in Nightingale. Try live demoInstall in 5 minutes The 30-second version Stay on Grafana Alerting if alert volume is modest, rules follow panels, Slack or PagerDuty contact points are enough, and the team already lives in Grafana. One system fewer is one system fewer to run. Move to Nightingale if the rule count has outgrown panel-level management, you need event pipelines, subscriptions or self-healing, on-call people need phone and SMS, or permissions should follow business groups rather than folders. Use both if the dashboard estate is large. Grafana data sources import into Nightingale in one step, dashboards stay exactly where they are, and a Nightingale dashboard can embed Grafana panels by URL. Their way Alerting as a module inside the visualization platform. The Nightingale way Alerting as the whole product; chart wherever you like. Where it shines Grafana is the visualization standard and its dashboard ecosystem has no real substitute. If alert volume is modest and Grafana is already in place, its built-in alerting is one system fewer to run. When Nightingale fits better Nightingale puts everything into the alerting side: event pipelines, subscriptions, self-healing. The two are not exclusive — plenty of users chart in Grafana and alert in Nightingale. Signs it is time to switch Alert volume has outgrown a panel-level rule model You need event pipelines, subscriptions or self-healing On-call people need phone and SMS, not only contact points Grafana · MySQL overview A Grafana panel embedded by URL in a Nightingale dashboard S1MySQL replica lag > 30s ident=mysql-prodbusigroup=DBA Delivered · phone and DingTalk Chart in Grafana, alert in Nightingale You Analyze this dashboard Nightingale AI Of 40 panels, 3 query metrics that no longer exist, and 2 show an abnormal trend in the last hour: connections and slow_queries. How the objects map Where each part of Grafana unified alerting lands once it is taken apart. Dashboards, panels and variables are not touched. Grafana Nightingale Data sources One-step import (Integrations → Data sources → Import from Grafana); secrets must be re-entered Grafana-managed alert rules Rewritten: Reduce + Threshold folded into PromQL Data-source-managed rules These are Prometheus ruler rules; follow the Alertmanager path Notification policy tree Flattened into notification rules Contact point Notification media + notification rule Silence / mute timing Fixed-time mute / recurring mute or a time window on the notification config NoData / Error state No-data switch on log and SQL rules; a separate up == 0 rule for Prometheus runbook_url The runbook link field on the rule When you cut over, pause the Grafana rules rather than delete them; rolling back is then one click. From Grafana Alerting →Coexistence and rollback plan → Questions about this comparison Can I keep using Grafana for charts? Yes, and it is the most common setup. Nightingale reads the same Prometheus or Loki, so Grafana panels are unaffected, and a Nightingale dashboard can embed Grafana panels by URL. Can Grafana alert rules be imported automatically? Rules cannot; data sources can. “Import from Grafana” pulls the data sources into a preview table, you tick the ones you want and re-enter secrets. Alert rules are rewritten following the guide, because the expression-chain and PromQL models differ. What happens to Grafana’s No data state? Nightingale has no such state machine. In Prometheus rules a series disappearing counts as recovery; to alert on missing data, write a separate up == 0 rule. Log and SQL rules have a no-data switch with its own severity and auto-recovery timeout. Does Nightingale have phone and SMS notifications? Yes, phone and SMS are built-in media types in the open-source edition. Grafana OSS contact points have no phone or SMS; Grafana OnCall OSS was archived in March 2026 and on-call capabilities live in Grafana Cloud. What about group_by in notification policies? Nightingale sends one event per notification and does no label aggregation. If the on-call flow depends on seeing a group of alerts in one message, accept that difference before switching; noise is cut by rule merging, mute rules and subscriptions instead. How to choose an open-source alerting platform "Alerting platform" means the last layer of monitoring: once the data exists, who evaluates it, how noise is cut, and who gets told. Collection and storage are out of scope here, and so is visualization. The open-source choices at this layer are few, but they differ a lot. First the tools are sorted into three kinds, then six questions are asked of each. Three kinds of tool​ Kind What it does Examples Alerting engine Runs queries itself, evaluates, cuts noise, delivers Prometheus + Alertmanager, Grafana Alerting, Nightingale Aggregation layer Receives alerts other systems already produced; deduplicates, correlates, delivers Keep, Alerta On-call delivery Schedules, escalations, phone wake-ups Mostly commercial; Grafana OnCall OSS is archived Step one is deciding which layer you lack. Data with no alerts yet: an engine. Three systems each already alerting: an aggregation layer. Alerts accurate enough but nobody answering the phone: on-call delivery. Do rules live in files or in a UI?​ In the Alertmanager world, rules are Prometheus YAML managed by reload and GitOps, with no UI editing and no permission model. Grafana Alerting and Nightingale both configure in the UI and both export and import. Ownership differs: Grafana uses folders and org roles, with fine-grained RBAC in Enterprise; Nightingale uses business groups, which are also the permission boundary and decide who can see, who can edit and where mutes apply. If only SREs maintain rules, files plus GitOps are the leanest option; if product teams configure their own, a UI and a permission boundary are hard requirements. Looking for an Alertmanager UI?​ Most people who search for an Alertmanager UI want one of two things, and they have different answers. A better view of firing alerts. Alertmanager's built-in web UI (port 9093) lists alerts and lets you create silences. karma adds grouping and a dashboard across several Alertmanagers, and Grafana can add Alertmanager as a data source to browse alerts and manage silences. All of these sit on top of Alertmanager and leave it unchanged. Editing rules and routing without touching YAML. None of the tools above do this: Prometheus rules and alertmanager.yml stay files. To manage rules, routing and mutes in a UI with per-team permissions, the alerting layer itself has to move. Grafana Alerting does that inside Grafana; Nightingale does it as a standalone engine that queries Prometheus directly, and Migrating from Prometheus + Alertmanager shows how alertmanager.yml maps onto it. Nightingale does not receive alerts from Alertmanager, so it replaces that layer rather than sitting on top of it. Is the data in one place or several?​ Alertmanager only handles alerts evaluated by Prometheus (Loki alerts go through its own ruler). Grafana Alerting spans any data source it supports alerting on. Nightingale registers Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Elasticsearch, Loki, ClickHouse, MySQL and others, 10+ types, so metric, log and SQL rules all live in one place. Keep and Alerta do not query data; they only receive alerts. What cuts the noise: grouping, inhibition, mutes, subscriptions​ This is where the three engines differ most. Alertmanager: label-based grouping into one message (group_by), cross-rule inhibition (inhibit_rules), one-off silences, recurring mute intervals on routes. A clean model, all in config files. Grafana Alerting: embeds an Alertmanager, so grouping and silences match, but Grafana-managed alerts do not support inhibition rules. Nightingale: no label grouping, one event per notification. Noise is cut by merging at the rule level (one rule covers every series its query returns), fixed and recurring mutes (optionally muting notifications while keeping the event), subscription rules (conditional copies, timeout escalation) and event pipelines (processors that rewrite, drop or call back). Cross-rule inhibition has no declarative form; it is a pipeline rewrite. Keep / Alerta: deduplication and correlation are their main job, on alerts some other system produced. If the on-call flow depends on seeing a group of alerts in one message, the Alertmanager family fits better. If events must be routed to different people by business condition and rewritten before delivery, Nightingale fits better. How does the on-call person get woken up?​ Among the open-source engines only Nightingale ships phone and SMS media types, alongside DingTalk, Feishu, WeCom, Slack, Telegram and others, 20 channels in total. Alertmanager receivers are email, Slack, PagerDuty and webhooks first; Grafana contact points cover the main chat tools and also lack phone and SMS. None of the three has a schedule: on-call rotation in the open-source world is mostly left to commercial products, and Grafana OnCall OSS was archived in March 2026. Who can change a rule, and where is the boundary?​ Alertmanager and Prometheus have no authentication or permissions; isolation happens at the deployment level. Grafana OSS has org roles and folder permissions. Nightingale has users, teams and business groups; rules, mutes, subscriptions and targets belong to a business group, and data sources can be granted per group. When several product teams share one alerting platform, this question usually decides. What can AI do here?​ Alertmanager has no built-in AI. Grafana Assistant is Cloud-only; OSS relies on the LLM plugin and a separate MCP server. Nightingale runs an AI assistant and 74 MCP tools in-process across 13 toolsets, read tools on by default, write tools off, no delete tools; clients such as Claude Code and Cursor connect to the /mcp endpoint directly and inherit the user's token permissions. Keep applies AI to alert correlation. One table​ Dimension Prometheus + Alertmanager Grafana Alerting Nightingale Keep Alerta Kind Engine Engine Engine Aggregation Aggregation Where rules live YAML files UI + provisioning UI + import/export Does not evaluate Does not evaluate Data sources Prometheus Any alerting-capable source 10+ types: metrics, logs, SQL Receives alerts Receives alerts Grouping into one message Yes Yes No Correlation Correlation Cross-rule inhibition Yes No Pipeline rewrite Correlation rules Correlation rules Phone and SMS Third party Third party Built in Third party Third party Permission model None Roles + folders Business-group RBAC Yes Yes Built-in AI None Cloud only Assistant + MCP Alert correlation None License Apache-2.0 AGPL-3.0 Apache-2.0 Open core with an enterprise directory Apache-2.0 Recommendations by team profile​ Small team, all data in Prometheus, comfortable with GitOps: Prometheus + Alertmanager. Fewest components, cleanest model. Heavy Grafana users, moderate alert volume, contact points suffice: Grafana Alerting. One system fewer. Several data sources, product teams configuring their own rules, phone and SMS and chat tools required, AI-assisted investigation wanted: Nightingale. Full comparisons: Nightingale vs Prometheus + Alertmanager and Nightingale vs Grafana Alerting. Three monitoring systems already alerting, want one inbox: an aggregation layer such as Keep or Alerta. Nightingale is not one. Coming from Zabbix: start with Zabbix alternatives, then Nightingale vs Zabbix. Questions​ Is an alerting platform the same thing as a monitoring system? No. A monitoring system usually has four layers: collection, storage, visualization and alerting. This page is about the last one only: evaluation, noise reduction, delivery. Prometheus is storage plus evaluation, Grafana is visualization plus an alerting module, Nightingale is an engine built for the alerting layer alone. Can Nightingale receive alerts from Alertmanager or Zabbix? No. Nightingale is an alerting engine that runs its own queries; it has no inbound alert endpoint. To consolidate alerts other systems already produce, look at aggregation layers such as Keep or Alerta. Is there a UI for Alertmanager? Alertmanager ships a web UI for viewing alerts and creating silences, and karma or Grafana add richer alert dashboards on top. None of them edit alert rules or routing; those stay in YAML files. If you want rules, routing and mutes managed in a UI with permissions, the alerting layer itself has to change, for example to Grafana Alerting or Nightingale. Do the open-source editions have phone and SMS? Nightingale does; phone and SMS are built-in media types in its open-source edition. Alertmanager and Grafana OSS have neither and rely on third parties such as PagerDuty; Grafana OnCall OSS was archived in March 2026. Based on each project's public documentation and open-source edition as of October 2026; a guide, not a verdict. Nightingale figures come from build-time data. If something here is out of date, open an issue on GitHub. On this page Three kinds of tool Do rules live in files or in a UI? Looking for an Alertmanager UI? Is the data in one place or several? What cuts the noise: grouping, inhibition, mutes, subscriptions How does the on-call person get woken up? Who can change a rule, and where is the boundary? What can AI do here? documents.t: Comparisons Prometheus + Alertmanager Nightingale vs Prometheus + Alertmanager Prometheus stays. The exporters stay. The Grafana panels stay. Alertmanager is the only component this comparison actually replaces: rules move from YAML into the UI, the routing tree is flattened into notification rules, and silences become mute rules with a business-group boundary. Try live demoInstall in 5 minutes The 30-second version Stay on Prometheus + Alertmanager if the team is comfortable with GitOps, the rule count fits in one head, and webhooks into PagerDuty or a similar on-call tool are all the delivery you need. The pair is mature and adds no components; nothing here says switch for its own sake. Move to Nightingale if rules must be maintained in a UI by teams who are not SREs, permissions have to follow business groups, someone has to be phoned rather than webhooked, or the data is no longer only in Prometheus: logs in Elasticsearch, business metrics in MySQL. Run both if you want evidence first. Register Prometheus as a data source and Nightingale evaluates the same rules while Alertmanager keeps delivering; switch one notification channel at a time and back out of any step in about a minute. Their way Rules live in YAML and ship through GitOps. The Nightingale way Rules live in the UI, scoped by business group. Where it shines Prometheus remains one of the best time-series foundations available, and Alertmanager’s grouping and silencing model is genuinely clean. At moderate scale, with a GitOps-comfortable team and a rule count you can hold in your head, the pair is enough and adds no components. When Nightingale fits better Nightingale earns its place when rules must be maintained by teams who are not SREs, when permissions need to follow business groups, when someone has to be phoned at 3am, or when the data is not all in Prometheus. Signs it is time to switch Rules must be maintained by teams who are not SREs Someone has to be phoned at 3am, not just webhooked The data is no longer all in Prometheus rules.yml + alertmanager.yml - alert: MysqlReplicaLag expr: mysql_slave_lag_seconds > 30 for: 5m labels: { team: dba }route: receiver: dba-webhook group_by: [alertname] Nightingale · alert rule Name MySQL replica lag Condition mysql_slave_lag_seconds > 30, for 5m Business group DBA Notify Phone, SMS, DingTalk Who can edit DBA group One rule, two ways to write it You Create in one sentence: page the DBA group by phone when mysql-prod replica lag stays above 30s for 5 minutes Nightingale AI PromQL and threshold drafted. I will not guess the business group; pick one from the list and I will create the rule. Side by side Capability comparison Capability comparison Nightingale v9 Prometheus + Alertmanager Data sources Built in: Metrics, logs and SQL stores, 10+ types Not available: Evaluates Prometheus data only Where rules live Built in: In the UI, owned by a business group; a whole rules.yml can be imported Not available: YAML files and a reload; no UI editing Rule language Built in: Same PromQL, threshold inside the expression Built in: PromQL Notification grouping Not available: One event per notification; no label-based batching into one message Built in: group_by / group_wait / group_interval Cross-rule inhibition Partial or via add-on: Built in across severity tiers of one rule; across rules it is an event pipeline rewrite Built in: inhibit_rules Silences / mutes Built in: Fixed and recurring windows, mute-notifications-only, scoped to a business group Partial or via add-on: One-off silences; recurring windows via mute_time_intervals on routes Notification channels Built in: 20 built in, including phone, SMS, DingTalk, Feishu and WeCom Partial or via add-on: Email, Slack, PagerDuty, Telegram, WeChat, webhooks; phone, SMS, DingTalk and Feishu need third parties Subscriptions and collaboration Built in: Subscription rules, timeout escalation, event pipeline processors Not available: None Permissions Built in: Users, teams, business-group RBAC Not available: No authentication or permission model Dashboards Partial or via add-on: Built in, can embed Grafana panels by URL Not available: Expression browser only; Grafana is the usual companion Self-healing Built in: Script execution via ibex Not available: None AI / MCP Built in: Built-in assistant and 74 MCP tools Not available: None License Built in: Apache-2.0 Built in: Apache-2.0, CNCF graduated Built in Partial or via add-on Not available Based on the publicly documented capabilities of each project’s open-source edition as of August 2026. We try to state what the other tools are good at — advice you cannot trust is worth nothing to a community. How the objects map Take a rules.yml and an alertmanager.yml apart, and here is where each piece lands. The entry-by-entry mapping, the method for flattening the routing tree and the four asymmetries are in the migration guide. Prometheus / Alertmanager Nightingale Alerting rules in rules.yml Alert rules; paste the whole file into “Import Prometheus alert rules” Recording rules Untouched, Prometheus keeps computing them receivers[] Notification media plus a notification config inside a notification rule The route tree Flattened: every root-to-leaf path becomes one notification config with its matchers ANDed group_by / group_wait / group_interval No equivalent; one event per notification inhibit_rules No declarative equivalent; rewrite as a drop processor in an event pipeline Silence Mute rule, which must belong to a business group Alertmanager cluster Several alert engine instances shard the rules; no gossip needed Two traps: a notification config with no severity ticked matches nothing, not everything; and an event that lacks a label never matches, even for != and !~, whereas Alertmanager treats a missing label as an empty string. From Prometheus + Alertmanager →Coexistence and rollback plan → Questions about this comparison Do I have to replace Prometheus? No. Prometheus keeps scraping and storing; Nightingale registers it as a data source and runs instant queries against it on a schedule, so nothing has to move. Thanos, Mimir and VictoriaMetrics connect the same way. Can alertmanager.yml be converted automatically? The alert rules can: paste rules.yml into Rules → Import → Import Prometheus alert rules. Routes, receivers and silences are rebuilt entry by entry following the migration guide, because Nightingale uses flat notification rules rather than a routing tree. Can Nightingale receive webhooks from Alertmanager? No. Nightingale has no inbound alert endpoint, only metric write endpoints, so Alertmanager cannot sit in front of it as a forwarder during a transition. Rules are rebuilt inside Nightingale. What happens to Alertmanager grouping? Nightingale sends one event per notification and does not batch alerts into one message by label. Noise is cut at the rule level instead (one rule covers every series the query returns), plus mute rules and subscriptions. If your on-call flow depends on grouped messages, accept that difference before you switch. Do I have to stop Alertmanager to switch? Only as the final step. Everything before it runs with Prometheus and Alertmanager untouched: import rules disabled, enable one business group as a canary, compare in parallel, then remove the alerting rules from rule_files and stop Alertmanager last. Other comparisons Nightingale vs Zabbix → Nightingale vs Grafana Alerting → Comparisons → Not sure? Run both. Nightingale reads the storage you already have. Installing it changes nothing about the alerting you run today. Try live demoInstall in 5 minutes

Comparisons Zabbix Nightingale vs Zabbix Zabbix is built around hosts and items: it collects, stores and alerts on its own. Nightingale is built around queries: it evaluates on the Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or Elasticsearch you already run, and Categraf fills only the gaps. This is not one product beating another; two architectures fit two kinds of infrastructure. Try live demoInstall in 5 minutes The 30-second version Stay on Zabbix if the estate is mostly network gear, SNMP and IPMI, you lean on auto-discovery and LLD, and the team has years of Zabbix experience. Two decades of work in that space has no complete open-source substitute. Move to Nightingale if metrics already live in Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics, logs in Elasticsearch or Loki, Kubernetes and cloud services outnumber racks, or you keep both a Zabbix agent and exporters running just to get one alert. Run both if you want to migrate in batches. Categraf and the Zabbix agent coexist on the same host; let Nightingale deliver to one dedicated channel first, compare what fired each day, and never stop Zabbix. Their way Collect everything with its own agents, then alert on that. The Nightingale way Alert on the stores you already fill; collect only where nothing does. Where it shines Two decades of work show in traditional IT monitoring: network gear, SNMP, agent-based collection and auto-discovery are its home ground, and the hiring pool knows it well. When Nightingale fits better If your telemetry already lives in Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or ElasticSearch, Nightingale reads it directly instead of asking you to pour it into a second collection stack. Signs it is time to switch Telemetry already lives in Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or ElasticSearch Kubernetes and cloud services outnumber network gear You maintain two collection stacks to get one alert Storage you already run PrometheusVictoriaMetricsElasticSearchClickHouse NightingaleReads in place, moves nothing 20 notification channels Phone / SMSEmailDingTalkSlack+16 Categraf fills only the gaps You Why did this host go offline? Nightingale AI The agent stopped reporting 3 minutes ago, but the host answers ping and its neighbours are healthy. That points to the Categraf process exiting, not the host going down. Side by side Capability comparison Capability comparison Nightingale v9 Zabbix Collection model Partial or via add-on: Categraf or your existing exporters, pushed over Remote Write Built in: Zabbix agent / agent 2, SNMP, IPMI, JMX, auto-discovery and LLD Storage Built in: Embedded TSDB for small, single-Center setups; also reads Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Elasticsearch and ClickHouse. Multi-Center deployments use an external TSDB Built in: Its own server with MySQL / PostgreSQL / TimescaleDB What a rule covers Built in: One rule covers every series the query returns Partial or via add-on: Triggers are generated per host; a template on 1,000 hosts is 1,000 trigger sets Rule language Built in: PromQL / SQL / LogQL, depending on the source Built in: Trigger expressions and function library Severity levels Partial or via add-on: Three: S1 / S2 / S3 Built in: Six Trigger dependencies Partial or via add-on: No declarative dependencies; rewrite with an event pipeline Built in: Trigger dependencies and event correlation Maintenance / mutes Built in: Fixed and recurring mutes, mute-notifications-only keeps the event Built in: Maintenance periods Notification channels Built in: 20 built in; phone, SMS, DingTalk, Feishu and WeCom work out of the box Partial or via add-on: Email, script and webhook media types; Chinese IM mostly via community templates Escalation Partial or via add-on: Subscription rules escalate after a duration Built in: Multi-step escalations Permissions Built in: Users, teams, business-group RBAC; the business group is the boundary Built in: User groups, roles, host-group permissions Kubernetes Built in: Reads Prometheus data as is; Categraf ships Kubernetes plugins Partial or via add-on: Official Helm chart and templates, needs its own agents Network gear / SNMP Partial or via add-on: Categraf has an SNMP plugin, no auto-discovery Built in: Home ground: SNMP, discovery, network templates Log alerting Built in: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Loki, VictoriaLogs, ClickHouse Partial or via add-on: Log items with regex, not queries against a log store AI / MCP Built in: Built-in assistant and 74 MCP tools Not available: None License Built in: Apache-2.0 Partial or via add-on: AGPL-3.0 since 7.0 Built in Partial or via add-on Not available Based on the publicly documented capabilities of each project’s open-source edition as of August 2026. We try to state what the other tools are good at — advice you cannot trust is worth nothing to a community. How the objects map What each kind of Zabbix object is called in Nightingale, and which have no equivalent at all. The full table and the rebuild order that keeps Zabbix running throughout are in the migration guide. Zabbix Nightingale Zabbix server Nightingale plus a time-series store (the embedded TSDB is on by default; move to an external one at scale) Zabbix agent Categraf, or exporters you already run; both coexist on one host Host / host group Target (ident) / business group, which is also the permission boundary Template A component in the template center, 83 built in; import is a one-time copy Item No equivalent; what is collected is decided in the collector config Trigger Alert rule; one covers every object the query returns Low-level discovery No equivalent; as many series as the query returns, that many objects Action + media type Notification rule + notification media + message template Maintenance Mute rule Nightingale has no importer for Zabbix templates or triggers and cannot read its XML or YAML. Coming from Zabbix is a rebuild, not a move; the good news is that it is smaller than it looks: built-in components replace most templates, and one rule replaces a whole set of triggers. From Zabbix →Coexistence and rollback plan → Questions about this comparison Can Nightingale read Zabbix data directly? No. Nightingale data sources are query backends such as Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and Elasticsearch; the Zabbix history and trends tables are not among them. Leave the history in Zabbix as a read-only archive; nothing needs to be moved. Can Zabbix templates be imported? Not mechanically. The template center ships 83 components covering operating systems, databases, middleware and Kubernetes, so most standard Zabbix templates have a counterpart; custom triggers are rewritten one by one using the merge method in the guide. Can Nightingale monitor switches and routers? It can collect them, but it is not home ground. Categraf has an SNMP plugin that polls OIDs and Nightingale alerts on the result, but there is no network auto-discovery or mature device template library like Zabbix has. For device-heavy estates, keep Zabbix on the devices and put Nightingale on cloud and applications. How do the six Zabbix severities map? Down to three: Disaster and High become S1, Average and Warning become S2, Information and Not classified become S3. Information is lost in that step, so compare severities against this mapping during the parallel run. Does Zabbix have to stop during the migration? Never. Install Categraf, settle the storage, import built-in templates, translate the remaining triggers, build notifications, move maintenance windows, compare in parallel, then stop the Zabbix actions first and the agents a week later. Rolling back is disabling the Nightingale rules in bulk. Other comparisons Nightingale vs Prometheus + Alertmanager → Nightingale vs Grafana Alerting → Comparisons → Not sure? Run both. Nightingale reads the storage you already have. Installing it changes nothing about the alerting you run today. Try live demoInstall in 5 minutes

Open-source Zabbix alternatives: pick by scenario, not by ranking Searching for "Zabbix alternatives" returns ten-item lists with two sentences per tool. This page goes the other way: first why you want to leave, then where your data and objects would go, then one honest paragraph per candidate, including where it does not fit. Nightingale (n9e, 夜莺) is our own project; it appears only in the rows where it genuinely belongs. Why people leave Zabbix​ Three common reasons, and one counter-example that gets skipped too often. The database becomes the bottleneck. The history and trends tables grow with hosts times items; partitioning, the housekeeper and TimescaleDB are all ways of fighting that. Metric time-series stores were built for exactly this data. The environment went cloud-native. Kubernetes pods appear and vanish by the minute; a host-and-item model needs discovery and agents to keep up, and the metrics for these environments usually already live in Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics. Collecting them again with Zabbix means running two collection stacks. The alerting layer has new requirements. Noise reduction, permissions by business group, phone and SMS, chat tools, self-healing, AI-assisted investigation. Zabbix can do parts of it, but through script media types and outside systems. The counter-example: if the estate is mostly network gear, SNMP and IPMI, the team has years of Zabbix experience and the system runs stably, there is no reason to move. Two decades of work in that space has no complete open-source substitute. Three questions before switching​ Where is the data now? If metrics are already in Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics and logs in Elasticsearch or Loki, the replacement should read those stores rather than collect again. If the data exists only inside Zabbix, the replacement needs its own collection. What are you monitoring? Switches, routers and out-of-band IPMI are one world; Kubernetes, cloud databases and microservices are another. The first is about discovery and device templates, the second about query languages and multiple data sources. Who maintains the alert rules? SREs only: config files plus GitOps are enough. Product teams: a UI and a permission boundary are hard requirements. Choose by scenario​ Your situation Better fit Why Mostly network gear, SNMP, IPMI Stay on Zabbix; LibreNMS for pure network Discovery and device template libraries are their home ground Metrics already in Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics, lots of Kubernetes Nightingale, or Prometheus + Alertmanager Alert on the stores you have; no second collection stack The team already lives in Grafana, modest alert volume Grafana Alerting One system fewer Product teams configure rules in a UI, permissions by business group, phone and SMS Nightingale Those are the things it is built around Unified APM with traces, metrics and logs SigNoz OpenTelemetry-native A few dozen hosts, want charts right after install Netdata; or Nightingale with its embedded TSDB Zero-config start Traditional IT, just want a nicer interface Checkmk Raw Same model family as Zabbix, lowest concept migration cost The seven candidates, one at a time​ Prometheus + Alertmanager (Apache-2.0)​ The de facto standard for cloud-native metrics: pull model, exporter ecosystem, PromQL. Rules live in YAML and are evaluated by Prometheus; Alertmanager groups, inhibits, silences and routes. It shines exactly where Zabbix struggles: dynamic environments, service discovery, high-cardinality labels. The price is no UI for rules, no permission model, and webhook-first delivery with phone, SMS and most chat tools left to third parties. At moderate scale with a GitOps-comfortable team it is the leanest choice. Nightingale (Apache-2.0)​ An open-source alerting engine hosted by the China Computer Federation's open-source committee. It does not need the data moved: Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Elasticsearch, ClickHouse and other sources (10+ types) are registered and queried in place; Categraf fills the gaps, with 83 built-in integrations bundling collector config, dashboards and rules. Rules are configured in the UI, business groups are the permission boundary, phone, SMS, DingTalk, Feishu and WeCom are among 20 built-in channels, and an AI assistant with 74 MCP tools runs in-process. Not its ground: network device discovery, Zabbix-style multi-step escalation ladders, and it is not an aggregation layer, so it cannot receive alerts from other systems. Full comparison: Nightingale vs Zabbix. Grafana Alerting (AGPL-3.0)​ Grafana's built-in unified alerting: rules across many data sources, an Alertmanager-style notification policy tree, contact points for the main chat tools. If the team already lives in Grafana it is the one-system-fewer option. Watch the OSS permission granularity (fine-grained RBAC is Enterprise), the lack of phone and SMS contact points, and the fact that Grafana OnCall OSS was archived in March 2026 with on-call living in Grafana Cloud. See Nightingale vs Grafana Alerting. Checkmk Raw Edition (GPL-2.0)​ The same generation of model as Zabbix: agents plus automatic service discovery, thousands of check plugins, complete SNMP and traditional-IT coverage, and a more modern interface. It is the lowest-cost move when what you want is "a nicer Zabbix". Raw is the open-source edition; the CMC core and several features are commercial. Netdata (GPL-3.0)​ Per-second collection, auto-configured dashboards, usable minutes after a single-host install, low footprint. Good for a few dozen machines and teams that want to see charts first; often used alongside Zabbix rather than instead of it. Multi-node views and long retention go through Netdata Cloud, which has free and paid tiers. LibreNMS (GPL-3.0)​ SNMP-centred network monitoring: discovery, device templates, topology, traffic graphs, alert rules. If Zabbix is mainly your switch-and-router view, LibreNMS is the closest open-source replacement; it is not a general metrics or log alerting platform. SigNoz (Apache-2.0)​ An OpenTelemetry-native observability platform with traces, metrics and logs in ClickHouse and built-in alerting. It solves unified APM rather than infrastructure monitoring; "Zabbix alternative" only holds when what you really want is APM. What moving from Zabbix to Nightingale involves​ It is a rebuild, not a move: Nightingale has no importer for Zabbix templates or triggers. The work is smaller than it looks, because one Nightingale rule covers every series its query returns; the thousand trigger sets a template generates on a thousand hosts are usually one rule. The order: install Categraf (the Zabbix agent stays), settle the storage, import built-in templates, translate the remaining triggers, build notifications, move maintenance windows, compare in parallel, then stop Zabbix actions first and agents a week later. Every step verifies on its own; rolling back is disabling the Nightingale rules in bulk. Step by step: From Zabbix and Coexistence and rollback plan. Questions​ Can Nightingale read Zabbix data directly? No. Nightingale data sources are query backends such as Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics and Elasticsearch; the Zabbix history and trends tables are not among them. Leave the history in Zabbix as a read-only archive; nothing has to be moved. How long does leaving Zabbix take? It depends on the number of custom triggers. Built-in templates cover most of the standard ones; custom triggers and notification actions are rewritten one by one. The usual approach is one business group at a time, each running in parallel for a week or two, with Zabbix never stopping. Is there one open-source tool for both network gear and cloud-native alerting? None is home ground on both sides. In practice the work is split: Zabbix or LibreNMS keeps the switches, routers and IPMI, Nightingale or Prometheus takes Kubernetes and applications, and notifications land in the same channels. Did the Zabbix license change? Yes. Zabbix 7.0 moved from GPL-2.0 to AGPL-3.0. Nothing changes for internal deployments; if you embed it in a service offered to others, read the AGPL network clause. Based on each project's public documentation and open-source edition as of October 2026; a guide, not a verdict. Nightingale figures come from build-time data. documents.t: Point Nightingale at the Prometheus, log stores and databases you already run, then set up rules, noise reduction, routing and delivery. Every step is written down here. Why isn't my alert rule firing? Bring it up in 5 minutesLive demo

This page lets hosts with Datadog Agent keep their collectors and send compatible metric series to Nightingale. Compatibility Nightingale v9 registers /datadog/api/v1/series. It is not a complete Datadog backend and does not provide a v2 series receiver. The settings below are checked against Datadog Agent 7.70.0. Verify that other versions still support v1 before using them.

Edit /etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml on Linux: api_key: "replace-with-agent-key" dd_url: "http://127.0.0.1:17000/datadog" use_v2_api: series: false Replace the URL and key. End dd_url at /datadog; the Agent appends the API path itself. Changing dd_url alone is insufficient: Agent 7.70.0 enables v2 series by default. Setting use_v2_api.series: false selects the v1 JSON format Nightingale receives. Enable [HTTP.APIForAgent].Enable on the server. If [HTTP.APIForAgent.BasicAuth] is configured, Nightingale matches the request's api_key against its configured password values. A web-login token is not interchangeable with that key. Without server authentication, Nightingale does not check this value, although the Agent still requires a valid nonempty configuration.

sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent sudo datadog-agent status sudo journalctl -u datadog-agent -n 100 --no-pager Expected result: the Agent starts and sends series to /datadog/api/v1/series without authentication or routing errors. In Nightingale's explorer, select the actual destination store and confirm that collected metrics appear and keep receiving new samples. Nightingale replaces dots and hyphens in metric names with underscores: system.cpu.user becomes system_cpu_user. Inspect both Agent and Nightingale logs; a running service alone does not prove delivery. Success on auxiliary compatibility endpoints does not prove that logs, APM, events or all service checks were stored. This guide covers the v1 metric-series path only. If your Agent cannot use it, choose Categraf or a verified Prometheus collection path.
Data ingestion protocols Connected datasource with no data Implementation: Pushgw routes and series parsing and authentication.

By the end of this page, your existing Telegraf will write metrics to the store used by Nightingale. The example targets Telegraf 1.36.3 and Nightingale v9. Nightingale writes received metrics to its embedded TSDB or a configured external store.

Both are MIT-licensed agents written in Go, and Nightingale accepts metrics from either. The differences that matter in practice: Telegraf Categraf Plugins 300+ inputs, plus processors and many outputs 90+ inputs covering operating systems, databases, middleware, network gear and Kubernetes How it sends to Nightingale outputs.http with data_format = "prometheusremotewrite" (configured below) Prometheus Remote Write by default Hosts list in Nightingale Does not send Nightingale's heartbeat Sends a heartbeat every 10 s with host metadata that fills Infrastructure → Hosts Built-in dashboards and rules A few templates include Telegraf rule groups (Linux, for example) Many integration templates ship a Categraf rule group and Categraf dashboards Metric names Telegraf plugin naming, for example cpu_usage_active Several host plugins use the same names, so some rules work for both Keep Telegraf if it is already deployed or you rely on plugins Categraf does not have; nothing about alerting in Nightingale requires switching. Choose Categraf for new hosts when you want the host list and the bundled dashboards and alert rules to work without rewriting metric names. The two can run side by side during a migration.

Nightingale is running and reachable from the Telegraf host on port 17000. [HTTP.APIForAgent].Enable is true. Choose the embedded TSDB or configure an external writer. Keep your existing Telegraf installation. For a new installation, use the official instructions rather than the old 1.20.4 download script.

Merge this into telegraf.conf and replace the URL. outputs.http is the output plugin; prometheusremotewrite is its serialization format. [agent] interval = "15s" flush_interval = "15s" [[outputs.http]] url = "http://127.0.0.1:17000/prometheus/v1/write" method = "POST" data_format = "prometheusremotewrite" [outputs.http.headers] Content-Type = "application/x-protobuf" Content-Encoding = "snappy" X-Prometheus-Remote-Write-Version = "0.1.0" [[inputs.cpu]] percpu = false totalcpu = true collect_cpu_time = false report_active = true [[inputs.mem]] If Nightingale configures [HTTP.APIForAgent.BasicAuth], add matching username and password inside [[outputs.http]], before its headers table. Leave them out when authentication is disabled. Review any default InfluxDB output already enabled in the file; an unrelated failing output can obscure the result. OpenTSDB remains a compatibility protocol, but its metric names differ. Check existing dashboards when switching formats.

telegraf --config /etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf --test telegraf --config /etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf --once Expected result: --test shows CPU and memory samples; --once performs collection and delivery without authentication, routing or connection errors. --test alone does not test delivery. In Nightingale's metrics explorer, select the destination store and query cpu_usage_active. You should see series with Telegraf tags. Then restart the existing service. An installation with the official systemd unit can use sudo systemctl restart telegraf. Telegraf does not send Categraf heartbeat metadata. Receiving metrics does not grant the same target-registration or self-healing capabilities. See the 1.36.3 format documentation for Histogram and Summary batching limitations.

Where this page ends: a Nightingale agent that a third-party agent platform can discover and call on its own, plus one verified message:send request.

/mcp /a2a What the caller gets 74 fine-grained tools to orchestrate themselves One agent that talks Interaction JSON-RPC tool calls Natural language in, natural language out Needs an LLM configured? No — tools hit Nightingale's API directly Yes — it drives the built-in assistant Suits Clients that bring their own model: Claude Code, Cursor Somebody else's agent orchestration platform Both endpoints are on by default and share one auth path. A question the assistant cannot answer in the UI, it cannot answer over A2A either — get a conversation working first, see Nightingale AI overview.

documents.t: curl -s https://n9e.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json This address needs no authentication (the spec requires it to be discoverable). /.well-known/agent.json is an alias for older clients. What the card declares: Field Value name Nightingale Agent supportedInterfaces One HTTP+JSON interface at <BaseURL>/a2a capabilities.streaming true defaultInputModes / defaultOutputModes Both text securitySchemes x-user-token (apiKey, in a header); an extra oidc scheme appears when RSAuth is on skills Every built-in skill, with its name, description and example prompts skills is generated from the built-in skills' frontmatter, so the caller sees what Nightingale is actually good at — diagnosing why a rule did not fire, analyzing a dashboard, generating PromQL — rather than one generic blurb. An empty BaseURL is inferred from request headers. Set it explicitly behind a reverse proxy, or the third party may end up with an internal address: [HTTP.A2A] BaseURL = "https://n9e.example.com"
documents.s: The agent card is the only address a third party needs

documents.t: The REST binding path is /a2a/message:send (no /v1 prefix). messageId, role and parts are all required, and the enum value for role is ROLE_USER: curl -s -X POST https://n9e.example.com/a2a/message:send \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'X-User-Token: YOUR_TOKEN' \ -d '{ "message": { "messageId": "req-0001", "role": "ROLE_USER", "parts": [{ "text": "Which alerts are firing right now?" }] }, "metadata": { "lang": "en_US" } }' Expected result: a task object carrying id, contextId, status.state, and n9e.chat_id / n9e.seq_id under metadata. A status.state of TASK_STATE_COMPLETED means the turn finished; the answer is in artifacts. This step can take tens of seconds while the model thinks and calls tools — that is normal. For multi-turn, put "contextId": "<the contextId you got back>" inside message. contextId maps one-to-one onto Nightingale's chat_id, which means an A2A conversation is the same conversation you see in the Nightingale AI conversation list.

Method Path Send a message (unary) POST /a2a/message:send Send a message (SSE stream) POST /a2a/message:stream Get a task GET /a2a/tasks/{id} Cancel a task POST /a2a/tasks/{id}:cancel Resubscribe POST /a2a/tasks/{id}:subscribe tasks/list is deliberately not implemented and returns UnsupportedOperation per the spec — enumerating tasks across users is meaningless for a built-in assistant and would leak other people's activity. A bare GET on /a2a returns a short JSON hint listing the paths above. That exists so a client still using the legacy JSON-RPC style (tasks/send) gets a sentence it can read, rather than being redirected into the frontend SPA. Task state lives in Redis with a 24-hour TTL, shared across instances. After it expires tasks/get returns task-not-found, but the conversation itself is still in the database.

A2A sits at the root path and holds long connections: location /.well-known/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:17000; } location /a2a/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:17000; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_buffering off; # without this, streaming answers never emit anything proxy_read_timeout 3600s; # the default 60s cuts answers in half proxy_send_timeout 3600s; } The server sends an empty "working" status heartbeat every 30 seconds precisely to survive gateway idle timeouts — but the gateway's own read timeout still has to be raised.

The repository ships a test client built on the official SDK: go run ./cmd/a2a-cli --server http://127.0.0.1:17000 --token YOUR_TOKEN \ --message "Show the alert events currently firing" # Continue the same conversation go run ./cmd/a2a-cli --server http://127.0.0.1:17000 --token YOUR_TOKEN \ --context-id CHAT_ID --message "Analyze the first one in more detail" It streams by default; --get calls tasks/get afterwards to prove the task really was stored.
[HTTP.A2A] Disable = true # closes /a2a, /mcp and the agent card together To close MCP only and keep A2A, use DisableMCP = true.

Two separate things share this page, and they are worth telling apart up front. Conversation history is a real, everyday feature. "Agent" is an internal binding in the open-source build, not something you create — the details are in the second half so you do not go looking for a page that is not there.

Every turn is written to the database as it happens, so a conversation survives a page reload, a different browser and a restart of n9e. Two tables hold it: Table What it holds ai_assistant_chat One row per conversation: its id, its owner, its title, when it was last touched ai_assistant_message One row per turn: your question, the answer, and the tool calls behind it Both bodies are compressed, so the rows are smaller than the transcripts suggest. Conversations are strictly per user. Every read and write checks that the requesting account owns the conversation, with no administrator override, so one person's chats are not visible to anyone else — including through the API. An /a2a conversation is the same object: the contextId a caller passes back is the chat_id, so an agent talking to Nightingale through A2A appears in that user's list alongside what they typed in the browser.

The Conversations section of the Nightingale AI sidebar lists yours, newest first, grouped into Today / Yesterday / older, with a box that filters on title. Hovering a row reveals a menu: Rename — inline. Titles are generated from the first question otherwise, and renaming pins yours so the automatic title never overwrites it; Share — copies a link that opens the conversation read-only. The server still checks ownership on every read, so the link works for you and nobody else; treat it as a bookmark to a read-only view, not as a way to hand a transcript to a colleague. To do that, copy the text.
documents.s: What you can do with one

documents.t: There is no delete button. The endpoint exists; nothing in the interface calls it. Until that changes, deleting is an API call with your own token: curl -s --request DELETE \ -H 'X-User-Token: YOUR_TOKEN' \ http://127.0.0.1:17000/api/n9e/assistant/chat/YOUR_CHAT_ID The chat id is the last path segment of the conversation's URL. Deleting removes its messages as well, and — the ownership check again — only works on your own conversations. There is no retention policy and no TTL. Nothing expires conversations, so on a busy instance these two tables only grow. If that matters, script the call above; they are also ordinary tables that your backup and archival routine can treat like any other.

There is an ai_agent table, and rows in it bind a use case to an LLM config and a list of skills. In the open-source build that is much less than it sounds: The only use case is chat, and exactly one enabled row for it is ever consulted; A row is created for you at startup — default-chat-agent, bound to no specific model — so the assistant works out of the box; There is no system prompt and no tool selection on the row. Both are compiled into the product; nothing on an agent changes how the assistant thinks or what it may call; The skills bound to the chat agent are ignored on the ordinary conversation path. Skills are discovered from the catalogue and loaded on demand instead — see Install, manage and write Skills; There is no menu entry, no permission point of its own, and the list page that does exist has had its create button removed. It is administrator-only and reachable by typing the address. So: do not build a workflow on named agents in the open-source build. If a page or a screenshot elsewhere shows agent management as a feature, it is not this edition.

What you actually want Where to do it A different model for the assistant Mark a different LLM config Default — it wins over any agent binding anyway (Configure an LLM provider) Different behaviour for a class of question Write a skill; its description decides when it applies (Install, manage and write Skills) More tools for one procedure builtin_tools in that skill's frontmatter A longer diagnostic chain max_iterations in that skill's frontmatter Restrict what the assistant can reach The asking account's role and business groups (Permission inheritance and RBAC)
