By the end of this page, a script will emit custom samples that Categraf sends to Nightingale's TSDB. The example uses Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9. The executable may be Shell, Python or a compiled program.

Create /opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh: #!/bin/sh printf 'custom_check_success{check="demo"} 1\n' chmod +x /opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh /opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh Expected result: stdout contains only the Prometheus metric line. Send diagnostics to stderr rather than mixing prose with samples. Resolve nonzero process-exit errors before diagnosing delivery.

In conf/input.exec/exec.toml: [[instances]] commands = ["/opt/categraf/scripts/collect_demo.sh"] timeout = 5 data_format = "prometheus" The format must match stdout. The input also supports influx and falcon, but their formats are not interchangeable. Command paths support globs; check which scripts they match before enabling them. See the exec input documentation.

./categraf --test --inputs exec Expected result: custom_check_success with check="demo" and value 1, without parsing or timeout errors. Restart the existing service and query the metric in the destination store to confirm new samples continue arriving. If foreground execution works but service execution fails, check the service account, permissions, working directory, PATH and environment. Use absolute paths and bounded execution times instead of relying on an interactive shell.

The constant value 1 verifies the pipeline only. A real check should report its actual result, such as queue length or last-success time. Emit an explicit failure value. No output and a value of zero require different alert conditions. Avoid random IDs, timestamps and full error messages as labels; they create unbounded series. Use Counter semantics for cumulative counts and Gauge semantics for current values. See Prerequisites.
Create your first alert Connected datasource with no data

By the end of this page, you will choose a suitable Java metrics endpoint and connect JVM or application metrics to Nightingale. Nightingale v9 does not scrape Java processes itself. Use Categraf v0.5.17, Prometheus or vmagent.

For a Spring Boot application, prefer Actuator. This example uses dependency management from Spring Boot 3.5.x: <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId> <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId> </dependency> Let the application's Spring Boot BOM manage versions instead of mixing Micrometer release lines. Expose the endpoint in application.properties: management.server.port=8081 management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,prometheus Allow the collector to access the management port. Adjust paths and credentials for Spring Security, proxies and custom application contexts. curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/prometheus Expected result: Prometheus text with JVM metrics, not a login page, JSON error or 404. See the Spring Boot 3.5 metrics documentation.

Without Spring Boot, use micrometer-registry-prometheus, register application meters with a shared PrometheusMeterRegistry, and serve its scrape() output over HTTP. Package names vary between Micrometer and Prometheus client versions. Follow the official example for your dependencies instead of copying old imports. A registry without an HTTP endpoint cannot be scraped. Adding a registry dependency without binding JVM meters does not create all JVM metrics automatically.

For an application you cannot modify but that exposes MBeans, use the JMX Exporter Java Agent. This HTTP-mode example uses JMX Exporter 1.3.0. Put the jar and jmx.yaml in the working directory: rules: - pattern: ".*" java -javaagent:./jmx_prometheus_javaagent-1.3.0.jar=9404:./jmx.yaml -jar ./app.jar curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:9404/metrics Expected result: port 9404 returns Prometheus metrics. The broad rule is for initial verification; narrow it to required MBeans and restrict endpoint access for production. Use the 1.3.0 documentation for the package and options.

Reuse a component's existing Prometheus endpoint rather than adding a second JMX collection path. Some middleware and service frameworks already expose /metrics; verify the format and authentication first. Metric names and labels vary, so choose matching dashboards and rules.

Add the actual endpoint to conf/input.prometheus/prometheus.toml. This example matches the Actuator configuration above: [[instances]] urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:8081/actuator/prometheus"] url_label_key = "instance" url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" ./categraf --test --inputs prometheus Expected result: metrics such as jvm_ without scraping or parsing errors. Restart collection and check that new samples arrive in Nightingale's destination store. If Prometheus or vmagent already scrapes the application, register its store as a datasource without adding another scrape path.
Prometheus datasource Process monitoring

By the end of this page, Linux host metrics will be queryable in Nightingale, and you will know why an online target and a populated dashboard are separate checks. The collector commands target Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9.

Configure writers and heartbeat using Install and register. Host metrics come from inputs such as cpu, mem, disk, diskio, net and system, configured under conf/input.<name>/. From the collector installation directory: ./categraf --test --inputs cpu:mem:disk Expected result: the terminal prints the corresponding metrics without permission or configuration errors. This proves local collection only. Select the destination store in Nightingale's explorer and verify that new samples arrive.

Check the two paths separately: Path Purpose heartbeat → /v1/n9e/heartbeat Target metadata and liveness writers → /prometheus/v1/write → TSDB Samples used by queries, dashboards and metric alerts Nightingale v9 can use its embedded TSDB. The old statement that it always forwards metrics without storing them is no longer generally correct. For external storage, also check the Pushgw.Writers destinations and the backend's receiver configuration. Work through these checks: Does --test produce samples? If not, fix collection first. Does writers in conf/config.toml point to the intended Nightingale or Edge? Do collector logs show authentication, connection or write failures? Is the destination accepting data? Prometheus needs its Remote Write receiver enabled. Is the query using the right source, and are clocks synchronized? Are dashboard variables excluding the business group, ident or instance? sudo journalctl -u categraf.service -n 100 --no-pager Expected result: a direct query against the correct store returns samples. Resolve dashboard filtering after that. See Connected datasource with no data for detailed troubleshooting.

Prometheus generates up when it actively scrapes a Node Exporter endpoint. Categraf pushes with Remote Write and does not automatically generate that scrape-status metric. Use a Host-type rule in Nightingale for missing-target detection. Select the intended targets, tags or business groups and configure the missing duration. Stop and restart collection on one test host to verify triggering and recovery before applying the rule broadly. Expected result: the test host produces an event after the configured duration and recovers when its heartbeat resumes. Independent Ping or port probes are also useful, but measure reachability or service response rather than collector health.
Targets and heartbeat Import dashboards and rules
By the end of this page, MySQL runtime metrics will be collected, and you will know how that differs from business-SQL alerting. The configuration targets Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9.

MySQL performance monitoring: a collector reads server status and writes metrics to a TSDB. Business-SQL alerts: Nightingale queries the business database directly, for example for failed-order counts. See SQL datasources. Nightingale metadata database: stores users and rules. See Database deployment. It does not automatically provide either monitoring path.

First install and register Categraf. Create a monitoring account reachable from the collector, then edit conf/input.mysql/mysql.toml: [[instances]] address = "127.0.0.1:3306" username = "monitor" password = "replace-with-monitor-password" parameters = "tls=false" timeout_seconds = 3 gather_table_size = false gather_slave_status = false labels = { instance = "mysql-local:3306" } Replace the address, password and unique instance label. Configure TLS for network connections; this example is for local verification. Grant the permissions required by enabled queries. Replication status, process lists and table-size collection have different permissions and costs; do not use root as a shortcut. Enable replication metrics only when needed, and check whether the server supports SHOW SLAVE STATUS or SHOW REPLICA STATUS. Use another [[instances]] for each target, with a distinct instance label. See the v0.5.17 configuration for the full option list.

From the collector installation directory: ./categraf --test --inputs mysql Expected result: metrics starting with mysql_, without authentication or SQL-permission errors. Restart the existing collector service, select the destination store in Nightingale's explorer, and check the metrics and instance labels. Import the MySQL dashboards and rules from integration templates. Confirm collection before enabling thresholds against absent data.

Order counts and failed jobs are not MySQL server-status metrics. Use custom SQL queries in the collector when you also need stored trends, or a Nightingale SQL datasource for direct query-based evaluation. Use read-only credentials and bounded queries with timeouts so monitoring does not impair the business workload.
Input plugins SQL alert rules

By the end of this page, Oracle samples will reach your TSDB, and you will know where shared and per-instance SQL belongs. The example uses the Categraf v0.5.17 Oracle configuration and the store used by Nightingale v9.

conf/input.oracle/oracle.toml: connections and [[instances]] for one or more targets. conf/input.oracle/metric.toml: shared collection queries. [[instances.metrics]]: queries specific to the owning instance. Reuse the writer configured during installation and registration; Oracle collection does not require another TSDB.

Use a monitoring account permitted to query the required views: interval = 15 [[instances]] address = "127.0.0.1:1521/ORCLPDB1" username = "monitor" password = "replace-with-monitor-password" is_sys_dba = false is_sys_oper = false max_open_connections = 5 labels = { instance = "oracle-local:1521" } [[instances.metrics]] mesurement = "sessions" label_fields = ["status", "type"] metric_fields = ["value"] timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT status, type, COUNT(*) AS value FROM v$session GROUP BY status, type ''' Replace the service name, credentials and instance label. mesurement is the plugin's actual key; do not correct it to measurement. The status and type columns become labels; value is numeric. Column names must match the mapping. Avoid SYS. Ask a DBA to grant access for each enabled query. This custom query needs v$session; the bundled queries may require additional views. Passing one query is not proof that the account can run the entire collection set.

./categraf --test --inputs oracle Expected result: Oracle metrics without connection, permission or column-mapping errors. For an ORA error, check the service and credentials, then the views used by the failing SQL. After local collection succeeds, restart the existing service and check oracle_ metrics and instance labels in the destination store. Give each target distinct labels to prevent collisions.

Put queries required by every instance in metric.toml; keep special queries under the target's [[instances.metrics]]. Have a DBA review execution plans and frequency before enabling queries against large tables. See the Oracle configuration directory for fields and bundled queries.
Input plugins Import dashboards and rules
By the end of this page, an independent probe will check service ports and HTTP responses rather than process existence alone. The configuration targets Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9.

Edit conf/input.net_response/net_response.toml: [[instances]] targets = ["127.0.0.1:22"] protocol = "tcp" timeout = "2s" labels = { probe = "ssh-local" } Replace the target. A successful TCP connection proves that the port accepts connections, not that the application is healthy. Configure a protocol-appropriate send and expect pair when response checking is required. UDP needs a meaningful request and expected reply. Changing protocol to udp alone does not make a complete probe. See the net_response configuration.

Edit conf/input.http_response/http_response.toml: [[instances]] targets = ["http://127.0.0.1:8080/health"] method = "GET" response_timeout = "5s" expect_response_status_code = 200 expect_response_substring = "ok" follow_redirects = false labels = { probe = "application-health" } Use the application's actual health endpoint and response. Check both status and body. Enable redirect following deliberately so a login redirect does not masquerade as health. HTTPS targets can also produce certificate-expiry metrics.

./categraf --test --inputs net_response:http_response Expected result: net_response_result_code or http_response_result_code for the intended target. Zero means the configured check succeeded; nonzero means failure. The plugins use different nonzero codes, so do not share their error-code descriptions. Restart collection after testing and check labels, result codes and timestamps in the destination store. Start with a result_code != 0 condition, an appropriate sustained duration and a meaningful severity. When an HTTPS target produces http_response_cert_expire_timestamp, this expression returns seconds until expiry: http_response_cert_expire_timestamp - time() Verify the metric exists before enabling an expiry threshold. DNS, network access and probe permissions also affect results; a failed probe does not necessarily mean a process exited.
Metric alert rules Import dashboards and rules Full HTTP options: v0.5.17 configuration.

By the end of this page, you will distinguish excessive system process counts from a missing service and collect per-service resource metrics. The configuration targets Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9.

processes counts system processes by state and helps detect runaway jobs. procstat matches a service and collects its count, CPU, memory and file descriptors. Application Prometheus metrics also describe requests, errors and runtime behavior. See Java monitoring. An existing process does not prove that a service works; add port or HTTP probes where needed.

Edit conf/input.procstat/procstat.toml: [[instances]] search_exec_substring = "nginx" gather_total = true gather_per_pid = false gather_more_metrics = ["cpu", "mem", "fd", "uptime"] labels = { service = "nginx" } Replace the match and confirm that it selects the intended service. Add another [[instances]] for another service. Select one suitable matching method per instance. gather_per_pid = true adds PID labels and can increase series counts when processes restart frequently.

./categraf --test --inputs processes:procstat Expected result: system counts and service metrics appear; the matched count agrees with the actual processes. Restart the collector service and query procstat_lookup_count in Nightingale. It is positive when matching processes exist and zero when none match. Verify on a test service before adding a sustained-duration alert to avoid noise from normal restarts. If the host or collector disappears, samples may disappear instead of becoming zero. Add missing-host detection separately.

The jvm option in gather_more_metrics requires jstat on the target host. If foreground testing works but systemd fails, check its PATH, the JDK location and permissions to inspect the process. Use sudo systemctl edit categraf.service with the actual JDK path: [Service] Environment="PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-17-openjdk-amd64/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin" Restart and inspect the logs. Replace the example path if that JDK is not installed. Configuration reference: procstat v0.5.17.
Java application monitoring Metric alert rules
By the end of this page, Redis runtime metrics will be available in Nightingale. An existing Redis Exporter can remain in place. The examples target Categraf v0.5.17 and Nightingale v9.

The input connects to Redis and reads status using commands such as INFO. After installing and registering Categraf, edit conf/input.redis/redis.toml: [[instances]] address = "127.0.0.1:6379" username = "monitor" password = "replace-with-monitor-password" pool_size = 2 labels = { instance = "redis-local:6379" } Replace the credentials and instance label. Older Redis installations without ACL users may require an empty username. Use a monitoring account with permissions for the enabled collection set. Allowing INFO alone does not necessarily cover every optional command. Slow-log and custom-command collection need their own permissions. See the configuration.

If Prometheus or vmagent already scrapes the exporter, register that store as a datasource without collecting it twice. Alternatively, add the exporter to conf/input.prometheus/prometheus.toml: [[instances]] urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:9121/metrics"] url_label_key = "instance" url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" This is the exporter's HTTP endpoint, not Redis port 6379. Fetching it from the collector host should return Redis metrics in Prometheus text format.

Test the selected path: ./categraf --test --inputs redis # For the exporter path: ./categraf --test --inputs prometheus Expected result: Redis metrics without authentication or scraping errors. Restart the collector service. Select the destination store in Nightingale's explorer and check redis_ metrics, instance labels and new samples. The native input and Redis Exporter do not use identical metric names. Import dashboards and rules matching the collector you chose.
Import dashboards and rules Remote Write
After this page, you will know the prerequisites for Nightingale and be able to separate missing data, missing alerts and missing notifications into specific checks.

For binaries, understand working directories, configuration files, stdout / stderr and systemd. For containers, understand port mappings, volumes, logs and where a container's 127.0.0.1 points. sudo journalctl -u n9e.service -n 100 --no-pager sudo journalctl -u categraf.service -n 100 --no-pager Use the actual service names. Expected result: recent logs for the component under investigation. If no such unit exists, use the log entry point for its real deployment.

A metric name describes the measurement. Labels distinguish hosts, services and instances; the name and labels identify a series. A timestamp and value form a sample. Incorrect clocks place data outside the intended range. A Gauge is a current value; a Counter accumulates and may reset when a process restarts. Histograms and summaries require understanding buckets, counts and sums. Avoid unique request IDs as labels. See the Prometheus data model.

Start with selecting series by labels, using rate() on counters and aggregating instances. Build thresholds around the meaning of the data; a cumulative count is not a requests-per-second value. An instant query evaluates a time; a range query returns a series over an interval. Range and step affect the display. Verify an expression in the metrics explorer before putting it into a metric rule. See the Prometheus query documentation.

Prometheus and vmagent scrape with Pull. The scraper knows whether a request succeeded and can generate up. Categraf sends Remote Write with Push. Its liveness cannot be treated as a Prometheus scrape-status check. Nightingale v9 can use embedded or external storage. If metrics already exist in Prometheus, register the datasource without moving them. Heartbeat metadata and sample delivery are separate paths; see Linux monitoring.

Find the failing stage first: Does the collector produce samples locally? Do they reach the correct store? Does Nightingale query that datasource? Does rule evaluation produce an event? Is the event muted, filtered or processed? Is notification delivery successful? Include versions, deployment method, expected and actual behavior, the incident time range, minimal configuration and relevant logs. Remove credentials and personal information first. Keep enough context to make the failure diagnosable.

Quick start Prerequisites
Where this page ends: charts from clicking metric names instead of writing PromQL, and your team's own queries added to the same catalogue so colleagues who do not write PromQL can use them too.

You have just connected a component, data is arriving, and you have no idea which metrics are worth looking at. Built-in metrics is that catalogue: organised by component type and category, each entry carrying a metric name, a unit, the PromQL and a plain-language description, and charting on one click. A fresh install ships with more than 1300 entries covering Linux, MySQL, Redis, Nginx, Kafka, ClickHouse, Kubernetes and other common components. Compared with the Metrics explorer: that one is for people writing PromQL during an incident; this one is for routine checks and for finding out what a newly connected component even exposes. Explorer → Metrics → Built-in metrics (/metrics-built-in).

The left column is Filters, and its job is to attach a set of label conditions to the query whenever you click a metric. In the product's own words: with {ident="n9e01"} configured and selected, clicking cpu_usage_idle actually issues cpu_usage_idle{ident="n9e01"}. Set one up before you start clicking. Without it, a metric like cpu_usage_idle returns every series in the environment — thousands of lines, and a stalled browser. Click + at the top of the left column: Field What to put in it Name Something recognisable, e.g. "Trading production" Data source Which source this filter applies to Filter conditions The label conditions, e.g. ident="n9e01" Authorized teams Which teams may use it, and whether read and write or read only
documents.s: 1. Set a filter before clicking a metric

documents.t: Four filters across the top: Component type (Linux, MySQL, Kubernetes…), Category (the second level, e.g. cpu / mem / disk under Linux), Unit, and a keyword search that matches the name, the PromQL and the description. The table shows five columns by default: component type, category, name, unit, PromQL. Display columns at the top right adds expression type, metric type, custom fields, description and updated-by. The Name column actually renders the metric's description, and it is a link; the real expression is in the PromQL column. Clicking it opens a query drawer that charts it straight away, and Add panel in that drawer stacks several metrics for comparison. With rows selected, More offers export (JSON), import and delete.

Click Add metric: Field What to put in it Component type Pick an existing one or create a new one Category The second level Expression type Metric name (just a name) or PromQL (a full expression with functions) Metric type Gauge / Counter / Histogram PromQL The query itself Unit Used for display conversion Custom fields Name plus value, for whatever context you want to carry Metric description Per language: Name (required) and Description — this is what the list shows Note: there is no top-level name field. The name lives inside the per-language description block, so a metric filled in only in Chinese will not show a name in the English UI. Creating, editing and deleting are gated by the /builtin-metrics/add, /put and /del permission points.

This decides where you go to change something: The 1300-odd built-in entries come from integrations/<Component>/metrics/*.json in the backend and are loaded when n9e-center starts. No UI action triggers it, and there is nothing for you to "import"; Metrics you create here are stored in the database. For the same PromQL, the database row wins over the file — so when a built-in entry cannot be edited, the workaround is to create a new one with the same PromQL; Integrations → Components has a Metrics tab under each component. That is another view onto the same data; editing either side is equivalent. Two other places consume this catalogue: the Built-in metrics button beside the PromQL input in the Metrics explorer, and the one-click drawer on the host list.
Write the PromQL yourself: Metrics explorer Look at things host by host: Object quick view What else a component template carries: Import dashboards and rules
Where this page ends: a dashboard owned by a business group, with at least one panel drawing real data, saved and exportable to hand to someone else.

Monitoring a common component (Linux, MySQL, Redis, Nginx…): a usable board almost certainly already ships with the template, and importing then adjusting beats drawing from scratch; Monitoring your own business metrics: start empty. Either way, note one thing first: the Add / Import / More buttons only appear once a specific business group is selected on the left. While the sidebar sits on the preset filters "My business group dashboards" or "Public dashboards", the buttons are hidden — that is not a permission problem, click a real group and they come back.
documents.s: First decide: import a template or start empty

documents.t: Explorer → Dashboards (/dashboards), pick a business group on the left, then Import. The dialog has four tabs: Tab When to use it Import built-in dashboard (default) Pick a component (MySQL, Redis…), then tick the dashboards shipped with it. This is the usual path Import Grafana dashboard URL (recommended) Converts nothing; creates an iframe-mode dashboard that embeds your Grafana page Import Nightingale dashboard JSON Paste JSON exported from another Nightingale Import Grafana dashboard (not recommended) Beta, converts Grafana dashboard JSON into Nightingale's model. Plenty of limits — see Use Grafana with Nightingale Expected result: the boards appear in the list and open with charts on them. If the charts are empty, do not start editing the board — the component's metrics probably are not arriving yet; go back to Verify incoming data. The templates themselves live under Integrations → Components, which offers the same set of dashboards. Importing collector config and alert rules alongside them is covered in Import dashboards and rules.

Click Add, give the dashboard a name (ident, tags and note are optional). Saving takes you straight to the detail page. Click Add panel. Besides the 12 visualization types, the dropdown offers Row (a collapsible horizontal divider) and Paste panel (panel config JSON copied elsewhere). Pick a type to open the panel editor. It is a full-screen modal with two columns, not tabs: Left: the variable bar on top, a live preview in the middle, the query editor below. That query editor is the same one the Metrics explorer uses, so the preview updates as you type. Text and Iframe panels have no query editor. Right: a stack of collapsible sections, of which a type-specific subset appears — Panel options (name, description, links, repeat by variable), Graph styles, Legend, Tooltip, Value mappings, Standard options, Thresholds, Colors, Links, Override. The modal header also carries the visualization-type selector and a time range picker. Change the chart type there rather than deleting the panel and adding a new one. Click Save to return to the dashboard, then drag a panel's edge to resize it and its title to move it.
documents.s: 2. Start empty and add the first panel

documents.t: Type What it is for Time series The default. One or more lines over time Bar chart Comparing categories, or counts bucketed by time Stat One big number, coloured by threshold Table NG (Beta) The newer table with more features; use it for new panels Table The older table, still used by existing panels Pie chart Proportions Hexmap Many instances on one screen, spot the outlier by colour Bar gauge Top N as horizontal bars Text Prose and links; queries nothing Gauge A single value against a range Heatmap How a distribution changes over time Iframe Embeds an external page Switching Table to Table NG raises a confirmation offering Auto upgrade (carry the old options over where possible) or Switch type only (start the options fresh).

Rows: Add panel → Row inserts a collapsible divider. Deleting one asks whether to delete the row and its panels or delete the row only. Time range and auto refresh: top right. The selected range goes into the URL (__from / __to / __refresh) and is remembered per dashboard in the browser. Refresh intervals are 5s / 10s / 20s / 30s / 1m / 2m / 3m / 5m / 10m. A refresh interval shorter than the query step buys nothing, and the UI says so. Links: the link icon in the title bar configures jump targets (name, URL, open in a new tab), which is how you chain related boards together. Dashboard settings (the gear): name, ident, tags, note, plus two behaviour switches — Graph tooltip (Default / Shared crosshair / Shared tooltip) and Graph zoom (Default / Update time range). Variables: the entry point sits at the end of the variable bar, showing "Add variable" while there are none. See Variables and filters.

Changes are not saved automatically. After adding panels and adjusting the layout, click Save dashboard in the title bar; leaving with unsaved changes prompts first. A whole board: Export on the list row gives you JSON, with Download JSON and Copy JSON to clipboard. Paste it back elsewhere through "Import Nightingale dashboard JSON". The JSON in that box can be selected and copied, but editing it writes nothing back — there is no edit-JSON feature. Into another business group: use Clone. The copy is independent; the two are maintained separately from then on. A single panel: the panel's own menu has Copy, which puts that panel's config JSON on the clipboard; on the target dashboard use Add panel → Paste panel. The same menu also holds Refresh / Edit / Clone / Share / Inspect / Delete, and table panels add Export (CSV).
documents.s: Save, export, move a panel elsewhere

documents.t: Make one board serve many hosts: Variables and filters Show it to someone without an account: Anonymous time-limited sharing Import the template's rules too: Import dashboards and rules
Where this page ends: extra entries in the Nightingale side menu that open your other systems, and a way to embed Nightingale pages into your own portal without asking people to log in a second time.
documents.s: Share, embed and integrate external systems

documents.t: Others come in. Embedded products hangs an external page into the Nightingale side menu as an iframe. It has a configuration page under Integrations. Nightingale goes out. Embedding Nightingale pages into another portal is done with URL parameters plus proxy authentication. There is no configuration page — you edit the config file and the link.

Integrations → Embedded products (/embedded-products), then Add. Field What to put in it Name The menu label in the side bar; keep it short URL The full URL to embed, e.g. https://cmdb.example.com/hosts Visibility Visible to logged-in users, or Visible to specific teams (then pick the teams) Save. Expected result: a new entry at the bottom of the side menu that loads the page in the main area (a browser refresh is sometimes needed). Each row in the list carries two more controls: Show in menu keeps the configuration but hides the entry — handy for taking something down temporarily; and the handle at the start of the row reorders the entries in the side menu. The usual candidates are a CMDB, a ticketing system, or the team's runbook wiki, so that acting on an alert does not mean switching browser tabs.
documents.s: Embed an external system into Nightingale

documents.t: Nightingale is only the iframe container here; whether embedding works is decided entirely by the other side's response headers: Their response header Result X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN The browser refuses, the iframe is blank Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' Same Neither header, or your domain explicitly allowed It embeds The browser console spells it out: Refused to display ... in a frame because it set 'X-Frame-Options', or Refused to frame ... because an ancestor violates ... frame-ancestors. Two fixes: have them add Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://<your-nightingale>, or put an nginx reverse proxy in front of their site that rewrites the headers and point the entry at the proxy. Cookies are the second layer. If their session cookie is SameSite=Lax/Strict it is not sent inside a cross-site iframe, so the user just sees a login page. Either they switch to SameSite=None; Secure, or both sides move behind the same SSO.
documents.s: A blank frame almost always means the other side refuses

documents.t: Nightingale honours three URL parameters, on any page: Parameter Effect ?menu=hide Hides the side menu; the page body renders normally ?viewMode=fullscreen Dashboard detail only: hides the page header too, leaving just panels &themeMode=dark / light Pins light or dark instead of following the browser For example, a dashboard embedded as a bare canvas: <iframe src="https://n9e.example.com/dashboards/12?viewMode=fullscreen&themeMode=dark" width="100%" height="800" frameborder="0"></iframe> There is no way out of viewMode=fullscreen from inside an iframe — the exit shortcut is blocked by iframe security, so the parameter has to be removed from the URL by hand. The product says as much in its own hint. If all you want is to expose one dashboard to someone outside, do not use this route. Use anonymous time-limited sharing instead: /dashboards/share/<id>?__token= already renders without the menu, and it expires on its own.
documents.s: Embed Nightingale in another portal: hide the chrome first

documents.t: When the portal already has its own login, use proxy authentication so nobody signs in twice: [HTTP.ProxyAuth] Enable = true # which request header carries the username HeaderUserNameKey = "X-User-Name" # roles given to a user auto-created from a username Nightingale has not seen DefaultRoles = ["Standard"] The portal or gateway adds X-User-Name: <username> when forwarding to Nightingale. Nightingale looks the user up by that header, and creates the account with DefaultRoles if it does not exist yet. Three things you must get right, or this becomes an open impersonation endpoint: Only a proxy you control may set that header, and it must unconditionally strip an incoming header of the same name at the edge — otherwise anyone can become anyone by adding a header; Bind Nightingale to an internal address reachable only from the gateway, never straight to the internet; Enabling ProxyAuth disables JWT login: Nightingale's own login page stops working and the logout endpoint returns an error. It is a one-way switch, so decide before you flip it.

Visibility only controls who sees the entry in the side menu. It is not a security boundary for the embedded system — Nightingale has no say once a user hits that URL directly, so the embedded system must authenticate on its own. There is no URL parameter that hides a named subset of menus. menu=hide is all or nothing; to tailor menus per person, use roles and permission points — see Roles and permissions.
Expose a single board: Anonymous time-limited sharing Already running Grafana: Use Grafana with Nightingale Who sees what: Users and teams
Where this page ends: your Grafana dashboards untouched, and Nightingale alerting on the same stores. No data is migrated and no panel is rebuilt.

This Goes to Why Charting and ad-hoc exploration Grafana You already have dozens of panels; rebuilding them buys nothing Alert evaluation Nightingale Rules carry business-group ownership, muting and subscriptions, and every evaluation leaves a record Notification routing and noise control Nightingale Notification rules, media types, templates and workflows are one coherent set Closing the loop on events Nightingale Active events, history and self-healing live in one place The split rests on one condition: both sides look at the same data. Sections 1 and 2 below are the two directions — pick the one that matches where your metrics live.

If metrics are already in Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics / Thanos, this is the least work: register the same query endpoint your Grafana data source uses in Nightingale too. Integrations → Data sources → Add → Prometheus, same URL. Field by field, see Prometheus. Two things to watch: The two sides do not need matching names. Nightingale's alert rules pick the source by its Nightingale name. If the Grafana data source uses Server (proxy) access, that URL is reached from the Grafana host. The Nightingale host must be able to reach it too, or the data source test fails.
documents.s: 1. Point both sides at the same stores

documents.t: If your metrics only live in Nightingale's embedded TSDB (Categraf pushes straight to Nightingale), Grafana can query it — the embedded store exposes a standard Prometheus query API at http://<nightingale>:17000/prometheus. But that endpoint only accepts requests from the local machine by default. To let Grafana reach it from another host, configure basic auth first: [EmbeddedTSDB] Enable = true BasicAuthUser = "grafana" BasicAuthPass = "<pick your own>" Setting these lifts the local-only restriction, and the auto-registered embedded-tsdb data source switches from 127.0.0.1 to the detected host IP with the same credentials attached. Restart Nightingale to apply. Then add a Prometheus data source in Grafana: URL http://<nightingale IP>:17000/prometheus Auth Basic auth, with the user and password above Save and test; a result for up means it works. This route suits small deployments only. The embedded store is a single-instance local-disk option, good to roughly 100k active series — see Embedded TSDB and external storage for the limits. Once you outgrow it and move to an external store, go back to section 1 and point both sides there.
documents.s: 2. The other direction: let Grafana query Nightingale's embedded TSDB

documents.t: PromQL in a Nightingale rule is the same PromQL you write in a Grafana panel; the only difference is that the threshold goes into the expression itself (... > 1). Start from scratch: Create the first rule Bring existing Grafana alert rules across: Migrate from Grafana alerting Run both in parallel before cutting over: Coexisting with what you already run

The Import dialog on the dashboard list has four tabs; two of them concern Grafana: Tab What it does Import Grafana dashboard URL (recommended) Converts nothing. It creates an iframe-mode dashboard that embeds your Grafana page. You supply a name, ident, tags and the Grafana dashboard URL Import Grafana dashboard (not recommended) Beta. Converts Grafana dashboard JSON into Nightingale's own model The limits of the second one are stated in the dialog itself: only dashboards using Prometheus data sources, and only the chart types and features Nightingale supports. JSON older than v7 is rejected outright; v7 to v8 warns first and lets you continue. Anything non-trivial needs manual cleanup afterwards — "not recommended" is not politeness. A third option is to hang all of Grafana off the side menu; see Share, embed and integrate external systems.

Both of the last two options need an iframe, and Grafana refuses to be framed by default. Edit grafana.ini: [security] allow_embedding = true That is enough when both run on the same domain. Across domains you also have to let Grafana's session cookie travel in a third-party context: [security] allow_embedding = true cookie_secure = true ; requires HTTPS cookie_samesite = none ; allow the cookie on cross-site requests cookie_secure = true means Grafana must be served over HTTPS; if it is plain HTTP today, put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front of it. The classic symptom of missing these two lines is that you are logged into Nightingale on the outside while the framed Grafana keeps showing its login page. If you would rather viewers did not log into Grafana at all, turn on anonymous read-only access: [auth.anonymous] enabled = true org_name = Main Org. org_role = Viewer Restart Grafana to apply.
Every field on the data source form: Prometheus Build boards in Nightingale itself: Build a dashboard Hang external systems off the side menu: Share, embed and integrate external systems

Where this page ends: one search running against your log store, narrowed to the lines you care about using the field sidebar, and "which indices, which time field" saved as an index pattern so you never type it again.

The open-source Log explorer supports three categories only: Elasticsearch, Loki and VictoriaLogs. OpenSearch, ClickHouse and Doris can be registered as data sources, but cannot be selected on this page. With none available, the page says "No available data source type" and points at data source management. Registering the source itself is covered in ElasticSearch / OpenSearch and Loki / VictoriaLogs.
documents.s: Before you start: which sources this page accepts

documents.t: Explorer → Logs (/log/explorer). The left column, top to bottom (this is the Elasticsearch shape): Control What to put in it Data source One of the three categories above Mode Indices (type the index directly) or Index patterns (use a saved pattern) Index An index name or wildcard such as app-log-*. The gear beside it manages index patterns Date field Which field is the time axis, usually @timestamp The top row holds the syntax switch (KQL / Lucene), Query conditions, the time range (last 1 hour by default) and Query. Click Query. Expected result: a histogram appears in the middle, the log table below it, and the duration and match count at the top right. The two syntaxes: Lucene status:active field equals title:(quick OR brown) field contains either term author:"John Smith" exact phrase bro* wildcard; ? matches one character quikc~ fuzzy count:[1 TO 5] age:>10 ranges quick AND brown NOT fox boolean KQL method: GET level: error* response_time >= 1 and response_time <= 5 method: POST and status_code: (500 or 502) user:{ first: "Alice" and last: "White" } nested fields The row above the table: Original / Table / Time series / Clustering switch the display form; Line break, Lines and Log time toggle columns; the gear opens field column settings.
documents.s: 1. Pick a source and run the first search

documents.t: Available fields at the bottom left lists every field seen in this batch. Hover one and three actions appear: Add to current query — adds field: value as a condition; Exclude from current query — adds the negation; Filter documents with this field. Clicking a field name also shows its top N values with their share — the fastest way to answer "which service is producing most of these errors". Filters → Add above the table builds explicit conditions as field / operator / value. Filters are combined with AND, and each one can be disabled instead of deleted, which makes trying combinations cheap. To put a colleague in front of the same screen, use ⋮ → Share link at the top right: it serialises the current query into the URL and copies it. That is for someone already logged in, not an anonymous link.
documents.s: 2. Narrow the results from the field sidebar

documents.t: Typing app-log-* and @timestamp every time gets old. Save them as an index pattern. The entry point is not in the side menu: switch Mode to Index patterns, and the gear next to the index box opens the manager (/log/index-patterns). Click Create index pattern: Field What to put in it Data source Required, Elasticsearch-type only Cross cluster Turn on for cross-cluster search Name An index wildcard such as app-log-*. A * is appended automatically if you omit it Time field Picked from the date-typed fields of that index, @timestamp by default Match any index, including hidden ones Whether indices starting with . count too Note The right half of the drawer previews which indices match, and says "No matching indexes" when none do — check the wildcard there rather than saving and wondering later. The page is gated by the /log/index-patterns permission point; without it, the gear is not even rendered.

Neither has the concept of an index or a date field, so those two boxes do not appear. Loki: the box takes LogQL, e.g. {job="varlogs"} |= "error". A builder drawer next to it assembles labels, line filters, parsers and range aggregations step by step, with a Preview QL before you run it; a log line can also open a context viewer showing what happened around it. VictoriaLogs: the box takes LogsQL, defaulting to * (match everything). It adds Limit entries and Total hits, and the display forms are Group / Table / JSON.

There is no "create alert rule" button on this page — do not go looking for it. The way to turn a working search into an alert is: write down four things: data source, index (or index pattern), date field, query conditions; go to Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → Add and pick a log rule type; fill those four in as they are, then decide how many matches count as a problem. Field semantics and picking the threshold are covered in Log rules.
documents.s: From a log line to a rule

documents.t: Write the log rule: Log rules Connect an ES / OpenSearch cluster: ElasticSearch / OpenSearch Connect Loki / VictoriaLogs: Loki / VictoriaLogs

Where this page ends: one PromQL query running against any registered Prometheus-type source, a clear idea of why Table and Graph do not show the same numbers, and four ways to take that query somewhere useful.

Explorer → Metrics (/metric/explorer) opens on the Explorer tab. The top row: Control What it does Filter views Saves a set of query conditions so you can pick them again later Data source Lists Prometheus-type sources only. A fresh install has exactly one, embedded-tsdb Enable autocomplete Completes metric names and labels in the input; turn it off when cardinality is very high Type PromQL into the box and click Execute: up Expected result: the Table tab lists series with their instant values, and "Series (N)" at the top left gives the count. If nothing comes back, start at Why does a data source connect but return no data?.
documents.s: 1. Pick a source and run the first query

documents.t: This is the part people misread: Tab What it queries When to use it Table An instant query at one point in time — the raw reported values Checking whether a metric is arriving at all, and whether its value and timestamp look right Graph A range query over a time window, resampled to a step Looking at a trend The Table side has three more controls: Time (empty means now; set a moment to query that moment), Unit (display only, e.g. SI short) and Export (CSV) for the current series and values. The Graph side has a time range picker plus Max data points and Min step. When the step does not line up with the scrape interval, the points on the chart are resampled, so they will not match the raw values in Table — that is expected, not a bug. Below the chart you also get load time, resolution and result-series count; that is where to look first when a query feels slow.
documents.s: 2. Table and Graph do not show the same data

documents.t: Three helpers sit around the input: Built-in metrics (left of the input): pick a metric by component type and category, and it drops straight into the box. How that catalogue is maintained is covered in Built-in metric views; The magnifier (right of the input): search metric names, see which labels they carry and what values those labels take; Historical records: the PromQL you have run against this source, up to 100 entries; click one to put it back in the box. It is stored in your own browser, so it does not follow you to another machine.
documents.s: 3. You do not have to write PromQL by hand

documents.t: Add panel at the bottom stacks another complete query panel below the current one, each with its own data source and PromQL — handy for putting the same metric from two sources next to each other. With more than one panel, each gets a close icon. It is not "add to dashboard". These panels live only on this page and disappear on refresh. To keep something, go to Build a dashboard.
documents.s: 4. Compare several queries side by side

documents.t: Once it works, the same PromQL has four destinations: An alert rule: Alerts & Notifications → Alert rules → Add, paste the source and the PromQL as they are, and put the threshold into the expression. See Metric rules; A panel: dashboard panels use the same query editor, see Build a dashboard; A new metric: if the query is expensive, precompute it — see Recording rules; A link for someone to glance at: switch to Graph, and the share icon at the top right stores the current query as a temporary chart and gives you a /chart/<id> link that opens without login. That link never expires and cannot be revoked, so do not treat it as controlled sharing — see Anonymous time-limited sharing.
Querying logs: Log explorer and index patterns Starting from one host instead: Object quick view Where metric names and labels come from: Metrics, labels and series
Where this page ends: metrics for a few selected hosts without having to work out the query first, and "the hosts and metrics I check every morning" saved as a view you just reopen.

What you want Route Look at a few hosts once and move on Tick rows on the host list, click the icon in the toolbar Look at the same hosts and the same metrics daily Quick view — configure it once and save it Both read the same built-in metric catalogue; they differ in where you enter and whether the selection is saved.

Infrastructure → Hosts (/targets), tick one or more hosts. The last button in the toolbar is icon-only; hovering it shows "View monitoring metrics of selected hosts". It stays disabled until at least one row is ticked. It opens a full-width drawer titled Built-in metrics: the catalogue on the left, already filtered to the hosts you ticked, and a chart on the right when you click a metric. Expected result: tick n9e-web-01, click cpu_usage_idle, and you get that host's line — not every host in the environment. It does not navigate and has no URL of its own; closing the drawer returns you to the host list. So it is for a look, not for keeping. To keep it, see the next section.
documents.s: 1. One click from the host list

documents.t: Explorer → Metrics → Quick view (/object/explorer). Pick a data source at the top right first. Without one, all three columns are empty — which is the most common reason the page "looks blank", and it is not a data problem. Each column does one job: Column What it does List The existing views. + at the top right creates one; a view marked Public is usable by others Filters Lists every value of the dimension the view defines (ident in the screenshot); tick a few to look at only those. Select all and Clear sit at the top right Metrics Categories across the top, derived from the metric-name prefix (all / cpu / disk / mem / net / processes / system…); click a metric name to chart it below Below the chart area: the time range, Max data points, Min step and Clear. Charts also accept a function, an offset comparison, an aggregation and its grouping labels.
documents.s: 2. Quick view: save the set you keep coming back to

documents.t: Click + at the top of the List column: Field What to put in it Name Public Turn on to let others use this view Filters Fixed label conditions, e.g. keeping only one set of hosts Dynamic labels Labels that can be chosen on the page itself Dimension labels Required. The middle column lists the values of this label; for hosts, use ident Ignore metric prefix The categories on the right come from the metric-name prefix. Setting monitor_ files monitor_cpu_usage under cpu Preview before saving; if the preview shows no values, fix the filters rather than saving. The list also exports a view's config JSON and imports one back.

It stores filters and dimensions, not a fixed set of charts. Everything is picked and drawn on the spot, which is also why it is not a wall display; It only accepts Prometheus-type data sources; For a fixed layout, for sharing outside, or for embedding elsewhere, use a dashboard — see Build a dashboard.
documents.s: What it stores, and what it does not

documents.t: Maintaining what is in the catalogue: Built-in metric views How hosts get into the list: Targets and heartbeat Charts you want to keep: Build a dashboard

Where this page ends: a recording rule evaluating on a fixed schedule, turning a PromQL expression that takes seconds to run into a new metric. Alert rules and panels then query that metric instead, and evaluation drops from seconds to milliseconds.

Three cases: one expensive query is reused by several alert rules and several panels; a single evaluation already takes seconds (multi-dimension joins, high-cardinality sum, histogram_quantile); the query carries a long range ([1h], [1d]) and alerting recomputes it every 30 seconds. If the query is already fast and used in exactly one place, a recording rule only adds something else to maintain.

This is the step people get stuck on. After evaluating, the result is written back into the data source that was queried, through the Remote Write URL configured on that source. Leave the field empty and the rule still runs, but the result has nowhere to land. Go to Integrations → Data sources, edit the Prometheus source you plan to use, and fill in Remote Write URL under Other (the form lists the shape for each product): Prometheus http://localhost:9090/api/v1/write Thanos http://localhost:19192/ VictoriaMetrics single-node http://localhost:8428/api/v1/write VictoriaMetrics cluster http://{vminsert}:8480/insert/0/prometheus/api/v1/write Prometheus itself needs --web.enable-remote-write-receiver before it accepts remote write. The auto-registered embedded-tsdb source does not have this field set, so fill it in: http://127.0.0.1:17000/prometheus/api/v1/write The embedded TSDB's /prometheus endpoint only accepts requests from the local machine by default, and recording rules run inside the Center process, so 127.0.0.1 is enough.
documents.s: Before you start: the data source must accept writes

documents.t: Explorer → Metrics → Recording rules (/recording-rules), then Add. Field What to put in it Business group Which group owns the rule, and therefore who can edit it Metric name The new metric this produces. Follow the Prometheus convention <level>:<metric>:<operations> Note One line saying who this is for Data source Prometheus-type only, multi-select. Each selected source runs its own copy and writes back through its own Remote Write URL PromQL The expression to precompute, without a threshold. Each run is an instant query, so the expression must return an instant vector Execution frequency A cron expression with second precision, @every 15s by default; the dropdown offers 15s to 300s Tags key=value, separated by Enter or Space, written onto the new metric as labels A typical rule looks like this: Metric name service:http_latency:p99_5m PromQL histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (service, le) (rate(http_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) Execution frequency @every 30s Save. Expected result: the rule appears in the list with Enable switched on.

Wait one or two evaluation cycles, then go to Explorer → Metrics, pick the same data source, and query the new metric name: service:http_latency:p99_5m Data points mean it works. If nothing comes back, check in this order: is Enable on for this rule in the list; is Remote Write URL filled in on the data source (the section above); paste the PromQL into the Metrics explorer and run it — if the source expression returns nothing, the recording rule has nothing to write; look for record_eval: lines in the n9e log; a failed query logs query error, a failed write logs write error.
documents.s: 2. Confirm the new metric is actually being written

documents.t: The rule used to query: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (service, le) (rate(http_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 1 Change it to: service:http_latency:p99_5m > 1 The threshold is unchanged; the cost per evaluation goes from recomputing a quantile to reading one lightweight metric.
documents.s: 3. Point the alert rule at the new metric

documents.t: The whole gain comes from the output being much smaller than the input. Done wrong, a recording rule is slower overall — it trades "slow query" for "slow write plus slightly faster query". use sum by (<subset of labels>) to collapse down to the labels you actually alert on; drop churning labels such as instance and pod, unless alerting really groups by them; the output should have one to two orders of magnitude fewer series than the input; do not evaluate more often than the source metric is collected — with a 15s scrape interval, running every 5s just re-reads the same points.
documents.s: Only useful if it reduces cardinality

documents.t: No backfill. The new metric starts at the moment the rule is enabled; earlier time ranges simply do not have it. To look at history you go back to the original expression. One PromQL per rule. The form has a single PromQL box — no multi-query composition, no cross-source arithmetic, no separate write target. No writing elsewhere. The result always goes back to the source that was queried, and that source's own Remote Write URL decides where it lands.

Where this page ends: a link that expires on its own, letting someone without a Nightingale account open exactly one dashboard — and that you can revoke at any point before it expires.

The entry point is not on the dashboard itself, it is on the list: Explorer → Dashboards, find the row, and click the pencil icon in the Public column. Top to bottom in the dialog: Option What it means Public Choose Public — the type selector only appears afterwards Type Anonymous access / Login access / Authorized access. For someone without an account, pick Anonymous access Note Required. One dashboard can carry several live links; without a note you cannot tell which one to revoke Expiration A number plus a unit (hours / days / months / years), 30 days by default Theme System / Dark / Light. Affects only the link you copy, not the token itself Once Anonymous access is selected, the lower half of the dialog expands into Sharing link (anonymous access). Fill in the note and expiration, then click Generate link. If the dashboard is not already stored as "Public — Anonymous access", a confirmation asks whether to change that too. Confirming saves the public setting first, then issues the link. Do not skip it: a link works regardless of the public setting, so if the setting is left alone, the Public column gives no hint that this dashboard is exposed. Expected result: a new row in the table below with note, link, expiry and creator. The link looks like this: https://<your-nightingale>/dashboards/share/<dashboard id>?__token=<uuid>

Open the link in a private window. It should render the dashboard directly, with no side menu and no redirect to the login page. Landing on the login page means the token did not take effect — most often because ?__token=... was lost while copying.
documents.s: 2. Check it yourself before sending it

documents.t: Back in the same dialog, click Revoke on the row. The link stops working immediately, and the action cannot be undone. Expired links stay in the table (marked expired) rather than disappearing, so you can clean them up in the same place.

They can: open that one dashboard without logging in, for as long as the link is valid; query the data sources the dashboard references — the ones hard-coded in panels, plus every source of the same category expanded from a "Datasource"-type variable. They cannot: Open a different dashboard. A token is bound to one dashboard id; using a valid link against another dashboard is rejected outright, even if that dashboard allows anonymous access on its own. Reach a data source outside the dashboard. A request for a source not in the dashboard's set returns 403. Write anything. SQL data sources are forced through a strict read-only check on this channel, and proxied requests only pass read-only query endpoints (/api/v1/query, _search, /select/logsql/ and similar). _bulk, /-/reload and the like are refused. Two things that catch people out: A link's validity is decoupled from the public setting. The token is checked before the public/login decision, so switching the dashboard back to "Not public" does not kill links already handed out. When you change the type, the UI warns that "this dashboard still has N sharing link(s) that have not expired" and offers to revoke them — answer it properly. There is no "never expires". The ceiling is 99 years; for long-term exposure set the unit to years. It stays a revocable link rather than becoming a permanent switch.
documents.s: What the link holder can do

documents.t: The dashboard uses a "Host ident" variable. That variable type needs an authenticated API, so an anonymous viewer would get nothing. The generate button is disabled with "The dashboard has been configured with a host_ident variable and cannot be accessed anonymously". Replace it with a plain query variable first. The dashboard config could not be read. Generation is disabled the same way ("Could not read the dashboard config"). That is deliberate: unknown means not allowed. Insufficient permission. Issuing, listing and revoking all require dashboard write permission plus read-write membership of the business group. A read-only member sees none of it — being able to list links is the same as being able to forward a working anonymous link.
documents.s: When the link cannot be issued

documents.t: Temporary chart link. The chart in the Metrics explorer has a share icon; it stores the current query as a temporary chart and gives you a /chart/<id> link that opens without login (it relies on PromQuerier under [Center.AnonymousAccess], on by default). It has no expiry and no revoke. Fine as a replacement for a screenshot; not a controlled way to expose data. Alert event detail sharing. An event detail page can issue its own time-limited link (7 days by default) with the same mechanism, but it shares one event rather than a dashboard. See Active and historical events.

Where this page ends: a few dropdowns at the top of a board so that picking a host or a cluster switches every chart at once — one board serving dozens of hosts instead of dozens of copies.

Open a dashboard; the variable bar sits under the title bar. With no variables yet it shows an Add variable link; once there are some, the entry point is the pencil icon at the end of the bar. Create a Query variable: Field What to put in it Name Letters, numbers and underscores only. Panels reference it as $name or ${name} Label The text shown above the dropdown; empty falls back to the name Type See the next section Hide A hidden variable has no dropdown, but its value is still substituted Data source Where the candidate values come from Definition The expression that produces the values, see below Regex Optional. A regular expression literal (/…/) filtering the options; named capture groups let the display text differ from the value Multi select / Include all option / Custom all value Dropdown behaviour Width Dropdown width; empty means 180px On a Prometheus source, Definition accepts these forms: label_names() every label name label_values(ident) every value of one label label_values(up{job="api"}, instance) filter series first, then take one label metrics(cpu_.*) metric names matching a regex query_result(up == 0) the instant result of a PromQL query Anything without a function name is treated as a PromQL instant query, equivalent to query_result(...). The form previews the result live. If the preview shows no options, do not save — you would only be storing an empty dropdown. Expected result: after saving, a dropdown appears on the variable bar; pick a value and the panels refresh.

Type Where the options come from Typical use Query Queried from a data source Hosts, instances, clusters, service names Custom A fixed comma-separated list you type prod,staging,dev Text box Typed by whoever is looking at the board A trace id, a keyword Constant One hard-coded value Factoring out a repeated prefix, usually with Hide on Datasource Every source of one category The same board across per-region Prometheus instances Datasource identifier The same, but yielding the identifier rather than the internal id Host ident The hosts the current user may see Filtering the host list by permission The last one has a side effect worth remembering: a dashboard using Host ident cannot be shared anonymously, because it depends on an authenticated API. The UI disables link generation outright — see Anonymous time-limited sharing.

Reference one variable from another variable's definition and they cascade: cluster label_values(up, cluster) instance label_values(up{cluster="$cluster"}, instance) Picking a cluster narrows the instance options to that cluster. Order matters: the referenced variable must come first, and the variable list can be dragged to reorder.

Panel queries, panel titles and text panels all accept ${name}: cpu_usage_idle{ident="$ident"} A multi-select variable expands to a|b|c, so it must become a regex match: cpu_usage_idle{ident=~"$ident"} Beyond your own variables, a set of built-ins is always available: Built-in What it is ${__field.name} / ${__field.value} The series name / value in the legend ${__field.labels.X} / ${__field.labels.__name__} One label's value / the metric name ${__interval} / ${__interval_ms} The interval, which defaults to the step ${__range} / ${__range_ms} The length of the current time range ${__rate_interval} __interval * 4 ${__from} / ${__to} Range bounds in milliseconds; __from_date_seconds and __from_date_iso also exist Panel options also carry Repeat: pick a multi-select variable and one identical panel is rendered per value, with a configurable maximum per row. Eight identical CPU charts for eight hosts come from this, not from copy-paste.

Two things people conflate: Variable options are resolved within the current time range. label_values(...) looks at the series that existed in that window. Widening from "last 1 hour" to "last 7 days" can therefore add hosts that were decommissioned; and a host that came online twenty minutes ago legitimately does not show up yet. Check this first when a dropdown is missing something. The time range itself is not a variable. It lives in the URL as __from / __to and is remembered per dashboard in the browser. To reference it inside a query, use the ${__from} / ${__range} built-ins above.
documents.s: How the time range takes part

documents.t: Names allow only letters, numbers and underscores, matching how $name is parsed; A multi-select variable needs =~. With = the query matches the literal string a|b|c and always returns nothing; With Include all option and no Custom all value, "all" expands to every current option joined together (a|b|c), so it too only works under =~. Put .* in Custom all value if that is what you want; This page is about dashboard variables. System → Variable (/system/variable-settings) is a different feature: global variables for notification templates and rules, covered in Global variables and secrets.

Every process exposes /metrics on its own HTTP port, in Prometheus format: curl http://n9e:17000/metrics Controlled by [HTTP] ExposeMetrics, which is on by default. An alerting system that is down will not alert you about being down, so these should be scraped by your monitoring and have rules on them — see Monitor Nightingale itself.

Ordered by how early they show a problem: Metric Why n9e_alert_rule_eval_total / n9e_alert_rule_eval_error_total How many evaluations ran and how many failed. Evaluation stopping shows here first n9e_alert_rule_eval_duration_ms Time per evaluation. A slowing data source surfaces here n9e_alert_alert_queue_size Event queue backlog. Sustained growth means the downstream cannot keep up n9e_alert_query_data_error_total Failed data source queries n9e_center_http_request_duration_seconds Web and API latency n9e_db_operation_latency_seconds Metadata database latency

Nightingale exposes 55 metrics of its own on every process's /metrics endpoint ([HTTP] ExposeMetrics is on by default). Go runtime and process metrics are left out below — every Go program has those, and they say nothing about Nightingale. The 16 marked † come from the source rather than from a live scrape: a labelled metric does not appear on /metrics until something first observes it, so a freshly started instance will not show them. That is expected — write rules against the name regardless.

Nightingale's command line is thin — configuration lives in the toml files under etc/, and there are three flags. There are no subcommands for managing alert rules and the like; that is what the HTTP API is for.

n9e (Center), n9e-alert, n9e-pushgw and n9e-edge take exactly the same flags: Flag Meaning Default --configs <dir> Configuration directory. Also settable as N9E_CONFIGS etc --crypto-key <key> Key for decrypting encrypted fields in the config file empty --version Print the version and exit ./n9e --configs /etc/n9e N9E_CONFIGS=/etc/n9e ./n9e ./n9e --version A process needs only the etc/ and integrations/ directories next to the binary.

The n9e-cli in the release does one thing: migrate v5 configuration to v6. Flag Meaning --config <path> Path to a v5.x webapi.conf --upgrade Run the migration --version Print the version Useful if you are still on v5, irrelevant otherwise.

To be clear up front: the project publishes no official support matrix. What follows was verified against the release artefacts and the code — it is not a promise. Treat this page as a starting set of known-good combinations, not as an exhaustive list of what works.

Configuration lives in the etc/ directory next to the binary. n9e, n9e-alert and n9e-pushgw read config.toml; n9e-edge reads etc/edge/edge.toml. Point them elsewhere with --configs, or the N9E_CONFIGS environment variable: ./n9e --configs /etc/n9e N9E_CONFIGS=/etc/n9e ./n9e

[EmbeddedTSDB] is handled by Center only. n9e-edge, n9e-alert and n9e-pushgw read the same etc directory and ignore this section. [DB] DBType = "sqlite" and [Redis] RedisType = "miniredis" are testing defaults. miniredis is an in-process stand-in that several instances cannot share. Production needs the real thing — see Choosing a metadata database. Turning on [HTTP.ProxyAuth] disables JWT login entirely; it is a one-way switch. MaxQueryBytes is the serialized-bytes budget of one query's result; a query that hits it returns the newest records it fits plus an explicit "truncated" note. Raising it costs roughly MaxConcurrentQueries x MaxQueryBytes x 3.7 of extra heap on this engine (decoded records measure ~2.7x their on-disk bytes, plus one marshalled copy in the handler), and it must stay below the 48MB per-node response cap on the center side. First, the thing to be clear about: Nightingale has no mechanism for overriding arbitrary config keys from the environment. There is no N9E_DB_DSN. Configuration comes from the toml files under etc/ and nowhere else. The containerised answer is to mount a config file, not to pile up environment variables — which is exactly what the compose bundles do (./etc-nightingale:/app/etc).

Variable Purpose Default N9E_CONFIGS Center's config directory; same as --configs etc N9E_ALERT_CONFIGS Config directory for n9e-alert etc N9E_PUSHGW_CONFIGS Config directory for n9e-pushgw etc N9E_EDGE_CONFIGS Config directory for n9e-edge etc/edge N9E_PROXY_URL Proxy for outbound HTTP empty N9E_GRAFANA_IMPORT_ALLOWLIST Allowed addresses when importing from Grafana empty N9E_SKILL_GATEWAY Egress gateway socket for the Skill sandbox (Linux sandbox) empty

These belong to other containers, not to Nightingale — worth knowing when reading a compose file: Variable Belongs to MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD the mysql container POSTGRES_USER / POSTGRES_PASSWORD / POSTGRES_DB / PGDATA the postgres container WAIT_HOSTS the wait-for-dependencies entrypoint HOST_PROC / HOST_SYS / HOST_MOUNT_PREFIX the categraf container, for collecting from the host GIN_MODE / TZ generic
documents.s: Variables you will see in the compose bundles

documents.t: Three approaches, best first: One config file per environment, selected with N9E_CONFIGS or --configs. Plainest, and the easiest to audit. Template plus render at start: have the container entrypoint substitute variables into the toml (envsubst or similar) before launching the process. Encrypted fields: store sensitive values encrypted in the config file against a --crypto-key, and keep the key itself in the environment or a secret manager. See Secret management.

The Nightingale web UI runs entirely on a public HTTP API — everything you can do in the interface has an endpoint behind it. That is good news: automation does not need a second API, it uses the same one the UI does. There is no OpenAPI / Swagger document today. The authority is the routing table itself, ccfos/nightingale/center/router/router.go, where all 413 /api/n9e/* endpoints are registered. The fastest way to find the endpoint for an action is to open your browser's network panel and perform the action in the UI.

Group Prefix Auth Purpose Page API /api/n9e/* JWT or X-User-Token What people and automation use — 413 endpoints Service API /v1/n9e/* basic auth For integrating external systems — 91 endpoints, off by default The service API is governed by [HTTP.APIForService], Enable = false by default. Edge mode requires turning it on.

Prefer a personal token. Generate one from the avatar menu; it is long-lived until deleted: curl -H "X-User-Token: <token>" \ http://n9e:17000/api/n9e/busi-groups Or exchange credentials for a JWT: curl -X POST http://n9e:17000/api/n9e/auth/login \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username":"root","password":"<password>"}' # take dat.access_token from the response, then send Authorization: Bearer <token> A token has no permissions of its own — it acts as its owner. Generate automation tokens from a dedicated least-privilege account; see Tokens and credential rotation.

Both success and failure return 200; the err field in the body is what distinguishes them: {"dat": {...}, "err": "", "request_id": "..."} {"err": "some message", "request_id": "..."} List endpoints return dat in two different shapes, and a script has to handle both: sometimes a bare array, sometimes {"list": [...], "total": N}.

An unmatched /api/n9e/* path returns 200 and an HTML page — the single-page app's entry point, not a 404. So: # this proves nothing; a typo returns 200 too curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://n9e:17000/api/n9e/does-not-exist To tell whether an endpoint exists, check that the response is JSON, or read the routing table. This trap comes back in troubleshooting.
documents.s: Warning: a status code does not prove an endpoint exists

documents.t: By object; the routing table has the complete list: Object Endpoints Business groups GET/POST /busi-groups, PUT/DELETE /busi-group/:id Alert rules GET/POST /busi-group/:id/alert-rules, POST /busi-group/:id/alert-rules/import, GET /alert-rule/:arid/pure Active events GET /alert-cur-events/list, GET /alert-cur-events/card, DELETE /alert-cur-events Historical events GET /alert-his-events/list Mute rules GET/POST /busi-group/:id/alert-mutes Subscriptions GET/POST /busi-group/:id/alert-subscribes Data sources POST /datasource/list, POST /datasource/upsert, DELETE /datasource/ Dashboards GET/POST /busi-group/:id/boards, GET/PUT /board/:bid, POST /busi-groups/boards/clones Targets GET /targets, PUT /targets/bgids, PUT /targets/note, POST /targets/tags Notification rules GET/POST /notify-rules, PUT /notify-rule/:id Media types GET/POST /notify-channel-configs, PUT /notify-channel-config/:id Message templates GET/POST /message-templates, PUT /message-template/:id Workflows GET /event-pipelines, POST/PUT /event-pipeline Users and teams GET/POST /users, GET/POST /user-groups, GET /roles Integration templates GET /builtin-components, GET /builtin-payloads A few create endpoints take an array rather than a single object: /notify-channel-configs, /message-templates and /notify-rules. Posting a bare object fails with cannot unmarshal object into Go value of type []....
/alert-cur-events and /alert-his-events only list and delete. Events come from rule evaluation and nowhere else. To produce test data, write a rule that is certain to fire.

Collector requests are separate from the management API. They are enabled by [HTTP.APIForAgent].Enable and write metrics into the embedded store or configured external writers. A web-login JWT is not the collector credential. Format Receiver Guide Prometheus Remote Write POST /prometheus/v1/write Telegraf, Categraf OpenTSDB JSON POST /opentsdb/put Data ingestion protocols Datadog v1 series POST /datadog/api/v1/series Datadog Agent compatibility Remote Write and OpenTSDB use the configured Agent BasicAuth when enabled. Datadog v1 series instead matches api_key against its password values. Check authentication and the actual destination store before treating an HTTP response as proof that a sample is queryable.
