documents.t: S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: {__name__=~"AliyunRds_MySQL_(SlaveIO|SlaveSQL)Running"} != 1 Runbook: Confirm the replication state and lag on the read-only instance page in the Alibaba Cloud console; The console usually offers a repair-replication entry — use it first; If it was caused by the primary's binlog being purged, the read-only instance must be rebuilt; Move read traffic off that read-only instance before you start.
documents.s: AliYun RDS MySQL / instance state abnormal alert

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: AliyunRds_ConnectionUsage{engine="MySQL"} > 80 Runbook: Check the connection count curve against the specification ceiling in the console; Group connections by source with SHOW PROCESSLIST (MySQL family) or db.currentOp() (MongoDB) to find the abnormal application; Tell business growth apart from a connection pool leak (many idle connections piling up); Upgrade as an emergency measure, and cap the application pool and shorten idle timeouts for the root cause.
documents.s: AliYun RDS MySQL / connection usage alert

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_amqp_instance_connections_value > 1000 Runbook: Confirm the connection count curve against the specification ceiling in the console; Check whether clients open a new connection for every send/receive — the correct pattern is a reused long-lived connection with one channel per thread; Confirm no client is reconnecting abnormally; If you genuinely need more connections, upgrade the instance specification.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_amqp_instance_consumers_value < 1 Runbook: Confirm in the console which vhost/queue has no consumers; On the consumer side, confirm the application process is alive and not reporting connection or auth errors; If the consumer is healthy but not connected, verify the vhost, queue name and credentials; Once consumption resumes, watch the backlog start to drain.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_amqp_instance_vhost_queue_message_accum_maximum > 1000 Runbook: Confirm in the console which queue has the largest backlog and how fast it is growing; Check whether the consumer count is zero or clearly insufficient — start or scale out consumers first; If consumers exist but are slow, check the consumer log for abnormal retries or downstream timeouts; For a huge backlog, consider temporarily increasing consumer concurrency.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)CpuUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)CpuUsage") > 80 Runbook: Check the CPU curve under console performance monitoring and use real-time key analysis to find hot keys; Use the slow log to find O(N) commands (KEYS, HGETALL, wide ZRANGE) and rework them; Splitting large keys is the single most effective optimisation; If it stays high, upgrade the specification or move to the cluster edition to spread the load.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)QPSUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)QPSUsage") > 80 Runbook: Confirm the QPS curve against the specification ceiling in the console; Determine whether it is business growth or cache breakdown letting requests through; Adding a local cache and batching requests on the application side reduces QPS significantly; If you genuinely need more capacity, upgrade or move to the cluster edition.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)MemoryUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)MemoryUsage") > 80 Runbook: Use the console's cache analysis to find the key prefixes consuming the most memory; Split large keys and add TTLs to keys that have none; Confirm maxmemory-policy matches expectations; If capacity is genuinely short, upgrade the specification in the console.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)HitRate"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)HitRate") < 30 Runbook: First rule out a cold start after a restart or resize; In the console, check whether it comes with heavy key eviction — if so treat it as insufficient memory; Review the cache key design and whether the TTL is too short; Confirm there is no flood of lookups for non-existent keys (cache penetration) — add null caching or a bloom filter if needed.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_StandardFailedCount"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)FailedCount") > 0 Runbook: Use the console audit log or the application log to identify the failing command type and error; Common causes are writes rejected for lack of memory, exceeding the connection limit, or a disabled command; Handle each accordingly (upgrade, reduce connections, use a supported command); Confirm the application has retry and fallback logic.

Unit: milliseconds S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)AvgRt"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)AvgRt") > 100000 Runbook: Use the console slow log to find the slowest commands; Focus on O(N) commands and big-key operations, switching to SCAN or batching; Check whether throttling was triggered (bandwidth/QPS over specification); Once those are ruled out, upgrade the specification in the console.
documents.s: AliYun Redis average response time alert

documents.t: Unit: milliseconds S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)SyncDelayTime"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)SyncDelayTime") > 5 Runbook: Confirm the lag curve and the instance architecture in the console; A spike in primary writes amplifies lag — check for bulk write jobs; Syncing large keys causes obvious latency spikes — use cache analysis to find and split them; If lag persists, move read traffic back to the primary.
documents.s: AliYun Redis data sync latency alert

documents.t: Unit: milliseconds S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)MaxRt"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)MaxRt") > 100000 Runbook: Use the console slow log to find the single slowest command; Tail latency usually comes from big-key operations or blocking commands — split large keys first; Check whether an RDB/AOF persistence fork is causing periodic stalls; If it persists after tuning, upgrade the specification in the console.
documents.s: AliYun Redis max response time alert

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)IntranetInRatio"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)IntranetInRatio") > 80 Runbook: Confirm the bandwidth curve against the specification ceiling in the console; Use cache analysis to find large keys — writing large keys is the main cause of saturated bandwidth; Split large keys and reduce one-shot bulk writes; If you genuinely need more bandwidth, upgrade the specification.
documents.s: AliYun Redis inbound bandwidth usage alert

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)IntranetOutRatio"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)IntranetOutRatio") > 80 Runbook: Confirm the bandwidth curve against the specification ceiling in the console; Use cache analysis to find large keys — reading large keys is the main source of outbound bandwidth; Split large keys and avoid one-shot HGETALL/SMEMBERS full reads; If you genuinely need more bandwidth, upgrade the specification.
documents.s: AliYun Redis outbound bandwidth usage alert

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|ShardingProxy|Splitrw|SplitrwProxy)ConnectionUsage"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)ConnectionUsage") Runbook: Confirm the connection count curve against the specification ceiling in the console; Check whether clients fail to reuse connections or the pool is oversized; As an emergency measure upgrade in the console to raise the connection limit; For the root cause, cap the application pool and enable connection reuse.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: label_replace({__name__=~"AliyunKvstore_(Standard|Sharding|Splitrw)Keys"},"redisType","$1","measure","(.+)Keys") > 80 Runbook: Use the console's cache analysis to count keys by prefix and find the fastest-growing prefix; Confirm whether those keys should have a TTL — cache keys without expiry are a classic memory leak; Add sensible expiry times and clean up the existing keys; Confirm the application is not using Redis as persistent storage.
documents.s: AliYun Redis cached key count alert

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_upstream_code5xx_average > 10 Runbook: In the console, confirm whether it is Upstream 5xx (returned by the backend) or instance 5xx (from SLB itself); For Upstream 5xx, check the application logs on the backend ECS for the root cause; Instance 5xx usually means all backends are unhealthy — check the health check configuration and backend state; If it lines up with a recent release, roll back first.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_status_code5xx_average > 10 Runbook: In the console, confirm whether it is Upstream 5xx (returned by the backend) or instance 5xx (from SLB itself); For Upstream 5xx, check the application logs on the backend ECS for the root cause; Instance 5xx usually means all backends are unhealthy — check the health check configuration and backend state; If it lines up with a recent release, roll back first.
documents.s: AliYun-SLB - L7 instance status code 5xx (Count/Second) above 10

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_qps_utilization_average > 50 Runbook: Confirm the QPS curve against the instance specification's performance ceiling in the console; Determine whether it is genuine business growth or abnormal traffic; For growth, upgrade the SLB specification (guaranteed-performance instances let you set the ceiling); For abnormal traffic, add WAF/DDoS protection and rate limiting.
documents.s: AliYun-SLB - L7 instance QPS usage exceeds 50%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_drop_connection_average > 0 Runbook: In the console, compare the drop curve against the instance specification's connection/bandwidth ceiling to see which one topped out; If it topped out, upgrade the specification immediately — shared-performance instances top out especially easily at peak; Check whether abnormal traffic is consuming the quota; After upgrading, confirm drops return to zero.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_drop_traffic_rx_average > 0 Runbook: In the console, compare the drop curve against the instance specification's connection/bandwidth ceiling to see which one topped out; If it topped out, upgrade the specification immediately — shared-performance instances top out especially easily at peak; Check whether abnormal traffic is consuming the quota; After upgrading, confirm drops return to zero.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_drop_traffic_tx_average > 0 Runbook: In the console, compare the drop curve against the instance specification's connection/bandwidth ceiling to see which one topped out; If it topped out, upgrade the specification immediately — shared-performance instances top out especially easily at peak; Check whether abnormal traffic is consuming the quota; After upgrading, confirm drops return to zero.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_new_connection_utilization_average > 50 Runbook: Confirm the max connection and new connection curves in the console; Check whether the backend is responding more slowly and causing connections to pile up — a high connection count is often a symptom of a slow backend; If the backend is fine, upgrade the SLB specification; Check whether clients are failing to reuse connections.
documents.s: AliYun-SLB - instance new connection usage exceeds 50%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: aliyun_acs_slb_dashboard_instance_max_connection_utilization_average > 50 Runbook: Confirm the max connection and new connection curves in the console; Check whether the backend is responding more slowly and causing connections to pile up — a high connection count is often a symptom of a slow backend; If the backend is fine, upgrade the SLB specification; Check whether clients are failing to reuse connections.
documents.s: AliYun-SLB - instance max connection usage exceeds 50%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: 100 * AliyunSlb_InstanceStatusCode4xx{} / on(loadBalancerId) group_left sum({__name__=~"AliyunSlb_InstanceStatusCode.+"}) by (loadBalancerId,loadBalancerName,regionId) > 10 Runbook: Check the 4xx breakdown in the console to see whether 404 or 403/401 dominates; A 404 spike usually means the frontend references a decommissioned endpoint — check the release log; A 403/401 spike points at an auth configuration change or expired credentials; For suspected scanning traffic, put a WAF in front to block it.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: 100 * AliyunSlb_InstanceStatusCode5xx{} / on(loadBalancerId) group_left sum({__name__=~"AliyunSlb_InstanceStatusCode.+"}) by (loadBalancerId,loadBalancerName,regionId) > 10 Runbook: In the console, confirm whether it is Upstream 5xx (returned by the backend) or instance 5xx (from SLB itself); For Upstream 5xx, check the application logs on the backend ECS for the root cause; Instance 5xx usually means all backends are unhealthy — check the health check configuration and backend state; If it lines up with a recent release, roll back first.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: AliyunSlb_InstanceQpsUtilization{} > 80 Runbook: Confirm the QPS curve against the instance specification's performance ceiling in the console; Determine whether it is genuine business growth or abnormal traffic; For growth, upgrade the SLB specification (guaranteed-performance instances let you set the ceiling); For abnormal traffic, add WAF/DDoS protection and rate limiting.
documents.s: AliYun SLB L7 instance QPS usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: AliyunSlb_InstanceMaxConnectionUtilization{} > 80 Runbook: Confirm the max connection and new connection curves in the console; Check whether the backend is responding more slowly and causing connections to pile up — a high connection count is often a symptom of a slow backend; If the backend is fine, upgrade the SLB specification; Check whether clients are failing to reuse connections.
documents.s: AliYun SLB instance max connection usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: AliyunSlb_DropConnection{} > 10 Runbook: In the console, compare the drop curve against the instance specification's connection/bandwidth ceiling to see which one topped out; If it topped out, upgrade the specification immediately — shared-performance instances top out especially easily at peak; Check whether abnormal traffic is consuming the quota; After upgrading, confirm drops return to zero.

The AMD ROCm SMI input is ported from Telegraf. It runs the rocm-smi binary that ships with ROCm and parses the output into per-GPU utilization, memory usage, temperature, power draw, fan speed and clock frequencies. ROCm must be installed on the host; the default binary path is /opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi, adjustable via bin_path. The rules fire on high temperature, exhausted memory and power close to the cap.
documents.s: Monitor AMD ROCm SMI with Nightingale

documents.t: 4 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.amd_rocm_smi

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.amd_rocm_smi/rocm.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.amd_rocm_smi started once the plugin is loaded. # Query statistics from AMD Graphics cards using rocm-smi binary # bin_path = "/opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi" ## Optional: timeout for GPU polling # timeout = "5s" Open the integration center in Nightingale, find AMD ROCm SMI, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
4 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: amd_rocm_smi_memory_used / (amd_rocm_smi_memory_total > 0) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Take gpu_id and name from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showmemuse --showpids to see which processes hold the memory; If a zombie process has exited without releasing memory, confirm nobody is using it and kill it to free the memory; If the training job genuinely needs that much memory, reduce the batch size or enable gradient accumulation and mixed precision; When several jobs share one card, switch to memory isolation or queued scheduling so they do not squeeze each other into failure.
documents.s: AMD GPU memory usage too high

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: amd_rocm_smi_temperature_sensor_junction > 95 Runbook: Take gpu_id from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showtemp --showfan --showpower to check temperature, fan speed, and power draw; If the fan speed is low, check whether the fan has failed or is clogged with dust and clean it during a maintenance window if needed; If the fan is already at full speed and it is still hot, check the chassis airflow and data centre intake temperature, and whether neighbouring slots are too densely populated; In the short term you can limit heat with rocm-smi --setpoweroverdrive to cap power, but the cooling problem must be fixed promptly.
documents.s: AMD GPU junction temperature too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: amd_rocm_smi_temperature_sensor_edge > 85 Runbook: Take gpu_id from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showtemp --showclocks to compare temperature with the current clocks and confirm whether it is already throttling; Check the temperature of the other GPUs on the same machine; if they are all high it is a chassis- or room-level cooling problem; If only one card is hot, check that card's fan, thermal paste, and mounting position; While fixing cooling, evaluate whether to reduce job concurrency on that card so it does not run throttled for long periods.
documents.s: AMD GPU edge temperature too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: amd_rocm_smi_temperature_sensor_memory > 95 Runbook: Take gpu_id from the alert labels and run rocm-smi --showtemp to compare the memory temperature with the junction temperature; A memory temperature well above the junction temperature usually means poor contact on the memory heatsink and requires a maintenance window to inspect; Check whether long-running high memory bandwidth workloads (such as large model inference) are involved and reduce concurrency to relieve it; Also run rocm-smi --showretiredpages to check for bad pages; growing bad pages mean the memory is degrading and the card should be scheduled for replacement.
documents.s: AMD GPU memory temperature too high

With mod_status enabled, Apache httpd serves a machine-readable status page at /server-status?auto. The input scrapes it for total accesses and traffic, requests per second, busy and idle workers, CPU load, uptime and the distribution of worker states. The rules cover idle workers running out, requests queuing, httpd being unreachable and restarts. Remember to restrict who can reach the status page.
5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.apache

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.apache/apache.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.apache started once the plugin is loaded. [[instances]] # https://statuslist.app/apache/apache-status-page-simple-setup-guide/ # scrape_uri = "http://localhost/server-status/?auto" # host_override = "" # insecure = false # custom_headers = {} # log_level = "info" Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Apache, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: apache_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status httpd (or apache2) to confirm whether the master process is alive; If the process is alive, run curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1/server-status?auto' to verify by hand whether the status page is blocked by a Require directive or a firewall; If the process is gone, run httpd -t to validate the configuration before starting it, and check the tail of error_log for the cause (port already in use, expired certificate, module load failure are common); Confirm the upstream load balancer has removed this node so traffic stops being sent to it.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: apache_workers{state="idle"} == 0 Runbook: Run curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1/server-status?auto' and read the Scoreboard to see which state workers are stuck in (W = sending reply, meaning a slow backend; R = reading request, meaning slow clients); If they are stuck in W, first check whether the backend (PHP-FPM, database, upstream API) has slowed down, and use tail -f access_log to find the slow URLs from the response-time column; As a stopgap, raise MaxRequestWorkers and ServerLimit and reload gracefully, but re-check memory first (per-worker memory x concurrency must not exceed physical memory); If slow clients are holding workers, enable mod_reqtimeout and lower KeepAliveTimeout.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: sum without (state) (apache_workers{state="busy"}) / sum without (state) (apache_scoreboard) * 100 > 85 Runbook: Run curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1/server-status?auto' and compare BusyWorkers against the open_slot headroom in the Scoreboard; Use tail -n 10000 access_log | awk to rank URLs by count and latency, and decide whether this is genuine traffic growth or one slow endpoint holding workers; For traffic growth, scale out instances or raise MaxRequestWorkers (recalculating ServerLimit against memory); For a slow endpoint, fix the backend first and apply mod_reqtimeout or rate limiting to that URL so a single endpoint cannot drain the whole process pool.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(apache_duration_ms_total[5m]) / (rate(apache_accesses_total[5m]) > 0) > 1000 Runbook: Confirm the access_log LogFormat includes %D (microsecond duration), then run awk '{print $NF, $7}' access_log | sort -rn | head -20 to find the slowest URLs; If the slow URLs are dynamic requests, move on to the backend (PHP-FPM slowlog, application logs, database slow queries); If static assets are slow, check disk IO and whether sendfile or caching was accidentally disabled; While investigating, apply mod_ratelimit or degrade that URL so workers are not held indefinitely.
documents.s: Apache average request duration too long

documents.t: S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: apache_uptime_seconds_total < 300 Runbook: First confirm whether this was a planned release by checking change records and shell history; If unplanned, run journalctl -u httpd --since '-30min' and tail -200 error_log to determine whether it was a segfault, an OOM, or a configuration error; For an OOM kill, confirm with dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' and lower MaxRequestWorkers based on real per-worker memory; For repeated crashes, keep core dumps (CoreDumpDirectory) and bisect by disabling third-party modules one at a time.

AutoMQ is a Kafka-compatible messaging system with separated compute and storage. It sends metrics to an OTel Collector's Prometheus exporter or exposes Prometheus-format data on its own endpoint (8890 in the reference test). Scrape that with the Categraf prometheus input, using whatever port your deployment configures. The template ships five dashboards (cluster overview, broker, topic, consumer group and detail) and metric descriptions for requests, throughput, latency, storage and object-store operations. The rules cover brokers going offline, request error rate, consumer lag and failed storage operations.
5 dashboards, 97 panels in total 12 alert rules, each with runbook steps 59 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.prometheus

These components expose Prometheus-format /metrics themselves, so the Categraf prometheus input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, add it as a Nightingale data source and the templates work as they are. Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.prometheus/采集OTEL-COLLECTOR的样例.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.prometheus started once the plugin is loaded. interval = 15 [[instances]] urls = [ "http://<automq-or-otel-collector>:8890/metrics" ] # AutoMQ metrics already contain an instance label; do not overwrite it. url_label_key = "otel_collector" url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" labels = { source = "automq" } Open the integration center in Nightingale, find AutoMQ, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels Broker Metrics 13 Cluster Overview 12 Detailed Metrics 60 Group Metrics 2 Topic Metrics 10
12 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(kafka_controller_active_count) by (job) != 1 Runbook: On each broker confirm the process is alive and can reach the controller quorum; In KRaft mode run kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server <broker> describe --status to check the quorum; When the count is 0, restore the failed controller nodes first — the cluster elects automatically once the majority is back; When it is above 1, investigate the network partition and then stop the minority side so the cluster reconverges.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(kafka_server_connection_count) by (job, instance) > 1000 Runbook: Run ss -tn state established '( sport = :9092 )' | awk '{print $5}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to see which clients the connections come from; Tell more client instances apart from a connection leak (producers/consumers not being reused); As an emergency measure raise the broker's file handle limit; For the root cause, make clients reuse connections and confirm there is no short-lived reconnect pattern.
documents.s: Kafka broker has too many connections

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: kafka_request_time_99p_milliseconds{type="Fetch"} > 1000 Runbook: Check broker disk IO and page cache hit rate — slow Fetch usually means cold data being read from disk; Check whether a consumer is replaying from a very old offset and pulling large amounts of cold data; Check whether network bandwidth is saturated; If it persists, add brokers or memory to raise the page cache hit rate.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: kafka_partition_count > 5000 Runbook: Run kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server <broker> --describe to count partitions per topic and find the ones that are clearly oversized; Check whether the partition count matches actual throughput — many topics are sized by guesswork; Partitions can only be added, never removed, so shrinking means creating a new topic and migrating; Delete long-idle abandoned topics — that is the quickest win.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: kafka_request_time_99p_milliseconds{type="Produce"} > 100 Runbook: Check broker disk write latency and whether network bandwidth is saturated; Check the acks setting — with acks=all latency follows the slowest replica, so look for lagging replicas; Run kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions to confirm replication is healthy; If the storage side is clearly the bottleneck, add brokers or move to faster disks.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(rate(kafka_request_count_total{type="Fetch"}[1m])) by (job, instance) > 1000 Runbook: Check the consumer count together with fetch.min.bytes / fetch.max.wait.ms — values that are too small cause busy high-frequency polling; Raising fetch.min.bytes makes consumers batch their fetches and significantly reduces request count; Check whether consumers are spinning (polling frequently with no data); Combine with broker CPU to judge whether to scale out.
documents.s: Kafka fetch requests exceed 1000 per second

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(rate(kafka_request_count_total{type="Produce"}[1m])) by (job, instance) > 1000 Runbook: Check the producer's batch.size and linger.ms — values that are too small mean one request per message; Raising linger.ms lets the producer batch and dramatically reduces the request count; Check whether producers have compression enabled (compression.type); Combine with broker CPU to judge whether to scale out.
documents.s: Kafka produce requests exceed 1000 per second

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(max(kafka_log_end_offset) by (job, topic, partition)) by (job, topic) - on (topic) group_left (consumer_group) sum(max(kafka_group_commit_offset) by (job, consumer_group, topic, partition)) by (job, consumer_group, topic) > 10000 Runbook: Take topic and consumer_group from the alert labels and run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group <group> to see the LAG distribution per partition; Lag concentrated on a few partitions means data skew — check the producer's partition key; Evenly spread lag means slow consumers: check the consumer logs for abnormal retries, then add consumer instances (never beyond the partition count); Confirm the consumers have not all dropped out.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(rate(kafka_stream_operation_latency_count{operation_type="S3Request", status="failed"}[1m])) by (job, operation_name) > 0.1 Runbook: Take operation_name from the alert labels to identify which operation is failing (upload, download, delete); Find the matching S3 error code in the broker log and separate permissions (403), throttling (503 SlowDown) and network timeouts; For throttling, ask the object storage side to raise the quota or reduce write concurrency; For permissions, verify the AK/SK and bucket policy; for network issues, check connectivity and bandwidth to the object store.
documents.s: Kafka S3 request failure rate high

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(rate(kafka_request_error_count_total{error!="NONE"}[1m])) by (job, instance, error) > 0.1 Runbook: Take the error field from the alert labels to identify the error type; NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER usually means partition leaders are moving — check whether the cluster is rebalancing; For REQUEST_TIMED_OUT, check broker load and disk IO; For authentication/authorization errors, verify the client's ACLs and credentials.
documents.s: Kafka request error rate too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="in"}[1m])) by (job) > 50 * 1024 * 1024 sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="in"}[1m])) by (job) > 20 * 1024 * 1024 Runbook: Use kafka-topics.sh together with per-topic traffic metrics to find the highest-traffic topic; Determine whether it is natural growth or a client resending abnormally; If producers have no compression, enable compression.type=lz4/zstd — that usually cuts bandwidth immediately; Once confirmed, add brokers or NIC bandwidth as needed.
documents.s: Kafka cluster inbound network traffic high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="out"}[1m])) by (job) > 50 * 1024 * 1024 sum(rate(kafka_broker_network_io_bytes_total{direction="out"}[1m])) by (job) > 20 * 1024 * 1024 Runbook: Identify the topics and consumer groups with the highest consume traffic; Check whether a consumer group is doing a full replay from the beginning — this is the most common cause of an outbound traffic spike; Check whether there are far more consumers than needed, and whether groups consuming the same topic can be merged; Add brokers or NIC bandwidth as needed.
documents.s: Kafka cluster outbound network traffic high

The Azure input calls the Azure Monitor metrics API and pulls metrics by subscription, resource group or resource type (virtual machines, storage accounts, SQL databases, App Service and so on). The config lets you name the metrics and aggregations to collect per resource type. Register a service principal, grant it the Monitoring Reader role, and put the tenant ID, client ID, secret and subscription ID into the config. The Azure API allows 12,000 reads per hour, so keep the interval and metric count within that budget.
Categraf collector config: input.azure

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.azure/azure.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.azure started once the plugin is loaded. # Gather Azure resources metrics from Azure Monitor API # 每2m查询一次azure monitor, 查询时间范围也为2m interval = "2m" [[instances]] # can be found under Overview->Essentials in the Azure portal for your application/service subscription_id = "" # can be obtained by registering an application under Azure Active Directory client_id = "" # can be obtained by registering an application under Azure Active Directory. # If not specified Default Azure Credentials chain will be attempted: # - Environment credentials (AZURE_*) # - Workload Identity in Kubernetes cluster # - Managed Identity # - Azure CLI auth # - Developer Azure CLI auth client_secret = "" # can be found under Azure Active Directory->Properties tenant_id = "" # Define the optional Azure cloud option e.g. AzureChina, AzureGovernment or AzurePublic. The default is AzurePublic. # cloud_option = "AzurePublic" # 聚合粒度 # 比如我采集周期是10m, 指标上报周期是30s, 那么在10m内会有20个原始点 # 经过该参数的聚合处理后，比如聚合粒度是1m, 那么就会获取到10个点 # 注意，最小值是1m # 支持的值为1m,5m,15m,30m,1h,6h,12h,1d # 且aggregation_interval不能大于interval aggregation_interval = "1m" ## 以下为采集目标配置，有三种方式，分别是指定资源、指定资源组、指定订阅 ## 三种方法可同时使用 # 方式一：指定具体的资源, 比如某台具体的主机 # [[instances.resource_target]] # can be found under Overview->Essentials->JSON View in the Azure portal for your application/service # must start with 'resourceGroups/...' ('/subscriptions/xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx' # must be removed from the beginning of Resource ID property value) # resource_id = "resourceGroups/flashcat/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/lfn-test" # the metric names to collect # leave the array empty to use all metrics available to this resource # metrics = [ "<<METRIC>>", "<<METRIC>>" ] # metrics aggregation type value to collect # can be 'Total', 'Count', 'Average', 'Minimum', 'Maximum' # leave the array empty to collect all aggregation types values for each metric # aggregations = [ "<<AGGREGATION>>", "<<AGGREGATION>>" ] # 方式二：指定资源组 # # resource group target #1 to collect metrics from resources under it with resource type # [[instances.resource_group_target]] # # the resource group name # resource_group = "flashcat" # # # defines the resources to collect metrics from # [[instances.resource_group_target.resource]] # # the resource type # resource_type = "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines" # metrics = [ "<<METRIC>>", "<<METRIC>>" ] # aggregations = [ "<<AGGREGATION>>", "<<AGGREGATION>>" ] # 方式三：指定订阅ID # # subscription target #1 to collect metrics from resources under it with resource type # [[instances.subscription_target]] # resource_type = "<<RESOURCE_TYPE>>" # metrics = [ "<<METRIC>>", "<<METRIC>>" ] # aggregations = [ "<<AGGREGATION>>", "<<AGGREGATION>>" ]

The BIND input is ported from Telegraf and reads the statistics channel of named (http://localhost:8053/xml/v3 by default): incoming queries by type, responses by rcode, recursive clients, socket and network counters, cache state per view and memory context usage. Configure statistics-channels in named.conf and restrict who can reach it. The rules cover rising SERVFAIL and REFUSED ratios, recursive clients near the limit, query volume dropping and named being unreachable.
5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.bind

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.bind/bind.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.bind started once the plugin is loaded. [[instances]] urls = [ # "http://localhost:8053/xml/v3", ] gather_memory_contexts = true gather_views = true timeout = "5s" # labels={app="bind"} Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Bind, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_SERVFAIL[5m])) / (sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_Response[5m])) > 0) * 100 > 5 Runbook: Run rndc querylog to turn on query logging (remember to run it again to turn it off afterwards) and find the domains that dominate the errors in the named log; Run dig +trace @127.0.0.1 <domain> against that domain to tell whether the upstream authoritative server is unreachable, DNSSEC validation is failing, or a forwarder is broken; For DNSSEC failures, verify with dig +cd first, then fix the trust anchor or temporarily add a negative-trust-anchor for that zone; For forwarder problems, check that the servers in forwarders are reachable and switch to a backup DNS server.
documents.s: BIND SERVFAIL response ratio too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: sum without (type) (bind_counter_RecursClients) > 900 Runbook: Run rndc status to see the live recursive client count and the configured limit; Spot-check a few slow domains with dig +trace to determine whether a slow upstream authoritative server is causing recursive requests to pile up; Once confirmed, raise recursive-clients in options (re-checking memory) and run rndc reload; If malicious queries are filling the quota, configure response-rate-limit and tighten the source networks allowed by allow-recursion.
documents.s: BIND recursive clients approaching the limit

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: sum without (type) (increase(bind_counter_RecLimitDropped[5m])) > 0 Runbook: Run rndc status immediately to confirm recursive client usage; Run rndc recursing to dump the queries currently being resolved and identify the domain or client consuming the quota; As an emergency measure raise recursive-clients and run rndc reload to restore service; Afterwards check the health of the upstream authoritative servers for the domain you identified, or restrict the offending source IPs with allow-recursion or RRL.
documents.s: BIND hit the recursive client limit and is dropping queries

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_QueryTimeout[5m])) / ((sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_Queryv4[5m])) + sum without (type) (rate(bind_counter_Queryv6[5m]))) > 0) * 100 > 10 Runbook: Run rndc dumpdb -all and inspect the dump file for slow upstream servers; From the BIND host run dig @<authoritative IP> plus ping/mtr to separate an upstream outage from packet loss on this host's egress; If IPv6 is unreachable and causing the timeouts, add -4 to the named start-up arguments or disable outbound IPv6 queries; Longer term, add forwarders and enable forward first to reduce the share of queries recursed directly to authoritative servers.
documents.s: BIND recursive query timeout ratio too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum without (type) (increase(bind_counter_QryDropped[5m])) > 0 Runbook: Look for client-related dropped entries in the named log and identify the source IPs and query names being dropped; If the source is a legitimate business network, check whether the allow-query / allow-recursion ACLs are missing that range; If the sources are scattered and the query names look random, treat it as a random-subdomain attack: enable response-rate-limit and consider adding a fetches-per-zone limit; After changing the configuration, validate it with named-checkconf before running rndc reload.

The cAdvisor input collects the container_* metrics that cAdvisor exposes: per-container CPU usage and throttling, memory working set and OOM events, filesystem reads and writes, network traffic and drops. Two ways to connect: type = "kubelet" scrapes the kubelet's /metrics/cadvisor (port 10250, authenticated) and can attach Pod labels and annotations to the metrics; type = "cadvisor" scrapes a standalone cAdvisor (port 8080 by default). The dashboard shows resource usage per container and the metric reference explains each container_* metric. The rules cover CPU throttling, memory near the limit, OOM kills and network drops.
1 dashboard, 5 panels in total 6 alert rules, each with runbook steps 45 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.cadvisor

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.cadvisor/cadvisor.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.cadvisor started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] # url = "https://1.2.3.4:10250" # type = "kubelet" ## url = "http://1.2.3.4:8080/metrics" ## type = "cadvisor" # url_label_key = "instance" # url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" # bearer_token_string = "eyJlonglongxxxx.eyJlonglongyyyy.oQsXlonglongZZZ" ## bearer_token_file = "/path/to/token/file" # ignore_label_keys = ["id","name", "container_label*"] ## choose_label_keys = ["id"] # timeout = "3s" # use_tls = true ## tls_min_version = "1.2" ## tls_ca = "/etc/categraf/ca.pem" ## tls_cert = "/etc/categraf/cert.pem" ## tls_key = "/etc/categraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification ## insecure_skip_verify = true Open the integration center in Nightingale, find cAdvisor, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels cAdvisor 5
6 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: container_memory_working_set_bytes{name!=""} / (container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{name!=""} > 0) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Take name from the alert labels and run docker stats <name> or kubectl top pod to confirm live usage; Use the application's own memory analysis inside the container (jmap -histo:live for Java, pprof heap for Go) to separate normal growth from a leak; If the limit is simply too small, raise it and redeploy, adjusting the application's own heap ceiling to match (-Xmx must leave room for off-heap memory); If it is a leak, estimate the remaining runway from the growth rate and add an automatic restart as a stopgap while you investigate the code.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(container_oom_events_total{name!=""}[10m]) > 0 Runbook: Take name from the alert labels and confirm the OOMKilled state via the State.OOMKilled field in docker inspect <name> output or with kubectl describe pod; Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to find the killed process and its memory usage at the time; Compare that usage against the limit and raise the limit if it is clearly too small; If usage looks abnormal, investigate it as a memory leak; for Java, -Xmx must be smaller than the container limit with room for off-heap memory or an OOM is guaranteed.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{name!=""}[5m]) / (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{name!=""}[5m]) > 0) * 100 > 25 Runbook: Take name from the alert labels and confirm the growth of nr_throttled and throttled_usec with cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat (cgroup v2); Compare actual CPU usage against the limit; being throttled while below the limit usually means bursts are being sliced up by the 100 ms period, so raise the limit slightly or lower in-period concurrency; A common trigger is a JVM or Go runtime sizing thread pools from the host core count; set GOMAXPROCS or -XX:ActiveProcessorCount to match the limit; If more compute is genuinely needed, raise the CPU limit and watch the throttling ratio fall.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: container_fs_usage_bytes{name!=""} / (container_fs_limit_bytes{name!=""} > 0) * 100 > 85 Runbook: Take name and device from the alert labels and run docker exec <name> du -sh /* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head to find the biggest consumers; In the vast majority of cases application logs are not being rotated: configure logrotate or switch to writing to stdout and let the runtime rotate them; If the writable layer is filling up, mount a volume for directories that need persistence rather than writing into the layer; As an emergency measure run docker system prune to reclaim host space from unused images and stopped containers.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: changes(container_start_time_seconds{name!=""}[1h]) > 3 Runbook: Take name from the alert labels and run docker logs --tail 200 <name> or kubectl logs --previous to read the logs from before the last exit; Run docker inspect <name> and check State.ExitCode and State.OOMKilled in the output to distinguish an OOM, a deliberate application exit, and a failing health check; Handle OOMKilled as a memory alert; for a non-zero exit code, find the start-up failure in the application logs (missing configuration, dependency not ready); If a health check is the cause, confirm the probe's initial delay is longer than the real start-up time and raise the start period if needed.

S3 Info · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(container_network_receive_packets_dropped_total{name!=""}[5m]) > 1 Runbook: Take name from the alert labels and run docker exec <name> cat /proc/net/dev plus ss -s to check drops and queue state; If the receive queue is overflowing, raise the kernel's net.core.netdev_max_backlog and the application's accept queue (somaxconn); Check whether the host NIC is also dropping packets (ethtool -S <nic> | grep -i drop); if the problem is at the host level, do not chase it inside the container; If traffic genuinely exceeds the container's networking capacity, evaluate switching to host networking or raising the bandwidth allocation.

Ceph's mgr ships a prometheus module: after ceph mgr module enable prometheus, /metrics is served on port 9283 and the Categraf prometheus input scrapes it without any dedicated plugin. The dashboard covers cluster health, OSD availability and capacity, PG state distribution, usage and IOPS per pool, and MON quorum. The rules cover HEALTH_WARN and HEALTH_ERR, OSDs down, abnormal PGs, pools near capacity and loss of MON quorum.
1 dashboard, 57 panels in total 15 alert rules, each with runbook steps

These components expose Prometheus-format /metrics themselves, so the Categraf prometheus input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, add it as a Nightingale data source and the templates work as they are. # conf/input.prometheus/ceph.toml [[instances]] urls = ["http://<ceph-mgr>:9283/metrics"] labels = { service = "ceph", cluster = "ceph-cluster-001" } Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Ceph, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels Ceph - Cluster By Categraf 57
15 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

Ceph is in Error state longer than 5m, please check status of pools and OSDs S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: ceph_health_status > 1 Runbook: Immediately run ceph health detail to see which ERR item it is; Common ones are inactive/incomplete PGs, many down OSDs, or a full OSD forcing the cluster read-only; Restore the down OSDs or free space on the full OSD first — this is the root cause of the vast majority of ERRs; Do not scale or adjust the crush map during recovery, as it worsens data migration.

OSD {{ $labels.ceph_daemon}} on cluster {{ $labels.cluster}} was reweighted for too long. Please either create silent or fix that issue S2 Warning · for 60 min · Trigger: ceph_osd_weight < 1 Runbook: Run ceph osd tree to see which OSD is down-weighted and to what; Determine whether it was a manual reweight or an automatic reweight-by-utilization; If the fault is resolved, run ceph osd reweight <id> 1.0 to restore the weight and let data backfill; If it was down-weighted to balance capacity, consider using the balancer module instead.

Osd free space for {{ $labels.osd }} is higher tan 90%. Please validate why its so big, reweight or add storage S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: ceph_osd_utilization > 90 Runbook: Run ceph osd df to see the utilization spread and whether it is one OSD or the cluster as a whole; For a single hot OSD, check ceph balancer status and run ceph balancer on if it is disabled; If the cluster as a whole is near full you must add OSDs, or first delete unused pools/snapshots to free space; Temporarily raising mon_osd_full_ratio buys time but is a dangerous operation and must be paired with real expansion.

Some groups are activating for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Those PGs are unavailable for too long! S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: ceph_pg_activating > 0 Runbook: Run ceph -s and ceph health detail for the overall state and the specific warnings; Use ceph pg dump_stuck and ceph pg <pgid> query to locate the stuck PGs and why; In most cases the root cause is a down OSD or a full disk — restore the OSD or free space and the PGs return to active+clean automatically; Watch with ceph -w during recovery and avoid other operations that add load.

Some groups are located on full OSD on cluster {{ $labels.cluster }}. Those PGs can be unavailable shortly. Please check OSDs, change weight or reconfigure CRUSH rules. S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: ceph_pg_backfill_toofull > 0 Runbook: Run ceph osd df to find the OSDs short on space; Freeing space or adding OSDs is the real fix; As an emergency measure raise osd_backfill_full_ratio so backfill continues, but only if the disks genuinely have headroom; Avoid taking further OSDs offline before backfill completes, or redundancy drops further.

Some groups are down (unavailable) for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Please ensure that all the data are available S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: ceph_pg_down > 0 Runbook: Run ceph pg <pgid> query to see why it is down, focusing on which OSDs blocked_by points to; Bringing those OSDs back online is the most direct fix — usually a disk or host failure; If an OSD genuinely cannot be recovered, assess the data loss risk of an osd lost operation before running it; Record every step: decisions involving data loss should be reviewed by a second person.

Some groups are incomplete (unavailable) for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Please ensure that all the data are available S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger: ceph_pg_incomplete > 0 Runbook: Run ceph -s and ceph health detail for the overall state and the specific warnings; Use ceph pg dump_stuck and ceph pg <pgid> query to locate the stuck PGs and why; In most cases the root cause is a down OSD or a full disk — restore the OSD or free space and the PGs return to active+clean automatically; Watch with ceph -w during recovery and avoid other operations that add load.

Some groups are inconsistent for too long on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Data is available but inconsistent across nodes S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: ceph_pg_inconsistent > 0 Runbook: Use ceph health detail to find the inconsistent PGs, then rados list-inconsistent-obj <pgid> for the specific objects; Run ceph pg repair <pgid> to trigger repair — Ceph overwrites from the authoritative copy; Before repairing, confirm which copy is bad: if the primary itself is corrupt, verify the authoritative copy is trustworthy first; An OSD that repeatedly produces inconsistencies should have its SMART checked — it is usually bad sectors and the disk should be replaced.

Some groups are unavailable on {{ $labels.cluster }}. Please check their detailed status and current configuration. S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: ceph_pg_total - ceph_pg_active > 0 Runbook: Run ceph -s and ceph health detail for the overall state and the specific warnings; Use ceph pg dump_stuck and ceph pg <pgid> query to locate the stuck PGs and why; In most cases the root cause is a down OSD or a full disk — restore the OSD or free space and the PGs return to active+clean automatically; Watch with ceph -w during recovery and avoid other operations that add load.

CEPH target down for more than 2m, please check - it could be a either exporter crash or a whole cluster crash S1 Critical · for 10 min · Trigger: up{job="ceph"} == 0 Runbook: Confirm the node running ceph exporter / mgr is alive and the process is running; Run ceph -s on any mon node to confirm by hand whether the cluster itself is healthy; A failed mgr causes many metrics to disappear — run ceph mgr fail to switch to the standby mgr; After collection resumes, note the data gap and remember there were no alerts during the blind window.

Ceph is in Warn state longer than 30m, please check status of pools and OSDs S2 Warning · for 30 min · Trigger: ceph_health_status == 1 Runbook: Run ceph health detail to see exactly which WARN items are present; Common ones are a single down OSD, PGs not clean, clock skew and pools without pg_autoscale; Work through them following the guidance — Ceph's health detail usually gives explicit instructions; Once done, confirm ceph -s returns to HEALTH_OK.

Monitor storage for {{ $labels.monitor }} less than 30% - please check why its too high S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: ceph_monitor_avail_percent < 30 Runbook: Run df -h to check the free space on the partition holding /var/lib/ceph/mon; The most common reason the mon directory grows is a cluster that has been unclean for a long time, preventing osdmap trimming — fix the cluster health first; Run ceph tell mon.<id> compact to trigger rocksdb compaction and reclaim space; Longer term, give mon its own larger disk.

Monitor clock skew detected on {{ $labels.monitor }} - please check ntp and hardware clock settings S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: abs(ceph_monitor_clock_skew_seconds) > 0.1 Runbook: On each mon node run chronyc tracking to check the offset and upstream source state; Confirm every mon node uses the same set of NTP sources; Start chronyd where it is not running and enable it at boot; where the offset is large, use chronyc makestep to step the clock; After correcting the time, confirm with ceph -s that the clock skew warning is gone.

OSD latency for {{ $labels.osd }} is too high. Please check if it doesn't stuck in weird state S2 Warning · for 90s · Trigger: ceph_osd_perf_apply_latency_seconds > 10 Runbook: Run ceph osd perf to see commit/apply latency per OSD and whether it is isolated or widespread; For a single slow OSD, go to that node and use iostat -x 1 and smartctl to check disk health and saturation; If it is widespread, check whether a large recovery/backfill is running and lower osd_max_backfills to reduce the impact; For a failing disk, follow the replacement procedure.

OSD is down longer than 30 min, please check what's the status S2 Warning · for 30 min · Trigger: ceph_osd_up == 0 Runbook: Run ceph osd tree to identify the OSD and its node; On that node use systemctl status ceph-osd@<id> and its logs to find the cause (disk failure, OOM, process crash); If the disk is fine, just start the OSD; if the disk failed, follow the replacement procedure and ceph osd out to migrate data away; Watch recovery progress with ceph -s and avoid taking more OSDs offline.

The ClickHouse input queries the system tables over HTTP (port 8123 by default): system.metrics, system.events, system.asynchronous_metrics, system.parts and others. That yields concurrent queries, merges and mutations, replication queue and lag, memory and caches, part counts and ZooKeeper sessions. Verified against a real ClickHouse 24.8 workload. The two dashboards use different metric families and are not interchangeable: ClickHouse_Categraf expects this input, ClickHouse_Exporter expects the clickhouse_* metrics from ClickHouse's built-in Prometheus endpoint. The rules cover query backlog, replication lag, too many parts, memory near the limit and lost ZooKeeper sessions.
2 dashboards, 26 panels in total 10 alert rules, each with runbook steps 81 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.clickhouse

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.clickhouse/clickhouse.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.clickhouse started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 # Read metrics from one or many ClickHouse servers [[instances]] ## Username for authorization on ClickHouse server username = "default" ## Password for authorization on ClickHouse server # password = "" ## HTTP(s) timeout while getting metrics values ## The timeout includes connection time, any redirects, and reading the ## response body. # timeout = 5 ## List of servers for metrics scraping ## metrics scrape via HTTP(s) clickhouse interface ## https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/interfaces/http/ # servers = ["http://127.0.0.1:8123"] ## If "auto_discovery"" is "true" plugin tries to connect to all servers ## available in the cluster with using same "user:password" described in ## "user" and "password" parameters and get this server hostname list from ## "system.clusters" table. See ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/system_tables/#system-clusters ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/server_settings/settings/#server_settings_remote_servers ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/table_engines/distributed/ ## - https://clickhouse.tech/docs/en/operations/table_engines/replication/#creating-replicated-tables # auto_discovery = true ## Filter cluster names in "system.clusters" when "auto_discovery" is "true" ## when this filter present then "WHERE cluster IN (...)" filter will apply ## please use only full cluster names here, regexp and glob filters is not ## allowed for "/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/remote.xml" ## <yandex> ## <remote_servers> ## <my-own-cluster> ## <shard> ## <replica><host>clickhouse-ru-1.local</host><port>9000</port></replica> ## <replica><host>clickhouse-ru-2.local</host><port>9000</port></replica> ## </shard> ## <shard> ## <replica><host>clickhouse-eu-1.local</host><port>9000</port></replica> ## <replica><host>clickhouse-eu-2.local</host><port>9000</port></replica> ## </shard> ## </my-own-cluster> ## </remote_servers> ## ## </yandex> ## ## example: cluster_include = ["my-own-cluster"] # cluster_include = [] ## Filter cluster names in "system.clusters" when "auto_discovery" is ## "true" when this filter present then "WHERE cluster NOT IN (...)" ## filter will apply ## example: cluster_exclude = ["my-internal-not-discovered-cluster"] # cluster_exclude = [] ## Optional TLS Config # tls_ca = "/etc/telegraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/telegraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/telegraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = false # [[instances.metrics]] # measurement = "sessions" # metric_fields = [ "value" ] # timeout = "3s" # request = ''' # SELECT count() AS value FROM system.processes # ''' Open the integration center in Nightingale, find ClickHouse, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. 10 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import. Rules are grouped by collector; import the group that matches how you collect.

ClickHouse Categraf replica is read-only​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: clickhouse_metrics_readonly_replica > 0 Runbook: Run SELECT database, table, is_readonly, zookeeper_exception FROM system.replicas WHERE is_readonly to find the read-only tables and the reason; Check that the ZooKeeper/Keeper cluster is healthy (echo ruok | nc <zk> 2181) and that ClickHouse can reach it; Once ZooKeeper is back, run SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA <db>.<table> so the replica re-establishes its session; If the metadata in ZooKeeper is lost, use SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA to rebuild it, after confirming another healthy replica exists. ClickHouse Categraf memory usage​ Memory usage alert S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: clickhouse_metrics_memory_tracking / clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_os_memory_total * 100 > 90 clickhouse_metrics_memory_tracking/ clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_os_memory_total * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run SELECT query, memory_usage, elapsed FROM system.processes ORDER BY memory_usage DESC LIMIT 5 to find the queries consuming memory, and KILL QUERY WHERE query_id='...' to stop the bleeding if needed; Check the highest memory_usage entries in system.query_log to find SQL missing filters or doing large JOINs; Use max_memory_usage / max_bytes_before_external_group_by to cap a single query and allow spilling to disk; Confirm the mark cache and uncompressed cache are not configured too large. ClickHouse Categraf disk usage​ Disk usage alert S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_disk_available_default / (clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_disk_available_default + clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_disk_used_default) * 100 < 10 clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_disk_available_default / (clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_disk_available_default + clickhouse_asynchronous_metrics_disk_used_default) * 100 < 20 Runbook: Run SELECT name, free_space, total_space FROM system.disks to check each disk; Run SELECT database, table, formatReadableSize(sum(bytes)) FROM system.parts WHERE active GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY sum(bytes) DESC to find the largest tables; For tables with a TTL, run ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL to trigger cleanup, or DROP PARTITION to remove expired partitions; Longer term, expand the disk or configure a multi-volume storage policy to move cold data down. ClickHouse Categraf concurrent network connections too high​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: clickhouse_metrics_network_send > 250 or clickhouse_metrics_network_receive > 250 clickhouse_metrics_network_send > 250 or clickhouse_metrics_network_receive > 250 increase(clickhouse_metrics_interserver_connection[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run SELECT count(), user, client_hostname FROM system.processes GROUP BY 2,3 ORDER BY 1 DESC to see which clients the connections come from; Compare with Query and TCPConnection in system.metrics to tell high query concurrency apart from a connection leak; For clients that do not reuse connections, switch to a connection pool on the application side; Check that max_concurrent_queries and max_connections match the instance size, and apply rate limiting if needed.

ClickHouse native endpoint authentication errors​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(ClickHouseErrorMetric_AUTHENTICATION_FAILED[5m]) > 0 increase(ClickHouseErrorMetric_RESOURCE_ACCESS_DENIED[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run SELECT event_time, user, client_hostname, exception FROM system.query_log WHERE type='ExceptionBeforeStart' AND exception LIKE '%AUTHENTICATION_FAILED%' ORDER BY event_time DESC LIMIT 20 to find the source IP and username; If it is your own application, verify the credentials in its config against users.xml; If the source is an unknown IP, treat it as an intrusion attempt: tighten the networks allowlist in users.xml and rotate the password; Confirm the ClickHouse port is not directly exposed to the internet. ClickHouse native endpoint replica is read-only​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: ClickHouseMetrics_ReadonlyReplica > 0 Runbook: Run SELECT database, table, is_readonly, zookeeper_exception FROM system.replicas WHERE is_readonly to find the read-only tables and the reason; Check that the ZooKeeper/Keeper cluster is healthy (echo ruok | nc <zk> 2181) and that ClickHouse can reach it; Once ZooKeeper is back, run SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA <db>.<table> so the replica re-establishes its session; If the metadata in ZooKeeper is lost, use SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA to rebuild it, after confirming another healthy replica exists. ClickHouse native endpoint memory usage​ Memory usage alert S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: ClickHouseMetrics_MemoryTracking / ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_OSMemoryTotal * 100 > 90 ClickHouseMetrics_MemoryTracking / ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_OSMemoryTotal * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run SELECT query, memory_usage, elapsed FROM system.processes ORDER BY memory_usage DESC LIMIT 5 to find the queries consuming memory, and KILL QUERY WHERE query_id='...' to stop the bleeding if needed; Check the highest memory_usage entries in system.query_log to find SQL missing filters or doing large JOINs; Use max_memory_usage / max_bytes_before_external_group_by to cap a single query and allow spilling to disk; Confirm the mark cache and uncompressed cache are not configured too large. ClickHouse native endpoint replica errors​ S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: ClickHouseErrorMetric_ALL_REPLICAS_ARE_STALE == 1 or ClickHouseErrorMetric_ALL_REPLICAS_LOST == 1 ClickHouseErrorMetric_NO_AVAILABLE_REPLICA == 1 ClickHouseErrorMetric_TOO_FEW_LIVE_REPLICAS == 1 Runbook: Run SELECT database, table, is_readonly, absolute_delay, zookeeper_exception FROM system.replicas to locate the failed tables; A large absolute_delay means the replica cannot keep up — check the replica node's IO and its merge queue (system.replication_queue); ALL_REPLICAS_LOST usually means the metadata in ZooKeeper is gone, so verify the data on a healthy replica and then run SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA; Route queries to healthy shards while recovering so they stop failing. ClickHouse native endpoint disk usage​ Disk usage alert S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskAvailable_default / (ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskAvailable_default + ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskUsed_default) * 100 < 10 ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskAvailable_default / (ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskAvailable_default + ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskUsed_default) * 100 < 20 ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskAvailable_backups / (ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskAvailable_backups + ClickHouseAsyncMetrics_DiskUsed_backups) * 100 < 20 Runbook: Run SELECT name, free_space, total_space FROM system.disks to check each disk; Run SELECT database, table, formatReadableSize(sum(bytes)) FROM system.parts WHERE active GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY sum(bytes) DESC to find the largest tables; For tables with a TTL, run ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL to trigger cleanup, or DROP PARTITION to remove expired partitions; Longer term, expand the disk or configure a multi-volume storage policy to move cold data down. The CloudWatch input is ported from Telegraf. It calls the GetMetricData API to pull statistics per namespace (AWS/EC2, AWS/RDS, AWS/ELB and so on), with dimension filters to limit collection to the resources you care about. Authentication follows the standard credential chain: role_arn, explicit access keys, a named profile, environment variables, the shared credentials file and the EC2 instance profile, tried in that order. CloudWatch bills per API call, so choose the interval and namespace scope with the invoice in mind. The template ships an RDS dashboard, and the rules cover EC2 status check failures, sustained high CPU, RDS connections and storage, ELB 5xx and unhealthy backends.
1 dashboard, 19 panels in total 8 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.cloudwatch

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.cloudwatch/cloud.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.cloudwatch started once the plugin is loaded. interval="5m" [[instances]] ## Amazon Region # list of region and endpoint, see https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/cw_region.html region = "us-east-1" ## Amazon Credentials ## Credentials are loaded in the following order ## 1) Web identity provider credentials via STS if role_arn and ## web_identity_token_file are specified ## 2) Assumed credentials via STS if role_arn is specified ## 3) explicit credentials from 'access_key' and 'secret_key' ## 4) shared profile from 'profile' ## 5) environment variables ## 6) shared credentials file ## 7) EC2 Instance Profile # access_key = "" # secret_key = "" # token = "" # role_arn = "" # web_identity_token_file = "" # role_session_name = "" # profile = "" # shared_credential_file = "" ## Endpoint to make request against, the correct endpoint is automatically ## determined and this option should only be set if you wish to override the ## default. ## ex: endpoint_url = "http://localhost:8000" endpoint_url = "https://monitoring.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com" ## Set http_proxy # use_system_proxy = false # http_proxy_url = "http://localhost:8888" ## The minimum period for CloudWatch metrics is 1 minute (60s). However not ## all metrics are made available to the 1 minute period. Some are collected ## at 3 minute, 5 minute, or larger intervals. ## See https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/faqs/#monitoring. ## Note that if a period is configured that is smaller than the minimum for a ## particular metric, that metric will not be returned by the CloudWatch API ## and will not be collected by Telegraf. # ## Collection Delay (required) ## Must account for metrics availability via CloudWatch API delay = "5m" ## Requested CloudWatch aggregation Period (required) ## Must be a multiple of 60s. period = "5m" ## Recommended if "delay" and "period" are both within 3 hours of request ## time. Invalid values will be ignored. Recently Active feature will only ## poll for CloudWatch ListMetrics values that occurred within the last 3h. ## If enabled, it will reduce total API usage of the CloudWatch ListMetrics ## API and require less memory to retain. ## Do not enable if "period" or "delay" is longer than 3 hours, as it will ## not return data more than 3 hours old. ## See https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/APIReference/API_ListMetrics.html #recently_active = "PT3H" ## Configure the TTL for the internal cache of metrics. # cache_ttl = "1h" ## Metric Statistic Namespaces (required) # namespaces = ["AWS/EC2"] ## Maximum requests per second. Note that the global default AWS rate limit ## is 50 reqs/sec, so if you define multiple namespaces, these should add up ## to a maximum of 50. ## See http://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch_limits.html # ratelimit = 25 ## Timeout for http requests made by the cloudwatch client. # timeout = "5s" ## Batch Size ## The size of each batch to send requests to CloudWatch. 500 is the ## suggested largest size. If a request gets to large (413 errors), consider ## reducing this amount. # batch_size = 500 ## Namespace-wide statistic filters. These allow fewer queries to be made to ## cloudwatch. # statistic_include = ["average", "sum", "minimum", "maximum", sample_count"] # statistic_exclude = [] ## Metrics to Pull ## Defaults to all Metrics in Namespace if nothing is provided ## Refreshes Namespace available metrics every 1h #[[instances.metrics]] # names = ["Latency", "RequestCount"] # # ## Statistic filters for Metric. These allow for retrieving specific # ## statistics for an individual metric. # # statistic_include = ["average", "sum", "minimum", "maximum", sample_count"] # # statistic_exclude = [] # # ## Dimension filters for Metric. # ## All dimensions defined for the metric names must be specified in order # ## to retrieve the metric statistics. # ## 'value' has wildcard / 'glob' matching support such as 'p-*'. # [[instances.metrics.dimensions]] # name = "LoadBalancerName" # value = "p-example" Open the integration center in Nightingale, find CloudWatch, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels AWS RDS Telegraf 19
8 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_cpu_utilization_average > 85 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier and region from the alert labels and sort by Top SQL in Performance Insights to find the statements burning the most CPU; Run EXPLAIN on the statements you find; a full scan from a missing index is the most common cause; Confirm no unusual batch jobs or analytical queries are hitting the primary, and move them to a read replica if they are; Only after optimisation should you upgrade the instance class, and that change must be made inside a maintenance window.
documents.s: RDS instance CPU utilization too high

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_free_storage_space_average < 10737418240 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier from the alert labels and confirm the allocated and used capacity in the console; Expand storage immediately (Modify > Allocated storage); RDS scaling is online but has a 6-hour cooldown, so do not wait until it is full; At the same time reclaim space: drop stale temporary tables, shorten binlog retention (call mysql.rds_set_configuration('binlog retention hours', N)), and archive historical partitions; Longer term enable Storage Autoscaling with a sensible upper bound.
documents.s: RDS instance free storage space low

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_burst_balance_average < 20 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier from the alert labels and compare ReadIOPS/WriteIOPS in CloudWatch against the volume's baseline IOPS to size the overrun; Reduce IO at the source first: use Performance Insights to find the queries with the most physical reads and add indexes; As an emergency measure switch the storage type to gp3 or io1/io2 for guaranteed IOPS; the gp3 change can be made online; Growing the volume also raises baseline IOPS, but is usually less cost-effective than moving to gp3.
documents.s: RDS instance IO burst balance low

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_freeable_memory_average < 536870912 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier from the alert labels and review the memory-related wait events in Performance Insights; Check whether innodb_buffer_pool_size (MySQL) or shared_buffers (PostgreSQL) in the parameter group is set too large; anything above 75% of instance memory tends to trigger this; Excessive connections also consume memory: confirm the application uses a connection pool and that max_connections is not far above what you actually need; Only once the configuration is sane should you move to an instance class with more memory.

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_read_latency_average > 0.05 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier from the alert labels and compare ReadIOPS and BurstBalance for the same period to rule out an exhausted IO burst balance first; If IOPS are not saturated but latency is high, check whether a large scan is flushing the buffer pool and use Performance Insights to find the SQL with the most physical reads; Adding indexes to cut physical reads is the most effective fix, followed by moving analytical queries to a read replica; If the workload is reasonable and latency is still high, upgrade the storage type to gp3/io1 for more predictable latency.
documents.s: RDS instance read latency too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_write_latency_average > 0.05 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier from the alert labels and first check whether Multi-AZ is enabled, since synchronous replication makes write latency higher than a single-AZ instance and that is expected; Compare WriteIOPS against the volume's IOPS ceiling and handle saturation via the burst balance / storage type path; Check whether a large transaction or bulk import is running; splitting it into smaller batches reduces latency substantially; If binlog/WAL write amplification is obvious, confirm sync_binlog and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit actually match the durability the business requires.
documents.s: RDS instance write latency too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_disk_queue_depth_average > 10 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier from the alert labels and look at ReadIOPS/WriteIOPS together with BurstBalance to see whether the IOPS ceiling has been reached; Sort by IO wait in Performance Insights to find the SQL generating the IO and optimise those statements first; Confirm that backups, snapshots, and index rebuilds do not overlap the business peak; If the workload genuinely needs more IOPS, switch to gp3 and set IOPS and throughput explicitly.
documents.s: RDS instance disk queue backing up

documents.t: S3 Info · for 15 min · Trigger: cloudwatch_aws_rds_swap_usage_average > 268435456 Runbook: Take db_instance_identifier from the alert labels and read it together with FreeableMemory to see how long the memory pressure has lasted; Check whether the buffer pool parameters in the parameter group are set too large and whether the connection count exceeds expectations; Look for large sorts or large temporary tables consuming memory, locate them in Performance Insights, and optimise them; If configuration and queries are both reasonable and swapping continues, move to an instance class with more memory.
documents.s: RDS instance swap usage too high
