The Consul input calls the Consul health API and turns every registered health check into a metric with service name, node, check name and current state (passing, warning, critical). It does not collect Consul's own telemetry, which Consul can emit over StatsD or its built-in Prometheus endpoint; its single job is answering "is anything registered in Consul unhealthy". The rules cover service instances turning critical, services with no healthy instance left, nodes dropping out, checks stuck in warning and Consul itself being unreachable. ACL tokens and TLS are supported.
7 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.consul

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.consul/consul.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.consul started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] ## Consul server address # address = "localhost:8500" ## URI scheme for the Consul server, one of "http", "https" # scheme = "http" ## ACL token used in every request # token = "" ## HTTP Basic Authentication username and password. # username = "" # password = "" ## Data center to query the health checks from # datacenter = "" ## Allows any Consul server (non-leader) to service a read. ## Default is true # allow_stale = true ## Forces the read to be fully consistent. ## Default is false # require_consistent = false ## Prefix from which to expose key/value pairs. # kv_prefix = "" ## Regex that determines which keys to expose. ## Default is ".*" # kv_filter = ".*" ## Optional TLS Config # tls_ca = "/etc/telegraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/telegraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/telegraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = true Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Consul, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
7 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: consul_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status consul and consul members to check the process and the cluster view; If the process is alive, run curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8500/v1/status/leader to verify the API; a 403 means the ACL token used for collection lacks permission or has expired; If the process is gone, check journalctl -u consul for the cause (a corrupted raft data directory or a port conflict are common); Before recovering, confirm the remaining nodes still form a quorum so you do not accidentally push the cluster out of quorum.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: consul_raft_leader == 0 Runbook: Run consul operator raft list-peers on each server node and confirm whether the number of surviving servers has fallen below a quorum; If quorum is lost, bring the failed servers back up first rather than jumping to a peers.json recovery; If enough servers survive but no leader is elected, check connectivity on ports 8300/8301 between servers and clock skew (chronyc tracking); Only once automatic recovery is ruled out should you rebuild the peer list by hand with raft/peers.json following the official outage recovery procedure.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: consul_autopilot_healthy == 0 Runbook: Run consul operator autopilot state and check Healthy and LastContact for every server; For nodes with Healthy=false, check that the process is alive and measure network latency to the leader; A LastIndex far behind means the node is still catching up on logs; watch whether it keeps converging, and note that slow disk IO is a common cause (confirm with iostat -x 1); Once a node is confirmed dead, remove it from the cluster with consul force-leave <node> or consul operator raft remove-peer.
documents.s: Consul Autopilot reports the cluster unhealthy

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: consul_autopilot_failure_tolerance == 0 Runbook: Run consul operator raft list-peers and count the healthy servers (a 3-node cluster tolerates 1 failure, a 5-node cluster tolerates 2); If a node is unhealthy, repair that node rather than adding a new one, so the peer count does not become even; When you genuinely need to grow, scale to an odd number such as 5 and confirm fault tolerance recovers once the new node has caught up on raft; Avoid any rolling restart or version upgrade until this is resolved.
documents.s: Consul cluster fault tolerance is zero

documents.t: categraf pushes one sample per status (passing/warning/critical/maintenance) with an identical metric name and label set, so the values overwrite each other once stored. This rule therefore tests for the presence of the status label rather than comparing values. S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: count by (address, node, service_name, check_name) (consul_health_service_status{status="critical"}) > 0 Runbook: Take node and service_name from the alert labels and run consul catalog nodes -service=<service_name> to see how many healthy instances remain; scale out immediately if only one is left; Log in to the node and run curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8500/v1/health/checks/\<service_name> to read the exact failure reason from the Output field; Follow that Output to the matching process and port (check script timeout, unexpected HTTP status, TCP connection refused); If the check itself is misconfigured (timeout too short, wrong path), fix the service definition and run consul reload.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: count by (address, node, check_name) (consul_health_node_status{status="critical"}) > 0 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels and run consul members to see whether the node's Serf state is alive or failed; failed means gossip is not getting through: check bidirectional connectivity on port 8301 and security groups, and whether the host is down; If the node is up but serfHealth flaps repeatedly, it is usually packet loss or high host load causing gossip timeouts; confirm with mtr and uptime; Once the node is confirmed decommissioned, clean it up with consul force-leave <node> so the stale entry stops alerting.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: consul_serf_lan_member_status != 1 Runbook: Take the node name from the member label and run consul members to confirm its current state; For Failed, first check that the host is up and the consul process is running; If the host is fine, check bidirectional TCP/UDP connectivity on port 8301 and the MTU (gossip relies on UDP, and an MTU mismatch causes intermittent loss of contact); If the node really is decommissioned, run consul force-leave <node>; entries left in the Left state are cleaned up automatically after 72 hours.

The dns_query input resolves the names in domains against the configured DNS servers (the host's own resolver or external public ones), supporting A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT and other record types. It reports query time, rcode, the number of records returned and the result values. You rarely need it on every host; pick one or two probe points, list your business domains and critical third-party domains, and label by probe point and DNS server. The rules cover failed resolution, slow queries and unexpected return codes.
documents.s: Monitor DNS resolution quality with Nightingale

documents.t: 4 alert rules, each with runbook steps 5 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.dns_query

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.dns_query/dns_query.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.dns_query started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] # # append some labels for series # labels = { region="cloud", product="n9e" } # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # # auto_detect_local_dns_server = false ## servers to query # servers = ["8.8.8.8"] servers = [] ## Network is the network protocol name. # network = "udp" ## Domains or subdomains to query. # domains = ["."] ## Query record type. ## Possible values: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, PTR, TXT, SOA, SPF, SRV. # record_type = "A" ## Dns server port. # port = 53 ## Query timeout in seconds. # timeout = 2 Open the integration center in Nightingale, find DNS Query, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
4 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: dns_query_rcode_value != 0 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with dig @<DNS server> <domain> and check the status and elapsed time; Compare against a public resolver (e.g. dig @223.5.5.5) to tell a DNS server problem from a problem with the domain itself; For a self-hosted resolver, check the service process, upstream forwarding config and network connectivity; Verify the probe's domain, record type and timeout settings are sensible so the config itself is not causing the alert.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: dns_query_time_ms > 5000 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with dig @<DNS server> <domain> and check the status and elapsed time; Compare against a public resolver (e.g. dig @223.5.5.5) to tell a DNS server problem from a problem with the domain itself; For a self-hosted resolver, check the service process, upstream forwarding config and network connectivity; Verify the probe's domain, record type and timeout settings are sensible so the config itself is not causing the alert.
documents.s: DNS query response time exceeds 5 seconds

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: dns_query_result_value == 1 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with dig @<DNS server> <domain> and check the status and elapsed time; Compare against a public resolver (e.g. dig @223.5.5.5) to tell a DNS server problem from a problem with the domain itself; For a self-hosted resolver, check the service process, upstream forwarding config and network connectivity; Verify the probe's domain, record type and timeout settings are sensible so the config itself is not causing the alert.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: dns_query_result_value == 2 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with dig @<DNS server> <domain> and check the status and elapsed time; Compare against a public resolver (e.g. dig @223.5.5.5) to tell a DNS server problem from a problem with the domain itself; For a self-hosted resolver, check the service process, upstream forwarding config and network connectivity; Verify the probe's domain, record type and timeout settings are sensible so the config itself is not causing the alert.

5 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Metric Meaning Unit dns_query_rcode_value DNS Response Code (RCODE) — 0 (NOERROR): the query succeeded with no error 1 (FORMERR): format error, the DNS server could not understand the query 2 (SERVFAIL): server failure, the DNS server encountered an internal error 3 (NXDOMAIN): the domain name does not exist 4 (NOTIMP): the query type is not supported 5 (REFUSED): the query was refused, usually for policy reasons. In monitoring, RCODE 0 means the query succeeded, while other values usually indicate an issue that needs attention dns_query_result_value Custom Query Result — 0 means success, 1 means timeout, 2 means error. dns_query_status_change DNS Resolution Status Change — When expect_query_ips is configured for the corresponding domain, categraf compares the IP list in the response with the configured IP list and emits this metric. 0 means the responded IPs match the expected IPs, 1 means the responded IPs differ from the expected IPs. dns_query_status_change_detail DNS Resolution Change Detail — 0 means the responded IPs match the expected IPs, 1 means the responded IPs differ from the expected IPs. {ips="responded IP list", diff="responded IP list minus expected IP list"} dns_query_time_ms Query Response Time ms

The Docker input is based on Telegraf's docker plugin. It connects to the Docker daemon socket (unix:///var/run/docker.sock) or a TCP endpoint and collects engine-level container counts and states, image count and storage driver information, plus CPU, memory, blkio and network IO for every container. Swarm services and extended memory statistics are optional. The bundled Docker Dashboard is written against these docker_* metrics and verified on real hosts, so this input must be enabled for it. cAdvisor is also a recommended way to collect containers, but it emits container_* metrics and needs the dashboards from the cAdvisor integration; the two do not mix. The rules cover container OOM kills, abnormal exits, CPU and memory over limits and the daemon being unreachable.
1 dashboard, 16 panels in total 6 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.docker

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.docker/docker.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.docker started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] # # append some labels for series # labels = { region="cloud", product="n9e" } # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 ## Docker Endpoint ## To use TCP, set endpoint = "tcp://[ip]:[port]" ## To use environment variables (ie, docker-machine), set endpoint = "ENV" # endpoint = "unix:///var/run/docker.sock" endpoint = "" ## Set to true to collect Swarm metrics(desired_replicas, running_replicas) gather_services = false gather_extend_memstats = false container_id_label_enable = true container_id_label_short_style = false ## Containers to include and exclude. Globs accepted. ## Note that an empty array for both will include all containers container_name_include = [] container_name_exclude = [] ## Container states to include and exclude. Globs accepted. ## When empty only containers in the "running" state will be captured. ## example: container_state_include = ["created", "restarting", "running", "removing", "paused", "exited", "dead"] ## example: container_state_exclude = ["created", "restarting", "running", "removing", "paused", "exited", "dead"] # container_state_include = [] # container_state_exclude = [] ## Timeout for docker list, info, and stats commands timeout = "5s" ## Specifies for which classes a per-device metric should be issued ## Possible values are 'cpu' (cpu0, cpu1, ...), 'blkio' (8:0, 8:1, ...) and 'network' (eth0, eth1, ...) ## Please note that this setting has no effect if 'perdevice' is set to 'true' perdevice_include = [] ## Specifies for which classes a total metric should be issued. Total is an aggregated of the 'perdevice' values. ## Possible values are 'cpu', 'blkio' and 'network' ## Total 'cpu' is reported directly by Docker daemon, and 'network' and 'blkio' totals are aggregated by this plugin. ## Please note that this setting has no effect if 'total' is set to 'false' total_include = ["cpu", "blkio", "network"] ## Which environment variables should we use as a tag ##tag_env = ["JAVA_HOME", "HEAP_SIZE"] ## docker labels to include and exclude as tags. Globs accepted. ## Note that an empty array for both will include all labels as tags docker_label_include = [] docker_label_exclude = ["annotation*", "io.kubernetes*", "*description*", "*maintainer*", "*hash", "*author*", "*org_*", "*date*", "*url*", "*docker_compose*"] ## Optional TLS Config # use_tls = false # tls_ca = "/etc/telegraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/telegraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/telegraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = false Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Docker, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels Docker Dashboard 16
6 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: docker_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status docker to confirm the daemon is alive; Run docker ps to verify by hand — if it hangs without returning, the daemon is stuck, use journalctl -u docker -n 200 to locate the cause; Confirm the permissions on /var/run/docker.sock match the collector account; Confirm the disk (especially the partition holding /var/lib/docker) is not full, a full disk is a common cause of a stuck daemon.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: docker_container_health_status == 2 Runbook: Take container_name from the alert labels and run docker inspect <container> and check the State.Health field in the output for the last few health check results; Run docker logs --tail 200 <container> to locate the application error; Reproduce the health check by hand (docker exec <container> <health check command>) to tell an application failure apart from a wrongly written check; If the application is broken and cannot be fixed quickly, first remove the instance from the upstream load balancer, then investigate.

S1 Critical · Trigger: docker_container_status_oomkilled == 1 Runbook: Take container_name from the alert labels and run docker inspect <container> | grep -i memory to confirm the current limit; Compare with the historical peak of docker_container_mem_max_usage to tell a too-small limit apart from an application memory leak; If the limit is too small, raise --memory and recreate the container; If a leak is suspected, capture a heap profile on the application side (jmap for Java, pprof for Go) instead of just raising the limit to hide the problem.

S1 Critical · Trigger: increase(docker_container_status_restart_count[10m]) > 3 Runbook: Take container_name from the alert labels and run docker logs --tail 200 <container> to see the error before each exit; Run docker inspect <container> and read the State.ExitCode exit code in the output (137 usually means OOM or killed; 1 or 2 usually means the application failed to start); For configuration or dependency problems (cannot reach the database, missing config file), fix the dependency before starting it again; To keep the restart loop from filling the disk with logs, docker stop the container and remove it from the load balancer while you investigate.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: docker_container_mem_usage_percent > 90 Runbook: Take container_name from the alert labels and run docker stats --no-stream <container> to confirm current usage against the limit; Check the history curve to tell a steady climb (likely a leak) apart from a normal traffic peak; For normal peaks, raise --memory leaving 20% headroom and recreate the container; For a steady climb, capture a heap profile on the application side to find the leak, and raise the limit meanwhile to buy investigation time.
documents.s: Docker container memory approaching its limit

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(docker_container_cpu_throttling_throttled_periods[5m]) / rate(docker_container_cpu_throttling_periods[5m]) > 0.25 Runbook: Take container_name from the alert labels and run docker inspect <container> | grep -iE 'cpuquota|cpuperiod|nanocpus' to confirm the current quota; Compare with docker_container_cpu_usage_percent to tell a traffic increase apart from a busy loop in the application; If traffic grew, raise --cpus and recreate the container, or scale out to several instances; If usage looks abnormal, capture a CPU profile on the application side to find the hot functions.

Doris FE (port 8030 by default) and BE (8040) processes both expose Prometheus metrics on /metrics, so no dedicated plugin is needed. Label each node type with group and job; the dashboards use those labels to separate FE from BE and one cluster from another. The templates cover query QPS and latency, load jobs, compaction backlog, tablet state, BE disk and memory, and node liveness.
1 dashboard, 91 panels in total 21 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.prometheus

These components expose Prometheus-format /metrics themselves, so the Categraf prometheus input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, add it as a Nightingale data source and the templates work as they are. Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.prometheus/collect_doris_examples.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.prometheus started once the plugin is loaded. # doris_fe [[instances]] # 配置 fe metrics 服务地址 urls = [ "http://127.0.0.1:8030/metrics" ] url_label_key = "instance" url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" # 指定 fe 服务 group 和 job 标签，这里是仪表盘变量调用，可根据实际需求修改。 labels = { group = "fe",job = "doris_cluster01"} # doris_be [[instances]] # 配置 be metrics 服务地址 urls = [ "http://127.0.0.1:8040/metrics" ] url_label_key = "instance" url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" # 指定 be 服务 group 和 job 标签，这里是仪表盘变量调用，可根据实际需求修改。 labels = { group = "be",job = "doris_cluster01"} Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Doris, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Dashboard Panels Doris Overview 91
21 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum by (ident) (jvm_heap_size_bytes{type="used"}) / sum by (ident) (jvm_heap_size_bytes{type="max"}) > 0.85 Runbook: Run jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 to watch GC frequency and old generation usage; High FE memory usually comes from too much metadata (an explosion of tables/partitions/tablets) — use SHOW PROC '/statistic' to see the scale; Raise the FE JAVA_OPTS -Xmx and restart (roll the restart to avoid impact); For the root cause, reduce partition counts and drop unused tables — Doris keeps all metadata in memory, so scale control is an ongoing discipline.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(doris_be_snmp_tcp_in_errs[1m]) > 0 Runbook: On that BE node run netstat -s | grep -i error to see the specific error types; Run ethtool -S <nic> to check for physical-layer errors; Check network quality between BEs and from FE to BE (mtr); Confirm the link is not saturated — Doris query fragment transfer is bandwidth intensive.
documents.s: Doris_BE TCP packet receive errors in the last 1 minute

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_be_add_batch_task_queue_size > 20 Runbook: Run SHOW PROC '/backends' to check whether BE load is balanced; Lower load job concurrency or increase batch size to reduce tiny loads; Raise doris_max_pending_batch_size and the related thread pool parameters in be.conf and restart the BE; Check whether disk IO is saturated — the final bottleneck for loading is usually the disk.
documents.s: Doris_BE batch thread pool queue backlog

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: (sum(doris_be_cpu)by(instance)-sum(doris_be_cpu{mode=~"idle|iowait"})by(instance))/sum(doris_be_cpu)by(instance)*100 > 70 Runbook: Run SHOW PROCESSLIST to find large running queries and KILL them to stop the bleeding if needed; Use fe.audit.log to find the SQL scanning the most rows and add partition pruning or materialized views; Check whether compaction is consuming CPU (search the BE log for compaction); If query volume genuinely grew, add BE nodes.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_be_scanner_thread_pool_queue_size > 0 Runbook: Check fe.audit.log for the SQL scanning the most rows and reduce the scan with partition pruning, prefix indexes or materialized views; Run SHOW PROC '/backends' to check whether BE load is unbalanced; Raise doris_scanner_thread_pool_thread_num in be.conf and restart, but only if CPU has headroom; If disk IO is saturated, consider SSDs or adding BE nodes.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_be_send_batch_thread_pool_queue_size > 0 Runbook: Check bandwidth and latency between BEs (iperf3, mtr); Check whether a large result set query is doing heavy shuffle, and use EXPLAIN to see whether a colocate join can reduce the transfer; Raise send_batch_thread_pool_thread_num in be.conf; Confirm the NIC is not saturated and upgrade to 10GbE if needed.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_query_latency_ms{quantile="0.95"} > 5000 Runbook: On the FE run SHOW PROCESSLIST to see current slow queries and KILL <id> to stop the bleeding if needed; Sort fe.audit.log by QueryTime to find the top slow SQL; Use EXPLAIN to check whether partition pruning and indexes are used, and whether a large-table JOIN is missing colocate; Combine with BE CPU and the scanner thread pool queue to tell FE planning from BE execution as the bottleneck.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_query_latency_ms{quantile="0.99"} > 10000 Runbook: On the FE run SHOW PROCESSLIST to see current slow queries and KILL <id> to stop the bleeding if needed; Sort fe.audit.log by QueryTime to find the top slow SQL; Use EXPLAIN to check whether partition pruning and indexes are used, and whether a large-table JOIN is missing colocate; Combine with BE CPU and the scanner thread pool queue to tell FE planning from BE execution as the bottleneck.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_txn_publish_latency_ms{quantile="0.95"} > 5000 Runbook: Check the transaction timing entries in fe.log to tell whether publish or execution is slow; Slow publish usually means slow BE responses or unhealthy tablet replicas — use SHOW PROC '/statistic' for the unhealthy replica count; Check whether load concurrency is too high and lower it or use larger batches; Check BE disk IO and compaction pressure.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_txn_publish_latency_ms{quantile="0.99"} > 10000 Runbook: Check the transaction timing entries in fe.log to tell whether publish or execution is slow; Slow publish usually means slow BE responses or unhealthy tablet replicas — use SHOW PROC '/statistic' for the unhealthy replica count; Check whether load concurrency is too high and lower it or use larger batches; Check BE disk IO and compaction pressure.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_txn_exec_latency_ms{quantile="0.95"} > 5000 Runbook: Check the transaction timing entries in fe.log to tell whether publish or execution is slow; Slow publish usually means slow BE responses or unhealthy tablet replicas — use SHOW PROC '/statistic' for the unhealthy replica count; Check whether load concurrency is too high and lower it or use larger batches; Check BE disk IO and compaction pressure.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_txn_exec_latency_ms{quantile="0.99"} > 10000 Runbook: Check the transaction timing entries in fe.log to tell whether publish or execution is slow; Slow publish usually means slow BE responses or unhealthy tablet replicas — use SHOW PROC '/statistic' for the unhealthy replica count; Check whether load concurrency is too high and lower it or use larger batches; Check BE disk IO and compaction pressure.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(doris_fe_txn_counter{type="failed"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Search fe.log for 'transaction failed' to find the reason; Common causes are insufficient tablet replicas, an unavailable BE, or timeouts — use SHOW PROC '/statistic' for unhealthy replicas; Confirm the loader has retry logic and add it if not; After fixing the BE or replica problem, rerun the failed load jobs.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum by (type) (doris_fe_txn_status{type=~"aborted|unknown"}) > 0 Runbook: Run SHOW TRANSACTION WHERE STATUS='ABORTED' to see the specific transactions and reasons; aborted is usually a timeout or insufficient replicas; unknown needs the most attention — it means the FE cannot confirm the final state; Fix the underlying problem (BE availability, replica health) and reload; For unknown transactions, verify with the business side whether data is duplicated or missing.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_editlog_write_latency_ms{quantile="0.95"} > 1000 Runbook: Slow editlog writes directly affect every metadata operation — first use iostat -x 1 to check whether the disk holding the FE metadata directory is saturated; Confirm the FE metadata directory does not share a disk with data; a dedicated SSD is recommended; Check network latency between FEs — multi-replica editlog must be synchronised; Look for a burst of DDL or load jobs submitted at the same time.
documents.s: Doris_FE P95 edit log write latency

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_editlog_write_latency_ms{quantile="0.99"} > 2000 Runbook: Slow editlog writes directly affect every metadata operation — first use iostat -x 1 to check whether the disk holding the FE metadata directory is saturated; Confirm the FE metadata directory does not share a disk with data; a dedicated SSD is recommended; Check network latency between FEs — multi-replica editlog must be synchronised; Look for a burst of DDL or load jobs submitted at the same time.
documents.s: Doris_FE P99 edit log write latency

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: doris_fe_query_err_rate > 1 Runbook: Filter fe.audit.log for State=ERR records and read the specific error; Separate syntax/permission errors (user-side) from resource/timeout errors (server-side); For resource errors, combine BE CPU, memory and scan queue to find the bottleneck; If it lines up with a recent change (upgrade, schema modification), roll back to verify.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(doris_fe_image_clean[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Search fe.log for image clean errors and determine whether it is permissions or disk; Use df -h and ls -lh <meta_dir>/image to check directory size and free space; For permissions, fix the directory owner; for a full disk, clean other files first; Longer term, give the FE metadata directory enough dedicated space.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(doris_fe_edit_log_clean[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Search fe.log for edit log clean errors; Confirm free space and permissions on the metadata directory; Check whether an FE node has fallen far behind and is preventing log trimming — use SHOW FRONTENDS to see node states; If a lagging node cannot recover, consider removing and re-adding it.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(doris_fe_image_write[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Search fe.log for image write errors — usually insufficient disk space or memory; Use df -h for the metadata directory and jstat to check whether the FE heap is tight; For low memory, raise the FE -Xmx; for low disk, clean up or expand; After fixing, confirm a new image file appears under <meta_dir>/image — this verification step is mandatory.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(doris_fe_txn_counter{type="reject"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Search fe.log for reject-related entries to confirm the reason; The most common cause is load concurrency exceeding the FE transaction limit (max_running_txn_num_per_db) — use SHOW PROC '/transactions' for the current count; As an emergency measure raise max_running_txn_num_per_db, but the real fix is lower load concurrency with larger batches; Confirm the loader has retry logic and rerun the rejected jobs.

Elasticsearch exposes its state over HTTP JSON. The input reads _cluster/health, _cluster/stats, _nodes/stats and index statistics: cluster colour, unassigned shards, node JVM heap and GC, circuit breakers, thread pool rejections, indexing and search latency, and disk watermarks. On a small cluster set local = false and scrape any one node to get data for all of them; on a large cluster run Categraf on every node with local = true. Dashboards come in Categraf and elasticsearch_exporter editions; the rules cover the cluster turning yellow or red, unassigned shards, JVM heap near the limit, thread pool rejections and disk watermarks.
5 dashboards, 307 panels in total 22 alert rules, each with runbook steps 30 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.elasticsearch

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.elasticsearch/elasticsearch.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.elasticsearch started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 ############################################################################ # !!! uncomment [[instances]] to enable this plugin [[instances]] # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # append some labels to metrics # labels = { cluster="cloud-n9e-es" } ## specify a list of one or more Elasticsearch servers # servers = ["http://localhost:9200"] servers = [] ## Timeout for HTTP requests to the elastic search server(s) http_timeout = "10s" # either /_nodes/stats or /_nodes/_local/stats depending on this setting local = false ## Set cluster_health to true when you want to obtain cluster health stats cluster_health = true ## Adjust cluster_health_level when you want to obtain detailed health stats ## The options are ## - indices (default) ## - cluster cluster_health_level = "cluster" ## Set cluster_stats to true when you want to obtain cluster stats. cluster_stats = true ## Indices to collect; can be one or more indices names or _all ## Use of wildcards is allowed. Use a wildcard at the end to retrieve index names that end with a changing value, like a date. # indices_include = ["zipkin*"] ## use "shards" or blank string for indices level indices_level = "" ## node_stats is a list of sub-stats that you want to have gathered. Valid options ## are "indices", "os", "process", "jvm", "thread_pool", "fs", "transport", "http", ## "breaker". Per default, all stats are gathered. node_stats = ["jvm", "breaker", "process", "os", "fs", "indices", "thread_pool", "transport"] ## HTTP Basic Authentication username and password. username = "elastic" password = "password" ## Optional TLS Config # use_tls = false # tls_ca = "/etc/categraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/categraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/categraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = true ## Sets the number of most recent indices to return for indices that are configured with a date-stamped suffix. ## Each 'indices_include' entry ending with a wildcard (*) or glob matching pattern will group together all indices that match it, and ## sort them by the date or number after the wildcard. Metrics then are gathered for only the 'num_most_recent_indices' amount of most ## recent indices. num_most_recent_indices = 1 Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Elasticsearch, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. The EMQX input calls the Dashboard API (port 18083 by default). It first reads /nodes for each node's version, running state, connection count, processes and memory, then the cluster-level subscription count, routes, message sent, received and dropped counters, sessions and retained messages. Listing several node addresses for one cluster makes it pick a reachable one at random; use separate [[instances]] blocks for separate clusters. Set version to match the EMQX major version (v3, v4 or v5), and supply Dashboard credentials. The rules cover nodes going offline, sudden drops in connections, rising message drops and process counts near the limit.
9 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.emqx

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.emqx/emqx.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.emqx started once the plugin is loaded. [[instances]] ## emqx的dashboard地址，ip:port, 单个集群监控使用逗号分割多个IP,会随机挑一个可用ip进行连接请求 ## 多个集群，拆分到多个instance配置 address="http://192.168.11.12:18083" ## 指定emqx的版本，支持v3/v4/v5, 分别对应emqx的3.X/4.X/5.X 版本 version="v3" ## api需要鉴权，输入用户名和密码 username="admin" password="public" Open the integration center in Nightingale, find EMQX, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
9 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: emqx_node_status != 1 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels, log in to that host, and run emqx ctl status and systemctl status emqx to check the process; If the process is alive but the status is abnormal, read the tail of log/emqx.log.1; an exhausted Erlang VM heap or a full disk driving the node into self-protection are the usual causes; If the process is gone, rule out resource problems with df -h and free -g before starting it; After recovery run emqx ctl cluster status to confirm the node rejoined the cluster and watch the connection count return.

S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger: emqx_cluster_node_stopped > 0 Runbook: Take cluster from the alert labels and run emqx ctl cluster status on any surviving node to see which nodes are stopped; Log in to the stopped node and troubleshoot it as a single-node failure (process, memory, disk, logs); If the node cannot be recovered soon, run emqx ctl cluster force-leave <node> to remove it so the routing table stops trying to sync with it; During recovery watch the connection count and memory on the remaining nodes and scale out before letting devices reconnect if needed.
documents.s: EMQX cluster has a stopped node

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: emqx_node_connections / (emqx_node_max_fds > 0) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels and run emqx ctl listeners to see the current and maximum connections per listener; Run cat /proc/$(pgrep -f beam.smp)/limits | grep 'open files' to confirm the actual fd limit; Raise LimitNOFILE in systemd and node.max_ports in emqx.conf and restart to apply, re-checking memory (each connection costs tens of KB); If misbehaving clients are consuming connections by reconnecting furiously, rate-limit them at the gateway and review the client reconnect backoff.
documents.s: EMQX connections approaching the file descriptor limit

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: emqx_node_process_used / (emqx_node_process_available > 0) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels and run emqx ctl vm to see the live process/used and process/limit values; Compare against connection growth to decide whether this is normal growth or a session leak (persistent sessions with clean_session=false accumulating); For accumulating persistent sessions, review the session expiry configuration and spot-check with emqx ctl sessions list; If you genuinely need more capacity, raise node.process_limit in emqx.conf and restart, re-checking memory.
documents.s: EMQX Erlang process count approaching the limit

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: emqx_node_memory_used_bytes / (emqx_node_memory_total_bytes > 0) * 100 > 85 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels and run emqx ctl vm memory to see the breakdown (processes/binary/ets); A high binary share usually means messages piling up in session queues; look for subscribers that are not consuming fast enough and confirm the hot topics with emqx ctl topics list; A high processes share usually means too many sessions; handle it as for the Erlang process alert; As a stopgap lower mqueue_max_len to cap per-session queue length so a single slow consumer cannot drag the node down.
documents.s: EMQX node memory usage too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(emqx_messages_dropped[5m]) > 1 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels and run emqx ctl metrics | grep dropped to separate the drop reasons (queue_full / no_subscribers / expired); queue_full means subscribers are consuming too slowly; investigate the consumers first, then consider raising mqueue_max_len; For no_subscribers, confirm the publisher's topic spelling and whether the subscriber has disconnected; For expired, check that the Message Expiry Interval matches the real delivery latency.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(emqx_packets_connack_auth_error[5m]) > 1 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels and read the authentication failure entries in log/emqx.log to see the clientid and source IP distribution; Concentrated sources with regular clientids usually mean a broken authentication backend; check that the data source configured in emqx ctl authn list (MySQL/Redis/HTTP) is reachable; Scattered sources with random clientids indicate brute forcing; rate-limit at the firewall or gateway and enable a blacklist; If a batch of credentials expired at once, allow them through temporarily and push the device side to update.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(emqx_actions_failure[5m]) / ((rate(emqx_actions_success[5m]) + rate(emqx_actions_failure[5m])) > 0) * 100 > 5 Runbook: Take node from the alert labels and check the per-rule failure counters on the rule engine page of the Dashboard to identify the failing rule and action; Read that action's error in log/emqx.log to distinguish an unreachable downstream, a timeout, and a data format mismatch; For an unreachable downstream, fix it first and confirm the bridge's connection pool and timeout settings are sensible; For format problems, review the field mapping in the rule SQL, verify with the Dashboard's test feature, and then publish.
documents.s: EMQX rule engine action failure rate too high

documents.t: S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: emqx_node_uptime_seconds < 300 Runbook: First confirm whether this was a planned release or a scaling operation; If unplanned, check log/emqx.log.1 and journalctl -u emqx --since '-30min' for the cause; Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to rule out an OOM kill, and handle it as a memory alert if that is the case; After the restart watch the connection recovery curve and CPU, and rate-limit reconnections at the gateway if needed so the storm does not take down the node again.

The exec input is Categraf's catch-all. You write a script, the script prints metrics to standard output, and Categraf runs it on a schedule and parses the result. Any language works; the output must be one of three formats, chosen with data_format: Prometheus text exposition, InfluxDB line protocol (measurement,label=v field=1) or Open-Falcon JSON. Use it for business metrics, health checks of legacy systems and one-off inspection scripts. Keep the script's run time below the collection interval, and remember that values must be numeric.
documents.s: Report custom metrics to Nightingale from scripts (Exec)

documents.t: Categraf collector config: input.exec

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.exec/exec.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.exec started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] # # commands, support glob commands = [ # "/opt/categraf/scripts/*.sh" ] # # timeout for each command to complete # timeout = 5 # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # # choices: influx prometheus falcon # # influx stdout example: measurement,labelkey1=labelval1,labelkey2=labelval2 field1=1.2,field2=2.3 # data_format = "influx"

The GitLab Linux Package comes with a full set of exporters: node_exporter (host), gitlab_exporter (Rails and Sidekiq), Gitaly, Workhorse, postgres_exporter, redis_exporter and NGINX VTS. The five dashboards (overview, machine performance, NGINX, PostgreSQL, Redis) each use part of that set, so scrape all of these endpoints rather than a single /metrics. The rules cover Sidekiq queue backlog, Gitaly and Workhorse error rates, database connections and Redis memory, HTTP 5xx and host resources.
5 dashboards, 52 panels in total 9 alert rules, each with runbook steps

For an external Categraf, make the exporters listen on reachable addresses in /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb and firewall them to the collector node: prometheus['enable'] = false node_exporter['listen_address'] = '0.0.0.0:9100' gitlab_workhorse['prometheus_listen_addr'] = '0.0.0.0:9229' gitlab_exporter['listen_address'] = '0.0.0.0' gitlab_exporter['listen_port'] = '9168' redis_exporter['listen_address'] = '0.0.0.0:9121' postgres_exporter['listen_address'] = '0.0.0.0:9187' gitaly['configuration'] = { prometheus_listen_addr: '0.0.0.0:9236' } After gitlab-ctl reconfigure, list each port in the urls of the Categraf prometheus input with job = "gitlab" in labels. If you keep GitLab's bundled Prometheus, adding it as a data source works too. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Gitlab, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels GitLab - Machine Performance 10 GitLab - NGINX VTS 7 GitLab - Overview 10 GitLab - PostgreSQL 15 GitLab - Redis 10
9 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

High gRPC ResourceExhausted error rate S2 Warning · for 60 min · Trigger: sum without (grpc_code, grpc_method, grpc_service, grpc_type) ( rate(grpc_server_handled_total{grpc_code="ResourceExhausted"}[5m]) ) / sum without (grpc_code, grpc_method, grpc_service, grpc_type) ( rate(grpc_server_handled_total[5m]) ) * 100 > 1 Runbook: On the Gitaly node, check the logs to see which RPCs are being limited (gitaly_concurrency_limiting related); Use gitlab-ctl status plus node CPU/IO to confirm Gitaly is overloaded; Determine whether an oversized repository or a misbehaving client is pulling repeatedly, and throttle that source temporarily; If capacity is genuinely short, raise Gitaly's concurrency limits and add nodes.

Puma instance {{ $labels.instance }} has more than 90% thread utilization ({{ $value | printf "%.1f" }}%) over the last 60 minutes. S2 Warning · for 60 min · Trigger: instance:puma_utilization:ratio * 100 > 90 Runbook: On the GitLab node run gitlab-ctl status to check the puma process and look for timeouts in /var/log/gitlab/puma/; Combine with the PumaQueueing alert to judge the queue depth; Short term, raise puma['worker_processes'] and max_threads then run gitlab-ctl reconfigure; Look for slow requests (large MR diffs, big repository pages) holding workers for a long time and rate limit them if needed.

Postgres database has deadlocks S2 Warning · Trigger: increase(pg_stat_database_deadlocks[5m]) > 0 Runbook: On PostgreSQL confirm log_lock_waits=on and take the full SQL of both deadlock participants from the log; Join pg_locks with pg_stat_activity to identify which two tables are waiting on each other; In GitLab this commonly comes from CI concurrently updating the same records — reduce concurrency or upgrade GitLab (upstream frequently fixes these); Check whether a long transaction is amplifying the deadlock probability.

The Postgres service {{ $labels.job }} instance {{ $labels.instance }} is not responding for more than 50% of the time for 5 minutes. S2 Warning · Trigger: avg_over_time(pg_up[5m]) * 100 < 50 Runbook: Log in to the PostgreSQL node and confirm the process is alive (gitlab-ctl status postgresql or systemctl status postgresql); If it is alive, connect by hand with psql to tell a hung instance from a network or pg_hba problem; If it is not running, read the tail of the PG log (full disk, full WAL directory, OOM) before starting it; If a standby exists, assess whether to fail over.

Puma instance {{ $labels.instance }} is queueing requests with an average of {{ $value | printf "%.1f" }} over the last 30 minutes. S2 Warning · Trigger: avg_over_time(puma_queued_connections[30m]) > 1 Runbook: Combine with HighPumaUtilization to confirm worker utilization; Check /var/log/gitlab/puma/puma_stdout.log and the gitlab-rails log for the slowest request paths; Short term, raise puma['worker_processes'] and run gitlab-ctl reconfigure; Longer term, find the root cause of the slow requests (large repositories, large MRs, unindexed queries) and add nodes if needed.

The Redis service {{ $labels.job }} instance {{ $labels.instance }} is not responding for more than 50% of the time for 5 minutes. S2 Warning · Trigger: avg_over_time(redis_up[5m]) * 100 < 50 Runbook: Log in to the Redis node and check the process with gitlab-ctl status redis or systemctl status redis; If it is alive, verify with redis-cli ping to tell a hang from a network or password problem; If it is not running, check the logs (OOM, or a full disk breaking the RDB write) before starting it; After recovery, check whether the Sidekiq queues are backed up and watch them drain.

The service {{ $labels.job }} instance {{ $labels.instance }} is not responding for more than 50% of the time for 5 minutes. S2 Warning · Trigger: avg_over_time(up[5m]) * 100 < 50 Runbook: Take job/instance from the alert labels to identify the component (gitaly/puma/sidekiq/registry, etc.); On that node run gitlab-ctl status to check the process state; Use gitlab-ctl tail <service> to find the exit reason in the logs; After restarting, run gitlab-rake gitlab:check for an overall health check.

Sidekiq has jobs queued S2 Warning · for 60 min · Trigger: sum by (name) (sidekiq_queue_size) > 0 Runbook: Take name from the alert labels to identify the backed-up queue; Check queue depth and failed jobs in the GitLab admin Background Jobs page or via gitlab-rails runner; Confirm the Sidekiq process is alive and that concurrency is not set too low (sidekiq['max_concurrency']); If it is caused by mass job failures and retries, find the failure root cause (Redis/PG problems, external timeouts) before clearing them.

Workhorse has high error rates S2 Warning · Trigger: ( sum without (job, code) ( job_route_method_code:gitlab_workhorse_http_request_duration_seconds_count:rate5m{code=~"5.."} ) / sum without (job,code) ( job_route_method_code:gitlab_workhorse_http_request_duration_seconds_count:rate5m ) < 10 ) * 100 > 50 Runbook: Run gitlab-ctl tail gitlab-workhorse to see the exact errors and the failing routes; The usual root cause is a puma timeout or Gitaly being unavailable — confirm both are healthy first; For large-file issues, check disk space and temporary directory permissions; If it lines up with a recent upgrade, roll back first.

The HAProxy input reads the CSV output of the stats page (/stats;csv) or the Runtime API Unix socket. It collects current and maximum sessions, queue length, request rate, status code classes, connection and response errors, retries and redispatches at frontend, backend and server level, plus the health-check result of every backend server. Verified against real backend traffic. The rules cover backend servers marked DOWN, backends with no servers left, queue buildup, rising 5xx and HAProxy itself being unreachable.
1 dashboard, 10 panels in total 8 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.haproxy

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.haproxy/haproxy.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.haproxy started once the plugin is loaded. [[instances]] # URI on which to scrape HAProxy. # e.g. # uri = "http://localhost:5000/baz?stats;csv" # uri = "http://user:pass@haproxy.example.com/haproxy?stats;csv" # uri = "unix:/run/haproxy/admin.sock" uri = "" # Flag that enables SSL certificate verification for the scrape URI ssl_verify = false # Comma-separated list of exported server metrics. See http://cbonte.github.io/haproxy-dconv/configuration-1.5.html#9.1 server_metric_fields = "" # Comma-separated list of exported server states to exclude. See https://cbonte.github.io/haproxy-dconv/1.8/management.html#9.1, field 17 status server_exclude_states = "" # Timeout for trying to get stats from HAProxy. timeout = "5s" # Flag that enables using HTTP proxy settings from environment variables ($http_proxy, $https_proxy, $no_proxy) proxy_from_env = false Open the integration center in Nightingale, find HAProxy, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels HAProxy By Categraf 10
8 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: haproxy_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status haproxy to confirm the process is alive; If it is alive, verify the stats endpoint by hand with curl -s http://<host>:<port>/stats;csv and check whether an ACL or firewall is blocking it; If it is not running, validate the config first with haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg, then start it and check /var/log/haproxy.log for the exit reason; Confirm the VIP layer (keepalived or similar) has failed over, otherwise move traffic to the standby node by hand.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: haproxy_backend_up == 0 Runbook: Take the backend name from the alert labels and run echo 'show stat' | socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock to see the state and down reason of every server in that backend; curl each backend address from the HAProxy host to tell a collective backend failure apart from a HAProxy-to-backend network problem; If the backends are healthy, check whether the backend's check configuration (probe path, timeout, rise/fall) is too aggressive; If it cannot be recovered quickly, switch traffic to a standby backend or a degraded page.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: haproxy_server_up == 0 Runbook: Take backend and server from the alert labels and log in to that backend host to confirm the application process and port are alive; curl the backend address from the HAProxy host to tell an application failure apart from a network problem; For an application failure, follow that application's own recovery procedure, then confirm HAProxy has automatically added it back (haproxy_server_up returns to 1); Run echo 'show stat' | socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock to see how many servers are still available in the backend, and scale out immediately if headroom is low.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: sum by (backend) (rate(haproxy_backend_http_responses_total{code="5xx"}[5m])) / sum by (backend) (rate(haproxy_backend_http_responses_total[5m])) > 0.05 Runbook: Take the backend name from the alert labels and first determine whether every server is erroring or only one (compare haproxy_server_http_responses_total{code="5xx"}); If it is one server, remove it from the backend to stop the bleeding; If all of them are erroring, check the backend application logs for the root cause (dependency timeouts, exhausted connection pool, a bug from a release); If it lines up with a recent release, roll back first rather than keep investigating.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: haproxy_backend_current_queue > 0 Runbook: Take the backend name from the alert labels and compare with haproxy_backend_http_response_time_average_seconds to tell a slower backend apart from rising concurrency; If the backend got slower, investigate on the application side (slow queries, GC, dependency timeouts); If concurrency rose, check whether maxconn on the backend and its servers is set too low, raise it and reload; If backend capacity is genuinely insufficient, add more servers.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: haproxy_frontend_limit_sessions > 0 and haproxy_frontend_current_sessions / haproxy_frontend_limit_sessions > 0.8 Runbook: Take the frontend name from the alert labels and determine whether this is natural traffic growth or abnormal traffic (slow connections, crawlers); For natural growth, raise the frontend maxconn and the global maxconn, confirm the system ulimit -n and memory are sufficient, then reload; For abnormal traffic, add a stick-table rate limit on the frontend or block the source IPs outright; Check whether many connections are sitting idle for a long time and tighten timeout client.
documents.s: HAProxy frontend sessions approaching the limit

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: haproxy_backend_http_response_time_average_seconds > 1 Runbook: Take the backend name from the alert labels and compare haproxy_backend_http_connect_time_average_seconds with http_queue_time_average_seconds to tell slow connects, long queueing and slow backend processing apart; For long queueing, handle it as request queueing (raise maxconn or scale out); For slow processing, investigate on the application side (slow queries, GC, downstream timeouts); You may raise timeout server temporarily so requests are not cut off while you investigate, but do not treat it as a long-term fix.
documents.s: HAProxy backend response time too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: increase(haproxy_backend_connection_errors_total[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Take the backend name from the alert labels and run echo 'show stat' | socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock to see which server's connection errors are growing; telnet or curl that backend address from the HAProxy host to tell a closed port, a refused connection and a connect timeout apart; If the backend process is healthy, check the network in between, the security groups, and whether the backend's backlog/somaxconn is saturated; Check whether the backend's timeout connect is set too short and causing false positives.

Huawei Cloud metrics come from the Cloud Eye service (CES). The cloudeye-exporter maintained by Huawei Cloud converts CES metrics per product namespace into Prometheus metrics named huaweicloud_sys_<service>_<metric>, which the Categraf prometheus input scrapes. The templates are split by product: ECS hosts, RDS (MySQL and PostgreSQL), DCS Redis instances and proxy nodes, ELB, distributed messaging (Kafka, RabbitMQ, RocketMQ), Cloud Search (CSS/ES) and WAF, one dashboard each. The rules cover ECS CPU and memory, RDS connections and disk, DCS memory and hit ratio, ELB backend health; the metric reference explains each product's metrics one by one.
14 dashboards, 330 panels in total 35 alert rules, each with runbook steps 286 metric descriptions

Deploy the cloudeye-exporter and configure it with an IAM account's AK/SK, the project and the namespaces to collect. Once http://<exporter>:8087/metrics?services=SYS.ECS responds, scrape it per namespace with the Categraf prometheus input: # conf/input.prometheus/huaweicloud.toml interval = 120 [[instances]] urls = ["http://<exporter>:8087/metrics?services=SYS.ECS,SYS.RDS,SYS.DCS,SYS.ELB"] labels = { job = "huaweicloud" } Cloud Eye metrics are at 60-second granularity or coarser, so do not collect more often than that. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Huawei Cloud, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

Dashboard Panels Huawei Cloud Search Service (CSS/ES) 25 Huawei Cloud Distributed Cache Service (DCS) 13 Huawei Cloud Elastic Load Balance (ELB) 24 Huawei Cloud ECS Host Monitoring Dashboard 13 Huawei Cloud Distributed Message Service (Kafka) 26 Huawei Cloud RDS for MySQL instance 22 Huawei Cloud RDS for PostgreSQL instance 21 Huawei Cloud Database (RDS) 22 Huawei Cloud RabbitMQ 53 Huawei Cloud Redis Instance Monitoring Dashboard 35 Huawei Cloud Redis Proxy Node Monitoring Dashboard 12 Huawei Cloud Redis Data Node Monitoring Dashboard 35 Huawei RocketMQ Monitoring 16 Huawei Cloud WAF 13
35 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage >80 Runbook: SSH in and use top -H to find the busiest processes and threads; Use perf top or a language profiler to find the hot functions; Tell business growth apart from a code fault (infinite loop, frequent GC); For growth, change to a larger flavour in the console or scale out horizontally.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS CPU usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_inodesUsedPercent >80 Runbook: Run df -i to find the mount point; Count files level by level to find the directories with the most small files; Common sources are log fragments, session files and container layers — confirm and bulk delete; Longer term, consider moving small-file workloads to a dedicated partition.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS inode usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_ntp_offset > 1000 Runbook: Run chronyc tracking to check the offset and upstream source state; Huawei Cloud ECS should use the internal NTP service (ntp.myhuaweicloud.com) — confirm it is configured; Start chronyd if it is not running and enable it at boot; For a large offset, use chronyc makestep to step the clock.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS NTP offset exceeds 1 second

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_net_tcp_close > 20000 Runbook: Run ss -s to see the real connection state distribution; Run ss -tan | awk '{print $5}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to find the peers; The root cause is usually too many short-lived connections — switch the application to long-lived connections or a pool; As an emergency measure enable net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse and widen ip_local_port_range.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS TIME_WAIT connections exceed 20000

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_proc_zombie_count >0 Runbook: Run ps -ef | awk '$2 ~ /Z/ || $8 ~ /Z/' or ps aux | grep 'Z' to find the zombie processes and their parent PPIDs; Once you have the parent, the problem is that it never calls wait() — this must be fixed in code; As an emergency measure restart the parent so init reaps the zombies; If the count keeps growing, the code fix is mandatory — restarting is only a stopgap.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS zombie processes above 0

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_mem_available < 20 Runbook: Run free -h to check available memory and swap; Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head to find the largest consumer and judge whether it is leaking; For a leak, capture a heap in the application — a restart alone is not enough; For growth, change to a larger memory flavour in the console.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS available memory below 20%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_net_dropout > 50 Runbook: Run ip -s link show to confirm TX dropped is growing; Confirm whether the instance flavour's bandwidth cap is saturated — cloud bandwidth is capped per flavour and exceeding it drops packets; If capped, adjust bandwidth or change the flavour in the console; If not capped, check security groups, the kernel transmit queue and the application's send logic.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS outbound packet loss rate exceeds 50%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_net_errout > 50 Runbook: Run ip -s link show and ethtool -S to confirm the error counters; In the cloud the physical layer is the provider's responsibility, so an abnormal error rate should go to a Huawei Cloud support ticket first; At the same time confirm whether the instance flavour's bandwidth cap was exceeded; If redundancy exists, move traffic away to stop the impact.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS outbound packet error rate exceeds 50%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_usedPercent > 80 Runbook: Run df -h to find the mount point and du -x --max-depth=1 for the largest directories; Clean logs and temporary files first, and use lsof +L1 for deleted-but-unreleased files; Expand the EVS disk online in the console, then use growpart plus resize2fs/xfs_growfs to grow the filesystem; Longer term, evaluate moving the data directory to a dedicated cloud disk.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS block device usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_net_dropin > 50 Runbook: Run ip -s link show to confirm RX dropped is growing; Confirm whether the instance flavour's bandwidth or PPS cap is saturated — cloud instances limit both; If capped, adjust bandwidth or change the flavour in the console; If not capped, raise the receive ring buffer with ethtool -G and consider enabling RPS.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS inbound packet loss rate exceeds 50%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_net_errin > 50 Runbook: Run ip -s link show and ethtool -S to confirm the error counters; In the cloud the physical layer is the provider's responsibility, so an abnormal error rate should go to a Huawei Cloud support ticket first; At the same time confirm whether the flavour's bandwidth/PPS cap was exceeded; If redundancy exists, move traffic away.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS inbound packet error rate exceeds 50%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_agt_write_requests_rate > 99 Runbook: Run iostat -x 1 to check actual IOPS and await; Run iotop -oP to find the process writing the most; Compare against the EVS disk type's IOPS ceiling to see whether it has topped out — ultra-high performance and general purpose disks differ greatly; If it has, upgrade the disk type or expand it in the console (IOPS usually scales linearly with capacity); if not, optimise the application's write pattern.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS disk write IOPS too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_agt_read_requests_rate > 99 Runbook: Run iostat -x 1 to check actual IOPS and await; Run iotop -oP to find the process reading the most; Compare against the EVS disk type's IOPS ceiling to see whether it has topped out; If it has, upgrade the disk type or expand it; if not, reduce disk reads with caching and better indexes.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ECS disk read IOPS too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_elb_l4_in_bps_usage > 80 Runbook: Check that ELB's bandwidth monitoring curve in the console to tell sustained growth from a spike; Determine whether it is normal business growth or abnormal traffic (crawlers, attacks); For genuine growth, adjust the ELB specification or bandwidth cap in the console; For abnormal traffic, use WAF/DDoS protection to rate limit or block.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB L4 inbound bandwidth usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_elb_l4_out_bps_usage > 80 Runbook: Check that ELB's bandwidth monitoring curve in the console to tell sustained growth from a spike; Determine whether it is normal business growth or abnormal traffic (crawlers, attacks); For genuine growth, adjust the ELB specification or bandwidth cap in the console; For abnormal traffic, use WAF/DDoS protection to rate limit or block.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB L4 outbound bandwidth usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_elb_l4_con_usage > 80 Runbook: Check that ELB's connection count monitoring in the console for the growth trend; Check whether the backend is responding more slowly and causing connections to pile up — a high connection count is often a symptom of a slow backend rather than the cause; If the backend is fine, upgrade the ELB specification for the growth; Check whether clients are failing to reuse connections.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB L4 concurrent connection usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_elb_l4_ncps_usage > 80 Runbook: Check that ELB's connection count monitoring in the console for the growth trend; Check whether the backend is responding more slowly and causing connections to pile up — a high connection count is often a symptom of a slow backend rather than the cause; If the backend is fine, upgrade the ELB specification for the growth; Check whether clients are failing to reuse connections.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB L4 new connection usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_elb_l7_in_bps_usage > 80 Runbook: Check that ELB's bandwidth monitoring curve in the console to tell sustained growth from a spike; Determine whether it is normal business growth or abnormal traffic (crawlers, attacks); For genuine growth, adjust the ELB specification or bandwidth cap in the console; For abnormal traffic, use WAF/DDoS protection to rate limit or block.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB L7 inbound bandwidth usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_elb_l7_out_bps_usage > 80 Runbook: Check that ELB's bandwidth monitoring curve in the console to tell sustained growth from a spike; Determine whether it is normal business growth or abnormal traffic (crawlers, attacks); For genuine growth, adjust the ELB specification or bandwidth cap in the console; For abnormal traffic, use WAF/DDoS protection to rate limit or block.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB L7 outbound bandwidth usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_elb_m9_abnormal_servers > 0 Runbook: In the console's backend server group, find the instances failing the health check; Log in to that instance and confirm the application process and port are alive; If the application is fine, verify the health check configuration (path, port, timeout, interval) matches reality; Confirm the remaining healthy instances can carry the traffic and scale out immediately if not.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB unhealthy hosts above 0

documents.s: Huawei Cloud ELB query rate usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: This metric samples the CPU usage of the measured object multiple times within the statistics period and reports the average. Only single-node/primary-standby/read-write-splitting instances are supported. S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_cpu_avg_usage > 80 Runbook: Run SLOWLOG GET 10 to find the slowest commands; Focus on O(N) commands such as KEYS, HGETALL and SMEMBERS and on big-key operations, switching to SCAN or batching; Check whether an RDB/AOF persistence run is causing the CPU spike; If it stays high after tuning, upgrade the instance flavour in the console.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis average CPU usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_memory_usage > 80 Runbook: Use redis-cli --bigkeys to find large keys and split them or add TTLs; Use INFO memory to check the fragmentation ratio and enable activedefrag if it is high; Check whether keys without an expiry keep accumulating; Confirm maxmemory-policy, then expand the flavour in the console.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis memory usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_is_slow_log_exist == 1 Runbook: Run SLOWLOG GET 10 for the specific slow commands and their timings; Focus on O(N) commands and big-key operations; Switching to SCAN with batching and splitting large keys is the real fix; If the slow commands come from a scheduled job, move it to off-peak hours.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis slow log detected

documents.t: This metric samples the CPU usage of the measured object multiple times within the statistics period and reports the average. Only single-node/primary-standby/read-write-splitting instances are supported. S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_bandwidth_usage > 90 Runbook: Use INFO stats to check instantaneous_input_kbps / output_kbps and determine the direction; Use redis-cli --bigkeys to find large keys — reading and writing large keys is the most common cause of saturated bandwidth; Split large keys and reduce one-shot bulk reads; If you genuinely need more bandwidth, upgrade the flavour in the console.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis bandwidth usage exceeds 90%

documents.t: For single-node and primary-standby instances the connection limit is 10000; adjust the threshold to your workload. S3 Info · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_total_connections_received > 10000 Runbook: Use CLIENT LIST grouped by source to find the clients reconnecting frequently; Switching the application to a connection pool with reused connections is the real fix; Check whether the client's connection timeout is set too short and causing repeated reconnects; Confirm no throttling or memory alarm is causing the server to close connections.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis new connections exceed 10000

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_cpu_usage > 80 Runbook: Identify the node with high CPU in the console; In cluster mode this is usually data skew — a hot key in one slot, findable with --hotkeys; Hot keys can be mitigated with a local cache or by splitting the key; If it stays high after rebalancing, upgrade the flavour.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis max CPU usage exceeds 80%

documents.t: For single-node and primary-standby instances the connection limit is 10000; adjust the threshold to your workload. S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_connected_clients > 8000 Runbook: Check that DCS instance's monitoring curves in the Huawei Cloud console; Connect with redis-cli and run INFO to confirm the real state of the relevant metric; Once the cause is identified, follow the usual Redis path (big keys, slow commands, connection leaks); If capacity is short, change the instance flavour in the console.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis active clients exceed 8000

documents.t: Check spec limits together with instantaneous inbound/outbound traffic to decide whether scaling up resolves it. Only Redis 4.0+ instances support this metric; Redis 3.0 instances do not. S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_rx_controlled > 0 Runbook: Check when the throttling occurred in the console and compare against the bandwidth and QPS curves to see which limit was exceeded; For bandwidth, use --bigkeys to find and split large keys; For QPS, add a local cache or batch requests on the application side; If you genuinely need more capacity, change the instance flavour in the console.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis flow control count above 0

documents.t: For single-node and primary-standby instances the connection limit is 10000; adjust the threshold to your workload. S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dcs_p_connected_clients > 20000 Runbook: Check that DCS instance's monitoring curves in the Huawei Cloud console; Connect with redis-cli and run INFO to confirm the real state of the relevant metric; Once the cause is identified, follow the usual Redis path (big keys, slow commands, connection leaks); If capacity is short, change the instance flavour in the console.
documents.s: Huawei Cloud Redis Proxy node active clients exceed 20000

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dms_broker_alive == 0 Runbook: Confirm the instance and broker state in the Huawei Cloud console; Confirm clients have failed over to other brokers — with multiple brokers only some partitions are unavailable; If the console looks fine but clients report errors, check the network and security groups plus the client's nameserver address; If it stays unavailable, open a ticket with Huawei Cloud.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dms_broker_cpu_core_load > 1.5 Runbook: Check that broker's TPS and message backlog curves in the console to tell producer-side from consumer-side pressure; For a heavy consume backlog, scale out consumers first; For a produce spike, evaluate upgrading the instance flavour; Confirm no oversized messages or huge batch sends are overwhelming the broker.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: huaweicloud_sys_dms_broker_memory_usage > 85 Runbook: Check the message backlog in the console — a backlog consumes significant memory; Restoring consumption to drain the backlog is the most direct fix; Check whether the message retention period is set too long; For sustained growth, upgrade the instance flavour.

286 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Collection method (Linux): The disk read rate is calculated from the change in the sixth column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./. Collection method (Windows): Disk I/O data is obtained from the WMI Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfDisk_LogicalDisk object. The object is read once per collection period, and the instantaneous value it returns represents the metric value for that period.
