Collection method (Linux): The disk write IOPS is calculated from the change in the eighth column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./. Collection method (Windows): Disk I/O data is obtained from the WMI Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfDisk_LogicalDisk object. The object is read once per collection period, and the instantaneous value it returns represents the metric value for that period. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./. Under high CPU usage, the query may time out, and monitoring data may fail to be collected. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_device_used_percent Block Device Usage — This metric measures the physical disk usage of the monitored object, in percent. It is calculated as: used storage of all mounted disk partitions / total disk storage. Collection method (Linux): The disk usage of each mount point is summed up, the total disk size is calculated from the disk sector size and sector count, and the overall disk usage is then derived. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_fs_rwstate (Agent) File System Read/Write Status — This metric indicates the read/write status of the file systems mounted on the monitored object. Status values: read/write (0) or read-only (1). Collection method (Linux): Obtained from the file system mount parameters in the fourth column of /proc/mounts. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_inodesTotal (Agent) Total inodes — This metric measures the total inode space of the current disk on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): Run the df -i command and check the Inodes column. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_inodesUsed (Agent) Used inodes — This metric measures the used inode space of the current disk on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): Run the df -i command and check the IUsed column. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_inodesUsedPercent (Agent) inode Usage — This metric measures the percentage of used inodes on the current disk of the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): Run the df -i command and check the IUse% column. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_ioUtils (Agent) Disk I/O Usage — This metric measures the disk I/O usage of the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The disk I/O usage is calculated from the change in the thirteenth column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_io_svctm (Agent) Average I/O Service Time — This metric measures the average duration of each read or write I/O operation in the specified period. Collection method (Linux): The average I/O service time is calculated by dividing the change in the thirteenth column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period by the sum of the changes in the fourth and eighth columns. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_queue_length (Agent) Average Queue Length — This metric reflects how busy the disk is in the specified period and can be used to evaluate disk I/O performance. A larger value indicates a busier disk and poorer I/O performance. Collection method (Linux): The metric value is calculated by dividing the change in the fourteenth column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period by the collection period duration. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_readTime (Agent) Average Read Time — This metric measures the average time taken by disk read operations on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The average disk read time is calculated from the change in the seventh column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_read_bytes_per_operation (Agent) Average Read Operation Size — This metric measures the average number of bytes transferred per read I/O operation in the specified period. Collection method (Linux): The average read operation size is calculated by dividing the change in the sixth column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period by the change in the fourth column. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_writeTime (Agent) Average Write Time — This metric measures the average time taken by disk write operations on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The average disk write time is calculated from the change in the eleventh column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. huaweicloud_sys_agt_SlAsH_disk_write_bytes_per_operation (Agent) Average Write Operation Size — This metric measures the average number of bytes transferred per write I/O operation in the specified period. Collection method (Linux): The average write operation size is calculated by dividing the change in the tenth column of the corresponding device in /proc/diskstats during the collection period by the change in the eighth column. The mount point prefix path cannot exceed 64 characters, must start with a letter, and can contain only 0-9/a-z/A-Z/-/./~. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage (Agent) CPU Usage — This metric measures the current CPU usage of the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The CPU usage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. You can check the %Cpu(s) value with the top command. Collection method (Windows): Obtained through the Windows API GetSystemTimes. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_idle (Agent) Idle CPU Usage — This metric measures the percentage of time the CPU of the monitored object is currently idle. Collection method (Linux): The idle CPU time percentage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. Collection method (Windows): Obtained through the Windows API GetSystemTimes. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_iowait (Agent) iowait CPU Usage — This metric measures the percentage of CPU time currently occupied by the iowait state on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The iowait percentage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. You can check the %Cpu(s) wa value with the top command. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_irq (Agent) CPU Interrupt Usage — This metric measures the percentage of CPU time currently spent handling interrupts on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The CPU interrupt time percentage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. You can check the %Cpu(s) hi value with the top command. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_nice (Agent) Nice Process CPU Usage — This metric measures the current CPU usage of nice processes on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The nice process CPU usage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. You can check the %Cpu(s) ni value with the top command. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_other (Agent) Other CPU Usage — This metric measures the CPU usage of other consumers on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): Other CPU usage = 1 - idle CPU usage (%) - kernel space CPU usage - user space CPU usage. Collection method (Windows): Other CPU usage = 1 - idle CPU usage (%) - kernel space CPU usage - user space CPU usage. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_softirq (Agent) CPU Soft Interrupt Usage — This metric measures the percentage of CPU time currently spent handling soft interrupts on the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The CPU soft interrupt time percentage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. You can check the %Cpu(s) si value with the top command. Collection method (Windows): Not supported yet. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_system (Agent) Kernel Space CPU Usage — This metric measures the current kernel space CPU usage of the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The kernel space CPU usage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. You can check the %Cpu(s) sy value with the top command. Collection method (Windows): Obtained through the Windows API GetSystemTimes. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_cpu_usage_user (Agent) User Space CPU Usage — This metric measures the current user space CPU usage of the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): The CPU usage is calculated from the change in /proc/stat during the collection period. You can check the %Cpu(s) us value with the top command. Collection method (Windows): Obtained through the Windows API GetSystemTimes. % huaweicloud_sys_agt_load_average1 (Agent) 1-Minute Load Average — This metric measures the average CPU load of the monitored object over the past 1 minute. Collection method (Linux): Obtained by dividing load1 in /proc/loadavg by the number of logical CPUs. You can check the load1 value with the top command. huaweicloud_sys_agt_load_average15 (Agent) 15-Minute Load Average — This metric measures the average CPU load of the monitored object over the past 15 minutes. Collection method (Linux): Obtained by dividing load15 in /proc/loadavg by the number of logical CPUs. You can check the load15 value with the top command. huaweicloud_sys_agt_load_average5 (Agent) 5-Minute Load Average — This metric measures the average CPU load of the monitored object over the past 5 minutes. Collection method (Linux): Obtained by dividing load5 in /proc/loadavg by the number of logical CPUs. You can check the load5 value with the top command. huaweicloud_sys_agt_mem_available (Agent) Available Memory — This metric measures the available memory of the monitored object. Collection method (Linux): Obtained from the /proc/meminfo file. If MemAvailable is present in /proc/meminfo, it is used directly; otherwise, MemAvailable = MemFree + Buffers + Cached. The IPMI input is ported from ipmi_exporter. It runs a set of FreeIPMI commands and turns the output into metrics: temperatures, fan speeds, voltages, power draw, the health of every sensor and the chassis power state. The data comes from the BMC, so it is still available when the operating system is down. Collect locally on each server, or point one collector at a list of remote BMC addresses and credentials. IPMI itself must already be configured so that commands such as ipmimonitoring return output; otherwise there is nothing to convert.
3 dashboards, 31 panels in total 4 alert rules, each with runbook steps 19 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.ipmi

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.ipmi/conf.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.ipmi started once the plugin is loaded. # Read metrics from the bare metal servers via freeipmi [[instances]] # target指定是本地采集还是远程采集 #target="localhost" # 指定采集的用户名和密码，这里务必保证ipmi命令能获取正确输出，不是网上查到一个用户名 密码就可以。 #user = "user" #pass = "1234" # ipmi协议版本，支持1.5 和 2.0 #driver = "LAN_2_0" # 指定特权用户名 #privilege = "user" ## session-timeout, ms #timeout = 100000 # 支持的采集器 bmc, bmc-watchdog, ipmi, chassis, dcmi, sel，sm-lan-mode # 默认使用 bmc, ipmi, chassis和dcmi，建议保持下列配置便于仪表盘更好的展示 collectors = [ "bmc", "ipmi", "chassis", "sel", "dcmi"] # 不关注的传感器，指定id 排除掉 #exclude_sensor_ids = [ 2, 29, 32, 50, 52, 55 ] # 如果你想使用定制化的参数覆盖内置的命令，可以修改以下内容； 建议保持注释 #[instances.collector_cmd] #ipmi = "sudo" #sel = "sudo" #[instances.default_args] #ipmi = [ "--bridge-sensors" ] #[instances.custom_args] #ipmi = [ "--bridge-sensors" ] #sel = [ "ipmi-sel" ] Open the integration center in Nightingale, find IPMI, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

4 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: ipmi_cpu1_temp{} > 90 or ipmi_cpu2_temp{} > 90 Runbook: Run ipmitool sdr type temperature to see the actual readings and thresholds of each temperature sensor; Check that all chassis fans are spinning (ipmitool sdr type fan) and that filters and heatsinks are not clogged with dust; Confirm the room air conditioning and cold aisle temperature are normal and whether other machines in the same rack are also hot; Short term, reduce load on this machine or move critical workloads off to buy time for a dust-clean or fan replacement.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: count by (agent_hostname, server) ({__name__=~"ipmi_vcpu[0-9]+", status_code=~"lcr|ucr"}) > 0 Runbook: Run ipmitool sdr type voltage to see each voltage sensor's reading against its upper and lower thresholds and which way it deviates; Check the power supply status (ipmitool sdr type 'Power Supply'); on dual-PSU machines confirm whether one feed has failed; Check the power line and PDU output stability, and whether other machines in the same rack are alarming at the same time; If a PSU is confirmed faulty, schedule a replacement and move critical workloads off meanwhile.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: count by (agent_hostname, server) ({__name__=~"ipmi_fan[0-9]+", status_code=~"lcr|lnc|unc|ucr"}) > 0 Runbook: Run ipmitool sdr type fan to see each fan's speed and thresholds and identify the faulty one; A fan reading 0 or far below its peers is almost certainly failed — schedule a replacement; If every fan is running fast, intake temperature or load is too high: check room temperature, dust in the filters and any airflow obstruction; Before swapping fans, run ipmitool sdr type temperature to see whether temperatures have already risen, and move workloads off if needed.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: ipmi_system_temp > 90 or ipmi_pch_temp > 90 Runbook: Run ipmitool sdr type temperature to identify which sensor is hot and what its threshold is; Check the chassis fans and airflow, especially whether cabling is blocking intake around the motherboard; Confirm the room air conditioning and in-rack temperature, and whether the machine is wedged into an enclosed spot; Clean the dust, tidy the cabling and re-measure; if it still does not drop, contact the vendor to inspect the heatsink assembly.

19 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Monitoring a Java application mostly means monitoring the JVM: heap and non-heap memory, GC count and pause time per generation, thread count and deadlocks, class loading, file descriptors. The two common ways of exposing these produce different metric names, so the templates are split: JMX and JMX - Kubernetes: the application loads the Prometheus JMX Exporter Java Agent and emits jvm_memory_*, jvm_gc_collection_seconds_* and friends. JVM by OpenTelemetry: the application loads the OpenTelemetry Java Agent and an OTel Collector converts the data to Prometheus metrics. The two sets do not mix. Spring Boot applications can also go through Actuator; see the Spring Boot integration.
3 dashboards, 74 panels in total

Taking the JMX Exporter as the example: add -javaagent:jmx_prometheus_javaagent.jar=9404:config.yaml to the JVM options, check that http://<host>:9404/metrics responds, then scrape it with the Categraf prometheus input: # conf/input.prometheus/java-jmx.toml [[instances]] urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:9404/metrics"] url_label_key = "instance" url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" labels = { job = "order-service" } Put the application name in the job label; the dashboards filter on it. If a Prometheus already scrapes these targets, add it as a data source instead. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Java, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

Kafka's core broker metrics are exposed over JMX; collect those with jolokia or jmx_exporter. The Categraf kafka input fills the gap JMX cannot: consumer group lag, per-partition offsets and consumption rate. It is forked from the davidmparrott flavour of kafka_exporter, whose metric names differ slightly from the danielqsj flavour; set rename_uncommit_offset_to_lag = true to switch to the more common kafka_consumergroup_lag naming. Dashboards come in Categraf and kafka_exporter editions. The rules cover steadily growing consumer lag, offline partitions, under-replicated partitions, shrinking ISR and brokers dropping out.
2 dashboards, 24 panels in total 5 alert rules, each with runbook steps 6 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.kafka

5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import. Rules are grouped by collector; import the group that matches how you collect.

Kafka partitions are under-replicated​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max by (topic) (kafka_topic_partition_under_replicated_partition) > 0 Runbook: Take topic from the alert labels and run kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic <topic> --bootstrap-server <broker>, comparing Isr against Replicas to find which broker holds the missing replica; Check that broker's server.log for a full disk, GC pauses or network timeouts; If the broker is down, bring it back and the replicas will catch up automatically; If it cannot catch up for a long time, use kafka-reassign-partitions.sh to move the replica to a healthy broker. Kafka broker count dropped​ S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: delta(kafka_brokers[10m]) < 0 Runbook: Run kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server <broker> to list the currently online brokers and compare against the configuration to find the missing node; On that node, confirm the process is alive and check server.log for OOM or disk errors; After bringing it back, run kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions to confirm the replicas caught up; If the node cannot be fixed soon, use kafka-reassign-partitions.sh to move its partitions away and restore redundancy. Kafka consumer group lag exceeds 10000 messages​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max by (topic, consumergroup) (kafka_consumergroup_uncommitted_offsets) > 10000 Runbook: Take consumergroup and topic from the alert labels and run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group <group> --bootstrap-server <broker> to see the LAG distribution per partition; Lag concentrated on a few partitions means data skew — check the partition key on the producer side; Evenly spread lag means consumers are slow: first check the consumer logs for abnormal retries, then scale out consumer instances (never beyond the partition count) or make per-message processing faster; Confirm the consumers have not all dropped out (MEMBERS at 0 means you must start the consumers first).

Kafka consumer group lag exceeds 10000 messages - exporter​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max by (topic, consumergroup) (kafka_consumergroup_lag) > 10000 Runbook: Take consumergroup and topic from the alert labels and run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group <group> --bootstrap-server <broker> to see the LAG distribution per partition; Lag concentrated on a few partitions means data skew — check the partition key on the producer side; Evenly spread lag means consumers are slow: first check the consumer logs for abnormal retries, then scale out consumer instances (never beyond the partition count) or make per-message processing faster; Confirm the consumers have not all dropped out (MEMBERS at 0 means you must start the consumers first). Kafka under-replicated partitions - exporter​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max by (topic) (kafka_topic_partition_under_replicated_partition) > 0 Runbook: Take topic from the alert labels and run kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic <topic> --bootstrap-server <broker>, comparing Isr against Replicas to find which broker holds the missing replica; Check that broker's server.log for a full disk, GC pauses or network timeouts; If the broker is down, bring it back and the replicas will catch up automatically; If it cannot catch up for a long time, use kafka-reassign-partitions.sh to move the replica to a healthy broker.

Every Kubernetes component exposes Prometheus-format /metrics. The recommended path is to scrape them directly with the Categraf prometheus input and deploy kube-state-metrics (workload state) and node-exporter (node resources). The old Categraf kubernetes input is deprecated, but the dashboards and rules in this template keep working. Dashboards cover each control-plane component, nodes, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Pods, containers and CoreDNS. Rules cover crash-looping and Pending Pods, missing replicas, NotReady nodes and resource pressure, apiserver latency and error rate, etcd and scheduling failures, and expiring certificates. The metric reference explains the metrics component by component.

These components expose Prometheus-format /metrics themselves, so the Categraf prometheus input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, add it as a Nightingale data source and the templates work as they are. Control-plane endpoints need a ServiceAccount token or client certificate; when Categraf runs as a DaemonSet inside the cluster, use bearer_token_file to read the mounted token. On distributions such as K3s, the scheduler, controller-manager and kube-proxy may listen on loopback only, so collect them on the control-plane node itself. Do not expose these unauthenticated endpoints to the internet for convenience. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Kubernetes, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

The LDAP input queries the server's monitoring backend (cn=Monitor) for current and total connections, counters for bind, search, modify, add, delete and other operations, pending reads and writes, thread pool state and uptime. OpenLDAP and 389ds dialects are both supported, with slightly different metric names. The server must have the monitor backend enabled (olcDatabase=monitor on OpenLDAP) and allow the monitoring account to read it. StartTLS and LDAPS are supported. The rules cover abnormal connection counts, rising operation errors, growing bind failures and the service being unreachable.

5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: openldap_current_connections / (openldap_max_file_descriptors_connections > 0) * 100 > 80 Runbook: Run ldapsearch -x -D <bind_dn> -w <pw> -b 'cn=Connections,cn=Monitor' to list current connections and find the client IP holding the most; Many connections from a single application means it is not reusing or closing connections; push the application team to use a connection pool; As a stopgap raise slapd's ulimit -n (LimitNOFILE under systemd) and restart; Also check whether olcIdleTimeout is configured, since without it idle connections hold descriptors forever.
documents.s: OpenLDAP connections approaching the file descriptor limit

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: openldap_pending_threads > 0 Runbook: Run ldapsearch -x -D <bind_dn> -w <pw> -b 'cn=Operations,cn=Monitor' to see which operation type (Search/Bind/Modify) dominates; When Search dominates, hunt slow queries: enable loglevel stats in slapd.conf and find the SRCH filters with high duration in the log, then index the matching attributes (olcDbIndex); After adding indexes rebuild them with slapindex (slapd must be stopped first); If indexing is not the problem, raise olcThreads (default 16) and check whether CPU core count has become the bottleneck.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: openldap_active_threads / (openldap_max_threads > 0) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Run ldapsearch -x -D <bind_dn> -w <pw> -b 'cn=Threads,cn=Monitor' to see the live Active and Max values; Enable stats logging to locate slow operations, paying particular attention to unindexed substring filters such as (cn=abc) that force a full scan; Add olcDbIndex for the frequently filtered attributes and rebuild with slapindex; this is the most effective way to shed load; If indexing is already complete and it is still saturated, raise olcThreads or add read-only replicas (syncrepl consumers) to offload queries.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: openldap_operations_initiated - openldap_operations_completed > 100 Runbook: Run ldapsearch -x -D <bind_dn> -w <pw> -b 'cn=Operations,cn=Monitor' and compare Initiated with Completed per operation type to find where things are stuck; If Modify/Add are stuck, check backend database locks and disk IO (iostat -x 1); the mdb backend blocks easily under write amplification; If Search is stuck, follow the slow-query path and add indexes; If replication (syncrepl) is holding the provider back, check the connectivity and lag of each consumer and detach a broken consumer if necessary.
documents.s: OpenLDAP completed operations lagging behind initiated

documents.t: S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: openldap_uptime_time < 300 Runbook: First confirm whether this was a planned change; If unplanned, run journalctl -u slapd --since '-30min' to find the cause; Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to check for an OOM kill; an oversized olcDbMaxSize on the mdb backend is a common trigger; After the restart verify service with ldapsearch -x -b '' -s base namingContexts and confirm replicas have caught up.

Linux hosts are where most monitoring starts. Categraf's cpu, mem, disk, diskio, net, netstat, kernel and processes inputs are enabled by default and report as soon as the agent starts. The configs listed below are the plugins that have options worth tuning. The templates come in three sets, written against Categraf, node_exporter and Telegraf metric names respectively. Import the set that matches your collector; mixing them produces empty panels. The rules cover the things that actually page people: disks predicted to fill up, busy IO, conntrack exhaustion, clock drift and hosts going silent.

These rules are not in the alert rule library, so they are listed here in full. Machine monitoring - agent lost for more than 60 seconds​ Runbook: First confirm the machine itself is alive with ping and ssh — if it is down, handle it as a host outage; If it is alive, run systemctl status categraf to check the agent process and journalctl -u categraf -n 100 to locate the cause; Common causes are an agent crash, a config error, or network/auth failure to the server — verify by curling the server's write endpoint by hand; After recovery, confirm the data is continuous, and note that failures during the blind window produced no alerts at all. Machine monitoring - time offset exceeds 3 seconds, attention​ for 1 min Runbook: Run date and chronyc tracking to check the local time and the offset; Confirm chronyd/ntpd is running, and if not, start it and enable it at boot; Check that 123/UDP to the NTP server is allowed, switching to an internal NTP source if needed; When the offset is large, use chronyc makestep to step the clock, preparing time-sensitive workloads first. Lost connection with monitoring target - categraf​ Runbook: First confirm the machine itself is alive with ping and ssh — if it is down, handle it as a host outage; If it is alive, run systemctl status categraf to check the agent process and journalctl -u categraf -n 100 to locate the cause; Common causes are an agent crash, a config error, or network/auth failure to the server — verify by curling the server's write endpoint by hand; After recovery, confirm the data is continuous, and note that failures during the blind window produced no alerts at all. 132 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Metric Meaning Unit cpu_usage_guest CPU Guest time ratio — The proportion of time the CPU spends running the virtual CPU for the Guest OS. Label cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the statistical value of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the statistical value of CPU number 0 % cpu_usage_iowait CPU iowait time ratio — Represents the proportion of time the CPU spends waiting for I/O operations (input/output) to complete; Tag cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the iowait occupancy rate of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating iowait usage rate of CPU # 0 % cpu_usage_steal CPU Steal time ratio — Represents the proportion of time that the virtual machine (Guest OS) CPU time is used by the virtualization manager (Hypervisor) to run other virtual machines. The value of this indicator in the physical machine is 0, which is useless; If the value of this indicator in the virtual machine is greater than 10 for a long time, it means that the competition is serious. [Reference] (https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/zlrfMNrDHJVE5lkTVow5zA); Label cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the statistical value of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the statistical value of CPU number 0 % cpu_usage_nice Time proportion of CPU low-priority processes — In Linux systems, each process has a "nice" value, which usually ranges from-20 to 19. The default nice value is 0. A negative nice value indicates high priority (faster CPU access), while a positive nice value indicates low priority (slower CPU access). This indicator counts the time proportion of processes with nice values of 1-19. Tag cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the statistical value of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the statistical value of CPU number 0 % cpu_usage_system CPU core mode time ratio — Represents the time ratio of CPU core mode; Tag cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the statistical value of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the statistical value of CPU number 0 % cpu_usage_active CPU utilization — -Tag CPU = "CPU-total", indicating the CPU utilization of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating single-core utilization of CPU # 0 % cpu_usage_user CPU user mode time ratio — Indicates the time ratio of CPU user mode; Tag cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the statistical value of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the statistical value of CPU number 0 % cpu_usage_irq CPU hard interrupt time ratio — Indicates the proportion of time spent by the CPU handling hard interrupts; Tag cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the statistical value of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the statistical value of CPU number 0 % cpu_usage_idle CPU idle rate — -Tag CPU = "CPU-total", indicating the CPU idle rate of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the single core idle rate of CPU # 0 % cpu_usage_softirq CPU soft interrupt time ratio — Indicates the proportion of time the CPU takes to process soft interrupts; Tag cpu = "cpu-total", indicating the statistical value of the whole machine; Tag CPU = "0", indicating the statistical value of CPU number 0 % netstat_tcp_established Number of network links with ESTABLISHED status netstat_tcp_fin_wait1 Number of network links in FIN _ WAIT1 state netstat_tcp_fin_wait2 Number of network links in FIN _ WAIT2 state 100 * conntrack_ip_conntrack_count / conntrack_ip_conntrack_max IP conntrack usage — If it is full, you will usually see errors such as: conntrack table full in the system log. You can adjust the maximum value of the system to solve the problem % netstat_tcp_last_ack Number of network links in LAST _ ACK state netstat_tcp_listen Number of network links in LISTEN status 100 * conntrack_nf_conntrack_count / conntrack_nf_conntrack_max NF conntrack usage % increase(kernel_vmstat_oom_kill[1m]) OOM number statistics within 1 minute — Taken from /proc/vmstat , requires a higher version of the kernel, if I remember correctly, it should be 4.13 or above netstat_tcp_syn_recv Number of network links in SYN _ RECV state netstat_tcp_syn_sent Number of network links in SYN _ SENT state netstat_tcp_time_wait Number of network links in TIME _ WAIT state — The default configuration of disable _ connection _ stats in the categraf configuration file conf/input.netstat/netstat.toml is true because on machines with many network connections, obtaining the number of connections in each state will consume more CPU, so the default disable is dropped. netstat_tcp_tw Number of network links in TIME _ WAIT state (recommended) — Read from /proc/net/sockstat . (mem_swap_total - mem_swap_free)/mem_swap_total * 100 and mem_swap_total > 0 Swap space usage — Swap space usage. The computational atom is taken from /proc/meminfo . % mem_swap_total - mem_swap_free Swap space usage — Swap space usage. The computational atom is taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes mem_swap_total Total swap space — Total amount of swap space. Taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes mem_swap_free Swap space free amount — Swap space free amount. Taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes mem_buffered Memory Buffered amount — The amount of memory used as a buffer. Taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes mem_cached Memory Cached amount — The amount of memory used as a file cache. Taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes mem_used_percent Memory usage — Memory usage % 100 - mem_available_percent Memory usage (based on MemAvailable) — Memory usage. Calculation based on MemAvailable is more accurate, but older versions of Linux do not support it. % mem_used Memory usage — Memory usage = Total-Free-Buffered-Cached bytes mem_available_percent Memory availability — The amount of available memory that can be immediately allocated to the process divided by the total amount of memory. The values of numerator and denominator are taken from /proc/meminfo . % mem_available Memory Availability — The amount of available memory that can be immediately allocated to a process. Taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes mem_total Total memory — Total amount of memory. Taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes mem_active Memory activity — This field indicates the total amount of memory currently actively used, that is, the memory pages that the system has recently visited and is expected to be used again soon. Taken from /proc/meminfo . bytes netstat_udp_socket Number of current UDP connections disk_inodes_used / disk_inodes_total * 100 Hard disk inode usage — If you store a lot of small files, you need to pay attention to inode usage. % disk_inodes_used Hard disk inode usage — If you store a lot of small files, you need to pay attention to inode usage. disk_inodes_free Remaining amount of hard disk inode — If you store a lot of small files, you need to pay attention to inode usage. disk_inodes_total Total amount of hard disk inode — If you store a lot of small files, you need to pay attention to inode usage. irate(diskio_write_time[2m])/irate(diskio_writes[2m]) Hard disk IO-Write request average time ms diskio_write_time Hard Drive IO-Time the write request waits to be processed — The time a write request waits on disk. Multiple write requests waiting simultaneously increase this number. For example, if 8 requests all wait an average of 1000 milliseconds, 8000 is reported. ms diskio_weighted_io_time Hard Disk IO-Weighted IO Processing Time — As long as the device is processing IO, no matter how many are processed at the same time, diskio _ IO _ time will be incremented; The number of simultaneously processed IOs is multiplied by time to obtain a weighted value: diskio _ weighted _ IO _ time. ms irate(diskio_io_time[2m])/1000*100 Hard Disk IO-Time Dimension Utilization — Count the proportion of hard disk IO time in the time dimension. For example, if the value is 50%, it means that 50% of the time is processing IO, and if the value is 100%, it means that IO has been processing all the time. However, note that modern disk devices have the ability to process multiple I/O requests in parallel, so even if the value is 100%, the hard disk may still be able to receive new processing requests. For example, someone has two hands and has been working with one hand in the last minute. From the time dimension, the utilization rate is 100%, but even if it is 100%, he can do it if he is given more work, because he still has one hand available. % irate(diskio_write_bytes[2m]) Hard disk IO-bytes written per second bytes/s irate(diskio_writes{}[2m]) Hard drive IO-writes per second irate(diskio_merged_writes[2m]) Hard Disk IO-Number of merged write requests per second — Adjacent reads and writes may be merged for efficiency. So two 4K reads may turn into an 8K read before finally handing it over to disk, so it will be counted (and queued) to have only one I/O. These fields let you know how often this happens. irate(diskio_merged_reads[2m]) Hard disk IO-merge read requests per second — Adjacent reads and writes may be merged for efficiency. So two 4K reads may turn into an 8K read before finally handing it over to disk, so it will be counted (and queued) to have only one I/O. These fields let you know how often this happens. irate(diskio_read_bytes[2m]) Hard Drive IO-bytes read per second bytes/s irate(diskio_reads{}[2m]) Hard drive IO-Reads per second diskio_io_time Hard Disk IO-Time the hard disk takes to process IO — The time it takes for the hard disk to process IO, in milliseconds. Assuming that 500 milliseconds are processing IO in the last 1 second, this value will be increased by 500. This is a monotonically increasing Counter value, which will continue to rise after the operating system is started. In actual use, this indicator is generally used to calculate the hard disk IO UTIL (percentage of time dimension). ms diskio_iops_in_progress Hard Disk IO-Number of IO being processed by the device driver — The number of requests that have been currently assigned to the device driver and have not been completed, Gauge type. If I/O requests have entered the queue, but have not been assigned to the device driver, they are not counted. irate(diskio_read_time[2m])/irate(diskio_reads[2m]) Hard disk IO-Read request average time ms diskio_read_time Hard Drive IO-Time for read requests to be processed — The time the read request waits on disk. Multiple read requests waiting simultaneously increase this number. For example, if 5 requests all wait an average of 100 milliseconds, 500 is reported. ms irate(diskio_weighted_io_time[1m])/1000 Hard Disk IO-Queue Depth — Assuming that there is a weighted waiting time of 5000 ms in the past 1000 ms, it is equivalent to an average of 5 IO requests waiting, that is, the queue depth is 5. disk_used_percent Hard Drive Usage — Hard disk space usage. % disk_used Hard drive usage — Use the SI standard to render data, consistent with the df command. bytes disk_device_error Is there an error in reading hard disk information — 0 means normal, no error; A non-0 For example, if the value is 50%, it means that 50% of the time is processing IO, and if the value is 100%, it means that IO has been processing all the time. However, note that modern disk devices have the ability to process multiple I/O requests in parallel, so even if the value is 100%, the hard disk may still be able to receive new processing requests. For example, someone has two hands and has been working with one hand in the last minute. From the time dimension, the utilization rate is 100%, but even if it is 100%, he can do it if he is given more work, because he still has one hand available. % Logstash serves an HTTP API on port 9600 by default. The input reads _node/stats: input, filter and output event counts and durations per pipeline, persistent queue capacity and backlog, JVM heap, GC and threads, and process CPU and file descriptors. If the API has Basic Auth or TLS enabled, configure the username, password and certificates accordingly. The throughput, queue and pipeline panels only show non-zero data once Logstash actually processes events. The rules cover stalled event processing, a steadily growing queue, heap near the limit and Logstash being unreachable.
1 dashboard, 11 panels in total 6 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.logstash

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.logstash/logstash.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.logstash started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 # Read metrics exposed by Logstash [[instances]] # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # append labels # labels = { instance="x" } ## The URL of the exposed Logstash API endpoint. # url = "http://127.0.0.1:9600" url = "" ## Use Logstash 5 single pipeline API, set to true when monitoring ## Logstash 5. # single_pipeline = false ## Enable optional collection components. Can contain ## "pipelines", "process", and "jvm". # collect = ["pipelines", "process", "jvm"] ## Timeout for HTTP requests. # timeout = "5s" ## Optional HTTP Basic Auth credentials. # username = "username" # password = "pa$$word" ## Optional HTTP headers. # [inputs.logstash.headers] # "X-Special-Header" = "Special-Value" ## Optional TLS Config # use_tls = false # tls_min_version = "1.2" # tls_ca = "/etc/categraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/categraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/categraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = true Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Logstash, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels logstash 11
6 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(logstash_events_out[5m]) == 0 and rate(logstash_events_in[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty to find the pipeline whose events.out is not increasing; For that pipeline, look at the per-plugin event breakdown; the blockage is usually in an output (Elasticsearch rejecting writes, Kafka unreachable); Check logstash-plain.log for retry/backoff errors and confirm whether the downstream is returning 429 or timing out; After the downstream recovers, watch events.out come back; if it stays flat, restart Logstash and check whether the persistent queue is corrupted.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: logstash_jvm_mem_heap_used_in_bytes / (logstash_jvm_mem_heap_max_in_bytes > 0) * 100 > 85 Runbook: Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/jvm?pretty to confirm heap_used_percent and GC counts; The most common trigger is an oversized pipeline.batch.size; estimate memory as batch.size x worker count x average event size and lower it; Check for filters that cache large amounts of state in memory (aggregate, ruby) and cap their cache size; Only once the configuration is sane should you raise -Xmx in jvm.options, generally staying under half of physical memory and under 8 GB.
documents.s: Logstash JVM heap usage too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(logstash_jvm_gc_collectors_old_collection_count[5m]) * 60 > 1 Runbook: Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/jvm?pretty and compare the growth of old collection_count and collection_time_in_millis; Start with the heap alert path: lower pipeline.batch.size and check stateful filters; Run jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -30 to see the object distribution; when abnormal it is usually a build-up of event objects; After tuning, confirm the old GC rate falls; if it does not, split the pipeline or scale Logstash horizontally.
documents.s: Logstash old generation GC too frequent

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(logstash_events_queue_push_duration_in_millis[5m]) / (rate(logstash_events_in[5m]) > 0) > 100 Runbook: Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty and compare duration_in_millis across plugins to find the biggest contributor; If the time is concentrated in an output, investigate the downstream first (Elasticsearch write rejection rate, bulk queue); when the downstream is the root cause, fix it there rather than in Logstash; If it is concentrated in filters, focus on grok: replace complex regexes with dissect or add anchors to avoid catastrophic backtracking; If the host CPU is already saturated, raising pipeline.workers will not help and you need to scale out.
documents.s: Logstash queue push latency too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(logstash_events_duration_in_millis[5m]) / (rate(logstash_events_out[5m]) > 0) > 100 Runbook: Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty and sort plugins by duration_in_millis to find the slow one; Slow grok is the usual cause: load-test with --config.debug on a small sample and replace broad regexes with dissect; Filters that make external lookups (jdbc_streaming, elasticsearch, dns) must have caching enabled and timeouts set; After tuning, re-run the same sample set and compare duration to confirm the improvement is real.
documents.s: Logstash per-event processing time too long

documents.t: S3 Info · for 10 min · Trigger: logstash_process_cpu_percent > 90 Runbook: Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty to find the pipeline and plugin burning the most CPU; Capture stacks with jstack <pid>; many threads inside regex methods point to grok overhead; If it is still high after tuning filters, check whether pipeline.workers exceeds the real CPU core count and is causing context-switch overhead; If the host is genuinely at its limit, scale out and spread the load at the collection layer.
documents.s: Logstash process CPU usage too high

MinIO exposes Prometheus metrics under /minio/v2/metrics/ on three paths: cluster, bucket and node. The two bundled dashboards use all three families, so scraping /cluster alone leaves the object count, bucket usage, process and disk panels without data. The endpoint requires a Bearer Token by default. MINIO_PROMETHEUS_AUTH_TYPE=public is fine for a test environment; in production keep authentication on, configure the token in Categraf, and do not expose the endpoint to the internet. The rules cover nodes offline, disks offline or near capacity, S3 request error rate and failed health checks.
2 dashboards, 64 panels in total 2 alert rules, each with runbook steps

These components expose Prometheus-format /metrics themselves, so the Categraf prometheus input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, add it as a Nightingale data source and the templates work as they are. # conf/input.prometheus/minio.toml [[instances]] urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:9000/minio/v2/metrics/cluster"] labels = { job = "minio", instance = "minio-01:9000" } [[instances]] urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:9000/minio/v2/metrics/bucket"] labels = { job = "minio", instance = "minio-01:9000" } [[instances]] urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:9000/minio/v2/metrics/node"] labels = { job = "minio", instance = "minio-01:9000" } Open the integration center in Nightingale, find MinIO, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels MinIO Dashboard 32 MinIO Dashboard New Version 32
2 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

Disks down in MinIO deployment S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: avg_over_time(minio_cluster_disk_offline_total{}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run mc admin info <alias> to identify which node and which disk went offline and how much redundancy the cluster has left; On that node use dmesg -T | grep -iE 'i/o error|ata|scsi' and smartctl -a to tell a dropped disk, a bad disk and a lost mount apart; For a lost mount, remount it and MinIO will pick it up automatically; for a bad disk, replace it and run mc admin heal -r <alias>; Avoid heavy writes during healing and confirm remaining redundancy still exceeds the erasure-code parity count.

Node down in MinIO deployment S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: avg_over_time(minio_cluster_nodes_offline_total{}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Run mc admin info <alias> to identify the offline node, then ping/ssh to confirm the machine is alive; If it is alive, run systemctl status minio and check the logs — the usual causes are OOM, a failed disk mount or an expired certificate; For intra-cluster network failures check networking and security groups: MinIO nodes must reach each other; Once the node is back, run mc admin heal -r <alias> and watch the healing progress.

The MongoDB input wraps Percona's mongodb_exporter and collects connections, op counters, queues, WiredTiger cache, replica set member state and oplog window via serverStatus, replSetGetStatus and related commands. For sharded clusters, the mongodb_cluster input collects from the mongos side. The bundled dashboards are written against the 0.1x-compatible metric names such as mongodb_ss_*, so the Categraf config must set compatible_mode = true and give every instance an instance label. The rules cover connection counts, replication lag, unhealthy replica set members and unreachable instances.
1 dashboard, 23 panels in total 8 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.mongodb, input.mongodb_cluster

Install Categraf and enable the plugins you need. Each config goes in its own conf/input.<plugin>/ directory; fill in addresses and credentials, then restart Categraf. conf/input.mongodb/mongodb.toml [[instances]] # log level, enum: panic, fatal, error, warn, warning, info, debug, trace, defaults to info. log_level = "info" # append some const labels to metrics # NOTICE! the instance label is required for dashboards labels = { instance="mongo-cluster-01" } # mongodb dsn, see https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/connection-string/ # mongodb_uri = "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017" mongodb_uri = "" # if you don't specify the username or password in the mongodb_uri, you can set here. # This will overwrite the dsn, it would be helpful when special characters existing in the username or password and you don't want to encode them. # NOTICE! this user must be granted enough rights to query needed stats, see ../inputs/mongodb/README.md # username = "<username>" # password = "<password>" # if set to true, use the direct connection way # direct_connect = true # collect all means you collect all the metrics, if set, all below enable_xxx flags in this section will be ignored collect_all = true # if set to true, collect databases metrics # enable_db_stats = true # if set to true, collect getDiagnosticData metrics # enable_diagnostic_data = true # if set to true, collect replSetGetStatus metrics # enable_replicaset_status = true # if set to true, collect top metrics by admin command # enable_top_metrics = true # if set to true, collect index metrics. interval_times = 1 # log_level = "error" # append some labels to metrics # labels = { instance="mongo-cluster-02" } # mongodb_uri = "mongodb://username:password@127.0.0.1:27017" # collect_all = true # The mtail input turns logs into metrics. Input is a log file, output is a set of counters, gauges and histograms defined in mtail syntax; underneath it is Go regular expressions plus expression evaluation. It suits cases such as status-code distribution from Nginx access logs or error counts from application logs, with no need to ship the logs into Elasticsearch or Loki first. Each [[instances]] block points at a set of progs (mtail program files or a directory) and the log paths to follow. Give different instances different progs, or distinguish them with labels, or their metrics will collide.

The MySQL input is straightforward: it connects to the instance, runs SHOW GLOBAL STATUS, SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES, SHOW SLAVE STATUS and friends, and turns the results into metrics. Basic status and replication are collected by default; extended InnoDB metrics, the processlist and schema and table sizes are opt-in. Custom SQL can also be turned into metrics. The bundled rules cover the incidents that actually happen: slow queries piling up, connections approaching max_connections, too many threads running, replica IO or SQL thread stopped, replication lag, unexpected restarts and open files near the limit, each with runbook steps. The dashboards come in three flavours for local collection, remote multi-instance by address, and by instance label, plus a set written for mysqld_exporter metric names. Grant the monitoring account PROCESS, REPLICATION CLIENT and SELECT; do not use root.

The net_response input opens a TCP connection or exchanges a UDP packet with each host:port in targets, optionally sending a payload and matching the reply against expect. The outcome is reported as net_response_result_code: 0 success, 1 timeout, 2 connection failed, 3 read failed, 4 response mismatch, along with the connect time. It answers "can this port be reached from here right now", which is a different question from process liveness or ping reachability. The rules cover unreachable ports and probes taking too long.
2 dashboards, 3 panels in total 1 alert rule, each with runbook steps 2 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.net_response

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.net_response/net_response.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. For TCP, they are ## optional. S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: net_response_result_code != 0 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with nc -vz <target> <port> or telnet <target> <port>; On the target host run ss -lntp | grep <port> to confirm a process is listening; If it is listening, check the firewall, security groups and whether it is bound only to 127.0.0.1; If nothing is listening, start the service through its own procedure and confirm the upstream load balancer has taken it out of rotation.

Nginx can be monitored at three levels. The built-in stub_status module reports active connections, accepts, handled, requests and reading/writing/waiting counts, enough for liveness and traffic trends. The VTS module (nginx-module-vts) breaks requests, status codes, response time and traffic down by server zone and upstream, which is the recommended path; scrape its /status/format/prometheus with the Categraf prometheus input. The third is the nginx_upstream_check input, which reads the results of the upstream_check module. The three dashboards map to stub_status, upstream health checks and VTS. The rules cover Nginx being unreachable, active connections spiking and upstream nodes marked down.
3 dashboards, 24 panels in total 3 alert rules, each with runbook steps 7 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.nginx, input.nginx_upstream_check

3 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: nginx_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status nginx or ps -ef | grep nginx to confirm the master process is alive; If it is alive, run curl -s http://127.0.0.1/nginx_status to verify by hand whether stub_status is blocked by allow/deny rules or a firewall; If it is not running, validate the config with nginx -t before systemctl start nginx, and read the tail of error_log for the exit reason; Confirm the upstream VIP or load balancer has taken this node out of rotation so traffic stops flowing to it.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: increase(nginx_accepts[5m]) - increase(nginx_handled[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Check error_log for worker_connections are not enough or too many open files; Estimate the connection ceiling as worker_processes × worker_connections, compare it with the current nginx_active level, and raise worker_connections; Raise worker_rlimit_nofile and the systemd LimitNOFILE to match; Run nginx -s reload and confirm the gap between accepts and handled stops growing.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: nginx_upstream_check_status_code == 2 Runbook: Take upstream and name (the backend address) from the alert labels and run curl -sv http://<backend address>/ on the Nginx host to confirm it is genuinely unreachable; If it is unreachable, log in to that backend host and confirm the application process and port are alive; If the backend is healthy, check the network and security groups between Nginx and the backend, and whether the probe path in the check directive matches the backend's health check endpoint; Run curl http://<nginx>/status?format=json to see how many nodes are left in the same upstream, and scale out immediately if only one remains.

The NSQ input is ported from Telegraf and reads the /stats HTTP endpoint of nsqd: message counts and depth per topic, depth, in-flight, deferred, requeue and timeout counters per channel, and ready and in-flight state per client connection. The rules cover channel depth growing steadily, rising timeouts and requeues, channels without consumers and nsqd being unreachable.
5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.nsq

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.nsq/nsq.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.nsq started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 # [[instances]] ## The Nsq API URI used to collect statistical information. # targets = ["http://localhost:4151"] # headers={Authorization="", X-Forwarded-For="", Host=""} # timeout="5s" # # basic auth # username="" # password="" ## append some labels for series # labels = { product="nsq" } ## interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 Open the integration center in Nightingale, find NSQ, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: nsq_channel_depth > 10000 Runbook: Take topic and channel from the alert labels and run curl -s http://<nsqd>:4151/stats?format=json to inspect client_count and in_flight_count for that channel; If client_count looks normal but in_flight stays at its ceiling, individual messages are slow to process; go to the consumer application logs and tracing to find the slow step; If the processing logic itself is slow, scale out consumer instances or raise max_in_flight on the consumer; If the backlog came from a one-off traffic spike, you may run curl -X POST 'http://<nsqd>:4151/channel/empty?topic=..&channel=..' after evaluating the impact, but note this drops messages and must be confirmed with the business first.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: nsq_channel_backend_depth > 0 Runbook: Run curl -s http://<nsqd>:4151/stats?format=json and compare depth with backend_depth to size the spill; The root cause is usually still slow consumption, so scale out consumers or optimise consumption logic as for a backlog; Check the free space on the disk holding the nsqd data directory (--data-path) with df -h so it cannot fill up; For an expected short spike you can raise --mem-queue-size to buy memory buffering, but re-check the nsqd process memory ceiling at the same time.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: nsq_channel_client_count == 0 and nsq_channel_depth > 0 Runbook: Take topic and channel from the alert labels and confirm whether the consuming service has been fully taken offline or has crashed; If the consumer is running, check its connections to nsqlookupd/nsqd (netstat -anp | grep 4150) and look for connection errors in the consumer logs; If a release changed the channel name and left the old channel orphaned, confirm it is unused and delete it with curl -X POST 'http://<nsqd>:4151/channel/delete?topic=..&channel=..'; If the consumer does need to come back, start it and watch depth begin to fall.
documents.s: NSQ channel has no consumer but has a backlog

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(nsq_channel_timeout_count[5m]) > 1 Runbook: Take topic and channel from the alert labels and look in the consumer application logs for handlers exceeding msg-timeout; If processing genuinely needs longer, call Touch() periodically on long tasks in the consumer, or raise --msg-timeout on nsqd; If a slow downstream dependency (database, third-party API) is dragging processing down, fix the dependency first and add timeouts and circuit breaking in the consumer; Make sure the business logic is idempotent, otherwise redelivery will cause duplicate writes.

S3 Info · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(nsq_channel_requeue_count[5m]) > 10 Runbook: Aggregate the failure reasons from the consumer logs and separate business validation failures (which should not be retried) from dependency flapping (which should); Validation failures should be FIN-ed and written to a dead-letter store rather than requeued forever; For dependency flapping, check that retry backoff is configured sensibly, since fixed-interval retries create storms; Read this together with nsq_channel_timeout_count: if both are high the consumer is simply overloaded and needs to be scaled out first.

There are two collection paths for NVIDIA GPUs. The nvidia_smi input runs the local nvidia-smi command and parses its output, so nothing else needs installing; utilization, memory, temperature, power and clocks are all there, and remote hosts can be reached over SSH. The dcgm input talks to NVIDIA DCGM for finer metrics such as SM activity, NVLink traffic and XID errors, but needs the with-cgo-plugin build of Categraf and DCGM on the host. The dashboards are written for each metric family: a fleet overview, per-card detail and a per-job view. The rules watch for full memory and high temperature.
3 dashboards, 66 panels in total 2 alert rules, each with runbook steps 38 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.dcgm, input.nvidia_smi

Install Categraf and enable the plugins you need. Each config goes in its own conf/input.<plugin>/ directory; fill in addresses and credentials, then restart Categraf. conf/input.dcgm/dcgm.toml [[instances]] # 指定使用的指标定义文件, 一般使用 default-counters.csv就够了，也可以尝试用其他两个csv文件 # path to the file, that contains the DCGM fields to collect collectors = "conf/input.dcgm/default-counters.csv" # 是否是K8s环境，设置为true会附件Pod的信息 # Enable kubernetes mapping metrics to kubernetes pods # kubernetes=false # 指标中是否附加 gpu id 作为一个标签 # Choose Type of GPU ID to use to map kubernetes resources to pods. Possible values: "uid", "device-name" # kubernetes-gpu-id-type = "uid" # 是否使用 1.x 的ns # Use old 1.x namespace # use-old-namespace = false # 支持的选项是f g i # f: FlexKey 如果MIG被禁用，则监控所有GPU；如果MIG被启用，则监控所有GPU实例 # g: MajorKey 监控top-level entities：GPU或NvSwitches或CPU # i: MinorKey 监控sub-level entities: GPU实例/NvLinks/CPU核心 - 如果MIG被禁用，则不能指定该选项 cpu-devices = "f" # 与cpu-devices的选项一样 # gpu devices devices = "f" # 与cpu-devices的选项一样 switch-devices = "f" # 使用ConfigMap # ConfigMap <NAMESPACE>:<NAME> for metric data configmap-data = "none" # 这里就是前置依赖的nvidia-dcgm服务, 如果是本机采集，则使用localhost:5555 ,如果是远程采集，则使用远端IP:5555 # Connect to remote hostengine at <HOST>:<PORT> remote-hostengine-info = "localhost:5555" # 允许用户在没有实际GPU硬件的环境中模拟GPU, 仅用于测试 # Accept GPUs that are fake, for testing purposes only # fake-gpus = false # 将GPU型号名称中的每个空格替换为破折号，确保标识符连续且无空格。 # Replaces every blank space in the GPU model name with a dash, ensuring a continuous, space-free identifier. # replace-blanks-in-model-name = false conf/input.nvidia_smi/nvidia_smi.toml # # collect interval # interval = 15 # exec local command # e.g. nvidia_smi_command = "nvidia-smi" nvidia_smi_command = "" # exec remote command # nvidia_smi_command = "ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null SSH_USER@SSH_HOST nvidia-smi" # Comma-separated list of the query fields. # You can find out possible fields by running `nvidia-smi --help-query-gpu`. # The value `AUTO` will automatically detect the fields to query. query_field_names = "AUTO" Open the integration center in Nightingale, find NVIDIA, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

XID error code reference: https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/xid-errors/analyzing-xid-catalog.html S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 32 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 38 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 48 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 61 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 62 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 63 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 64 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 68 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 74 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 79 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 92 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 94 or DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS == 95 Runbook: Run nvidia-smi -q -d PAGE_RETIREMENT,ECC and dmesg -T | grep -i xid to identify the exact XID code and the affected card; Compare against the NVIDIA XID documentation to tell a software (driver/CUDA) problem from a hardware fault; Xid 48/63/64 (ECC) and 79 (fallen off the bus) are effectively hardware faults — remove that card from the scheduling pool first (taint the node on Kubernetes); For software issues upgrade the driver/CUDA and retest; for hardware, start the RMA process.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: sum by (Hostname, modelName, gpu) (DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 85) Runbook: Run nvidia-smi -q -d TEMPERATURE,PERFORMANCE to check the current temperature and whether SW/HW Slowdown has already triggered; Check chassis airflow, fan speeds and dust in the filters, and confirm the room intake temperature is normal; On multi-GPU machines check whether every card is hot — a single hot card usually means a heatsink contact or fan problem; Short term, use nvidia-smi -pl to lower the power cap or reduce job concurrency to buy time for a dust-clean.

38 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Metric Meaning Unit DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL GPU Utilization — Indicates GPU utilization, which refers to the time that one or more kernel functions are in the Active state within a cycle (1s or 1/6s, depending on the GPU product). This metric can only show the GPU resources used by kernel functions, but cannot display the specific usage details. % DCGM_FI_DEV_MEM_COPY_UTIL Memory Bandwidth Utilization — Indicates memory bandwidth utilization. For example, the maximum memory bandwidth of NVIDIA GPU V100 is 900 GB/sec; if the current memory bandwidth is 450 GB/sec, the memory bandwidth utilization is 50%. % DCGM_FI_DEV_ENC_UTIL Encoder Utilization — Indicates encoder utilization. % DCGM_FI_DEV_DEC_UTIL Decoder Utilization — Indicates decoder utilization. % DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_FREE Free Framebuffer Memory — Indicates the free amount of Framebuffer Memory. Note: Framebuffer Memory is generally also referred to as video memory. MiB DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED Used Framebuffer Memory — Indicates the used amount of Framebuffer Memory. This value corresponds to the used value of Memory-Usage in the nvidia-smi command. MiB DCGM_FI_PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE Graphics/Compute Engine Active Time Ratio — Indicates the proportion of time that the Graphics or Compute engine is in the Active state within a time interval. This value represents the average of all Graphics and Compute engines. A Graphics or Compute engine is in the Active state when the Graphics or Compute Context is bound to a thread and the Graphics or Compute Context is in the Busy state. % DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE SM Active Time Ratio — Indicates the proportion of time that at least one warp is in the Active state on a Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) within a time interval. This value represents the average of all SMs and is not sensitive to the number of threads per block. A warp is in the Active state when it is scheduled and allocated resources, which may be in the Computing state or non-Computing state (e.g., waiting for a memory request). A value less than 0.5 indicates inefficient GPU utilization, and a value greater than 0.8 is necessary. Assume a GPU has N SMs: if a kernel function runs N thread blocks on all SMs for the entire time interval, the value is 1 (100%). If a kernel function runs N/5 thread blocks within a time interval, the value is 0.2. If a kernel function uses N thread blocks but only runs for 1/5 of the cycle within a time interval, the value is 0.2. % DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_OCCUPANCY SM Warp Occupancy — Indicates the ratio of warps resident on an SM to the maximum number of warps that can reside on the SM within a time interval. This value represents the average of all SMs over a time interval. A higher occupancy does not mean a higher GPU utilization rate. Only in the case of workloads limited by GPU memory bandwidth (DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE), a higher occupancy indicates a more effective GPU utilization rate. % DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE Tensor Pipe Active Cycle Ratio — Indicates the fraction of cycles that the Tensor (HMMA/IMMA) Pipe is in the Active state. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. A higher value indicates higher utilization of Tensor Cores. A value of 1 (100%) means a Tensor instruction is issued every other instruction cycle throughout the time interval (one instruction is completed in two cycles). Assuming the value is 0.2 (20%), possible scenarios include: 20% of the SMs' Tensor Cores run at 100% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' Tensor Cores run at 20% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' Tensor Cores run at 100% utilization for 1/5 of the time interval; other combination modes. % DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_FP64_ACTIVE FP64 Pipe Active Cycle Ratio — Indicates the fraction of cycles that the FP64 (Double Precision) Pipe is in the Active state. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. A higher value indicates higher utilization of FP64 Cores. A value of 1 (100%) means an FP64 instruction is executed every four cycles (taking Volta-type cards as an example) throughout the time interval. Assuming the value is 0.2 (20%), possible scenarios include: 20% of the SMs' FP64 Cores run at 100% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' FP64 Cores run at 20% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' FP64 Cores run at 100% utilization for 1/5 of the time interval; other combination modes. % DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_FP32_ACTIVE FP32 Pipe Active Cycle Ratio — Indicates the fraction of cycles that the Fused Multiply-Add (FMA) pipe is in the Active state, where FMA operations include FP32 (Single Precision) and integers. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. A higher value indicates higher utilization of FP32 Cores. A value of 1 (100%) means an FP32 instruction is executed every two cycles (taking Volta-type cards as an example) throughout the time interval. Assuming the value is 0.2 (20%), possible scenarios include: 20% of the SMs' FP32 Cores run at 100% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' FP32 Cores run at 20% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' FP32 Cores run at 100% utilization for 1/5 of the time interval; other combination modes. % DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_FP16_ACTIVE FP16 Pipe Active Cycle Ratio — Indicates the fraction of cycles that the FP16 (Half Precision) pipe is in the Active state. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. A higher value indicates higher utilization of FP16 Cores. A value of 1 (100%) means an FP16 instruction is executed every two cycles (taking Volta-type cards as an example) throughout the time interval. Assuming the value is 0.2 (20%), possible scenarios include: 20% of the SMs' FP16 Cores run at 100% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' FP16 Cores run at 20% utilization throughout the time interval; 100% of the SMs' FP16 Cores run at 100% utilization for 1/5 of the time interval; other combination modes. % DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE DRAM Active Cycle Ratio — Indicates the fraction of cycles for memory bandwidth utilization (Memory BW Utilization) to send data to or receive data from device memory. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. A higher value indicates higher utilization of device memory. A value of 1 (100%) means a DRAM instruction is executed in each cycle throughout the time interval (in practice, a peak of about 0.8 (80%) is the maximum achievable value). Assuming the value is 0.2 (20%), it means 20% of the cycles are used to read or write device memory within the time interval. % DCGM_FI_PROF_PCIE_TX_BYTES PCIe Transmit Data Rate — Indicates the data rate transmitted over the PCIe bus, including protocol headers and data payloads. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. The rate is averaged over the time interval. For example, if 1 GB of data is transmitted in 1 second, the rate is 1 GB/s regardless of whether the data is transmitted at a constant rate or in bursts. The theoretical maximum PCIe Gen3 bandwidth is 985 MB/s per lane. B/s DCGM_FI_PROF_PCIE_RX_BYTES PCIe Receive Data Rate — Indicates the data rate received over the PCIe bus, including protocol headers and data payloads. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. The rate is averaged over the time interval. For example, if 1 GB of data is transmitted in 1 second, the rate is 1 GB/s regardless of whether the data is transmitted at a constant rate or in bursts. The theoretical maximum PCIe Gen3 bandwidth is 985 MB/s per lane. B/s DCGM_FI_PROF_NVLINK_RX_BYTES NVLink Receive Data Rate — Indicates the data rate received over NVLink, excluding protocol headers. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. The rate is averaged over the time interval. For example, if 1 GB of data is transmitted in 1 second, the rate is 1 GB/s regardless of whether the data is transmitted at a constant rate or in bursts. Theoretically, the maximum NVLink Gen2 bandwidth is 25 GB/s per link in each direction. B/s DCGM_FI_PROF_NVLINK_TX_BYTES NVLink Transmit Data Rate — Indicates the data rate transmitted over NVLink, excluding protocol headers. This value represents the average over a time interval, not an instantaneous value. The rate is averaged over the time interval. For example, if 1 GB of data is transmitted in 1 second, the rate is 1 GB/s regardless of whether the data is transmitted at a constant rate or in bursts. Theoretically, the maximum NVLink Gen2 bandwidth is 25 GB/s per link in each direction. B/s DCGM_FI_DEV_SM_CLOCK SM Clock Frequency — Indicates the SM clock frequency. MHz DCGM_FI_DEV_MEM_CLOCK Memory Clock Frequency — Indicates the memory clock frequency. MHz DCGM_FI_DEV_APP_SM_CLOCK SM Application Clock Frequency — Indicates the SM application clock frequency. MHz DCGM_FI_DEV_APP_MEM_CLOCK Memory Application Clock Frequency — Indicates the memory application clock frequency. MHz DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCK_THROTTLE_REASONS Clock Throttle Reasons — Indicates the reasons for the clock slowing down. MHz DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS XID Error Number — Indicates the last XID error number that occurred over a period of time. DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_VIOLATION Power Violation Duration — Indicates violations caused by power caps, and this value is the duration of the violation. μs DCGM_FI_DEV_THERMAL_VIOLATION Thermal Violation Duration — Indicates violations caused by thermal limits, and this value is the duration of the violation. μs DCGM_FI_DEV_SYNC_BOOST_VIOLATION Sync Boost Violation Duration — Indicates violations caused by sync boost limits, and this value is the duration of the violation. μs DCGM_FI_DEV_BOARD_LIMIT_VIOLATION Board Limit Violation Duration — Indicates violations caused by board limits, and this value is the duration of the violation. μs DCGM_FI_DEV_LOW_UTIL_VIOLATION Low Utilization Violation Duration — Indicates violations caused by low utilization limits, and this value is the duration of the violation. μs DCGM_FI_DEV_RELIABILITY_VIOLATION Board Reliability Violation Duration — Indicates violations caused by board reliability limits, and this value is the duration of the violation. μs DCGM_FI_DEV_BAR1_USED Used BAR1 Memory — Indicates the used amount of BAR1. MB DCGM_FI_DEV_BAR1_FREE Free BAR1 Memory — Indicates the free amount of BAR1. MB DCGM_FI_DEV_MEMORY_TEMP Memory Temperature — Indicates the memory temperature. °C DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP GPU Temperature — Indicates the GPU temperature. °C DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE GPU Power Usage — Indicates the power consumption. W DCGM_FI_DEV_TOTAL_ENERGY_CONSUMPTION Total Energy Consumption — Indicates the total energy consumed since the driver was loaded. J DCGM_FI_DEV_RETIRED_SBE Retired Pages due to Single-bit Errors — Indicates the pages retired due to single-bit errors. DCGM_FI_DEV_RETIRED_DBE Retired Pages due to Double-bit Errors — Indicates the pages retired due to double-bit errors.

The OpenStack input calls each service's API with a read-capable account: Nova instances, hypervisors and quotas; Neutron networks, subnets, ports, floating IPs and security groups; Cinder volumes and snapshots; Glance images; Keystone projects and users; Heat stacks. Every instance's state, project and flavor is reported as a metric too. Required API versions: blockstorage v3, compute v2, identity v3, networking v2. The rules cover instances entering ERROR, hypervisor resources near the limit, exhausted quotas and service APIs being unreachable.
5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.openstack
