Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: openstack_neutron_agent_alive == 0 Runbook: Take agent_host and agent_type from the alert labels and confirm the state with openstack network agent list; Log in to that node and run systemctl status neutron-openvswitch-agent (or the matching agent) to check the process and logs; If the process is alive but the heartbeat has timed out, check connectivity from that node to the message queue (RabbitMQ); agent heartbeats travel over RPC, so an unreachable MQ is the most common cause; After recovery run openstack network agent list to confirm alive is True and spot-check networking on one VM on that node.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: openstack_nova_service_forced_down == 1 Runbook: Take host_machine and name from the alert labels and confirm the state with openstack compute service list; Check the change record to determine whether this is planned maintenance; If unplanned, log in to the compute node and check the nova-compute process and connectivity to the MQ and database; Once the node is confirmed healthy, clear the flag with nova service-force-down <host> nova-compute --unset and verify VM scheduling works again.

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: openstack_hypervisor_vcpus_used / (openstack_hypervisor_vcpus > 0) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Take hypervisor_hostname from the alert labels and run openstack hypervisor show <host> to confirm vcpus_used and vcpus; Read it together with cpu_allocation_ratio to see whether overcommit headroom remains; at the default 16:1 ratio the vcpus value is already the post-overcommit figure; If idle VMs sit on this node, clean them up or migrate them with openstack server migrate; If the whole cluster is short on headroom, add compute nodes, and first confirm the scheduler filters are not concentrating load on a few nodes.

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: openstack_hypervisor_memory_mb_used / (openstack_hypervisor_memory_mb > 0) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Take hypervisor_hostname from the alert labels and run openstack hypervisor show <host> to compare memory_mb_used with memory_mb; Log in to the node and compare with free -g; high allocation but low real usage means VM flavors are oversized and the business can be pushed to right-size them; To free capacity, migrate some instances to idle nodes with openstack server migrate; If the cluster as a whole is tight, add compute nodes and double-check that ram_allocation_ratio has not been set above 1 by mistake.

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: openstack_hypervisor_local_gb_used / (openstack_hypervisor_local_gb > 0) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Take hypervisor_hostname from the alert labels, log in to the node, and run df -h plus du -sh /var/lib/nova/instances/* | sort -rh | head to find the biggest consumers; Clean up leftover directories from deleted instances and old base image caches (they accumulate indefinitely when nova's image cache manager is disabled); To free capacity, migrate instances to other nodes or switch root disks to Cinder volume boot; Longer term give /var/lib/nova/instances its own volume with a capacity alert.

The Oracle input connects to the instance and runs the queries defined in metric.toml: session counts, active sessions, tablespace usage, wait events, SGA and PGA, cache hit ratios, archive logs and more. Every query can be edited or extended. Connection settings and query definitions live in separate files so they can be trimmed per version and environment. The input does not run on Windows itself, but a Categraf on Linux can connect to an Oracle instance hosted on Windows. The monitoring account needs CREATE SESSION and SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE; if a query fails with ORA-00942 or ORA-01031, grant read access on that view rather than switching to an application account.
1 dashboard, 26 panels in total 5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.oracle

Install Categraf and enable the plugins you need. Each config goes in its own conf/input.<plugin>/ directory; fill in addresses and credentials, then restart Categraf. conf/input.oracle/metric.toml [[metrics]] mesurement = "sessions" label_fields = [ "status", "type" ] metric_fields = [ "value" ] timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT status, type, COUNT(*) as value FROM v$session GROUP BY status, type ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "lock" metric_fields = [ "cnt" ] timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM ALL_OBJECTS A, V$LOCKED_OBJECT B, SYS.GV_$SESSION C WHERE A.OBJECT_ID = B.OBJECT_ID AND B.PROCESS = C.PROCESS ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "slow_queries" metric_fields = [ "p95_time_usecs", "p99_time_usecs" ] timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT percentile_disc(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY elapsed_time) AS p95_time_usecs, percentile_disc(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY elapsed_time) AS p99_time_usecs FROM v$sql WHERE last_active_time >= sysdate - 5/(24*60) ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "resource" label_fields = [ "resource_name" ] metric_fields = [ "current_utilization", "limit_value" ] timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT resource_name, current_utilization, CASE WHEN TRIM(limit_value) = 'UNLIMITED' THEN '-1' ELSE TRIM(limit_value) END AS limit_value FROM v$resource_limit ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "asm_diskgroup" label_fields = [ "name" ] metric_fields = [ "total", "free" ] timeout = "3s" ignore_zero_result = true request = ''' SELECT name, total_mb * 1024 * 1024 AS total, free_mb * 1024 * 1024 AS free FROM v$asm_diskgroup_stat WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM v$datafile WHERE name LIKE '+%') ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "activity" metric_fields = [ "value" ] field_to_append = "name" timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT name, value FROM v$sysstat WHERE name IN ('parse count (total)', 'execute count', 'user commits', 'user rollbacks') ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "process" metric_fields = [ "count" ] timeout = "3s" request = "SELECT COUNT(*) AS count FROM v$process" [[metrics]] mesurement = "wait_time" metric_fields = [ "value" ] label_fields = [ "wait_class" ] timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT n.wait_class AS wait_class, ROUND(m.time_waited / m.INTSIZE_CSEC, 3) AS value FROM v$waitclassmetric m, v$system_wait_class n WHERE m.wait_class_id = n.wait_class_id AND n.wait_class != 'Idle' ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "tablespace" label_fields = [ "tablespace", "type" ] metric_fields = [ "bytes", "max_bytes", "free" ] timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT dt.tablespace_name AS tablespace, dt.contents AS type, dt.block_size * dtum.used_space AS bytes, dt.block_size * dtum.tablespace_size AS max_bytes, dt.block_size * (dtum.tablespace_size - dtum.used_space) AS free FROM dba_tablespace_usage_metrics dtum, dba_tablespaces dt WHERE dtum.tablespace_name = dt.tablespace_name ORDER BY tablespace ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "sysmetric" metric_fields = [ "value" ] field_to_append = "metric_name" timeout = "3s" request = ''' SELECT metric_name, value FROM v$sysmetric WHERE group_id = 2 ''' [[metrics]] mesurement = "applylag" metric_fields = [ "value" ] timeout = "3s" ignore_zero_result = true request = ''' SELECT ROUND( EXTRACT(DAY FROM TO_DSINTERVAL(value)) * 86400 + EXTRACT(HOUR FROM TO_DSINTERVAL(value)) * 3600 + EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM TO_DSINTERVAL(value)) * 60 + EXTRACT(SECOND FROM TO_DSINTERVAL(value)) ) AS value FROM v$dataguard_stats WHERE name = 'apply lag' ''' conf/input.oracle/oracle.toml # # collect interval # interval = 15 #[[instances]] # address = "10.1.2.3:1521/orcl" # username = "monitor" # password = "<password>" # is_sys_dba = false # is_sys_oper = false # disable_connection_pool = false # max_open_connections = 5 # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # labels = { region="cloud" } # [[instances.metrics]] # mesurement = "sessions" # label_fields = [ "status", "type" ] # metric_fields = [ "value" ] # timeout = "3s" # request = ''' # SELECT status, type, COUNT(*) as value FROM v$session GROUP BY status, type # ''' # [[instances]] # address = "192.168.10.10:1521/orcl" # username = "monitor" # password = "<password>" # is_sys_dba = false # is_sys_oper = false # disable_connection_pool = false # max_open_connections = 5 # # labels = { region="local" } Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Oracle, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Dashboard Panels Oracle by categraf 26
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

Job:{{$labels.job}};Address:{{$labels.address}};Region:{{$labels.region}}; S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: oracle_archivelog_count>100 Runbook: Run SELECT * FROM V$RECOVERY_FILE_DEST to check the FRA quota and used space; Use RMAN's crosscheck archivelog all; delete expired archivelog all; to clear already-backed-up archives; Confirm the archive backup job is running — a pile-up of archives is usually caused by failed backups; Longer term, raise db_recovery_file_dest_size or move the archive destination to larger storage.

Job:{{$labels.job}};Address:{{$labels.address}};Region:{{$labels.region}}; S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: oracle_process_count > 500 oracle_process_count > 800 Runbook: Compare SELECT COUNT(*) FROM V$PROCESS against SHOW PARAMETER processes to see the current level versus the limit; Run SELECT machine, program, COUNT(*) FROM V$SESSION GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC to find the application with an abnormal connection count; Tell business growth apart from an application connection pool leak (many INACTIVE sessions piling up); As an emergency measure raise the processes parameter (requires an instance restart); for the root cause, cap the application connection pool.

Job:{{$labels.job}};Address:{{$labels.address}};Region:{{$labels.region}}; S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: sum by (instance) (oracle_sessions_value{status='ACTIVE',type='USER'}) > 100 Runbook: Run SELECT sid, serial#, sql_id, event, seconds_in_wait FROM V$SESSION WHERE status='ACTIVE' AND type='USER' ORDER BY seconds_in_wait DESC to see what the active sessions are waiting on; If the wait events cluster on one type (such as enq: TX - row lock contention) there is lock contention — follow blocking_session to the source; Use the sql_id against V$SQL to find the slow statement, and ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION to stop the bleeding if needed; Once located, add indexes or rewrite the SQL, and check upstream for a traffic spike.

S1 Critical · for 90s · Trigger: oracle_up != 1 Runbook: Log in to the host and check the pmon process and listener state (ps -ef | grep pmon, lsnrctl status); If they are alive, connect by hand with sqlplus to tell a hung instance from a listener or account problem; If not running, read the tail of alert_<SID>.log to identify the cause (ORA-00600, full FRA, full disk) before starting it; If Data Guard is in place, immediately assess whether to fail over.

documents.t: Job:{{$labels.job}};Address:{{$labels.address}};Tablespace:{{$labels.tablespace}};Region:{{$labels.region}}; S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: oracle_tablespace_bytes/oracle_tablespace_max_bytes*100>95 Runbook: Use SELECT tablespace_name, bytes/1024/1024 mb FROM DBA_DATA_FILES together with DBA_FREE_SPACE to identify the tablespace and whether the data file has reached its maximum; Expand it: ALTER DATABASE DATAFILE '<path>' RESIZE <larger value>, or ADD DATAFILE; Check whether large tables or historical data can be archived and deleted — after deletion you still need shrink or move to actually release space; Check whether the data file has AUTOEXTEND enabled and what its MAXSIZE is.

The PHP-FPM input is adapted from Telegraf's phpfpm plugin and reads the pool status page: accepted connections, listen queue length and maximum, idle and active processes, total processes, how often max_children was reached and the slow request count. These are the direct indicators of a saturated PHP application. Enable pm.status_path = /status in php-fpm.conf or the pool config. Over HTTP the input supports timeouts, Basic Auth, custom headers and TLS; over a Unix socket, Categraf must run on the same host with read access to the socket. The rules cover a full process pool, listen queue backlog, rising slow requests and FPM being unreachable.
5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.phpfpm

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.phpfpm/phpfpm.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.phpfpm started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] ## An array of Nginx stub_status URI to gather stats. urls = [ ## HTTP: the URL must start with http:// or https://, ie: # "http://localhost/status", # "https://www.baidu.com/phpfpm-status", ## fcgi: the URL must start with fcgi:// or cgi://, and port must be present, ie: # "fcgi://127.0.0.1:9001", # "cgi://192.168.0.1:9000/status", ## Unix socket: path to fpm socket, ie: # "/run/php/php7.2-fpm.sock", ## or using a custom fpm status path: # "/var/run/php5-fpm.sock:/fpm-custom-status-path", ## glob patterns are also supported: # "/var/run/php*.sock" ] ## append some labels for series # labels = { region="cloud", product="n9e" } ## interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 ## Set response_timeout (default 5 seconds),HTTP urls only response_timeout = "5s" ## Whether to follow redirects from the server (defaults to false),HTTP urls only # follow_redirects = false ## Optional HTTP Basic Auth Credentials,HTTP urls only #username = "admin" #password = "admin" ## Optional headers,HTTP urls only # headers = ["X-From", "categraf", "X-Xyz", "abc"] ## Optional TLS Config,only http # use_tls = false # tls_ca = "/etc/categraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/categraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/categraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = false Open the integration center in Nightingale, find PHP, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(phpfpm_max_children_reached[10m]) > 0 Runbook: Take pool from the alert labels and run grep -i 'server reached pm.max_children' /var/log/php-fpm.log to see how often this happens; Compute the average per-process memory with ps --no-headers -o rss -C php-fpm | awk '{s+=$1} END {print s/NR/1024" MB"}', then derive a safe max_children from available memory divided by that figure; Raise pm.max_children to the computed value and run systemctl reload php-fpm; do not raise it blindly or you will trigger an OOM; If per-process memory or duration is abnormal, use the slowlog to find the slow scripts and reduce concurrency demand at the source.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: phpfpm_listen_queue / (phpfpm_listen_queue_len > 0) * 100 > 30 Runbook: Take pool from the alert labels and run curl -s http://127.0.0.1/status?full to see each worker's state and the URI it is serving; Many workers stuck on the same URI means that endpoint has slowed down; use the slowlog and application logs to locate it (database slow queries and external API timeouts are the usual causes); In the short term raise pm.max_children to add concurrency, after confirming there is enough memory; If the queue itself is too small (listen.backlog defaults to 511), raise it for your concurrency level and raise the kernel's net.core.somaxconn to match.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: phpfpm_idle_processes == 0 Runbook: Run curl -s http://127.0.0.1/status?full and watch the request duration of each worker to find processes held by long requests; Decide whether concurrency has grown or a slow script is holding workers: scale out or raise pm.max_children for the former, fix the script for the latter; With pm=dynamic, check whether pm.start_servers and pm.min_spare_servers are too low, which prevents new workers being spawned fast enough at peak; For sustained high load, switch to pm=static with a process count computed from memory to avoid fork churn.

S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(phpfpm_slow_requests[10m]) > 5 Runbook: Run tail -100 /var/log/php-fpm/www-slow.log to read the full call stack of the slow requests; the top frame is where they are stuck; Stacks stuck in PDO/mysqli point to the database, so check the slow query log and add indexes; stacks stuck in curl/file_get_contents need timeouts on the external call; Stacks stuck in session_start are usually file-based session lock contention; switch to Redis sessions and call session_write_close early; If request_slowlog_timeout is set too low and creates noise, adjust that parameter instead of ignoring the alert.

S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: phpfpm_start_since < 300 Runbook: First confirm whether this was a planned release or reload; If unplanned, run journalctl -u php-fpm --since '-30min' and tail -200 /var/log/php-fpm.log to find the cause; Run dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to check for an OOM kill, and if so lower pm.max_children based on real per-process memory; For repeated restarts, check whether an extension is segfaulting by ruling out third-party extensions one by one with php -m.

The ping input sends ICMP probes to the addresses in targets and reports packet loss, minimum, average, maximum and standard deviation RTT, and TTL. As long as the targets do not block ping, it is the cheapest liveness check; running one Categraf per site and pinging across sites also gives a picture of link quality. Split targets into several [[instances]] blocks with labels such as region or product; the dashboards and rules filter on them. With many targets, raise the file descriptor limit of the Categraf process. The rules cover unreachable targets and rising packet loss.
2 dashboards, 6 panels in total 1 alert rule, each with runbook steps 6 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.ping

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.ping/ping.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.ping started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] # send ping packets to targets = [ # "www.baidu.com", # "127.0.0.1", # "10.4.5.6", # "10.4.5.7" ] # # append some labels for series # labels = { region="cloud", product="n9e" } # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 ## Number of ping packets to send per interval. Corresponds to the "-c" ## option of the ping command. # count = 1 ## Time to wait between sending ping packets in seconds. Operates like the ## "-i" option of the ping command. # ping_interval = 1.0 ## If set, the time to wait for a ping response in seconds. Operates like ## the "-W" option of the ping command. # timeout = 3.0 ## Interface or source address to send ping from. Operates like the -I or -S ## option of the ping command. # interface = "" ## Use only IPv6 addresses when resolving a hostname. # ipv6 = false ## Number of data bytes to be sent. Corresponds to the "-s" ## option of the ping command. # size = 56 # max concurrency coroutine # concurrency = 50 Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Ping, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: ping_result_code != 0 Runbook: Reproduce it on the collector host with ping -c 5 <target>, then use mtr -n <target> to find which hop drops packets; If the target is alive, check whether it blocks ICMP — many security policies do, in which case this probe does not apply and you should switch to a port probe; For loss at an intermediate hop, involve the network team; Confirm the target host is not down or suffering a NIC failure.

6 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Metric Meaning Unit ping_ttl Ping ttl time — Time To Live refers to the limited time that a packet can "survive" in the network s ping_percent_packet_loss Ping packet loss rate % ping_average_response_ms Ping average time consumed ms ping_result_code Ping probe result status code — A value of 0 is normal, and a non-0 value is abnormal. If the Ping fails, there should be an exception log in the Categraf log ping_maximum_response_ms Ping maximum time consumption ms ping_minimum_response_ms Ping minimum time consumption ms

The PostgreSQL input connects as a client and reads the pg_stat_* monitoring views: connections per database, commits and rollbacks, cache hit ratio, deadlocks, temp files and replication lag. Custom queries can turn numbers from your own tables into metrics as well. A dedicated account with the pg_monitor role is all it needs; only custom queries require extra SELECT grants on the relevant schemas. The rules cover connection exhaustion, long-running transactions, falling cache hit ratio and replication lag.
1 dashboard, 14 panels in total 5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.postgresql

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.postgresql/postgresql.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.postgresql started once the plugin is loaded. # Read metrics from one or many postgresql servers # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] ## specify address via a url matching: ## postgres://[pqgotest[:password]]@localhost[/dbname]?sslmode=[disable|verify-ca|verify-full] ## or a simple string: ## host=localhost user=pqgotest password=... sslmode=... dbname=app_production ## ## All connection parameters are optional. ## ## Without the dbname parameter, the driver will default to a database ## with the same name as the user. This dbname is just for instantiating a ## connection with the server and doesn't restrict the databases we are trying ## to grab metrics for. ## # address = "host=localhost user=postgres sslmode=disable" ## A custom name for the database that will be used as the "server" tag in the ## measurement output. If not specified, a default one generated from ## the connection address is used. # outputaddress = "db01" ## connection configuration. ## maxlifetime - specify the maximum lifetime of a connection. ## default is forever (0s) # max_lifetime = "0s" ## A list of databases to explicitly ignore. If not specified, metrics for all ## databases are gathered. Do NOT use with the 'databases' option. # ignored_databases = ["postgres", "template0", "template1"] ## A list of databases to pull metrics about. If not specified, metrics for all ## databases are gathered. Do NOT use with the 'ignored_databases' option. # databases = ["app_production", "testing"] ## Whether to use prepared statements when connecting to the database. ## This should be set to false when connecting through a PgBouncer instance ## with pool_mode set to transaction. #prepared_statements = true # [[instances.metrics]] # measurement = "sessions" # label_fields = [ "state" ] # metric_fields = [ "value" ] # timeout = "3s" # request = ''' # SELECT COALESCE(state, 'unknown') AS state, # COUNT(*)::double precision AS value # FROM pg_stat_activity # GROUP BY COALESCE(state, 'unknown') # ''' Open the integration center in Nightingale, find PostgreSQL, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels postgresql by categraf 14
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

Time spent reading data files. A high value means memory is insufficient and data files are frequently read from disk S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: rate(postgresql_blk_read_time[5m]) > 100 Runbook: First confirm SHOW track_io_timing is on, otherwise this metric stays at 0 and the rule is meaningless until you enable it; Use pg_stat_statements sorted by shared_blks_read to find the SQL doing the most disk reads, then add indexes or rewrite them; Compare shared_buffers against instance memory — usually about 25% of physical memory; Run iostat -x 1 to confirm whether the disk holding the data directory is saturated.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: postgresql_up!=1 Runbook: Log in to the host and run systemctl status postgresql or docker ps to confirm the process is alive; If it is alive, connect by hand with psql -h <host> -p <port> -U <user> to tell a hung instance apart from a network or pg_hba authentication problem; If it is not running, read the tail of the log under $PGDATA/log to identify the cause (OOM, full disk, full WAL directory) before starting it; If a streaming replica exists, immediately assess whether to promote it (pg_ctl promote).

Time spent writing data files. In PG dirty pages are normally written to the page cache; a high value means the cache is small and the OS cache has to flush more aggressively S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: rate(postgresql_blk_write_time[5m]) > 100 Runbook: First confirm SHOW track_io_timing is on, otherwise this metric stays at 0; Check whether buffers_backend in pg_stat_bgwriter is much larger than buffers_checkpoint — if so, shared_buffers is too small or the bgwriter is too conservative; Raise checkpoint_timeout and checkpoint_completion_target to spread the flushing out and avoid IO spikes; Run iostat -x 1 to confirm whether the disk is saturated, and move to faster storage if needed.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(postgresql_deadlocks[10m]) > 0 Runbook: In postgresql.conf, confirm log_lock_waits=on and a sane deadlock_timeout, then take the full SQL of both sides of the deadlock from the log; Join pg_locks with pg_stat_activity to identify which two tables and which lock modes are waiting on each other; The root cause is usually two transactions updating the same rows in opposite order — enforcing a single locking order in the application removes it; Long transactions amplify deadlocks, so check for transactions that stay open without committing.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: rate(postgresql_blks_hit[5m])*100/(rate(postgresql_blks_hit[5m])+rate(postgresql_blks_read[5m])) < 50 Runbook: First rule out a cold cache after a restart (check the instance uptime); Use pg_stat_statements sorted by shared_blks_read to find the SQL doing the most disk reads, and add indexes to eliminate sequential scans first; Compare shared_buffers against instance memory — 25% of physical memory is the usual target; Check whether a full table scan or a batch job is flushing the cache, and move it off peak hours.

RabbitMQ 3.8 and later ship the rabbitmq_prometheus plugin: run rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_prometheus and /metrics appears on port 15692, which the Categraf prometheus input scrapes. Versions below 3.8 enable rabbitmq_management instead and use the Categraf rabbitmq input against the management API on 15672. The two paths produce different metric names, so the dashboards are split into 3.8+ and 3.8- editions; import the right one. The rules cover message backlog, too many unacked messages, queues without consumers, memory and disk alarms, and nodes going down. The throughput and backlog panels only show data once real exchanges, queues and traffic exist.
4 dashboards, 184 panels in total 6 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.rabbitmq, input.rabbitmq_exporter

Install Categraf and enable the plugins you need. Each config goes in its own conf/input.<plugin>/ directory; fill in addresses and credentials, then restart Categraf. conf/input.rabbitmq/rabbitmq.toml # As of 3.8.0, RabbitMQ ships with built-in Prometheus & Grafana support. # Support for Prometheus metric collector ships in the rabbitmq_prometheus plugin. # The plugin exposes all RabbitMQ metrics on a dedicated TCP port, in Prometheus text format. # # enable prometheus plugin: # `rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_prometheus` # `curl http://localhost:15692/metrics` # # then use categraf prometheus plugin scrape http://localhost:15692/metrics instead of this rabbitmq plugin # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] # # Management Plugin url # url = "http://localhost:15672" # username = "guest" # password = "guest" ## Optional TLS Config # use_tls = false # tls_min_version = "1.2" # tls_ca = "/etc/categraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/categraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/categraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = true ## Optional request timeouts ## ## ResponseHeaderTimeout, if non-zero, specifies the amount of time to wait ## for a server's response headers after fully writing the request. # header_timeout = "3s" ## ## client_timeout specifies a time limit for requests made by this client. ## Includes connection time, any redirects, and reading the response body. # client_timeout = "4s" ## A list of nodes to gather as the rabbitmq_node measurement. If not ## specified, metrics for all nodes are gathered. # nodes = ["rabbit@node1", "rabbit@node2"] ## A list of exchanges to gather as the rabbitmq_exchange measurement. If not ## specified, metrics for all exchanges are gathered. # exchanges = ["categraf"] ## Metrics to include and exclude. Globs accepted. ## Note that an empty array for both will include all metrics ## Currently the following metrics are supported: "exchange", "federation", "node", "overview", "queue" # metric_include = [] # metric_exclude = [] ## Queues to include and exclude. Globs accepted. ## Note that an empty array for both will include all queues # queue_name_include = [] # queue_name_exclude = [] ## Federation upstreams to include and exclude specified as an array of glob ## pattern strings. Federation links can also be limited by the queue and ## exchange filters. # federation_upstream_include = [] # federation_upstream_exclude = [] # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # important! use global unique string to specify instance # labels = { instance="rabbitmq-001" } conf/input.rabbitmq_exporter/rabbitmq_exporter.toml # rabbitmq_exporter 插件，在 categraf 内部集成了 kbudde/rabbitmq_exporter 的采集逻辑， # 走 RabbitMQ Management API（默认 15672 端口），指标名与 kbudde 版 exporter 保持兼容， # 适合原来就在用独立 rabbitmq_exporter 进程、希望看板和告警规则不改的场景。 # # 前置条件：RabbitMQ 开启 management 插件 # rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_management # # rabbit_url 是必填项，保持注释状态时该插件不会启用，填上地址才开始采集。 # # 采集间隔，不配置则沿用 categraf 全局 interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] ## RabbitMQ Management API 地址，必填 # rabbit_url = "http://127.0.0.1:15672" ## Management API 的账号密码，不填默认 guest/guest # rabbit_user = "guest" # rabbit_pass = "guest" ## 连接模式：direct 直连节点，loadbalancer 走负载均衡（前面挂了 LB 时用） # rabbit_connection = "direct" ## 启用哪些 exporter，默认 exchange、node、overview、queue ## 可选：exchange、node、overview、queue、connections、federation、shovel、memory、aliveness ## connections、memory、shovel 基数较高，生产环境按需开启 # enabled_exporters = ["exchange", "node", "overview", "queue"] ## 请求超时时间，单位秒，默认 30 # timeout = 30 ## 正则过滤，控制采集哪些 exchange / queue / vhost # skip_exchanges = "^$" # include_exchanges = ".*" # skip_queues = "^$" # include_queues = ".*" # skip_vhost = "^$" # include_vhost = ".*" ## 队列数超过这个值就跳过队列采集，0 表示不限制，队列特别多时用来兜底 # max_queues = 0 ## 排除上游的指标字段，例如 ["messages_ready", "mem_used"] # exclude_metrics = [] ## 请求能力声明，除非确认 RabbitMQ 只接受 JSON，否则保持默认 # rabbit_capabilities = "no_sort,bert" ## aliveness exporter 探测哪个 vhost # aliveness_vhost = "/" ## Management API 是 https 时按需配置 # use_tls = false # tls_min_version = "1.2" # tls_ca = "/etc/categraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/categraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/categraf/key.pem" ## 跳过证书链和域名校验 # insecure_skip_verify = false ## 采集间隔 = 全局 interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 ## 附加标签，多实例时建议用 instance 区分 # labels = { instance = "rabbitmq-001" } Open the integration center in Nightingale, find RabbitMQ, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. The file descriptors are near to the limit S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: sum (max_over_time(rabbitmq_process_open_fds[5m])) / sum (rabbitmq_process_max_fds) > 0.8 Runbook: On the node, run rabbitmq-diagnostics status and read total_used against total_limit under file_descriptors; Run rabbitmqctl list_connections to check whether the connection count is abnormal and whether clients fail to reuse connections; Raise the limit by changing LimitNOFILE in systemd or the container ulimit, then restart the node (RabbitMQ reads it once at startup); Also cap the client connection pools instead of relying only on a higher limit.

There are a high connection churn S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: ( sum(rate(rabbitmq_connections_closed_total[5m]) ) + sum(rate(rabbitmq_connections_opened_total[5m]) ) )/sum (rabbitmq_connections) > 0.1 unless sum (rabbitmq_connections) < 100 Runbook: Run rabbitmqctl list_connections peer_host user connected_at to see which clients keep reconnecting; Check whether the client opens a new connection for every message — the correct pattern is a reused long-lived connection with one channel per thread; Check whether heartbeat timeouts or network jitter are causing the server to close connections; Confirm no resource alarm (memory/disk watermark) is blocking connections and driving reconnects.

Insufficient established erlang distribution links S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: count(erlang_vm_dist_node_state) < count(rabbitmq_build_info) * (count(rabbitmq_build_info) - 1) Runbook: Run rabbitmq-diagnostics cluster_status on each node and compare the Running Nodes lists to find the unreachable node; Check connectivity on ports 4369 (epmd) and 25672 (distribution) between nodes; Confirm the Erlang cookie is identical across nodes (/var/lib/rabbitmq/.erlang.cookie); If a partition already happened, follow the configured cluster_partition_handling strategy and, if needed, restart the minority nodes so they rejoin.

The predicted free disk space in 24 hours from now is low S2 Warning · for 60 min · Trigger: ( predict_linear(rabbitmq_disk_space_available_bytes[24h], 60*60*24) < rabbitmq_disk_space_available_limit_bytes )and( count_over_time(rabbitmq_disk_space_available_limit_bytes[2h] offset 22h) > 0) Runbook: Run rabbitmq-diagnostics status and read the current disk_free against disk_free_limit; Run rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages message_bytes to find the most backed-up queues and determine whether consumers dropped out or are simply too slow; Restoring consumption to drain the backlog is the most direct fix; Also clean up other large files on that partition or expand the disk so the watermark never actually blocks publishers.

The TCP sockets are near to the limit S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: sum (max_over_time(rabbitmq_process_open_tcp_sockets[5m]))/sum (rabbitmq_process_max_tcp_sockets)> 0.8 Runbook: Run rabbitmq-diagnostics status and read sockets_used against sockets_total; Run rabbitmqctl list_connections grouped by source to find the client with an abnormal connection count; For clients that open a new connection per operation, switch to a long-lived connection with multiple channels; If more connections are genuinely needed, raise the node's file descriptor limit (the socket limit derives from it) and restart the node.

There were unroutable message within the last 5 minutes in RabbitMQ cluster S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: sum (increase(rabbitmq_channel_messages_unroutable_dropped_total[5m])) >= 1 or sum (increase(rabbitmq_channel_messages_unroutable_returned_total[5m])) >= 1 Runbook: Run rabbitmqctl list_exchanges and list_bindings to confirm the target exchange is not missing a binding; Verify the routing key used by the producer matches the binding rules (mind the wildcards for topic exchanges); Configure an alternate-exchange so unroutable messages land in a fallback queue instead of being dropped; Set the mandatory flag on the producer and handle Basic.Return so routing failures surface immediately.

S.M.A.R.T. is the self-monitoring built into hard drives and SSDs. The Categraf smart input runs smartctl (and the nvme tool for NVMe devices) and emits smart_device for overall health plus smart_attribute for individual attributes: reallocated sectors, pending sectors, temperature, power-on hours, SSD wear and more. The bundled rules watch the precursors of data loss: failed health checks, growing reallocated-sector counts and high temperature. The host needs smartmontools installed and Categraf needs permission to run smartctl, usually via passwordless sudo.
1 dashboard, 20 panels in total 6 alert rules, each with runbook steps 14 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.smart

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.smart/smart.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.smart started once the plugin is loaded. # Read metrics from storage devices supporting S.M.A.R.T. [[instances]] ## Optionally specify the path to the smartctl executable # path_smartctl = "/usr/bin/smartctl" ## Optionally specify the path to the nvme-cli executable # path_nvme = "/usr/bin/nvme" ## Optionally specify if vendor specific attributes should be propagated for NVMe disk case ## ["auto-on"] - automatically find and enable additional vendor specific disk info ## ["vendor1", "vendor2", ...] - e.g. "Intel" enable additional Intel specific disk info # enable_extensions = ["auto-on"] ## On most platforms used cli utilities requires root access. ## Setting 'use_sudo' to true will make use of sudo to run smartctl or nvme-cli. ## Sudo must be configured to allow the telegraf user to run smartctl or nvme-cli ## without a password. # use_sudo = true ## Skip checking disks in this power mode. Defaults to ## "standby" to not wake up disks that have stopped rotating. ## See --nocheck in the man pages for smartctl. ## smartctl version 5.41 and 5.42 have faulty detection of ## power mode and might require changing this value to ## "never" depending on your disks. # nocheck = "standby" ## Gather all returned S.M.A.R.T. attribute metrics and the detailed ## information from each drive into the 'smart_attribute' measurement. # attributes = true ## Optionally specify devices to exclude from reporting if disks auto-discovery is performed. # excludes = [ "/dev/pass6" ] ## Optionally specify devices and device type, if unset ## a scan (smartctl --scan and smartctl --scan -d nvme) for S.M.A.R.T. devices will be done ## and all found will be included except for the excluded in excludes. # devices = [ "/dev/ada0 -d atacam", "/dev/nvme0"] # devices = ["dev/nvme0 -d nvme", "/dev/nvme0"] ## Timeout for the cli command to complete. timeout = "30s" ## Optionally call smartctl and nvme-cli with a specific concurrency policy. ## By default, smartctl and nvme-cli are called in separate threads (goroutines) to gather disk attributes. ## Some devices (e.g. disks in RAID arrays) may have access limitations that require sequential reading of ## SMART data - one individual array drive at the time. In such case please set this configuration option ## to "sequential" to get readings for all drives. ## valid options: concurrent, sequential # read_method = "concurrent" Open the integration center in Nightingale, find SMART, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. 6 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

Disk self-assessed overall health is FAILED, serious failure risk, handle immediately S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: smart_device_health_ok == 0 Runbook: Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX for the full attribute list, focusing on Reallocated_Sector_Ct, Current_Pending_Sector and Offline_Uncorrectable; Immediately confirm the data on this disk has a replica or backup — this is the highest priority action; In a RAID array, check the array state and let it evict this disk and rebuild onto a hot spare; Schedule downtime to replace the disk and stop writing to it.

SSD flash wearout is nearly exhausted and may fail at any time; back up data and replace the drive immediately S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: smart_attribute_media_wear_percentage >= 90 Runbook: Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check Media_Wearout_Indicator / Percentage_Used together with Total_LBAs_Written; Combine with the write rate to estimate remaining life and plan the replacement window; Confirm the data on this disk has a replica and prepare the migration plan in advance; Review the source of write amplification (log level, frequent small writes, no TRIM) so the replacement does not repeat it.

Disk operating temperature too high, which accelerates aging or causes outright failure; check cooling immediately S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: smart_device_temp_c > 65 Runbook: Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and compare the temperature against the vendor's rated maximum; Check chassis airflow, fan speeds and dust in the filters, plus the room's ambient temperature; Check whether the bay layout is too dense and whether neighbouring disks are equally hot; Short term, reduce IO pressure on this disk (shift backups off peak, move hot data) to buy time.

Growing CRC failures on the data link, a possible precursor of interface, cable or disk controller failure S1 Critical · for 60 min · Trigger: increase(smart_attribute_crc_error_count[1h]) > 0 Runbook: Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check how fast UDMA_CRC_Error_Count is growing; Take the machine down, reseat the SATA/SAS data and power cables, and preferably just replace the cable; After replacing the cable, watch whether the counter stops growing — SMART counters never reset, so judge by the delta, not the absolute value; If a new cable does not help, suspect the backplane or HBA and swap them one at a time.
documents.s: CRC error count keeps growing within 1 hour

documents.t: SSD flash block erase failures indicate aging flash chips and a risk of write failures S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(smart_attribute_erase_fail_count[1h]) > 0 Runbook: Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check Erase_Fail_Count together with the remaining Reallocated/Available_Reservd_Space; A shrinking spare block pool means the disk is near end of life — confirm the data has a replica immediately; Schedule a replacement rather than waiting for writes to fail outright; Reduce write pressure on the disk beforehand so it does not degrade faster.

SSD flash block program failures; flash chip health is degrading rapidly, back up data immediately S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(smart_attribute_program_fail_count[1h]) > 0 Runbook: Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX and check Program_Fail_Count together with the remaining spare block ratio; Immediately confirm the data on this disk has a replica or backup — this is the highest priority action; Schedule a replacement soon: program failures often come with a risk of silent data corruption; Before replacing it, make the disk read-only or move hot data off to stop further writes.

14 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Metric Meaning Unit smart_attribute_crc_error_count SMART CRC Error Count — The number of Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) failures during hard disk data transmission, reflecting the reliability of the data transmission link. smart_attribute_end_to_end_error_detection_count SMART End-to-End Error Detection Count — The number of end-to-end verification failures in internal hard disk data transmission, associated with the health of hard disk firmware or physical storage units. smart_attribute_erase_fail_count SMART Erase Fail Count — The number of failures when a Solid State Drive (SSD) erases flash memory blocks; an excessive number may indicate flash chip aging or an increase in bad blocks. smart_attribute_host_reads SMART Host Reads Count — The total number of times the operating system reads data from the hard disk, which is a statistical indicator of hard disk usage with no direct fault warning significance. smart_attribute_media_wear_percentage SMART Media Wear Percentage — A core indicator dedicated to Solid State Drives (SSDs) that reflects the wear level of flash memory chips; the closer the value is to 100%, the shorter the lifespan. % smart_attribute_pll_lock_loss_count SMART PLL Lock Loss Count — The number of times the hard disk clock synchronization module (Phase-Locked Loop, PLL) loses lock, which can cause data transmission timing errors. smart_attribute_program_fail_count SMART Program Fail Count — The number of failures when a Solid State Drive (SSD) writes data (program operation) to flash memory blocks, which is a core indicator of flash memory health. smart_attribute_retry_buffer_overflow_count SMART Retry Buffer Overflow Count — The number of times the data buffer overflows when the hard disk automatically retries after a read/write failure, indicating a decline in hard disk read/write performance or hardware failure. smart_attribute_thermal_throttle_status SMART Thermal Throttle Status — The state where the hard disk triggers automatic speed reduction protection due to high temperature (1=triggered, 0=not triggered), which will cause slow read/write speeds after triggering. smart_attribute_timed_workload_timer SMART Timed Workload Timer — Accumulates the operating time of the hard disk in a preset load mode, used to evaluate the long-term working intensity of the hard disk and assist in judging the wear rate. s smart_attribute_wear_leveling_count SMART Wear Leveling Count — An indicator dedicated to Solid State Drives (SSDs) that records the number of executions of the wear leveling algorithm to ensure uniform wear of flash memory blocks and extend lifespan. smart_device_exit_status SMART Device Exit Status — The exit status code of the hard disk SMART self-test; 0 means the self-test is completed normally, and a non-zero value indicates self-test interruption or abnormality. smart_device_health_ok SMART Device Health Status — The overall health status identifier of the hard disk; 1=healthy (no fault warning), 0=unhealthy (potential faults exist). smart_device_temp_c SMART Device Temperature — The current operating temperature of the hard disk (in ℃); the safe operating range for mainstream hard disks is 0-60℃, and prolonged overheating will accelerate hardware aging. ℃

Categraf has included Telegraf's snmp input since v0.2.13. The idea is simple: list the OIDs for the metrics you want. [[instances.field]] reads single values, [[instances.table]] walks a table into multiple rows, and selected OIDs in a table (interface names, say) can become labels. Generic OIDs for interface traffic, errors and state work on almost every device; vendor-specific OIDs for CPU and memory are configured per vendor and model. The template ships dashboards for a generic switch overview, device traffic, access switches, and Cisco and Juniper device detail. The rules cover interfaces going down, traffic near bandwidth, errors and discards, high CPU and memory, and unreachable devices. The Cisco.toml in the template directory is a starting point for per-model configs.

37 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import. Rules are grouped by collector; import the group that matches how you collect.

H3C power supply state abnormal​ Normal state is 2 alert after 3 consecutive checks != 2 S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: snmp_system_power_status{Brand='H3C'} != 2 Runbook: Log in and run display power to identify the faulty power slot; On site, check the power module indicator, the supply line and the PDU output; If the line is fine, treat it as a power module hardware fault and start the replacement process; Before replacing, confirm the other feed is healthy so the device does not lose power mid-operation. H3C device CPU usage exceeds 70%​ CPU usage above 70% for 10 consecutive minutes S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: snmp_system_cpuuse{Brand='H3C'}>70 Runbook: Log in and run display cpu-usage (Huawei/H3C) or show system processes (Juniper) to see which process is busy; Common root causes are route flapping, an ARP/broadcast storm, an excessive number of ACL rules, or being scanned; Use display interface brief to spot abnormal port traffic and capture packets to find the broadcast storm source; Isolate the offending port or tune the configuration; if load stays high, evaluate whether the device has hit its capacity limit. H3C device memory usage exceeds 70%​ Memory usage above 70% for 2 consecutive minutes S2 Warning · for 2 min · Trigger: snmp_system_memuse{Brand='H3C'}>70 Runbook: Log in and run display memory-usage to see the memory breakdown; Check whether the routing table or ARP table has grown abnormally (display ip routing-table statistics, display arp statistics); Common root causes are route leaks, ARP attacks, or fragmentation on a device that has not been restarted for a long time; Improve route aggregation and ARP ageing, and schedule a maintenance window restart if needed. H3C device fan state abnormal​ Normal state is 2 alert after 3 consecutive checks != 2 S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: snmp_system_fan_status{Brand='H3C'} != 2 Runbook: Log in and run display fan to identify the faulty fan slot; At the same time run display temperature to confirm whether temperature has already risen; On site, check whether the fan is seized and whether the filter is clogged; clean and retest; Replace the fan module promptly once a hardware fault is confirmed; if temperature is already high, reduce device load or improve room cooling first. ICMP timeout​ 0 = no response 1 = responding If all requests within 1 minute get no response, the device is considered lost S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: max_over_time(snmp_icmp_up{}[1m]) == 0 Runbook: Ping again from another subnet to rule out a single-path problem, and use traceroute to find where it breaks; Try SSH/Telnet to the device — if you can log in, ICMP is being blocked by policy rather than the device being down; If it is completely unreachable, go on site and check the power and indicator lights; Confirm whether the services behind it have failed over to a redundant path, and restore traffic first if not. Incoming bandwidth usage high​ snmp_interface_incoming is the cumulative inbound traffic in bytes per second; rate(snmp_interface_incoming{}[1m]) * 8 gives inbound traffic per second in bit/s snmp_interface_speed is the maximum transmission rate of the interface This condition means actual inbound traffic exceeds 90% of the bandwidth S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: (rate(snmp_interface_incoming{}[1m]) * 8 / 10^9) > ((snmp_interface_speed{}/ 10^3) *0.9) and snmp_interface_speed >0 Runbook: Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface <port> to confirm the actual rate and peak; Use NetFlow/sFlow or capture traffic on the upstream device to find which sources/destinations consume the bandwidth; Determine whether it is normal growth, a backup job, or abnormal traffic (attack, loop); For genuine growth, upgrade the link or use link aggregation; for abnormal traffic, rate limit or isolate it first. Interface Down​ SNMP metric notes: snmp_interface_admin_status: up = 1, down = 2, testing = 3 Alert rule: latest snmp_interface_admin_status == up was up at least once in the last 14 days (offset 1h avoids alerting right at the down-to-up transition) latest ostatus != 1 checked every 60s, alert after 3 consecutive matches S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: snmp_interface_admin_status{ifname!~'^(vlan|Vlanif|VLAN|V|irb|gr-).*'} == 1 and min_over_time(snmp_interface_ostatus{ifname!~'^(vlan|Vlanif|VLAN|V|irb|gr-).*'}[14d] offset 1h) == 1 and snmp_interface_ostatus{ifname!~'^(vlan|Vlanif|VLAN|V|irb|gr-).*'} != 1 Runbook: Take the device and ifname from the alert labels, log in and run display interface <port> for the down reason and error counters; On site, check whether the cable or optical module is loose — for optics use display transceiver to read the TX/RX power; Confirm the port state on the peer device as well: only when both sides are down can you tell a link fault from a one-sided fault; Confirm whether a redundant link has taken over, and restore first if there is none. Juniper device power supply state abnormal​ Normal state is 2, abnormal state is 6 alert after 3 consecutive checks == 6 S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: snmp_system_power_status{Brand='Juniper'} == 6 Runbook: Log in and run display power to identify the faulty power slot; On site, check the power module indicator, the supply line and the PDU output; If the line is fine, treat it as a power module hardware fault and start the replacement process; Before replacing, confirm the other feed is healthy so the device does not lose power mid-operation. Inbound CRC errors​ incoming_errors: cumulative port error packets, incoming_ucastpkts: cumulative port packets 1-minute delta of incoming_errors above 100 1-minute delta of incoming_errors divided by 1-minute delta of incoming_ucastpkts above 1% checked every 60s, alert after 5 consecutive matches S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(snmp_interface_incoming_errors{}[2m]) > 100 and rate(snmp_interface_incoming_errors{}[2m]) / rate(snmp_interface_incoming_ucastpkts{}[2m]) > 0.01 Runbook: Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface <port> to see how fast CRC/errors are growing; Check the cable and optical module; for optical ports use display transceiver to confirm TX/RX power is within spec; Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match on both ends — a mismatch is the classic source of errors; After replacing the cable or module, clear the counters (reset counters interface) and retest. Outbound CRC errors​ outgoing_errors: cumulative port error packets, outgoing_ucastpkts: cumulative port packets 1-minute delta of outgoing_errors above 100 1-minute delta of outgoing_errors divided by 1-minute delta of outgoing_ucastpkts above 1% checked every 60s, alert after 5 consecutive matches S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(snmp_interface_outgoing_errors{}[2m]) > 100 and rate(snmp_interface_outgoing_errors{}[2m]) / rate(snmp_interface_outgoing_ucastpkts{}[2m]) > 0.01 Runbook: Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface <port> to see how fast CRC/errors are growing; Check the cable and optical module; for optical ports use display transceiver to confirm TX/RX power is within spec; Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex match on both ends — a mismatch is the classic source of errors; After replacing the cable or module, clear the counters (reset counters interface) and retest. Device interrupted​ snmp_uptime is the device uptime in units of 10ms delta(snmp_uptime{}/100 [2m]) means the device has not updated its uptime within 2 minutes S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: delta(snmp_uptime{}/100 [2m]) == 0 Runbook: Run an snmpwalk of the device's sysUpTime by hand to confirm whether it is still responding; If it responds, the problem is on the collector side — check categraf's snmp configuration, community string and timeouts; If it does not respond, treat it as a device outage and check power and the management network; After recovery, note the data gap — there were no alerts during the blind window. Device lost connection​ no response == 0, responding == 1 checked every 60s; alert when both snmp and icmp are 0 for 3 consecutive checks if not recovered, the alert repeats after 24h S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max_over_time(snmp_icmp_up{}[3m]) == 0 and max_over_time(snmp_up{}[3m]) == 0 Runbook: Immediately confirm whether the services behind the device have failed over to redundant equipment, and handle traffic first if not; On site, check the device power, indicators and whether the console produces output; If you can reach the console, check whether it is rebooting or in an abnormal state and collect logs; For a hardware fault, start the replacement process and keep traffic on the redundant path meanwhile. Device rebooted​ Alert when device uptime is below 600.00 seconds S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: resets(snmp_uptime{}[10m]) == 1 and resets(snmp_enginetime{}[10m]) == 1 Runbook: Log in and run display version for the uptime, and display logbuffer or display trapbuffer for the restart reason; Separate a manual restart, a power loss and an abnormal reset (memory exhaustion, software defect); For an abnormal reset, collect logs, contact the vendor and consider a firmware upgrade; Confirm all interfaces and routing neighbours recovered after the restart.

Abnormal fan status​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_fan_status == 1[3m]) == count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_fan_status[3m]) or count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_fan_present == 1[3m]) == count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_fan_present[3m]) Runbook: Log in and run display fan to identify the faulty fan slot; At the same time run display temperature to confirm whether temperature has already risen; On site, check whether the fan is seized and whether the filter is clogged; clean and retest; Replace the fan module promptly once a hardware fault is confirmed; if temperature is already high, reduce device load or improve room cooling first. Abnormal power status​ S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_power_status == 1[3m]) == count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_power_status[3m]) or count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_power_present == 1[3m]) == count_over_time(snmp_h3c_system_power_present[3m]) Runbook: Log in and run display power to identify the faulty power slot; On site, check the power module indicator, the supply line and the PDU output; If the line is fine, treat it as a power module hardware fault and start the replacement process; Before replacing, confirm the other feed is healthy so the device does not lose power mid-operation. Bgp Down​ the 2nd latest peer_status = 6 (established) peer_status changed within the last 5 minutes admin_status == 2 (up) S3 Info · Trigger: snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_peer_status offset 1m == 6 and delta(snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_peer_status[5m]) != 0 and snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_admin_status == 2 Runbook: Log in and run show bgp neighbor <peer> for the session state and the last disconnect reason; Check layer-3 connectivity to the neighbour (ping/traceroute) and whether TCP 179 is reachable; If the network is fine, verify the AS numbers, authentication password and prefix limits on both sides (exceeding the limit disconnects deliberately); Confirm whether the traffic is already carried by another neighbour, and restore it first if not. Bgp peer flap​ S3 Info · Trigger: delta(snmp_juniper_bgp_prefix_peer_up_count[1h]) >= 3 Runbook: Run show bgp neighbor <peer> to see the reasons for previous disconnects; For link-layer instability, check interface errors and optical power; For repeated disconnects caused by exceeding the prefix limit, adjust maximum-prefix or aggregate routes on the peer side; Check whether BGP damping is configured to suppress flapping, and evaluate enabling it if not. SNMP probe failed (device online)​ The device is reachable by ICMP but the SNMP probe keeps failing. This means the device is not down: SNMP is not enabled, an ACL is blocking it, UDP 161 is unreachable, or the credentials (community string / v3 authentication) are wrong. S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: max_over_time(snmp_icmp_up{}[3m]) == 1 and max_over_time(snmp_up{}[3m]) == 0 Runbook: On the device, confirm SNMP is enabled and the community string / v3 user is configured correctly; Check whether the device ACL and any firewall in between allow UDP 161 from the collector to the device; On the collector host, verify the credentials by hand with snmpwalk; If the credentials changed recently, update the SNMP authentication settings of this device on the platform as well and verify with Test on the page. SNMP collection interrupted (previously had data)​ The SNMP probe of this device succeeded at some point in the last hour, but there has been no snmp_up sample in the last 10 minutes. Common causes: the collection agent is offline or its configuration was removed, the device was disabled, or the network is down. Unlike a probe failure, this means the collection link as a whole produces no data at all. S2 Warning · Trigger: max_over_time(snmp_up{}[1h]) == 1 unless max_over_time(snmp_up{}[10m]) Runbook: Open the network device list and read the Health column of this device to tell an unreachable collection agent from a failed device probe; Confirm the configured collection agent (categraf) process and heartbeat are healthy; Confirm collection is not disabled for the device and the collect templates are still attached; On the device detail page, run Test to quickly verify the collection link. Bandwidth Usage Too High​ traffic value: delta(snmp_network_status_incoming [1m]) #delta() computes the increment (difference) of the time series /8 unit conversion factor min_over_time(metric_name [3m]) 3 max_over_time(snmp_network_status_speed [30m])/1000 * 0.7 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 alert at 70% and 90% of the physical port capacity S3 Info · for 2 min · Trigger: min_over_time(delta(snmp_network_status_incoming[3m]) * 8 / 180 / 1024 / 1024 [3m]) > snmp_network_status_speed / 1000 * 0.7 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 and snmp_network_status_speed > 0 min_over_time(delta(snmp_network_status_incoming[3m]) * 8 / 180 / 1024 / 1024 [3m]) > snmp_network_status_speed / 1000 * 0.9 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 and snmp_network_status_speed > 0 Runbook: Take the device and port from the alert labels and run display interface <port> to confirm the actual rate and peak; Use NetFlow/sFlow or capture traffic on the upstream device to find which sources/destinations consume the bandwidth; Determine whether it is normal growth, a backup job, or abnormal traffic (attack, loop); For genuine growth, upgrade the link or use link aggregation; for abnormal traffic, rate limit or isolate it first. Interface Down​ admin == 1 ops status was 2 (down) for the last 3 checks and 1 (up) on the 4th latest S3 Info · for 2 min · Trigger: snmp_network_status_admin_status == 1 and snmp_network_status_ostatus offset 4m == 1 and min_over_time(snmp_network_status_ostatus[3m]) == 2 Runbook: Take the device and ifname from the alert labels, log in and run display interface <port> for the down reason and error counters; On site, check whether the cable or optical module is loose — for optics use display transceiver to read the TX/RX power; Confirm the port state on the peer device as well: only when both sides are down can you tell a link fault from a one-sided fault; Confirm whether a redundant link has taken over, and restore first if there is none.

5 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Metric Meaning Unit snmp_interface_admin_status SNMP Interface Admin Status — SNMP interface administrative status, MIB name is ifAdminStatus. up(1): The interface is administratively enabled, the device is configured to allow the interface to operate. down(2): The interface is administratively disabled, the device is configured to prevent data transmission or operation. testing(3): The interface is in testing mode. Rarely seen in practice but exists in standard definitions. snmp_interface_ostatus SNMP Interface Operational Status — Interface operational status up(1): The interface is currently in normal working state and can send/receive data. down(2): The interface is currently unable to work, possibly due to physical link disconnection, configuration issues, or hardware failure. testing(3): The interface is in testing mode and temporarily not processing normal data flow, generally rare. snmp_interface_outgoing_ucastpkts Total Unicast Packets Sent by Interface — The total number of unicast packets sent by the interface in the outgoing direction. snmp_interface_outgoing_errors Total Outgoing Errors on Interface — The number of errors that occurred during data transmission on the interface. These errors typically include network layer or link layer issues, such as packet corruption, checksum errors, or other reasons that prevent normal data transmission. snmp_interface_speed Interface Bandwidth — snmp_interface_speed is an object in SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) used to represent the speed or bandwidth of a network interface, typically in bits per second (bps). It indicates the maximum data transfer rate of the network interface, i.e., the maximum traffic the interface can handle under ideal conditions. bit/s

Spring Boot applications need no external agent. Add the spring-boot-starter-actuator and micrometer-registry-prometheus dependencies, expose the prometheus endpoint, and the application serves JVM, HTTP request, datasource pool, executor and custom metrics on /actuator/prometheus. Actuator is built on Micrometer underneath. The two JVM dashboards are written against Actuator metric names (jvm_memory_used_bytes, http_server_requests_seconds and so on); one of them separates services by the application label. The rules cover heap near the limit, long GC pauses, rising HTTP 5xx and abnormal thread counts.
documents.s: Monitor Spring Boot applications with Nightingale

documents.t: 2 dashboards, 71 panels in total 5 alert rules, each with runbook steps

For Spring Boot 3.x, add to application.properties: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus management.endpoint.prometheus.enabled=true management.prometheus.metrics.export.enabled=true On 2.x the last line is management.metrics.export.prometheus.enabled=true. Check that http://localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus responds, then scrape it with the Categraf prometheus input and set an application label to the service name. Do not set exposure.include to *. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find SpringBoot, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels JVM (Actuator) with application name 37 JVM Dashboard 34
5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"}) * 100 / sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"}) > 85 Runbook: Check jvm_gc_pause_seconds to see whether full GC became more frequent and how long the pauses are; Capture a heap with jmap -histo:live <pid> or the arthas heapdump, then sort by object count to find the abnormally growing classes; Tell traffic growth (raise -Xmx) apart from a memory leak (must be fixed in code — a bigger heap only postpones it); You can restart the instance to recover, but capture the heap snapshot first or you lose the evidence.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max by (instance, uri) (http_server_requests_seconds_max{status!~"5.."}) > 10 Runbook: Take uri from the alert labels to identify the endpoint; Use arthas trace or APM distributed tracing to see which segment consumes the time (database, downstream RPC, or local computation); For a slow database, follow the slow-query path and add indexes; for a slow downstream, check its state and add a circuit breaker or fallback; Check whether the thread pool is saturated by slow requests and amplifying the queue — isolate the pool if so.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum by (instance, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) > 0 Runbook: Take uri from the alert labels to identify the endpoint, then search the application log for stack traces on that path; Tell total failure from partial failure — partial failure usually means one bad downstream instance or a data edge case; If it lines up with a recent release, roll back rather than keep investigating; Check whether downstream dependencies (database, cache, third-party APIs) are failing at the same time.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="nonheap"}) > 0 and sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="nonheap"}) * 100 / sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="nonheap"}) > 85 Runbook: Run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary (requires NativeMemoryTracking) or the arthas memory command to see each region's usage; Steadily growing Metaspace usually means a class loader leak — common with repeated hot deploys, dynamic proxies and script engines; As an emergency measure raise -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize and restart; For the root cause, look for a custom ClassLoader that is never released, and check jmap -clstats for an abnormal class loader count.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum by (instance) (increase(logback_events_total{level="error"}[5m])) > 0 Runbook: Take instance from the alert labels, then search your log system for ERROR-level stack traces in that time window; Group by exception type to tell an intermittent problem (downstream jitter, timeout retries) from a reproducible one (code bug, misconfiguration); Fix reproducible ones in code; for intermittent ones confirm retry and fallback logic actually works; If the ERROR volume spiked in line with a release, roll back first.
