The SQL Server input is based on the Telegraf plugin of the same name and reads dynamic management views (DMVs) and performance counters: connections and requests, wait statistics, buffer cache hit ratio, page life expectancy, transaction log usage, database state and size, and Always On availability group health. It has been verified against SQL Server 2022. Create a login in master and grant VIEW SERVER STATE and VIEW ANY DEFINITION; on 2022 and later add VIEW SERVER PERFORMANCE STATE. The rules cover blocking, deadlocks, log space, falling cache hit ratio and databases going offline.
1 dashboard, 10 panels in total 11 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.sqlserver

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.sqlserver/sqlserver.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.sqlserver started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 [[instances]] ## Specify instances to monitor with a list of connection strings. ## All connection parameters are optional. ## By default, the host is localhost, listening on default port, TCP 1433. ## for Windows, the user is the currently running AD user (SSO). ## See https://github.com/denisenkom/go-mssqldb for detailed connection ## parameters, in particular, tls connections can be created like so: ## "encrypt=true;certificate=<cert>;hostNameInCertificate=<SqlServer host fqdn>" # servers = ["Server=server.xxx.com;Port=1433;User Id=monitor;Password=xxxxxx;app name=categraf;log=1;"] # servers = [ ] ## Authentication method ## valid methods: "connection_string", "AAD" # auth_method = "connection_string" ## "database_type" enables a specific set of queries depending on the database type. If specified, it replaces azuredb = true/false and query_version = 2 ## In the config file, the sql server plugin section should be repeated each with a set of servers for a specific database_type. ## Possible values for database_type are - "SQLServer" or "AzureSQLDB" or "AzureSQLManagedInstance" or "AzureSQLPool" database_type = "SQLServer" ## A list of queries to include. If not specified, all the below listed queries are used. include_query = [] ## A list of queries to explicitly ignore. exclude_query = ["SQLServerAvailabilityReplicaStates", "SQLServerDatabaseReplicaStates"] ## Queries enabled by default for database_type = "SQLServer" are - ## SQLServerPerformanceCounters, SQLServerWaitStatsCategorized, SQLServerDatabaseIO, SQLServerProperties, SQLServerMemoryClerks, ## SQLServerSchedulers, SQLServerRequests, SQLServerVolumeSpace, SQLServerCpu, SQLServerAvailabilityReplicaStates, SQLServerDatabaseReplicaStates, ## SQLServerRecentBackups ## Following are old config settings ## You may use them only if you are using the earlier flavor of queries, however it is recommended to use ## the new mechanism of identifying the database_type there by use it's corresponding queries ## Optional parameter, setting this to 2 will use a new version ## of the collection queries that break compatibility with the original ## dashboards. ## Version 2 - is compatible from SQL Server 2012 and later versions and also for SQL Azure DB # query_version = 2 ## Toggling this to true will emit an additional metric called "sqlserver_telegraf_health". ## This metric tracks the count of attempted queries and successful queries for each SQL instance specified in "servers". ## The purpose of this metric is to assist with identifying and diagnosing any connectivity or query issues. ## This setting/metric is optional and is disabled by default. # health_metric = false ## Possible queries across different versions of the collectors ## Queries enabled by default for specific Database Type ## database_type = SQLServer by default collects the following queries ## - SQLServerPerformanceCounters ## - SQLServerWaitStatsCategorized ## - SQLServerDatabaseIO ## - SQLServerProperties ## - SQLServerMemoryClerks ## - SQLServerSchedulers ## - SQLServerRequests ## - SQLServerVolumeSpace ## - SQLServerCpu ## - SQLServerRecentBackups ## and following as optional (if mentioned in the include_query list) ## - SQLServerAvailabilityReplicaStates ## - SQLServerDatabaseReplicaStates ## Version 2 by default collects the following queries ## Version 2 is being deprecated, please consider using database_type. ## - PerformanceCounters ## - WaitStatsCategorized ## - DatabaseIO ## - ServerProperties ## - MemoryClerk ## - Schedulers ## - SqlRequests ## - VolumeSpace ## - Cpu ## Version 1 by default collects the following queries ## Version 1 is deprecated, please consider using database_type. ## - PerformanceCounters ## - WaitStatsCategorized ## - CPUHistory ## - DatabaseIO ## - DatabaseSize ## - DatabaseStats ## - DatabaseProperties ## - MemoryClerk ## - VolumeSpace ## - PerformanceMetrics Open the integration center in Nightingale, find SQLServer, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels SQLServer 10
11 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: sqlserver_up == 0 Runbook: On the database host run systemctl status mssql-server (Linux) or Get-Service MSSQLSERVER (Windows) to check the service; If the service is running, connect by hand with sqlcmd -S <host>,1433 -U <user> to separate a network problem, a port not listening, and a locked account; If the service is down, check /var/opt/mssql/log/errorlog (Linux) or the SQL Server error log; a full disk, tempdb creation failure, or an expired certificate are common causes; After recovery run SELECT name, state_desc FROM sys.databases to confirm every database is back ONLINE.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: sqlserver_server_properties_db_suspect > 0 Runbook: Run SELECT name, state_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE state_desc <> 'ONLINE' to identify the database; Look for the most recent errors for that database in the SQL Server error log to tell an IO error from log corruption; Restoring from the most recent good backup (RESTORE DATABASE) is the path with the least data loss and should be preferred; Only if no backup exists should you use EMERGENCY mode plus DBCC CHECKDB(..., REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS); that operation loses data, so take a file-level snapshot first.
documents.s: SQL Server has a database in SUSPECT state

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: sqlserver_server_properties_db_offline > 0 Runbook: Run SELECT name, state_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE state_desc = 'OFFLINE' to list the offline databases; Confirm against the change record whether this is planned maintenance or a migration; If unplanned, try ALTER DATABASE [db] SET ONLINE and read the error log for the exact reason if it fails; Once online run DBCC CHECKDB([db]) WITH NO_INFOMSGS to confirm data consistency.
documents.s: SQL Server has a database in OFFLINE state

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: sqlserver_volume_space_available_space_bytes / (sqlserver_volume_space_total_space_bytes > 0) * 100 < 10 Runbook: Take volume_mount_point from the alert labels and run SELECT DB_NAME(database_id), name, size*8/1024 AS size_mb FROM sys.master_files ORDER BY size DESC to find the largest files; For an oversized log file, run BACKUP LOG to truncate it first and then DBCC SHRINKFILE; under the full recovery model it cannot shrink without a log backup; If the data files genuinely need that space, clean up historical partitions or archive cold data; As an emergency measure move tempdb or backup files to another volume, but plan a disk expansion.
documents.s: SQL Server data volume free space low

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 5 min · Trigger: sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Percent Log Used", instance!="_Total", instance!="Total"} > 85 Runbook: Take instance (the database name) from the alert labels and run SELECT name, log_reuse_wait_desc FROM sys.databases WHERE name = '<db>' to see why the log cannot be reused; For LOG_BACKUP, run BACKUP LOG [db] TO DISK='...' immediately; this is by far the most common cause; For ACTIVE_TRANSACTION, run DBCC OPENTRAN to find the long transaction and decide whether to KILL it; For REPLICATION or AVAILABILITY_REPLICA, investigate whether replication/AlwaysOn synchronisation is stuck and repair the replication link first.
documents.s: SQL Server transaction log usage too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Page life expectancy", object="SQLServer:Buffer Manager"} < 300 Runbook: Run SELECT * FROM sys.dm_os_performance_counters WHERE counter_name LIKE '%Page life%' to confirm the live value; Run SELECT TOP 20 * FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats ORDER BY total_logical_reads DESC to find the statements with the highest logical reads, usually full scans caused by missing indexes; Take the suggestions from sys.dm_db_missing_index_details, review them, and create the indexes; this pays off faster than adding memory; If queries are already optimised and it is still low, check whether max server memory is set too small or is being squeezed by other processes before adding RAM.
documents.s: SQL Server page life expectancy too low

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Memory Grants Pending"} > 0 Runbook: Run SELECT session_id, requested_memory_kb, granted_memory_kb, wait_time_ms FROM sys.dm_exec_query_memory_grants to see who is waiting and who is holding; For sessions with huge grants, pull the statement with sys.dm_exec_sql_text; it is usually a large sort or hash join, and a missing index amplifies the memory requirement significantly; As an emergency measure KILL the largest consumer to release memory; Longer term add the indexes suggested by dm_db_missing_index_details, split large queries, or raise max server memory.
documents.s: SQL Server has queries waiting for memory grants

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Processes blocked"} > 5 Runbook: Run SELECT blocking_session_id, session_id, wait_type, wait_time, wait_resource FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0 to find the head of the blocking chain; For the head session use DBCC INPUTBUFFER(<spid>) or sys.dm_exec_sql_text to see what it is running; Once confirmed as a runaway long transaction, run KILL <spid> to stop the bleeding; Afterwards check whether that transaction lacks an index (widening the lock range) or the application forgot to commit, and consider enabling READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT to reduce reader/writer conflict.
documents.s: SQL Server blocked process count too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(sqlserver_performance_value{counter="Number of Deadlocks/sec"}[10m]) > 0 Runbook: Query the system_health extended event session for the deadlock graph: SELECT XEvent.query('.') FROM (SELECT CAST(target_data AS XML) AS TargetData FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets ...) and extract xml_deadlock_report; Read the lock acquisition order and the indexes involved from the graph; The usual fix is to make multi-table updates follow the same order everywhere in the application code, plus indexes on the participating queries to narrow the lock range; In the short term the application can retry on error 1205, but that does not replace fixing the root cause.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(sqlserver_database_io_read_latency_ms[5m]) / (rate(sqlserver_database_io_reads[5m]) > 0) > 50 Runbook: Take database_name and logical_filename from the alert labels to identify the slow file; On the host run iostat -x 1 (Linux) or watch Avg. Disk sec/Read in Performance Monitor to tell slow storage from read amplification inside SQL Server; If the storage is fine, optimise queries and add indexes as for page life expectancy to reduce physical reads; If the storage really is slow, consider moving the file to SSD, splitting filegroups to spread IO, or checking whether backup jobs overlap the business peak.
documents.s: SQL Server data file read latency too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(sqlserver_database_io_write_latency_ms[5m]) / (rate(sqlserver_database_io_writes[5m]) > 0) > 50 Runbook: Take database_name and file_type from the alert labels and handle file_type=LOG first, since slow log writes stall every commit; On the host run iostat -x 1 and check that disk's await and %util to see whether it is saturated; If the log file shares a disk with the data files, move the log to a dedicated low-latency disk; Check whether backups, DBCC CHECKDB, or index rebuilds overlap the business peak and move them to off-peak hours.
documents.s: SQL Server data file write latency too high

The switch_legacy input is forked from swcollector and targets the "just get the switches in quickly" case. List IPs in the config (single addresses, subnets or ranges), and the input detects the device model and uses generic OIDs to collect CPU and memory usage plus traffic, packets, errors, discards and up/down state for every port. No OIDs to write. It supports SNMP v2c only, so authentication is a single community string. Set switch_id_label to ident and each switch appears in Nightingale's host list keyed by its IP. For custom OIDs or SNMP v3, use the SNMP integration instead. The rules cover ports going down, traffic near bandwidth, rising errors and unreachable devices.
documents.s: Monitor switches with zero config (Switch Legacy) in Nightingale

documents.t: 1 dashboard, 14 panels in total 7 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.switch_legacy

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.switch_legacy/switch_legacy.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.switch_legacy started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = "300s" switch_id_label = "ip" [mappings] "192.168.88.160" = "switch001.bj" "192.168.88.161" = "switch002.bj" [[instances]] # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # use global unique string to specify instance # labels = { region="beijing" } ips = [ # "172.16.2.1", # "172.16.4/24", # "192.168.56.102-192.168.56.120" ] community = "public" # whether use index tag index_tag = false ignore_ifaces = ["Nu", "NU", "Vlan", "Vl"] concurrency_for_address = 1000 concurrency_for_request = 4 ping_enable = true ping_mode_fastping = true ping_timeout_ms = 300 ping_retries = 4 # true: use gosnmp, false: use snmpwalk snmp_mode_gosnmp = true snmp_timeout_ms = 1000 snmp_retries = 5 gather_ping_metrics = true gather_flow_metrics = true gather_cpu_metrics = true gather_mem_metrics = true gather_oper_status = false gather_pkt = false gather_broadcast_pkt = false gather_multicast_pkt = false gather_discards = false gather_errors = false gather_unknown_protos = false gather_out_qlen = false # ignore metrics if limit > 0 and collected value > limit speed_limit = 0 pkt_limit = 0 broadcast_pkt_limit = 0 multicast_pkt_limit = 0 discards_pkt_limit = 0 errors_pkt_limit = 0 unknown_protos_pkt_limit = 0 out_qlen_pkt_limit = 0 # [[instances.customs]] # metric = "AnyconnectSession" # tags = {} # oid = "1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.392.1.3.35.0" # [[instances.customs]] # metric = "ConnectionStat" # tags = {} # oid = "1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.147.1.2.2.2.1.5.40.6" # [[instances.customs]] # metric = "TempStatus" # tags = {} # oid = "1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.13.1.3.1.3.1004" Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Switch (legacy), and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels Network Switch 14
7 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger: switch_legacy_ping_up == 0 Runbook: Take the device identifier from the alert labels and double-check with ping and traceroute from a different machine to rule out a problem on the collector side; If it does ping from elsewhere, the problem is on the path from the collector; check the intermediate links and ACLs; If it does not ping at all, ask the data centre to check the power and status LEDs and try logging in over the console port; Once the device is confirmed failed, switch to the redundant link (check whether stacking/VRRP already failed over) and arrange a replacement.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: switch_legacy_cpu_util > 80 Runbook: Log in to the device and run display cpu-usage (Huawei) or show processes cpu sorted (Cisco) to see which process is consuming CPU; High usage is commonly an ARP or broadcast storm, or heavy punting of packets to the CPU; check with display cpu-defend statistics; For a broadcast storm, locate the source port and configure storm-control, and check for a loop at the same time (STP state); If a protocol process is the consumer, check the routing table size and neighbour count and apply route summarisation if needed.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: switch_legacy_mem_util > 80 Runbook: Log in to the device and run display memory-usage or show memory statistics to see the breakdown; Check whether the MAC table, ARP table, and routing table sizes are approaching the device's specification limits; If entries are growing abnormally, check for a MAC flooding attack and configure port security to cap MAC learning per port; If this is genuine business growth, evaluate whether the device model needs upgrading and clean up unused configuration and ACLs.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: changes(switch_legacy_if_oper_status[10m]) > 2 Runbook: Take the port identifier from the alert labels, log in to the device, and run display interface <port> to see the up/down count and the last transition time; Suspect the physical layer first: check whether the optical module's transmit and receive power (display transceiver diagnosis) are within thresholds and whether the fibre and connectors are loose; For copper ports, check cable quality and whether speed/duplex negotiation matches on both ends; Once physical problems are ruled out, check whether the peer device is restarting repeatedly, and shut down the port if necessary to stop it triggering network-wide reconvergence.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(switch_legacy_if_in_errors[5m]) > 1 Runbook: Take the port identifier from the alert labels and run display interface <port> to see the detailed CRC, Frame, and Giants error counters; Predominantly CRC errors are essentially always physical: replace the cable or fibre, clean the optical connectors, and confirm the cable length is within spec; Check that speed and duplex negotiation match on both ends, since a half/full duplex mismatch produces large numbers of collision errors; After replacing the cable, clear the counters with reset counters interface <port> and confirm they stop growing.

S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: switch_legacy_if_in_speed_percent > 80 Runbook: Take the port identifier from the alert labels and run display interface <port> to confirm the live rate against the negotiated port speed; Use NetFlow/sFlow, or capture on the server side, to identify which workloads generate the traffic and rule out anomalies (backup jobs or data sync running in the wrong window); If this is genuine business growth, evaluate link aggregation (Eth-Trunk / port-channel) to add capacity; In the short term apply QoS rate limiting to non-critical traffic to protect the important flows.
documents.s: Switch port inbound bandwidth utilization too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 10 min · Trigger: switch_legacy_if_out_speed_percent > 80 Runbook: Take the port identifier from the alert labels and run display interface <port> to see the outbound rate and queue drop counters; For a saturated uplink, link aggregation is the most direct fix; Use traffic analysis to confirm whether high-volume workloads should be taking a different path, and adjust routing or apply traffic engineering if so; Before adding capacity, apply QoS queue rate limiting to secondary traffic to protect the critical business.
documents.s: Switch port outbound bandwidth utilization too high

The systemd input talks to systemd over D-Bus and collects each unit's active state, enabled flag, restart count, task count and startup time. Unlike a plain process check, it tells "the service exists but is failed" apart from "the service keeps getting restarted". All units are collected by default, minus the noisy automount, device, mount, scope and slice types. In production, narrow it down with unit_include to the services you actually care about. Requires Linux with systemd 212 or newer.
1 dashboard, 7 panels in total 3 alert rules, each with runbook steps 12 metric descriptions Categraf collector config: input.systemd

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.systemd/systemd.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.systemd started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 # 是否启用 systemd 插件 enable = true # 包含的 unit 正则表达式，默认为 ".+"（所有unit） unit_include = '''.+''' # 排除的 unit 正则表达式，默认排除 automount、device、mount、scope、slice 类型 unit_exclude = '''.+\.(automount|device|mount|scope|slice)''' # 是否采集 service unit 的启动时间信息（单位：秒） enable_start_time_metrics = true # 是否采集 service unit task 的 metrics enable_task_metrics = true # 是否采集 service unit 重启次数信息 enable_restarts_metrics = true # 是否使用私有 systemd 连接 systemd_private = true Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Systemd, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels Systemd Monitoring Dashboard 7
3 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: systemd_unit_state{state!="active"} == 1 Runbook: Run systemctl --failed to list every failed unit, then systemctl status <unit> for its state and recent logs; Use journalctl -u <unit> -n 100 --no-pager to find the exit reason; For configuration problems, fix the config before systemctl restart <unit>; For repeated failures, check systemctl show <unit> -p NRestarts for a restart loop and find the root cause before restarting again.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: increase(systemd_service_restart_total[5m]) > 3 Runbook: Run journalctl -u <unit> -n 200 --no-pager to see the error before each exit; Check the exit code and whether it was OOM-killed (dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'); If an unready dependency is the cause (cannot reach the database, mount not finished), add After=/Requires= to the unit and fix the dependency; While investigating you can systemctl stop the service so it does not flood the disk with logs.

S2 Warning · for 3 min · Trigger: systemd_system_running == 0 Runbook: Run systemctl status for the overall state, then systemctl --failed to list the failed units; Use journalctl -u <unit> on each to find and fix the failure; Confirm whether the failed units affect critical services — some are unrelated one-shot jobs whose state can be cleared with systemctl reset-failed; After fixing, confirm systemctl is-system-running returns running.

12 metrics, the ones the dashboards and rules above are built on. Metric Meaning Unit systemd_service_restart_total Total Service Restarts systemd_socket_accepted_connections_total Total Accepted Socket Connections systemd_socket_current_connections Current Socket Connections systemd_socket_refused_connections_total Total Refused Socket Connections systemd_system_running System Running State — Whether the system is in running state (1 = running, 0 = not running) systemd_timer_last_trigger_seconds Timer Last Trigger Timestamp systemd_unit_start_time_seconds Unit Start Timestamp — Unix timestamp ms systemd_unit_state Unit State — The state value is one of activating | active | deactivating | failed | inactive systemd_unit_tasks_current Current Task Count systemd_unit_tasks_max Maximum Task Limit systemd_units Systemd Units — Total number of units in each state. The state is one of activating | active | deactivating | failed | inactive systemd_version Systemd Version Information

Tencent Cloud metrics come from its Cloud Monitor service. The tencentcloud-exporter maintained by Tencent Cloud converts them per product into Prometheus metrics named qce_<product>_<metric>, which the Categraf prometheus input scrapes. The templates ship one dashboard per product: CVM instances, CKafka, Cloud PostgreSQL, Redis (memory edition), TDSQL-C for MySQL, and public and private load balancers. The metric reference further down lists Tencent Cloud's monitoring metrics per product with meaning, unit and dimensions.
7 dashboards, 137 panels in total

Deploy the tencentcloud-exporter and configure it with an API key plus the products and regions to collect. Once http://<exporter>:9123/metrics responds, scrape it with the Categraf prometheus input: # conf/input.prometheus/tencentcloud.toml interval = 60 [[instances]] urls = ["http://<exporter>:9123/metrics"] labels = { job = "tencentcloud" } Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Tencent Cloud, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.

Every TiDB component ships a Prometheus endpoint: TiDB Server on 10080, PD on 2379, TiKV on 20180, with TiFlash and TiCDC on whatever ports they are configured with. Scrape them with the Categraf prometheus input, or add the Prometheus that TiUP deploys as a Nightingale data source. The dashboards depend on four labels: k8s_cluster, tidb_cluster, job and instance. Give the first two fixed values even outside Kubernetes. The rules cover failed and slow queries on TiDB, Region anomalies on PD, storage and Raft latency on TiKV, and components going down.
1 dashboard, 58 panels in total 28 alert rules, each with runbook steps

These components expose Prometheus-format /metrics themselves, so the Categraf prometheus input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, add it as a Nightingale data source and the templates work as they are. # conf/input.prometheus/tidb.toml interval = 15 [[instances]] urls = ["http://<tidb>:10080/metrics"] labels = { job = "tidb", k8s_cluster = "", tidb_cluster = "prod" } [[instances]] urls = ["http://<pd>:2379/metrics"] labels = { job = "pd", k8s_cluster = "", tidb_cluster = "prod" } [[instances]] urls = ["http://<tikv>:20180/metrics"] labels = { job = "tikv", k8s_cluster = "", tidb_cluster = "prod" } Open the integration center in Nightingale, find TiDB, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels tidb-Overview 58
28 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: avg(irate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) by(instance) * 100 <= 20 Runbook: Run top -H to see whether tidb-server, tikv-server or something else is busy; High TiKV CPU usually means too many coprocessor requests — use the TiDB slow log to find SQL scanning large ranges; High TiDB CPU usually means complex computation or many small queries — check the Grafana TiDB Query Summary; If it stays high after SQL tuning, add nodes.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="node_exporter"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (instance,job,le) ) > 1 Runbook: On the PD node run iostat -x 1 to check disk util and await — PD requires SSDs; Confirm the PD data directory does not share a disk with TiKV data; Check whether another process is competing for that disk's IO; If disk performance is genuinely insufficient, moving PD to a dedicated SSD is the only real fix.
documents.s: TiDB - PD disk write latency exceeds 1s; slow leader writes cause leader switches

documents.t: TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(etcd_server_is_leader) !=1 Runbook: Run pd-ctl member to check each PD member's state and whether the surviving nodes still form a majority; Without a majority, restore the failed PD nodes immediately; If all nodes are alive but no leader is elected, check connectivity and clock skew between PDs; Check each PD's log for the election failure reason and follow the official PD recovery procedure if needed.

TiDB (Control Plane) S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(etcd_network_peer_round_trip_time_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (To,instance,job,le) ) > 1 Runbook: Run mtr between PD nodes to find where latency and loss appear; Confirm PD nodes are not spread across data centres — PD is very sensitive to network latency and should be co-located; Check the NIC for errors and drops and whether bandwidth is saturated; Involve the network team, and avoid large data migrations meanwhile.
documents.s: TiDB - network latency between PD nodes exceeds 1s

documents.t: TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: node_netstat_Tcp_CurrEstab > 50000 Runbook: Run ss -s to see the connection state distribution and whether ESTABLISHED or TIME_WAIT dominates; Run ss -tan | awk '{print $5}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn to locate the sources; If the application does not reuse connections, switch to a connection pool; If TIME_WAIT dominates, enable tcp_tw_reuse and widen the port range.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="tidb"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="blackbox_exporter"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="drainer"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="grafana"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="pd"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="pump"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{job="tidb"}[1m]) > tidb_server_maxprocs{job="tidb"} * 0.8 Runbook: Check the Grafana TiDB Query Summary for the statement types with the highest QPS and latency; Use the TiDB slow log to find the specific SQL and check for missing indexes causing heavy row lookups; Confirm tidb_server_maxprocs matches the container/machine size; If it stays high after tuning, add tidb-server instances.
documents.s: TiDB - tidb CPU usage exceeds 80% of available CPU

documents.t: TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(tidb_session_schema_lease_error_total{type="outdated"}[15m]) > 0 Runbook: Search that tidb-server's log for schema lease errors; The usual root causes are an unstable network to PD/TiKV, or GC pressure preventing lease renewal; Check whether a long-running large transaction is blocking schema changes; For a single-instance problem, drain traffic and restart that instance; for a cluster-wide problem, investigate PD and the network.
documents.s: TiDB - tidb schema load errors in the last 15 minutes

documents.t: TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase( tidb_server_critical_error_total[5m] ) > 0 Runbook: Search the tidb-server log for critical error and binlog entries to confirm what was skipped and the scope; Check whether pump/drainer are available — failure to write binlog is the most common cause; Confirm whether downstream data is already missing and use tooling to verify and backfill if needed; After fixing the binlog path, keep watching to confirm nothing else is skipped.
documents.s: TiDB - tidb skipped binlog in the last 5 minutes

documents.t: TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: increase( tidb_domain_load_schema_total{type="failed"}[10m] ) > 10 Runbook: Check that instance's log for the specific failure; Investigate connectivity and latency to PD/TiKV; Check whether a DDL is stuck (ADMIN SHOW DDL JOBS) and blocking schema version advancement; Cancel stuck DDL with ADMIN CANCEL DDL JOBS and redo it.
documents.s: TiDB - tidb schema load failed more than 10 times in the last 10 minutes

documents.t: TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="tiflash"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S3 Info · for 1 min · Trigger: process_resident_memory_bytes{job=~"tikv",instance=~".*"} - (process_resident_memory_bytes{job=~"tikv",instance=~".*"} offset 5m) > 5*1024*1024*1024 Runbook: Use the TiDB slow log and the Grafana TiKV Coprocessor panel to find SQL doing very large range scans; KILL that query to stop the bleeding if needed; Check whether block-cache-size exceeds a sensible share of physical memory (45% is the usual ceiling); If the instance just started, this may be normal warm-up — but confirm it levels off.
documents.s: TiDB - tikv memory grew more than 5G within 5 minutes

documents.t: TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: changes(process_start_time_seconds{job="tikv"}[5m]) > 0 Runbook: Check the tail of the tikv log and dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' to tell a crash, an OOM kill and a manual restart apart; For OOM, compare block-cache-size against machine memory; For a panic, collect the logs and check the known issues for your TiDB version; After the restart, run pd-ctl store to confirm the store is Up and regions have rebalanced.

TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum(tikv_store_size_bytes{type="available"}) by (instance) / sum(tikv_store_size_bytes{type="capacity"}) by (instance) < 0.2 Runbook: Run pd-ctl store to see each store's capacity and usage and whether it is isolated or widespread; For a single full node, check whether regions are unevenly distributed and adjust scheduling with pd-ctl; If it is widespread, you must add TiKV nodes; Confirm GC is running normally (a GC life time set too long lets old versions accumulate).

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: probe_success{group="tikv"} == 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and first confirm the machine is alive with ping/ssh; On that node confirm the process is running and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the probe fails, check the listening port and firewall; Run tiup cluster display <cluster> for the overall topology state and confirm the remaining nodes still form a majority.

TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: (((node_memory_MemTotal_bytes-node_memory_MemFree_bytes-node_memory_Cached_bytes)/(node_memory_MemTotal_bytes)*100)) >= 80 Runbook: Run ps aux --sort=-%mem | head to find the largest consumer; For high TiKV memory, check block-cache-size first; for high TiDB memory, look for large queries without mem-quota-query; Set tidb_mem_quota_query to cap per-query memory; If there is no leak and it is still short, add memory or move instances.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: node_filesystem_readonly{fstype=~"(ext.|xfs)"} == 1 Runbook: Run dmesg -T | grep -iE 'i/o error|remount|read-only' to confirm what triggered it; Run smartctl -a /dev/sdX to check disk health — it is usually bad sectors; Immediately take the services on that node out (pd-ctl store delete or remove it with tiup) so nothing keeps trying to write; After replacing the disk, rejoin the cluster and wait for data to backfill.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: node_filesystem_files_free{fstype=~"(ext.|xfs)"} / node_filesystem_files{fstype=~"(ext.|xfs)"} * 100 < 20 Runbook: Run df -i to find the mount point; Count files level by level to find the directories with the most small files; In TiDB deployments it is usually unrotated log files — clean the old ones first; Longer term, tune log retention or raise inode density at format time.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{fstype=~"(ext.|xfs)", mountpoint!~"/boot"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{fstype=~"(ext.|xfs)", mountpoint!~"/boot"} * 100 <= 20 Runbook: Use df -h and du -x --max-depth=1 to find the largest directories; On TiDB nodes it is usually logs and slow logs piling up — clean those first; For a full TiKV data disk, expand or add nodes and confirm GC is running; Use lsof +L1 to check for deleted files whose handles are still open.

TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(net_drop_in[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> and ethtool -S <nic> to confirm the drop counters and the reason; If ring buffers are too small, raise them with ethtool -G <nic> rx; Check whether bandwidth is saturated — large-scale region migration will saturate a NIC; If needed, lower the scheduling concurrency with pd-ctl (leader-schedule-limit, region-schedule-limit).

TiDB (Control Plane) S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: increase(net_drop_out[1m]) > 0 Runbook: Run ip -s link show <nic> and ethtool -S <nic> to confirm transmit-side drops; Raise txqueuelen and the transmit queue; Check whether bandwidth is saturated and lower PD scheduling concurrency if so; Investigate the NIC driver and the peer switch port state.

TiDB (Control Plane) S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: (sum(pd_cluster_status{type="store_down_count"}) by (instance) > 0) and (sum(etcd_server_is_leader) by (instance) > 0) Runbook: Run pd-ctl store to identify the store and how long it has been down; On that node check the tikv process and disk state; If it can be recovered quickly, do so — that avoids PD triggering large-scale replica replenishment and extra load; If it genuinely cannot be recovered, run pd-ctl store delete <id> for a graceful decommission so data migrates in an orderly way.
documents.s: TiDB - tikv instances in down state above 0

The Tomcat input calls the Manager app's /manager/status/all endpoint and parses JVM heap and memory pool usage, thread pool size and busy count per connector (HTTP, AJP), request counts, processing time, errors and bytes sent and received. The endpoint requires authentication: add a user with the manager-gui role in tomcat-users.xml and relax the RemoteAddrValve in webapps/manager/META-INF/context.xml, which only allows localhost by default, or you get a 403. The rules cover thread pool exhaustion, heap near the limit, rising error rate and unreachable instances.
1 dashboard, 12 panels in total 6 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.tomcat

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.tomcat/tomcat.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.tomcat started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 # Gather metrics from the Tomcat server status page. [[instances]] ## URL of the Tomcat server status # url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/manager/status/all?XML=true" url = "" ## HTTP Basic Auth Credentials # username = "tomcat" # password = "s3cret" ## Request timeout # timeout = "5s" # # interval = global.interval * interval_times # interval_times = 1 # important! use global unique string to specify instance # labels = { instance="192.168.1.2:8080", url="-" } ## Optional TLS Config # use_tls = false # tls_min_version = "1.2" # tls_ca = "/etc/categraf/ca.pem" # tls_cert = "/etc/categraf/cert.pem" # tls_key = "/etc/categraf/key.pem" ## Use TLS but skip chain & host verification # insecure_skip_verify = true Open the integration center in Nightingale, find Tomcat, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels Tomcat - categraf 12
6 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: tomcat_up == 0 Runbook: Log in to the host and run ps -ef | grep catalina and ss -lntp | grep 8080 to check the process and port; If the process is alive, verify with curl -u <user>:<pass> 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/manager/status?XML=true'; a 401/403 means the manager account or a RemoteAddrValve restriction is blocking the collector's IP; If the process is gone, check the tail of logs/catalina.out for the cause (port conflict, insufficient memory, application start-up failure); Confirm the upstream load balancer has removed this node before restarting so traffic stops arriving.

S1 Critical · for 3 min · Trigger: tomcat_connector_current_threads_busy / (tomcat_connector_max_threads > 0) * 100 > 85 Runbook: Take name (the connector name) from the alert labels, capture thread stacks with jstack <pid>, and count which method the http-nio-* threads are stuck in; Many threads blocked on the database or an outbound HTTP call means a slow downstream: fix it and add timeouts to the call; As a stopgap raise maxThreads for that connector in server.xml, re-checking memory and the downstream capacity; Longer term add circuit breaking around external dependencies (for example Resilience4j) so downstream flapping cannot saturate the Tomcat thread pool.

S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(tomcat_connector_error_count[5m]) / (rate(tomcat_connector_request_count[5m]) > 0) * 100 > 5 Runbook: Run grep -E ' (5[0-9]{2}|4[0-9]{2}) ' logs/localhost_access_log.*.txt | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head to find the URLs where the errors concentrate; For 5xx, look for the matching exception stack in logs/catalina.out and the application logs; 4xx concentrated on a few endpoints usually means a caller changed parameters or authentication; confirm with the calling team; If the errors come from dependency timeouts, add timeouts and fallbacks to those calls first so the errors stop amplifying.
documents.s: Tomcat request error rate too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: rate(tomcat_connector_processing_time[5m]) / (rate(tomcat_connector_request_count[5m]) > 0) > 1000 Runbook: Confirm the access log pattern includes %D, then run awk '{print $NF, $7}' localhost_access_log.*.txt | sort -rn | head -20 to find the slowest URLs; Capture jstack <pid> three times in a row and diff them to find methods that persist across captures; If threads are stuck on the database, check slow queries and connection pool waits (threads block in getConnection when the pool is exhausted); If they are stuck in GC, confirm the Full GC frequency with jstat -gcutil <pid> 1s and then resize the heap or hunt the memory leak based on heap usage.
documents.s: Tomcat average request duration too long

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: (tomcat_jvm_memory_total - tomcat_jvm_memory_free) / (tomcat_jvm_memory_max > 0) * 100 > 85 Runbook: Run jstat -gcutil <pid> 1s 10 and watch the Full GC frequency and the old-generation occupancy after collection; if it stays high after collection there is a leak; Run jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -30 to rank objects and identify the class growing abnormally; If you suspect a leak, dump the heap with jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=/tmp/heap.hprof <pid> and analyse the reference chain in MAT; If it is simply undersized, raise -Xmx after checking physical memory, leaving room for off-heap memory.
documents.s: Tomcat JVM heap usage too high

documents.t: S2 Warning · for 5 min · Trigger: tomcat_jvm_memorypool_used{name=~".*Old Gen|Tenured Gen"} / (tomcat_jvm_memorypool_max{name=~".*Old Gen|Tenured Gen"} > 0) * 100 > 90 Runbook: Run jstat -gcold <pid> 1s 10 and watch whether the old generation drops after each Full GC; If it does not, run jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -30 to find the largest object types; The usual leak sources are static collections, uncleaned ThreadLocals, and class loader leaks from repeated hot deployments; jcmd <pid> GC.class_stats helps confirm; Once a leak is ruled out, consider raising -Xmx or switching to G1 and tuning -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis.
documents.s: Tomcat old generation usage too high

VictoriaMetrics is often both Nightingale's time-series store and something that needs monitoring itself. The single-node edition exposes /metrics on port 8428; the cluster edition must be scraped per component, vmstorage (8482), vmselect (8481) and vminsert (8480), or you only see part of the picture. There is one dashboard for single-node and one for cluster. The rules cover rejected writes, slow inserts, query timeouts, disk space, storage nodes going offline and merge backlog.
2 dashboards, 85 panels in total 9 alert rules, each with runbook steps

These components expose Prometheus-format /metrics themselves, so the Categraf prometheus input scrapes them without a dedicated plugin. If a Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics instance is already scraping them, add it as a Nightingale data source and the templates work as they are. # conf/input.prometheus/victoriametrics.toml [[instances]] urls = ["http://127.0.0.1:8428/metrics"] url_label_key = "instance" url_label_value = "{{.Host}}" labels = { job = "victoriametrics", service = "vmsingle" } For the cluster edition, point urls at each component and set the service label to vmstorage, vmselect or vminsert accordingly. Open the integration center in Nightingale, find VictoriaMetrics, and import the dashboards and alert rules into a business group. Imported rules start disabled. Check that the metrics are arriving first, then enable the rules one by one with thresholds that fit your environment.
Dashboard Panels VictoriaMetrics - Cluster 56 VictoriaMetrics - Single 29
9 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: sum by (job, level) (rate(vm_log_messages_total{level!="info"}[5m])) > 0 Runbook: Check the logs on that instance (journalctl -u victoria-metrics or the container logs) and filter by level for the specific error; Common causes are malformed data from the write side, rejected high-cardinality labels and insufficient disk space; For cardinality issues, use /api/v1/status/tsdb to see the top offenders and fix them at the write side; For disk issues, follow the disk space alert path.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max(rate(vm_rpc_send_duration_seconds_total{job_name=~".+"}[5m])) by(addr) / 1000 > 9 Runbook: Check CPU, disk IO and vm_slow_row_inserts_total on the vm-storage side to see whether the bottleneck is compute or disk; Use /api/v1/status/tsdb to check whether high-cardinality metrics are amplifying writes; Short term, reduce write concurrency or relabel-drop the high-cardinality metrics; Longer term, add vm-storage nodes or move to faster disks.
documents.s: Connection saturation between vm-insert and vm-storage exceeds 9

documents.t: S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger: net_response_result_code{service="vm-insert"}!=0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and reproduce it on the collector host with nc -vz <address> <port>; On that machine confirm the process is alive and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the port is unreachable, check the firewall and the listen address configuration; In cluster mode, confirm the remaining node count still satisfies read/write requirements — recover the node rather than restarting the whole cluster.

S1 Critical · for 1 min · Trigger: net_response_result_code{service="vm-select"}!=0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and reproduce it on the collector host with nc -vz <address> <port>; On that machine confirm the process is alive and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the port is unreachable, check the firewall and the listen address configuration; In cluster mode, confirm the remaining node count still satisfies read/write requirements — recover the node rather than restarting the whole cluster.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: max(vm_request_duration_seconds{job_name=~".+"}) by (path) > 15 Runbook: Take path from the alert labels to identify which kind of query is slow; Use /api/v1/status/top_queries to find the slowest and most frequent queries; The usual root causes are an over-wide time range or high-cardinality labels — narrow the dashboard time range and reduce group by dimensions; On the storage side, check whether disk IO and CPU are saturated and scale vm-select/vm-storage if needed.

S1 Critical · for 2 min · Trigger: net_response_result_code{service="vm-storage"} != 0 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and reproduce it on the collector host with nc -vz <address> <port>; On that machine confirm the process is alive and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the port is unreachable, check the firewall and the listen address configuration; In cluster mode, confirm the remaining node count still satisfies read/write requirements — recover the node rather than restarting the whole cluster.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: up{service=~"vminsert.+"} < 1 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and reproduce it on the collector host with nc -vz <address> <port>; On that machine confirm the process is alive and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the port is unreachable, check the firewall and the listen address configuration; In cluster mode, confirm the remaining node count still satisfies read/write requirements — recover the node rather than restarting the whole cluster.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: up{service=~"vmselect.+"} < 1 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and reproduce it on the collector host with nc -vz <address> <port>; On that machine confirm the process is alive and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the port is unreachable, check the firewall and the listen address configuration; In cluster mode, confirm the remaining node count still satisfies read/write requirements — recover the node rather than restarting the whole cluster.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: up{service=~"vmstorage.+"} < 1 Runbook: Take the instance address from the alert labels and reproduce it on the collector host with nc -vz <address> <port>; On that machine confirm the process is alive and check the log for a panic or OOM; If the process is alive but the port is unreachable, check the firewall and the listen address configuration; In cluster mode, confirm the remaining node count still satisfies read/write requirements — recover the node rather than restarting the whole cluster.

The vSphere input pulls performance data through the vCenter Server API across five levels: datacenter, cluster, ESXi host, virtual machine and datastore. That includes CPU ready time and usage, active memory and ballooning, disk latency and IOPS, network throughput and datastore capacity. A vCenter is required; connecting to a bare ESXi host does not work. Give Categraf a vCenter account with a read-only role rather than administrator. The config lets you narrow the counters per object type, which is advisable on large vCenters. The rules cover hosts disconnecting, high VM CPU ready time, memory ballooning, datastores near capacity and disk latency.
2 dashboards, 74 panels in total 5 alert rules, each with runbook steps Categraf collector config: input.vsphere

Install Categraf, put the config below in conf/input.vsphere/vsphere.toml, fill in your own address and credentials, and restart Categraf. The startup log prints input: local.vsphere started once the plugin is loaded. # # collect interval # interval = 15 # Read metrics from one or many vCenters [[instances]] ## vCenter URLs to be monitored. These three lines must be uncommented ## and edited for the plugin to work. #vcenter = "https://vcenter.local/sdk" #username = "user@corp.local" #password = "secret" ## VMs ## Typical VM metrics (if omitted or empty, all metrics are collected) # vm_include = [ "/*/vm/**"] # Inventory path to VMs to collect (by default all are collected) # vm_exclude = [] # Inventory paths to exclude vm_metric_include = [ "cpu.demand.average", "cpu.idle.summation", "cpu.latency.average", "cpu.readiness.average", "cpu.ready.summation", "cpu.run.summation", "cpu.usagemhz.average", "cpu.used.summation", "cpu.wait.summation", "mem.active.average", "mem.granted.average", "mem.latency.average", "mem.swapin.average", "mem.swapinRate.average", "mem.swapout.average", "mem.swapoutRate.average", "mem.usage.average", "mem.vmmemctl.average", "net.bytesRx.average", "net.bytesTx.average", "net.droppedRx.summation", "net.droppedTx.summation", "net.usage.average", "power.power.average", "virtualDisk.numberReadAveraged.average", "virtualDisk.numberWriteAveraged.average", "virtualDisk.read.average", "virtualDisk.readOIO.latest", "virtualDisk.throughput.usage.average", "virtualDisk.totalReadLatency.average", "virtualDisk.totalWriteLatency.average", "virtualDisk.write.average", "virtualDisk.writeOIO.latest", "sys.uptime.latest", ] # vm_metric_exclude = [] ## Nothing is excluded by default # vm_instances = true ## true by default ## Hosts ## Typical host metrics (if omitted or empty, all metrics are collected) # host_include = [ "/*/host/**"] # Inventory path to hosts to collect (by default all are collected) # host_exclude [] # Inventory paths to exclude host_metric_include = [ "cpu.coreUtilization.average", "cpu.costop.summation", "cpu.demand.average", "cpu.idle.summation", "cpu.latency.average", "cpu.readiness.average", "cpu.ready.summation", "cpu.swapwait.summation", "cpu.usage.average", "cpu.usagemhz.average", "cpu.used.summation", "cpu.utilization.average", "cpu.wait.summation", "disk.deviceReadLatency.average", "disk.deviceWriteLatency.average", "disk.kernelReadLatency.average", "disk.kernelWriteLatency.average", "disk.numberReadAveraged.average", "disk.numberWriteAveraged.average", "disk.read.average", "disk.totalReadLatency.average", "disk.totalWriteLatency.average", "disk.write.average", "mem.active.average", "mem.latency.average", "mem.state.latest", "mem.swapin.average", "mem.swapinRate.average", "mem.swapout.average", "mem.swapoutRate.average", "mem.totalCapacity.average", "mem.usage.average", "mem.vmmemctl.average", "net.bytesRx.average", "net.bytesTx.average", "net.droppedRx.summation", "net.droppedTx.summation", "net.errorsRx.summation", "net.errorsTx.summation", "net.usage.average", "power.power.average", "storageAdapter.numberReadAveraged.average", "storageAdapter.numberWriteAveraged.average", "storageAdapter.read.average", "storageAdapter.write.average", "sys.uptime.latest", ] # host_instances = true ## true by default # host_include = [] ## Nothing included by default # host_exclude = [] ## Nothing excluded by default # host_metric_include = [] ## Nothing included by default # host_metric_exclude = [] ## Nothing excluded by default ## Clusters # cluster_include = [ "/*/host/**"] # Inventory path to clusters to collect (by default all are collected) # cluster_exclude = [] # Inventory paths to exclude # cluster_metric_include = [] ## 5 rules. Each lists its trigger condition (PromQL) and the steps to take when it fires. Thresholds are meant to be adjusted after import.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: (sum(vsphere_host_cpu_usage_average{}) by(esxhostname)/count(vsphere_host_cpu_usage_average{}) by(esxhostname)) > 70 Runbook: Locate the ESXi host in vCenter and see which virtual machines contribute most of the load; Use vSphere DRS or a manual vMotion to move some VMs to a less loaded host; Confirm no VM is squeezing the others through over-provisioned vCPUs; If the whole cluster is running hot, add physical hosts.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: (sum(vsphere_host_mem_usage_average{}) by(esxhostname)/count(vsphere_host_mem_usage_average{}) by(esxhostname)) > 70 Runbook: Locate the ESXi host in vCenter and see which virtual machines contribute most of the load; Use vSphere DRS or a manual vMotion to move some VMs to a less loaded host; Confirm no VM is squeezing the others through over-provisioned vCPUs; If the whole cluster is running hot, add physical hosts.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: (sum(vsphere_vm_cpu_usage_average{}) by(vmname)/count(vsphere_vm_cpu_usage_average{}) by(vmname))>70 Runbook: Log in to the VM and use top or Task Manager to find the busiest process; Tell traffic growth apart from a program fault (infinite loop, frequent GC); Check the VM's CPU Ready value in vCenter — high means host contention rather than the VM being undersized; Add vCPUs once confirmed, or migrate the VM to a less loaded host.

S2 Warning · for 1 min · Trigger: (sum(vsphere_vm_mem_usage_average{}) by(vmname)/count(vsphere_vm_mem_usage_average{}) by(vmname))>70 Runbook: Log in to the VM and find the largest memory consumer, judging whether it is a leak; In vCenter check the VM's Balloon and Swapped metrics — non-zero means the host is reclaiming its memory; If the host is tight, migrate VMs or expand the host first; If the VM itself is short, add memory; if it is a leak, locate it in the application.

S2 Warning · for 15s · Trigger: sum(vsphere_datastore_disk_used_latest{vcenter=~".+"}/vsphere_datastore_disk_capacity_latest{vcenter=~".+"}) by(source)*100 > 70 Runbook: Locate the datastore in vCenter and sort by capacity to find the largest VMs and snapshots; Clean up leftover snapshots first — snapshots are the most common reason a datastore fills up; Remove unused ISOs, templates and leftover files from decommissioned VMs; Use Storage vMotion to move some VMs to a datastore with headroom, and expand capacity longer term.

Categraf runs on Windows too, and the basic CPU, memory, disk and network metrics keep the same names as on Linux. Host-level alert rules and dashboards therefore do not need a separate Windows edition. The template also ships a set of dashboards written against windows_exporter metric names, covering Windows Server itself plus Active Directory, DNS and ADFS. Import the "by Categraf" dashboard if you collect with Categraf, or the "exporter" set if you run windows_exporter.
6 dashboards, 203 panels in total 14 alert rules, each with runbook steps

Categraf installs as a Windows service; see Install Categraf. The basic inputs are on by default, so no Windows-specific collector config is needed. For windows_exporter, scrape http://<host>:9182/metrics with the Categraf prometheus input, or add your existing Prometheus as a data source. Lost connection with monitoring target - categraf [Windows]​ Runbook: First confirm the machine itself is alive (ping, Remote Desktop) — if it is down, handle it as a host outage; If it is alive, run Get-Service categraf to check the service state and Start-Service categraf if it is stopped; Check the logs under the categraf log directory — the usual causes are a config error or network/auth failure to the server; After recovery, confirm the data is continuous, and note that failures during the blind window produced no alerts at all.
